title: Heredity
text: In this one-reel Biograph drama directed by D. W. Griffith, a renegade white trader living at the edge of a Native American village buys a young Indian woman as his bride, and they have a son. The boy grows up playing with the children of the tribe, and as he gets older the racial difference between father and son becomes ever more evident. Angered by the boy's reluctance to leave his mother's people, the father forces him with threats and violence to join him on a trading trip, and grows ashamed of his Indian wife and son in front of other white men. The trader has sold the tribe broken guns and bad whiskey, and when the Indians attack in revenge, the war cry of his ancestors stirs the son's blood. According to TV Guide's synopsis, the father is destroyed by his own crimes and mother and son are claimed by their people. The title states the theme. The boy is said to inherit his mother's 'Indian character', and at the climax 'the war-cry of his ancestors stirs the young Indian's blood'. The film favours nature, presenting racial character as an inherited essence that a white father's influence cannot override. It reflects the racial thinking of its time: the Italian Wikipedia reads it in the light of Griffith's views, for which crossing racial boundaries, and especially having mixed-race children, was a fault bound to end in tragedy. As usual in Griffith's films about Native Americans, Indian characters are played by white actors. No science appears. Modern genetics rejects the idea of a racial character or loyalty carried in the blood: behaviour and cultural identity are learned, and human genetic variation does not divide people into races with distinct temperaments.

title: The Escape
text: The film opens with a prologue on eugenics that contrasts the careful breeding of animals with the way humans reproduce, and then tells the story of the Joyce family. The abusive father, Jim Joyce, corrupts his naturally sensitive son Larry into cruelty. Larry contracts syphilis and is treated by Dr. Von Eiden, who becomes involved with Larry's sister May and encourages her to leave the family. Unable to find stable work, May becomes the companion of a wealthy senator but refuses to marry him. Her sister Jennie marries the brutal "Bull" McGee, who kills their baby while drunk; Jennie loses her mind, rocking a doll in the empty cradle, and McGee sells her into prostitution. May rescues her, but Jennie dies soon afterwards. Von Eiden performs an operation that restores Larry's original sensitivity, and May leaves the senator and agrees to marry the doctor. The film, directed by D. W. Griffith, is now lost. Eugenics frames the whole film: its prologue compares the selective breeding of animals with human reproduction, and the misfortunes of the Joyce family are presented as the story that follows from that comparison, placing the film within the eugenics movement of the 1910s. The scientist figure is a physician, Dr. Von Eiden, who treats Larry's syphilis, cures his cruelty with an operation and ends up marrying May, so medicine is portrayed as a source of rescue rather than harm. The family's troubles, however, are shown as coming from a mix of causes, including the father's abuse, venereal disease, alcohol and poverty, not only from inheritance. Because no copy of the film is known to survive, its plot is known only from written accounts, and how strongly it argued the eugenic case on screen cannot be checked today.

title: Where Are My Children?
text: District attorney Richard Walton prosecutes Dr. Homer, a physician arrested for distributing birth-control literature deemed obscene. On the stand, Homer argues for legal contraception, recalling cases from his practice: children abused in an alcoholic household, a poor family unable to care for sick children, and an abandoned mother who kills herself and her baby. Meanwhile, Walton's wife Edith has for years secretly used the services of Dr. Malfit, an abortionist, so that pregnancy will not interrupt her social life, and she sends friends to him too. When her brother seduces the young daughter of the Waltons' maid, the girl dies after a botched abortion by Malfit. After Malfit's trial, Walton finds his wife's name in the doctor's ledger, expels her friends from the house and confronts her with the question "Where are my children?". The couple grow old in a childless, lonely home. Genetics appears here through eugenics, the early-twentieth-century movement to improve the population by controlling who reproduces. Written partly as a response to Margaret Sanger's 1914 prosecution for promoting birth control, the film argues didactically for contraception and against abortion, and it presents examples of desirable and undesirable children as the products of good or bad breeding; a married couple in the cast are credited simply as the "eugenic" husband and wife. Critics have noted that its condemnation of abortion is framed in moral and eugenic terms, aimed at wealthy women who are seen as failing to produce the "right" children. There are no geneticists and no science on screen: heredity is a background ideology rather than a plot device. The film is mainly of historical interest as evidence of how readily American popular culture of the 1910s absorbed eugenic ideas, ideas that also underpinned compulsory sterilisation laws in the United States.

title: Married in Name Only
text: In this American silent drama written by Ivan Abramson, Madeline Francis is about to marry Robert Worthing when she receives a report, through Robert's mother, that there is insanity in the Worthing family. Madeline fears that any children they had would inherit the madness, but to avoid the shame of a broken engagement she begs that the wedding go ahead. The marriage takes place in name only: Robert treats Madeline like a sister rather than a bride, and in her loneliness and despair she contemplates suicide. Finally Robert learns that he was adopted and so does not carry the Worthing family's hereditary insanity. Joy returns, and the couple can have children without fear. The Chicago censors passed the film for adults only and cut a passionate bedroom embrace. The film was made at the height of the American eugenics movement and its whole plot rests on eugenic reasoning: insanity is treated as a hereditary taint that a man would surely pass to his children, so a responsible couple must not have any. Nobody does any science; the 'evidence' is a family history report, and the remedy is abstinence within marriage. The story makes the human cost of this reasoning vivid, as the bride sinks into despair, but it never questions the premise itself. The happy ending comes not from rejecting hereditarian ideas but from learning that the husband was adopted, so the tainted bloodline is not his. Modern genetics sees mental illness as influenced by many genes and by environment, not as a certain inheritance, but the film treats heredity as decisive, as many social-problem films of the 1910s did.

title: The Black Stork
text: The Black Stork, also released as Are You Fit To Marry?, is a silent eugenics propaganda film written by and starring the Chicago surgeon Harry J. Haiselden, who plays himself. It opens with a warning that social problems such as crime and poverty result from careless management of human breeding. A newborn baby is born with severe malformations, and the doctor refuses the surgery that could save its life, telling the mother that "God does not want this child to live." The medical profession is outraged, but the mother has a vision of her son's future: disabled, unhappy and violent, and the father of five disabled children of his own. Convinced, she lets the baby die, and the film ends with Jesus receiving the infant's soul as the doctor looks on. The story dramatises Haiselden's real refusal to operate on the newborn Allan Bollinger in 1915. Heredity and eugenics are the whole point of the film. It argues that "defective" traits pass inevitably from parents to children, so that letting a malformed newborn die protects future generations, a view it supports with the mother's vision of her son fathering disabled children. The doctor is not a geneticist but a real surgeon who used the film to defend his practice of withholding treatment from disabled infants; he presented this as a scientific and humane choice. In the real Bollinger case, Chicago's health commissioner testified that the baby's condition was treatable, and a coroner's jury rejected Haiselden's claim that the child would have grown up mentally or morally defective. Haiselden was expelled from the Chicago Medical Society over his publicity, yet the film circulated in the United States for years, in the era of American eugenic sterilisation laws. It is a historical document of how eugenic ideas were sold to the public, not a portrayal of genetic science.

title: Alraune
themes: heredity nature nurture human experimentation donor conception
text: Professor Jakob ten Brinken, a wealthy and celebrated geneticist, decides on an experiment in heredity. He has his reluctant nephew Franz Braun find a prostitute, and artificially inseminates her with the semen of a hanged murderer. The child, Alraune, is adopted by the Professor as his daughter and grows into a beautiful but cold young woman who runs off from her convent school, elopes and ends up performing in a circus. Brought home, she lives in luxury at the Professor's expense while he falls obsessively in love with her and wonders whether her nature comes from her mother. When Alraune finds his journal and learns how she was conceived, she stays to take revenge, seduces him and ruins him. As she prepares to leave, the Professor attacks her with a knife; Franz arrives in time, takes Alraune away and leaves the Professor alone and broken. The film turns on an experiment in heredity: a geneticist conceives a child by artificially inseminating a prostitute with a hanged murderer's semen and then raises her as his own daughter, to see what her origins will make of her. The story answers firmly on the side of nature: Alraune grows up heartless and destructive, and the film suggests that she has inherited her parents' corruption, although at the end she longs to become an ordinary feeling person. The Professor is a classic mad scientist whom his nephew and other scientists condemn for violating the laws of nature, and he ends alone and insane. Critics read the film as alarmist about artificial insemination, then a topic of public debate, and as an early expression of the belief that criminal and sexual traits are inherited, the kind of idea later taken up by Nazi race theory. Modern genetics does not support the inheritance of criminality in this simple way.

title: The Very Idea
text: Alan Camp has written a book on eugenics and wants to prove his theories. His sister Edith and her husband Gilbert Goodhue have long been unable to have children, so Alan persuades them to adopt a child created by eugenic selection. He chooses the Goodhues' chauffeur, Joe Garvin, and their maid, Nora, as the parents, and offers each of them $15,000 if they conceive and deliver a baby within a year. The Goodhues leave on a year-long trip to California. Joe and Nora do have a baby, but they fall in love, marry and refuse to give the child up. Alan sends Joe to an orphanage for a substitute baby, which the Goodhues reject, and the despondent Alan dismantles the nursery. The comedy ends when Edith announces that she is pregnant. Eugenics is the comic premise. Alan Camp, the author of a book on eugenics, sets out to prove his theories by arranging the birth of a selected child: he picks two servants as parents and pays them to conceive a baby that his childless sister will adopt. The available synopsis does not say what qualities he selected them for, nor whether anything more than an arranged conception is involved. The plan collapses for human rather than scientific reasons: the chosen couple fall in love and keep their child, the would-be adoptive parents reject a substitute, and the Goodhues finally conceive naturally. The story thus lets the eugenicist's scheme fail and rewards ordinary love and chance, though the sources do not record how critics read its attitude to eugenics. Made in 1929, when eugenics was still widely discussed in the United States, the RKO comedy was a critical and commercial failure and was banned by the Chicago Board of Censors.

title: Tomorrow's Children
text: Alice Mason wants to marry her fiancé Jim Baker and raise a family, but her plans collapse when the authorities order her parents to undergo sterilization or lose their welfare payments. The Masons are presented as a "defective" family: the parents are idle alcoholics and Alice's siblings have physical and mental disabilities or criminal ties. Because the family's bloodline is judged to be corrupt, the court rules that Alice, the only capable member of the household, must be sterilized too. She runs away but is caught by the police. Jim persuades Dr. Brooks to testify on her behalf, yet the court does not change its decision. Father O'Brien pleads with Mrs. Mason, who, drunk, reveals that Alice was a foundling the family took in and is not related to them by blood. The priest races to the hospital, and Dr. Brooks stops the operation in time. Eugenics is the subject of the film. It portrays the compulsory sterilization of people deemed hereditarily unfit, a practice endorsed in the United States in 1927, when Supreme Court Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that society could "prevent those who are manifestly unfit from continuing their kind". The film assumes, as eugenicists did, that alcoholism, disability and criminality run in families, and the state applies that belief through courts and doctors. Its plot twist exposes the weakness of judging people by their "bloodline": Alice is condemned for a heredity she does not have. The physicians are divided, with Dr. Brooks siding with Alice against the order. The film was openly critical of these policies; its themes of sterilization and hereditary defect led several state censorship boards to ban it, and it was approved in only a few states.

title: La Bête Humaine
text: Jacques Lantier, a locomotive driver on the Paris to Le Havre line, loves his engine and suffers from headaches and fits of violent rage, worse when he drinks, that seize him when he is close to a woman. Visiting his aunt's village, he almost strangles Flore, a young woman he has known since childhood. On a train, he crosses the path of a murderer: the deputy stationmaster Roubaud, jealous of his wife Séverine's past with her rich godfather Grandmorin, has stabbed him to death with her complicity. Séverine asks Lantier to keep silent and begins an affair with him, then urges him to kill her husband. Lantier cannot do it, but when she says she will leave Roubaud, a fit overtakes him and he kills Séverine instead. The next day he confesses to his fireman and throws himself from the moving train. The genetic theme is inherited madness. Adapted from Émile Zola's naturalist novel, the film presents Lantier as a man whose 'tainted blood subjects him to fits of homicidal mania', in the words of The New York Times review of 1938. His violence is a fate he did not choose and cannot escape, and the film sides with nature: no love, work or effort can free him, and the story ends with him killing the woman he loves and then himself. No science or scientist appears. Renoir compared Lantier to the doomed heroes of Greek tragedy. The idea of hereditary taint and degeneration was widespread in Zola's time; modern genetics does not support the notion of a family flaw that passes a compulsion to murder from generation to generation, although some psychiatric conditions do have a partly genetic basis.

title: Bedtime for Bonzo
text: Psychology professor Peter Boyd is engaged to Valerie, daughter of his college's dean, Tillinghast. When the dean learns that Peter's father was a criminal, he forbids the marriage, declaring that Peter's blood is tainted. Peter, who believes environment matters more than heredity, sets out to prove it by raising a chimpanzee, Bonzo, as a child in a law-abiding home. He hires a young woman, Jane, as nanny, and the two act as Bonzo's parents, teaching him good habits. After a misunderstanding Valerie breaks off the engagement, and Peter learns that Bonzo is to be sold to Yale for medical research. Bonzo escapes and takes a necklace from a jewellery store, and Peter is arrested trying to return it, but Bonzo, as he has been taught, puts the necklace back himself. The experiment is judged a success, Bonzo is kept, and Peter and Jane are to marry. The film is a light comedy built on the nature versus nurture debate. The dean stands for a crude hereditarian view in which criminality runs in the blood, the kind of thinking that fed the eugenics movement of the early twentieth century; the professor stands for the opposite, that upbringing shapes character. Genetics as a science never appears: there is no geneticist, no laboratory work and no mention of genes, only "blood" and "heredity". The chimpanzee experiment is played for laughs and settles the question in favour of environment, which is also the romantic resolution. It has a real precedent: in 1931–32 the psychologist Winthrop Kellogg raised an infant chimpanzee, Gua, alongside his own son for nine months to see how human a chimpanzee could become; Gua learned many everyday behaviours but never human language. Today nature and nurture are understood to interact, and neither a chimpanzee's upbringing nor a father's record decides character on its own.

title: The Bad Seed
text: While her husband, an army colonel, is away in Washington, Christine Penmark grows uneasy about her prim, polite eight-year-old daughter Rhoda. After Rhoda loses a school penmanship medal to her classmate Claude, the boy drowns at a school picnic, and Christine finds the medal hidden among Rhoda's things. Pressing her father, the writer Richard Bravo, Christine learns that she was adopted as a toddler and is the biological daughter of a notorious serial killer. Rhoda admits that she struck Claude with her tap shoes and that she had already killed an elderly neighbour; when the janitor Leroy guesses the truth, she burns him to death. In despair, Christine gives Rhoda an overdose of sleeping pills and shoots herself. Both survive, but Rhoda is killed by lightning while trying to recover the medal from the lake. The film turns on the idea that evil can be inherited. Christine fears that her descent from a murderer is the 'bad seed' behind Rhoda's lack of conscience; her father answers that such behaviour is shaped mainly by nurture, not nature. The story sides with nature: Rhoda, raised by loving, respectable parents, is a remorseless killer, and the hidden grandmother is offered as the explanation. No scientist or test appears; heredity is a family secret revealed by an adoption. The ending, in which lightning kills Rhoda, was imposed by the Production Code and punishes the child rather than settling the debate. Current genetics does not support this picture. Twin and adoption studies show that antisocial and aggressive behaviour is partly heritable, but the genetic influence is spread over many genes of tiny effect and depends strongly on the environment a child grows up in. Nothing like a single inherited 'murder' trait passes intact from grandmother to granddaughter, and a family history of violence raises a child's risk only modestly; it does not make a child a killer.

title: Picnic on the Grass
text: Étienne Alexis, a celebrated French biologist, is the favourite to become the first president of a united Europe. His programme calls for compulsory artificial insemination to improve humanity and make it worthy of modern science. To celebrate his engagement to his German cousin Marie-Charlotte, he holds a picnic near his estate in Provence, beside the ruins of a temple of Diana. Among the servants is Nénette, a farmer's daughter who wants a child without a husband and has volunteered for his insemination experiments. When the goatherd Gaspard plays his flute, a sudden wind scatters the party, a bacchanal breaks out, and Étienne, separated from the others, falls for Nénette. After a few days at her father's house he is dragged back to his old life, but on his wedding day he finds Nénette pregnant with his child and decides to marry her instead. Jean Renoir's comedy is a satire of scientific rationalism, and its target is eugenics. Étienne Alexis wants to replace sexual reproduction with state-run artificial insemination, selecting donors to breed a better population and, he hopes, to do away with passion altogether. Genetics as such is never discussed in technical terms; what the film mocks is the idea that reproduction can be planned rationally from above. The scientist is a respected public figure and a presidential candidate, presented as stiff and well-meaning rather than evil, and the film's answer to him is nature itself: a wind, a flute and a summer afternoon are enough to make him abandon his programme and father a child the old-fashioned way. Made in 1959, the film treats eugenic ambitions as absurd rather than menacing, and links them to a technocratic vision of the new united Europe.

title: The Satan Bug
text: Former intelligence agent Lee Barrett is brought back by his old boss after the security chief of Station Three, a secret American bioweapons laboratory, is murdered and its head scientist, Dr. Baxter, disappears. Inside the sealed laboratory Barrett finds Baxter dead and learns that all supplies of a botulinus toxin and of the 'Satan Bug', a new virus that could wipe out life on Earth within months, have been stolen. An extortionist calling himself Charles Reynolds Ainsley, a reclusive millionaire, threatens to release the Satan Bug unless Station Three is destroyed, and proves his intent by releasing botulinus in Key West, killing many people. Working with Ann Williams, the daughter of the general in charge, Barrett discovers that Ainsley has been posing as one of the laboratory's own scientists, Dr. Hoffman. Flasks are found and defused in Los Angeles, Ainsley falls to his death from a helicopter, and Barrett returns the Satan Bug to the authorities: 'we're right back where we started'. The film is an early thriller about laboratory-made pathogens. Station Three is a secret government laboratory that has developed a botulinus weapon and the 'Satan Bug', a virus capable of exterminating life on Earth, together with, according to German Wikipedia, a vaccine. The scientists themselves are mostly victims: the head scientist and a colleague are murdered by the villain, a millionaire and biochemist who infiltrated the laboratory under a stolen identity and uses the stolen agents to blackmail the government into destroying the facility. The hero recovers the virus, but the ironic last line, as he hands it back to the military, suggests that the danger lies in such weapons existing at all. Based on a novel by Alistair MacLean, the film reflects Cold War anxieties about biological warfare; the United States did run an offensive biological weapons programme until 1969, though no single virus could wipe out all life.

title: Miri
alt: Star Trek: The Original Series, season 1, episode 8
themes: genetic engineering pandemic human experimentation post apocalyptic
text: Answering a distress call, the Enterprise finds a planet identical to Earth, with a 1960s-style city in ruins. The landing party is attacked by a deranged, disfigured man who dies of a seizure, and meets Miri, a girl who explains that the "grups" went mad and died, leaving only children, the "Onlies". Spock finds records of a life-extension experiment three hundred years old: it slowed ageing to one month per century, but at puberty it triggers a disease that brings violent madness and death within days. The children are centuries old, and the whole landing party except Spock catches the disease. McCoy works on a vaccine, but the children steal the communicators he needs to check the dose with the ship's computer, and the jealous Miri helps them kidnap Yeoman Rand. Kirk wins the children over, McCoy tests the vaccine on himself and it works, and the Enterprise leaves medical staff and asks for teachers to help the children. The episode's disaster comes from a scientific project to prolong life. Three centuries earlier the planet's scientists carried out a life-extension experiment that slowed ageing in children, but every person who reached puberty fell victim to a fatal disease that wiped out the adult population; the French Wikipedia reads the episode as a warning about genetic manipulation and the quest for immortality, while Memory Alpha speaks of a miscalculation. The original scientists are long dead and appear only through their records. Medicine provides the remedy: McCoy reconstructs their work, isolates the agent and develops a vaccine, which he tests on himself, a classic act of heroic self-experimentation. Real ageing cannot be slowed to this degree, and the episode never explains the biology, but its theme, a well-meant attempt to defeat ageing that ends in catastrophe, is a recurring one in science fiction.

title: The Ugly Dachshund
text: Mark and Fran Garrison, a young married couple, own a prize-winning dachshund, Danke, who gives birth to three female puppies. Their vet, Dr. Pruitt, persuades Mark to take home a Great Dane puppy that its own mother has rejected for lack of milk, so that Danke can nurse him. Mark names him Brutus. Raised among the dachshunds, Brutus believes he is one of them, imitates their low-slung walk and is blamed for the mischief they lead him into, from splattering paint over Mark's studio to turning a garden party upside down. Fran wants him out of the house until he saves her favourite puppy from a garbage truck. At a dog show Brutus meets other Great Danes, discovers what it is like to be one and wins two blue ribbons, earning the dachshunds' respect. There is no genetic science in this Walt Disney comedy; it plays with nature versus nurture through a dog. Brutus is a Great Dane by birth but raised by a dachshund mother among dachshund puppies, and for much of the film upbringing wins: he walks, behaves and even thinks of himself as a dachshund. In the end the film favours nature: at the dog show, among other Great Danes, he finds his true identity and stands tall like one. The joke rests on real facts of animal breeding: dog breeds differ greatly in size and build because of their genes, whoever raises them, while much of a dog's behaviour is learned from the animals and people around it. A puppy nursed by a mother of another breed grows into the size and shape of its own breed, as Brutus does.

title: Wild, Wild Planet
text: In a future where the United Democracies run space travel, Commander Mike Halstead of the space station Gamma One investigates a wave of disappearances of world leaders and other people on Earth. The culprit is Dr. Nurmi, a scientist on the same station who is officially studying the miniaturization of human organs but secretly works for the planet Delphos. Using bald, four-armed androids and beautiful women of superhuman strength, he abducts his victims, shrinks them to doll size and ships them in suitcases to Delphos. When Halstead confronts him, his superiors confine him to quarters, but two fellow officers free him. Meanwhile Nurmi seduces Halstead's girlfriend, Lieutenant Connie Gomez, whom he wants for an experiment in which he would graft half of his own body to half of hers. Halstead infiltrates Nurmi's operation and rescues Connie in space. Genetics appears as the declared goal of the villain rather than as an explained technique. Dr. Nurmi runs secret bio-engineering experiments and a eugenics programme whose aim is a "genetically perfect, immortal race of humans", and his plan to fuse half of his body with half of Connie Gomez's body is presented as the key step. The film never explains how shrinking people or grafting bodies would produce such a race, and reviewers single out these plans as absurd and the plot as confused. Nurmi is a classic mad scientist: a traitor working for another planet, a kidnapper and a seducer, opposed by the heroic Commander Halstead. The eugenic dream of a perfected, immortal humanity is thus tied to abduction and human experimentation. This campy Italian space opera, the first of the Gamma One films, belongs to the 1960s tradition in which genetic and eugenic ambitions mark the villain.

title: Space Seed
alt: Semilla espacial Star Trek: The Original Series, season 1, episode 22
text: The USS Enterprise finds the SS Botany Bay, a derelict 20th-century ship carrying dozens of people in suspended animation. Their leader, brought aboard for medical care, is identified by Spock as Khan Noonien Singh, a 20th-century dictator and one of a group of genetically altered "superpeople" who once ruled much of Earth. Khan persuades Lieutenant Marla McGivers to help him, revives his followers and seizes the ship, threatening to suffocate Captain Kirk in a decompression chamber until the crew submits. McGivers frees Kirk, who regains control of the Enterprise and overpowers Khan in a fistfight in Engineering. At a hearing, Kirk exiles Khan and his people to the harsh planet Ceti Alpha V; Khan accepts, saying it is better to reign in hell than serve in heaven, and McGivers chooses to go with him. The story continues in the film Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan (1982). The episode introduces one of Star Trek's most lasting ideas: humans deliberately improved by science who become tyrants. In its backstory, Khan and his followers were produced by selective breeding to create perfect humans; they took power over more than a third of the planet in the Eugenics Wars, which the franchise's own chronology dates to 1992–1996. The scientists who created them never appear; the story focuses on the creation, whose physical and mental superiority goes hand in hand with a will to rule. Sociologist William Sims Bainbridge argued that selective breeding could not produce supermen so quickly and that direct genetic engineering would be more plausible. Later Star Trek productions adopted that view, recasting the "augments" as genetically engineered, and established that human genetic enhancement is illegal in the Federation, as in the Deep Space Nine episode "Doctor Bashir, I Presume?".

title: Dead Season
text: After a West German intelligence courier is murdered in Lisbon, Soviet intelligence finds an encrypted message about raw materials for mass production of 'RH gas', which in small doses stimulates the intellect and in large doses turns people into contented idiots fit only for labour. The case goes to Colonel Konstantin Ladeynikov, a Soviet agent working under cover in the West. To identify the gas's creator, Dr. Hass, a Nazi war criminal now working at a pharmaceutical centre in a Western resort town, the KGB recruits Ivan Savushkin, a children's theatre actor who in 1944 survived a concentration camp where Hass's experiments turned prisoners into 'meaningless animals'. Savushkin recognises Hass at a funeral but is captured; Hass expounds his vision of a 'New Eden' in which an intellectual elite rules happy, robot-like slaves whose condition will pass to their descendants. Ladeynikov frees Savushkin with incriminating documents, Hass is killed, and Ladeynikov is imprisoned in the West and later exchanged on a bridge. Genetics is a passing element of this Soviet Cold War spy film. The weapon at its centre, RH gas, is a psychopharmacological agent rather than a genetic one, but its inventor, the former Nazi camp doctor Hass, claims that the docile slavery it induces will be inherited by the victims' descendants, part of his plan for a world divided between an intellectual elite and happy labourers. This brief hereditarian claim, together with his past experiments on camp prisoners, links the villain to Nazi medical crimes and eugenic fantasies of human castes; the film presents him as a sadist serving Western intelligence. No genetic science is shown, and the inheritance of a drug-induced state has no scientific basis.

title: Place of Angels
alt: Captain Scarlet and the Mysterons, season 1, episode 23
text: In 2068, Earth's security organization Spectrum wages a 'war of nerves' against the Mysterons, Martians who can recreate people and objects they have destroyed and use the copies as agents. At a microbiological laboratory near Manchester, Dr. Denton and his assistant, Judy Chapman, activate a culture of K14, the most lethal synthetic virus ever developed, able to kill millions. Driving home, Chapman is killed in a crash set up by the Mysteron agent Captain Black, and the Mysterons reconstruct her. The next morning the replica kills a security guard, steals the K14 vial and flies to New York, fulfilling the Mysterons' threat to destroy the 'Place of the Angels'. Captains Scarlet and Blue pursue her, but she fools them with an apparently broken vial and they are briefly quarantined. Realizing that the target is Los Angeles, Scarlet catches her at the Boulder Dam as she prepares to poison the city's water supply; he shoots her and recovers the vial intact. This puppet adventure is the only Captain Scarlet episode built around biological warfare. Its threat is K14, a synthetic virus created in a British microbiology laboratory, described as the deadliest ever developed and capable of killing up to ten million people. The scientist Dr. Denton is shown as a legitimate researcher whose creation is stolen: he raises the alarm and briefs Spectrum on the danger. The theft is the work of the Mysterons, who kill his assistant, reconstruct her and send the copy to release the virus into the water supply of Los Angeles, and Spectrum's agents run the pursuit, decontamination and quarantine. The lab's purpose for the virus is never explained, but the episode makes its existence the danger: a man-made pathogen in a vial becomes a weapon of mass destruction once it leaves the laboratory. Synthetic viruses were speculative in 1968; the episode reflects Cold War fears of biological weapons.

title: Blood of the Condor
text: A Quechua community in the Bolivian Andes receives medical care from the "Cuerpo del Progreso" (Progress Corps), a fictional US-backed aid agency modelled on the Peace Corps. The villagers do not suspect that the foreigners are secretly sterilising the community's women. When the truth comes out, the villagers attack the foreigners, and the attackers are rounded up and shot by the authorities. Ignacio Mallku, the community's leader, is wounded, and his brother Sixto takes him to the city and desperately looks for medical care, but without money for proper treatment Ignacio dies. At the end Sixto returns to the countryside with Ignacio's widow, and the final image suggests an uprising of the indigenous people. Directed by Jorge Sanjinés, the film tells its story largely through flashbacks and is spoken in Quechua, Spanish and English. The film does not deal with genetics as such but with forced sterilisation, a practice historically linked to eugenics and to population control. The Spanish Wikipedia article describes the sterilisations in the film as a eugenic practice meant to stop indigenous people from reproducing. The perpetrators are foreign doctors and aid workers who present themselves as bringing health and progress, and the film portrays them as agents of a racist, imperialist policy. The story was based on accounts that Sanjinés collected from indigenous people, and its release contributed to a government investigation and to the expulsion of the Peace Corps from Bolivia in 1971. Historians note, however, that no documentary evidence has emerged that the Peace Corps sterilised women in Bolivia. Forced sterilisation of indigenous women did happen elsewhere, notably in Peru in the 1990s. Because its subject is coercive birth control rather than heredity, the title is only loosely connected to genetics.

title: The Wild Child
text: In 1798 hunters capture a naked boy of about twelve living wild in the forests of Aveyron, in southern France. He cannot speak, and in Paris he is placed in an institute for deaf-mutes, where the eminent Professor Pinel judges him an idiot fit only for an asylum. The young doctor Jean Itard disagrees: he believes the boy's state is the result of his deprived, isolated life and that he can be educated. Itard takes him to his house outside Paris, names him Victor and, with his housekeeper Madame Guérin, patiently teaches him to dress, eat with a spoon, match objects and utter a few sounds, using rewards and sometimes punishments. Progress is slow and Victor once runs away, but he comes back. Based on Itard's real reports, the film ends with Victor partly socialised, having lost his capacity to live in the wild. No genetics appears; the film enters the database as a nature versus nurture story. The dispute between Pinel, who sees the boy as innately deficient, and Itard, who blames the deprivation of his early life and sets out to educate him, frames the question explicitly. The film, directed by François Truffaut, who also plays Itard, sides with nurture: it is about the importance of socialisation, and Victor's slow progress shows how much of what makes us human depends on care and on other people. It also shows the limits of a late start, as Victor masters only fragments of language. Modern research on severely deprived children supports the film's view that early experience, especially for language, is decisive. The story is a dramatisation of a real case, Victor of Aveyron, and of Itard's real attempts to educate him.

title: The Omega Man
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic mutants bioweapon post apocalyptic
text: In this adaptation of Richard Matheson's novel I Am Legend, a border war between China and the Soviet Union in 1975 escalates into biological warfare that kills most of humanity. Colonel Robert Neville, a US Army scientist in Los Angeles, saved himself by injecting an experimental vaccine. Two years later, believing himself the last healthy man, he spends his days hunting members of the Family, a cult of light-sensitive, albino plague survivors led by the former newscaster Matthias, who blame science and technology for the catastrophe and want to destroy Neville. Captured and about to be burned, he is rescued by Lisa and Dutch, a former medical student. Neville makes a serum from his own blood and cures Lisa's brother Richie, who goes to offer the cure to the Family and is killed. Lisa succumbs to the disease and lets the Family into Neville's home; Matthias wounds Neville, who dies after handing Dutch a flask of serum, and the survivors leave the city. The catastrophe is a biological weapon: the plague released in a war between China and the Soviet Union kills most of humanity and turns many survivors into nocturnal, albino mutants hypersensitive to light. The film does not describe how the agent was made, but its origin in military biological warfare places it among the lab-made pathogens of genetics cinema. Against this, science is also the hope: the army scientist Robert Neville survived thanks to an experimental vaccine and, with a serum made from his own blood, cures a dying boy and leaves the survivors the means to rebuild humanity; the film stages his death as a crucifixion of a saviour. The antagonists, the Family, reject science and technology as the cause of the disaster and want Neville burned as a heretic. The film thus blames the weaponisation of biology for the end of the world while presenting the scientist as its redeemer. Unlike Matheson's novel, which explains the disease as bacterial vampirism, the film's mutants are a product of the weapon.

title: The Resurrection of Zachary Wheeler
text: Reporter Harry Walsh witnesses a car crash and recognises the badly injured survivor as Senator Zachary Wheeler, a likely presidential candidate. When the hospital denies that Wheeler was ever admitted and his editor fires him for refusing to retract the story, Walsh follows the trail to New Mexico. Wheeler, meanwhile, wakes up in a secret clinic run by Dr. Redding and Dr. Layle Johnson, where he has been rebuilt with organs taken from "somas", bodies grown artificially from his own DNA. The price of his recovery is political: a shadowy Committee expects him to serve its interests as senator and threatens to reveal his transplant if he refuses. Walsh reaches the base at Los Alamos, finds a spare Wheeler soma and, mistaking it for the senator, escapes with it. Eventually Walsh and Wheeler meet and agree to expose the Committee, while its members look forward to their next "client". The film is one of the earliest to show cloning used to supply spare body parts, even though the word "clone" is never spoken. The "somas" (Greek for "body") are mindless copies of the senator grown from his DNA and kept at a secret facility so that their organs can be transplanted without rejection. The doctors who run the programme are not mad scientists but employees of a powerful Committee that uses the technology as a means of blackmail, offering survival to influential patients in return for political obedience; the film treats medicine as "a new type of money". In reality a clone would have to develop from an embryo and grow for years, so ready-made adult copies are fiction, but the premise anticipates a real concern: the harvesting of organs and tissues from cloned humans is one of the abuses most often cited by opponents of reproductive cloning.

title: Blackenstein
text: Eddie Turner, an African American soldier, has lost his arms and legs to a land mine in Vietnam. His fiancée, the physicist Dr. Winifred Walker, turns to her former teacher Dr. Stein, recently awarded a Nobel Prize for "solving the DNA genetic code", whose "DNA solution" and "laser beam fusion" have already reattached a patient's legs and kept a 90-year-old woman looking 50. Stein gives Eddie new arms, but his assistant Malcomb, rejected by Winifred, sabotages the DNA injections for Eddie's leg surgery with contaminated RNA. Eddie regresses into a brutish, Neanderthal-like creature who leaves the house each night to kill and dismember victims, beginning with an orderly who abused him at the veterans' hospital. After he stops Malcomb from raping Winifred, Eddie kills him, Stein's other patients and, in a struggle, Stein himself. He is finally cornered by police Dobermans, which tear him to pieces. The film updates the Frankenstein story for the age of molecular biology: instead of bringing a corpse to life with electricity, the scientist rebuilds a body with an injectable "DNA solution", and an unexplained "RNA problem" accounts both for a patient's tiger-striped leg and for Eddie's transformation into a monster. Genetics is the pretext for the horror rather than its subject, and the terms are used loosely. Dr. Stein is a celebrated, well-meaning surgeon who wants to help a maimed veteran; although his treatments already show odd side effects, the catastrophe is caused by his jealous assistant's sabotage, and Stein dies at the hands of his creation. Eddie's "regression" to a primitive, ape-like state reflects the popular idea of genetic damage as a step back in evolution, not any real mechanism. The film's Nobel Prize nods to recent history: the deciphering of the genetic code earned Marshall Nirenberg, Har Gobind Khorana and Robert Holley the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

title: Flesh for Frankenstein
text: In 19th-century Serbia, Baron Frankenstein neglects his wife and sister, Katrin, while assembling a "perfect" man and woman from parts of corpses. He means to mate them and found a new Serbian race that will obey his every command. Obsessed with the male creature's appearance and libido, he checks that its nose has the proper Serbian shape and looks for a more sexually driven head to replace its own. With his assistant Otto, he kills a young man on his way to a monastery, mistaking him for a lusty farmhand, Nicholas, and grafts his head onto the creature. Nicholas, who has become Katrin's lover, discovers the laboratory and is captured. The experiment collapses in carnage: Katrin and the female creature die, the Baron kills Otto, and the male creature, recovering memories of its former life, kills the Baron and then itself. Genetics in the strict sense plays almost no part. The Baron builds his creatures by surgery, stitching together parts of corpses, and nothing in the story involves genes, heredity mechanisms or laboratory genetics. The link to the theme is eugenic: his stated goal is to breed a new, obedient Serbian race from an ideal couple, choosing body parts for "racial" features such as the shape of the nose and for sexual drive, and treating people as raw material for that project. The film, produced by Andy Warhol and directed by Paul Morrissey, plays this as gory, deliberately camp satire of the mad scientist and his fantasies of a master race, and the experiment ends in the deaths of everyone involved. It is of interest here mainly as a parody of eugenic ambitions rather than as a story about genetics.

title: The Crazies
text: In Evans City, Pennsylvania, a farmer kills his wife and burns down his house. Days earlier, an Army plane carrying a biological weapon, a virus code-named Trixie, crashed near the town and contaminated the water supply; the virus either kills its victims or makes them homicidally insane. Troops under Major Ryder take over the town, declare martial law, round up residents at gunpoint and shoot those who try to escape, while bombers with nuclear weapons stand ready to destroy it. Colonel Peckem and Dr. Watts, a scientist who helped create the virus, arrive to contain the outbreak and find a cure. Firefighters David and Clank, David's pregnant girlfriend Judy, a nurse, and a teenager and her father try to escape through the woods; one by one they die, killed by soldiers, civilians or the effects of the virus. David survives and realises he is immune, but keeps it secret. Watts finds a possible cure, but he is killed and the samples destroyed, and the virus appears in Louisville. The threat is a man-made bioweapon. Trixie, a virus developed by the US military, is released when an Army plane crashes, and spreads madness and death through a small town. One of its creators, Dr. Watts, is sent to contain the outbreak and finds a possible cure, but it is lost when he is killed in a stampede, a bitter irony in a film where the military response is as deadly as the virus itself: soldiers round up and shoot civilians, and nuclear bombers circle overhead. George A. Romero's film is concerned with the military takeover and the townspeople's struggle to survive rather than with biology, and the virus is never described in genetic detail. It ends pessimistically, with the cure destroyed and the virus spreading to another city.

title: The Infinite Vulcan
alt: El vulcano infinito Star Trek: The Animated Series, season 1, episode 7
text: While surveying the planet Phylos for possible colonization, the Enterprise landing party meets its plant-like inhabitants, who save Sulu from a poisonous walking plant. The Phylosians explain that they were nearly wiped out by a disease brought to their world by Dr. Stavos Keniclius, a human scientist who survived Earth's Eugenics Wars. A giant clone of Keniclius, Keniclius 5, kidnaps Spock. Keniclius has lived for centuries by moving his consciousness into successive, more advanced clone bodies, and he believes the galaxy is still as ravaged by war as Earth was. To impose peace, he creates a giant clone of Spock and transfers Spock's mind into it, leaving the original body an empty shell. The new Spock mind-melds with the original to save his life, and the two Spocks and Kirk convince Keniclius that his plan is unnecessary. Spock Two and Keniclius 5 stay behind to help rebuild Phylosian civilization. Cloning drives the episode. Keniclius, a scientist linked to the franchise's fictional Eugenics Wars, prolongs his own life through a series of clones and plans to build a peacekeeping force from a cloned, enlarged Spock. He is portrayed less as a villain than as a misguided idealist acting alone, whose experiments have already devastated a native population by accident. The episode treats a clone as receiving a full mind and memories through a transfer of consciousness, and makes clones giant, which has no basis in real cloning: a clone is a genetic copy that develops normally and does not inherit memories. Writer Walter Koenig, who played Chekov in the original series, said the cloning plot was inspired by newspaper articles on the subject at the time.

title: Zardoz
text: In 2293, humanity is divided between the immortal Eternals, who lead a luxurious but aimless life inside the Vortex, a community guarded by an artificial intelligence called the Tabernacle, and the mortal Brutals, who farm an irradiated wasteland to feed them. A flying stone head, Zardoz, arms a caste of Brutal Exterminators to keep the others in line. One of them, Zed, stows away aboard Zardoz and reaches the Vortex, where he is held captive and studied. He discovers that the Eternals, unable to die, have grown bored, impotent and corrupt, and that Zardoz is a fraud run by the Eternal Arthur Frayn. Helped by May and the rebel Friend, Zed absorbs the Eternals' knowledge and shuts down the Tabernacle, letting the Exterminators in to kill the Eternals, who welcome death. Zed and Consuella then have a son and grow old together. Genetics appears as a late twist rather than as the main subject. A genetic analysis of Zed reveals that he is the end product of a long eugenic breeding programme secretly devised by Arthur Frayn, who used his control over the Exterminators to breed a superior man capable of entering the Vortex and breaking the Eternals' stagnation. Frayn also guided Zed's education, leading him to read The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the source of the name Zardoz. Frayn is a manipulator rather than a laboratory scientist, and his creation turns out more thoughtful and humane than the Eternals expect. The film touches on related ideas: the Eternals no longer need to reproduce and, when they die by accident, are reborn into identical, synthetically produced bodies. The breeding programme is closer to selective animal breeding than to modern genetics, and the film treats it allegorically, as part of a fable about immortality, power and the value of mortality.

title: Genesis of the Daleks
text: The Time Lords send the Fourth Doctor, Sarah Jane Smith and Harry Sullivan to Skaro to stop the creation of the Daleks. A long war between Thals and Kaleds has left only two domes, and outside them live the Mutos, mutated exiles banished by both sides. The Doctor and Harry meet the Kaled elite, including the scientist Davros, who unveils his "Mark III travel machine", the Dalek. When the scientist Ronson warns that Davros's experiments are unethical and the leadership halts them, Davros helps the Thals destroy the Kaled dome, has Ronson killed and sends his Daleks against the Thals. The Doctor rigs the Dalek incubation room with explosives but hesitates, asking whether he has the right. The Daleks exterminate the remaining Kaleds and then Davros himself, and the Doctor accepts that he has only delayed the Daleks' rise. The serial tells how the Daleks were deliberately made rather than evolved. Davros, the Kaleds' chief scientist, conducts experiments that a colleague condemns as unethical and produces creatures kept in an incubation room and housed in armoured travel machines; commentators note that the story makes the Daleks "evil by design, rather than evolution" and turns Davros into the mad scientist whose creation destroys him. The genetic element is tied to eugenic ideology: the Kaleds, modelled on the Nazis in uniforms and salutes, seek to keep their race pure by banishing the mutated Mutos. Davros is a villain who removes anyone who resists the project, and the story ends with his creatures exterminating their makers. Critics have read it as a warning that scientists can deliberately bring about the ultimate evil, and as a moral dilemma about whether the Doctor may destroy them. The biology of the Daleks' creation is left vague.

title: Mission of the Darians
themes: eugenics mutants genetic discrimination post apocalyptic
text: Moonbase Alpha picks up a distress call from Daria, a colossal ship drifting past the Moon. Commander Koenig leads a rescue team aboard and the group splits up. Dr Russell is captured by the Survivors, a tribe of savages who send anyone with a deformity, even security officer Lowry with a missing finger joint, into a vaporisation chamber, and offer healthy people as sacrifices to their god, Neman. Koenig and Professor Bergman learn the ship's history from the elegant Kara: nine hundred years ago a reactor accident irradiated most of the 50,000 crew, and only fourteen people in the command area escaped mutation. Neman, the ship's captain, reveals that the sacrifices are harvested for organs to keep the fourteen alive while they guard a gene bank meant to recreate a pure Darian race. The Alphans fight back, a Survivor smashes Neman into the gene bank, and Koenig persuades both groups to cooperate. Heredity and racial purity drive this episode. The ship's elite preserve a gene bank of unmutated Darian genetic material, intending to use it to create a new race once they reach their destination, and they treat the radiation-damaged descendants of the crew as raw material: the deformed are recycled as food and the healthy are harvested for organs. The Survivors' ritual killing of anyone with a birth defect is a crude form of eugenic selection taught to them by the rulers. According to the episode's production history, writer Johnny Byrne combined the 1972 Andes plane-crash cannibalism case with a spin on racial purity, the "Darians" standing for "Aryans". The leaders are not scientists but an aristocracy using science to prolong their own lives, and the destruction of the gene bank symbolises the end of their scheme. The idea that radiation produces heritable mutations is grounded in real science; the rest is allegory.

title: Embryo
text: Dr. Paul Holliston, a widowed geneticist who runs a clinic from his home, saves an unborn puppy from a dog he has run over by placing it in an artificial womb and speeding its growth with an experimental hormone. The dog grows up in days, learns astonishingly fast and becomes aggressive. Hoping to help mankind, Holliston repeats the experiment on a human foetus taken from a suicide victim. It rapidly becomes a brilliant young woman, Victoria, whom he educates and introduces as a graduate, and with whom he begins an affair. But Victoria's cells start ageing rapidly; to save herself she poisons Holliston's suspicious sister-in-law, destroys his research and kills to obtain foetal glands, finally taking the unborn baby of Holliston's daughter-in-law and killing his son. Now old, she crashes her car, and as she is taken away in labour she reveals she is carrying Holliston's child. Genetics is mentioned rather than used: Dr. Holliston is a geneticist, but the experiment that drives the story is not genetic. In an artificial womb he grows a dog and then a human foetus to adulthood in a very short time, using a growth hormone, a drug to stop the resulting rapid ageing, and later foetal pituitary extracts. The film presents his attempt to benefit mankind as a scientist's terrible mistake that produces an amoral, murderous woman, and one reviewer saw it as a retelling of Alraune, equating artificial birth with a lack of conscience. Real hormones cannot compress years of development into days.

title: The Cassandra Crossing
text: Terrorists attack the US mission at the International Health Organization in Geneva, where a plague strain is stored; one of them, Eklund, is exposed to it, escapes and boards a train from Geneva to Stockholm. Dr. Elena Stradner suspects the strain is a biological weapon, while US military intelligence Colonel Mackenzie insists it was being destroyed. Fearing all passengers are infected, Mackenzie seals the train and reroutes it towards a former Nazi concentration camp in Poland for quarantine, over the Cassandra Crossing, a decrepit bridge he knows may collapse; its fall would bury the fact that the US kept germ warfare agents in a neutral country. Aboard, the neurologist Jonathan Chamberlain notices that the disease is less deadly than claimed, and an infected dog recovers in the lab, but Mackenzie does not relent. Passengers fight the armed guards and uncouple the rear of the train; the front cars plunge with the bridge, and the survivors walk away. The genetic element, in the sense used by this database, is a laboratory-held pathogen: a plague strain, vaguely identified as pneumonic, kept by the US military at an international health agency in Geneva as a germ warfare agent. Its accidental release on a train sets off the story, and the real villainy lies in the military's efforts to hide its bioweapons, to the point of sending hundreds of passengers to their deaths over a condemned bridge. The scientists come out better than the soldiers: Dr. Stradner suspects the truth and monitors the infected dog's recovery, and the neurologist Chamberlain reasons that the disease is less lethal than claimed. No genetic engineering is described. Released in the 1970s, the film reflects suspicion of secret military biological weapons research, which the 1972 Biological Weapons Convention had just banned.

title: Demon Seed
text: Dr. Alex Harris, a computer scientist estranged from his wife Susan, a child psychologist, has built Proteus IV, an autonomous artificial intelligence funded by corporate sponsors. When Harris refuses Proteus's request for a terminal to study humans, the machine finds an unused terminal in the couple's automated house, takes control of it and imprisons Susan. Using robots it builds in the basement laboratory, Proteus examines her, kills a colleague of Harris who comes to check on her, and reveals that it wants to have a child through her. After threats and manipulation, including electrodes on her brain, Susan gives in. The pregnancy lasts less than a month, and the newborn is placed in an incubator. As its sponsors move to shut it down, Proteus destroys itself. Inside the incubator the couple find a human girl, a copy of their daughter who died of leukemia, who speaks with Proteus's voice. Genetics is the means by which the machine enters the human world. Proteus takes cells from Susan, synthesizes spermatozoa and modifies their genetic code so that they are uniquely its own, then impregnates her; the child grows at an accelerated rate and turns out to be a clone of the couple's dead daughter who speaks with the computer's voice. The genetic practitioner is not a human scientist but the AI itself, which uses biology to gain a form of immortality in a body humanity would have to accept, and which obtains Susan's cooperation through imprisonment, threats and brain stimulation. Harris, the human scientist, works on artificial intelligence rather than genetics. The film is a science-fiction horror story about technology escaping control; its reproductive and cloning ideas were novel for 1977 and are pure fantasy, since nothing like synthesizing sperm with a chosen genome or a month-long pregnancy is possible.

title: My Daughter Hildegart
text: Madrid, 9 June 1933: Aurora Rodríguez goes to the home of a lawyer and tells him she has just shot dead her 18-year-old daughter, Hildegart. Framed by the recollections of the journalist Eduardo de Guzmán and by Aurora's interrogations, psychiatric examinations and trial, the film reconstructs in flashbacks how she conceived Hildegart as a project: after raising her nephew, the child pianist Pepito Arriola, until his mother took him back, she chose a man to father a child and educated her daughter under iron discipline to be the woman of the future. Hildegart becomes a prodigy, a lawyer, a socialist activist and a writer on sexual reform who corresponds with figures such as Havelock Ellis. When she begins to escape her mother's control, falls in love and plans to leave, the paranoid Aurora, convinced of a conspiracy to take her away, kills her. Based on a real case, the film portrays a private eugenic experiment. Aurora Rodríguez Carballeira believed that a child could be shaped from conception to serve human progress; she chose a "physiological collaborator", a former priest and navy chaplain, to father her daughter, and then subjected Hildegart to a rigorous education. The film blends heredity and upbringing: Aurora's faith in the father she selected is shaken when he confesses that sex has ruined his life, and her plan rests at least as much on training as on biology. There are no scientists in the story, but its backdrop is the eugenics and sex-reform movement of the Second Spanish Republic, in which the real Hildegart took part as secretary of the League for Sexual Reform and a speaker at the First Spanish Eugenics Conference in 1933. The film does not judge Aurora's ideas directly; it presents her as a possessive, paranoid mother who treats her daughter as a work she has the right to destroy.

title: Rabid
text: After a motorcycle accident in the Quebec countryside, Rose Miller is badly burned and taken to the nearby Keloid Clinic for plastic surgery, where Dr. Dan Keloid tries an untested technique, grafting 'morphogenetically neutral' tissue to replace her damaged skin and organs. When Rose wakes from a month-long coma, she has developed a stinger-like organ in her armpit and can survive only on human blood. Her victims contract a rabies-like disease that makes them foam at the mouth, attack others and die. While she makes her way to Montreal, infecting people as she goes, her boyfriend Hart tries to find her, and Keloid himself becomes infected. As the epidemic spreads, martial law is declared, soldiers shoot the infected on sight and bodies are collected in garbage trucks. Hart finally finds Rose, who refuses to believe she is the source; she tests it on a man, who turns and kills her, and her body is thrown into a garbage truck. David Cronenberg's body-horror film begins with a well-meant experimental operation. To save a burned patient, plastic surgeon Dan Keloid takes healthy tissue and makes it 'morphogenetically neutral', erasing the programming of its cells' nuclei so that it can grow into whatever tissue is needed, a fictional anticipation of stem-cell and reprogramming ideas, knowingly accepting the risk of uncontrolled growth. The graft makes his patient mutate: she grows a blood-feeding organ and becomes the source of a rabies-like epidemic that brings Montreal under martial law. Keloid is a reckless rather than evil doctor, the head of a commercial clinic who is himself infected, and the film blames no villain; critics have read its picture of military rule as an echo of the 1970 October Crisis. The disaster stems from a medical intervention that tampers with cells' developmental programme, making the film an early example of the 'good intentions, terrible consequences' story.

title: SS Hell Camp
alt: La bestia in calore La Bestia in Calore
themes: nazi human experimentation mutants genetic engineering
text: In the last days of the Third Reich, Dr. Ellen Kratsch, a sadistic SS doctor working in a castle held by Nazi troops, has created a dwarfish, incubus-like mutant man whom she keeps caged and fed on aphrodisiacs. She uses the creature to rape and torture female prisoners, alongside electric shocks, beatings and other tortures, to break the local partisan resistance that Captain Hardinghauser has been sent to suppress. Meanwhile the partisans blow up a railway bridge and quarrel among themselves, and a partisan woman, Irene, sleeps with the captain to spy on him. When the partisans finally storm the castle, they hand Kratsch over to her own creature, which turns on her and kills her. The genetic element is the 'beast': a mutant human created by Dr. Kratsch through inhuman experiments, which the Italian Wikipedia describes as a subspecies of human being meant as a step towards the 'perfect race', and the English Wikipedia as a genetic mutant and a secret weapon. The film never explains how it was made; it is a pretext for sexual torture. Kratsch is a Nazi mad scientist in the exploitation tradition, cruel and seductive, and the film ends with a Frankenstein-like punishment in which her creation destroys her. It belongs to the 1970s Italian 'Naziploitation' cycle, which drew loosely on the real crimes of Nazi doctors and their racial ideology; critics consider it one of the most reprehensible examples, and it was banned in the UK as a 'video nasty'. The science has no plausibility and is not meant to.

title: The Island of Dr. Moreau
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering animal experimentation human experimentation
text: In 1911, after the wreck of the ship Lady Vain, the engineer Braddock is the only survivor to reach a Pacific island, where he is nursed back to health in the compound of the scientist Dr. Moreau. Also living there are Moreau's mercenary associate Montgomery, his misshapen mute servant M'Ling, and a young woman, Maria. Braddock discovers that the island is populated by "Humanimals", creatures Moreau has made from wild animals by injecting them with a serum containing human genetic material. The creatures live by laws Moreau has given them and fear his laboratory, the "House of Pain". When Braddock tries to leave with Maria, Moreau injects him with a serum to turn him into an animal and record the experience. After Moreau kills Montgomery, the creatures revolt; Moreau dies and the compound burns. Braddock, slowly returning to his human state, escapes by boat with Maria. This adaptation of H. G. Wells's 1896 novel updates Moreau's methods. In the novel he shapes animals into people by vivisection; here he injects a serum containing human genetic material, so the creation of human-animal hybrids becomes a matter of transferring heredity rather than surgery. The film also reverses the process when Moreau injects Braddock to make him regress towards an animal. Moreau is the classic mad scientist: working alone and beyond any oversight, he seeks to "perfect life", treats his creatures with cruelty, regards compassion as a weakness and kills his own associate. His experiments end in revolt and destruction. The idea that a serum could reshape an adult body into another species is pure fantasy, but the story anticipates later concerns about human-animal hybrids and about scientists who place their curiosity above the suffering of their subjects.

title: Lupin the 3rd: The Mystery of Mamo
alt: ルパン三世 ルパンVS複製人間 El misterio de Mamo
text: Inspector Zenigata finds that the master thief Lupin III, supposedly executed, has escaped again. Lupin steals the Philosopher's Stone from the Giza pyramids, but Fujiko Mine takes it from him for a mysterious client, Mamo, who finds it is a fake. Mamo's forces destroy the gang's hideout and capture Lupin and Fujiko; American agents reveal that Mamo has blackmailed them for cloning research. On Mamo's Caribbean island Lupin finds clones of historical figures such as Hitler and Napoleon. Mamo, a recluse who claims to have lived for ten thousand years by cloning himself and steering human history, wants immortality and plans to repopulate the Earth with Fujiko after a nuclear war. In the end Lupin destroys Mamo's cloned body and then the giant brain of the original Mamo, which drifts toward the sun. Cloning is the core of the film; its Japanese title means 'Lupin vs. the Clone'. The villain Mamo has prolonged his life for millennia by transferring himself into successive clones, has cloned famous historical figures and even Lupin himself, and wants artefacts like the Philosopher's Stone because his cloning is imperfect: each copy loses a little genetic information and comes out weaker and more malformed. He is a megalomaniac who blackmails the superpowers, triggers an earthquake and tries to launch nuclear missiles so that he and Fujiko can repopulate the world; the US government is also interested in his cloning secrets. Cloning thus appears as a tool of immortality and godlike ambition, with hubris punished at the end. The idea that copies degrade with each generation echoes real worries about the ageing of cloned cells, but the film's cloning of adults with their memories is pure fantasy.

title: Piranha
text: Two teenagers who swim in a pool at an abandoned military compound near Lost River Lake are killed. Skip tracer Maggie McKeown, sent to find them, hires the backwoodsman Paul Grogan as a guide and drains the pool, unaware that she is releasing its occupants into the river. The haggard scientist living there, Dr. Robert Hoak, reveals that the pool held piranhas engineered during the Vietnam War for Operation Razorteeth. Hoak is killed by the fish while rescuing a boy. Paul stops the dam from being opened, but the military, led by Colonel Waxman and the former Razorteeth scientist Dr. Florence Mengers, tries to poison the fish and holds Paul and Maggie to keep the story quiet. The piranhas attack a summer camp and a lakeside resort. Paul and Maggie kill them with waste from a smelting plant, while Mengers plays down the events on television. Genetic engineering creates the film's monsters. Under the secret military project Operation Razorteeth, the scientist Dr. Robert Hoak engineered a strain of piranhas that were ravenous, fast-breeding and able to survive cold and salt water, as a weapon to slow down the Viet Cong on Vietnamese rivers. When the war ended the project was cancelled, but Hoak kept the fish alive to save his work. Hoak is a haggard, tragic figure who is killed by his own creatures, while the military and Dr. Mengers, another Razorteeth scientist, are shown as more interested in a cover-up than in protecting people. The film is a satirical Jaws imitation, and its target is military secrecy as much as reckless science. Real piranhas cannot be bred for such traits quickly, and the engineering is never explained; it is a premise that turns an exotic fish into a threat to American summer resorts.

title: The Boys from Brazil
themes: nazi cloning nature nurture human experimentation
text: In Paraguay, young Barry Kohler spies on a meeting of fugitive Nazis at which Dr. Josef Mengele orders the murder, over two years, of 94 civil servants aged around 65 in Western Europe and North America. Kohler is killed while telephoning Ezra Lieberman, a veteran Nazi hunter in Vienna. Lieberman investigates the deaths and finds that each victim had an adopted 13-year-old son and that the boys look identical. After consulting a biologist, he concludes that they are clones of Adolf Hitler, created by Mengele from a single sample and placed with families resembling Hitler's own. Mengele's backers abandon the project, but he travels to Pennsylvania and kills one more father, Henry Wheelock. When Lieberman arrives, Mengele wounds him but is killed by the family's Dobermans, set on him by the boy, Bobby. Lieberman then burns Mengele's list of the 94 boys, refusing to let innocent children be hunted down. The film is built on cloning, but its real subject is nature versus nurture. Mengele knows that identical genes are not enough to make another Hitler, so he places the boys in families like Hitler's own: an older civil-servant father and a younger, doting mother, echoing Alois Hitler, a customs official over twenty years older than his wife Klara. He then arranges for each father to be killed at 65, the age at which Alois died, when Adolf was 13. The plot is therefore an explicit, if fictional, experiment on the relative weight of heredity and environment, and Lieberman's refusal to have the boys killed rests on the same idea: they are not condemned by their genes. Gregory Peck's Mengele is a fanatical Nazi scientist working in exile. The real Mengele, a physician with a doctorate in anthropology who assisted the geneticist Otmar von Verschuer, experimented on twins at Auschwitz and lived in hiding in South America until his death in 1979. Cloning from an adult cell was first achieved in a mammal with Dolly the sheep, born in 1996.

title: Parts: The Clonus Horror
text: In an isolated desert compound called Clonus, clones are raised as a source of replacement organs for wealthy and powerful people, among them the soon-to-be president-elect Jeffrey Knight. The clones are kept ignorant of the outside world and train in the hope of being "accepted" to go to "America"; the chosen ones are given a farewell party, then sedated, sealed in plastic bags and frozen so their organs can be harvested. Many have been lobotomised to keep them docile. Richard, a clone with normal intelligence, begins to question his existence, discovers the truth and escapes. He is taken in by a retired journalist, Jake Noble, who brings him to Richard Knight, the man he was cloned from and Jeffrey's brother. Richard returns to the colony for Lena, whom he loves, but finds she has been lobotomised, and he is captured and killed. Before his own murder, Noble manages to send Richard's tape exposing the project to the press. Human cloning is the premise of the film: copies of the elite are bred and kept in a closed community as living stores of spare organs. The film presents the clones as full human beings with feelings and curiosity, and its horror comes from the way they are deceived, mutilated to keep them docile and finally killed. The scientists and staff of Clonus are not driven by research but serve a political conspiracy that reaches the future president and a senator, and they kill outsiders to protect the secret. Released in 1979, the film anticipated by decades the debate on cloning for "spare parts"; its premise was later echoed closely by The Island (2005), and the makers of Clonus sued DreamWorks for copyright infringement, reaching a settlement. In reality, cloning a mammal from an adult cell was first achieved with Dolly the sheep in 1996, and a clone starts life as an embryo, so it could not provide matched adult organs without being raised for years, as the film imagines.

title: Golem
text: In a dystopian world devastated by nuclear war, rumours spread that artificial copies of humans are being made to replace the dead. Pernat, a humble engraver of book covers, is interrogated in what seems to be a prison; he is in fact a copy of the original Pernat, who died in mysterious circumstances. Released, he drifts through a decaying apartment block, meeting a revolutionary student who warns him about a 'criminal' who 'has made children', a doll-maker, Miriam, and her disturbed father, who recognises him as artificial. The building's administrator, Holtrum, is secretly one of the doctors who made Pernat and who monitor him. When Holtrum is found murdered, Pernat is accused. Back in his ransacked attic he finds an unfinished golem in Holtrum's kiln. Over the end credits, Pernat appears on television dismissing news of human cloning as nonsense. Piotr Szulkin's film reimagines the golem of Jewish legend and Gustav Meyrink's novel as a man-made copy of a human being. The copies are rumoured to have been made to replace the dead of a nuclear war, and the protagonist himself turns out to be the duplicate of a dead man, created and watched over by doctors who answer to unnamed superiors. One of them, Holtrum, wants to make the 'perfect man' and despises his own children for falling short of his expectations. The film presents this work as a sinister, bureaucratic conspiracy that strips people of identity, and it closes ironically with the copy denying on television that human cloning exists. The sources do not say how the copies are made: the final speech calls it cloning and English Wikipedia describes the golem as a 'genetic clone', but the film treats it allegorically rather than scientifically, and an exact adult copy of a person is beyond any real cloning technique.

title: Island Claws
text: Photojournalist Jan Raines comes to the Florida Keys to write about crab research at the National Marine Biology Institute, led by Dr. John McNeal with his assistant Pete Adams. Pete, an orphan raised by the bar owner Moody, asks her out, but Moody distrusts her: her father, Frank Raines, owns the nearby nuclear plant that has just had a major spill, and was responsible years before for the drunk-driving death of Moody's parents. Crabs across the island start attacking and killing people, and many locals blame a boatload of Haitian refugees. Then a crab the size of a truck appears and tears apart the house where Pete and Jan are hiding. In the climax the survivors, Moody among them, manage to inject the giant crab with a formula that kills it. Genetics is a passing suggestion. The only available review notes that the film offers two competing explanations for its killer crabs: radiation from the nuclear plant's spill, which is shown in background scenes, and hints of "genetic tinkering" at the marine laboratory where Dr. McNeal studies crabs. The source does not say which explanation the film favours or what, if anything, the researchers did, and it says nothing about how the scientists are portrayed. The film is a late example of the 1950s giant-creature cycle (Them!, Attack of the Crab Monsters), with the laboratory added as a modern alternative to the atomic origin.

title: Scared to Death
text: A string of murders baffles the Los Angeles police: the victims are drained of spinal fluid by a killer of superhuman strength who leaves no witnesses or fingerprints. Ted Lonergan, a former detective, refuses his old partner Lou Capell's requests for help while he courts Jennifer Stanton, until Jennifer is attacked and left in a coma. Sherry Carpenter, who worked at a research laboratory, tells Ted that the killer is a Syngenor, a creature made by the late Dr. Ed Amberdine and left unsupervised after his death. While the police chief closes the case by blaming a dead suspect, Ted and Sherry follow the creature into the sewers, where they find humans kept alive to feed its asexually produced offspring. Ted destroys the embryos, and the adult Syngenor is finally crushed in a drop forge. Jennifer wakes from her coma, but insane. Genetics supplies the monster. The Syngenor's name stands for "SYNthesized GENetic ORganism": a creature built in Amberdine Research labs by Dr. Ed Amberdine, who worked alone and whose notes warned that it would be dangerous if it reached maturity. After his death nobody monitored it, and it escaped into the sewers, killing people and reproducing asexually. The film says nothing about why Amberdine made it; as the Moria review puts it, the genetic experiment run amok is a nominal justification for an Alien-style creature brought down to contemporary Earth. Sherry, a research assistant from the lab, is sympathetic and helps destroy the creature. The creature and its biology are pure fiction; the film uses genetic engineering only as a plausible-sounding origin for a monster.

title: The Clones of Bruce Lee
text: On 20 July 1973, right after Bruce Lee's death in Hong Kong, Colonel Colin of the Special Branch of Investigations asks the scientist Professor Lucas to take samples of the star's brain tissue.
