From them Lucas creates three clones of Lee, who are trained in martial arts and sent to fight crime in Southeast Asia. Bruce Lee #1 goes undercover as an actor for a corrupt, gold-smuggling film producer who plans to have him killed on camera. The other two travel to Thailand to stop Dr. Ngai, a mad scientist who injects men with a formula that turns their skin to bronze and plans to conquer the world with them. After the clones return, Lucas, resentful that he was not properly rewarded, turns them against each other and then sends his henchmen after them. One clone is killed, but the others defeat Lucas's men and the professor is arrested. Cloning provides the premise but is treated as a pretext for the fights. The film never explains how the clones are made beyond taking brain tissue from Lee's body, and they appear as fully grown adult fighters soon afterwards, played by different Bruce Lee imitators. The scientist Professor Lucas works for a state security agency, and when he feels insufficiently rewarded he turns his creations against one another, a cheap version of the mad scientist who sees his clones as his property. The film belongs to the "Bruceploitation" cycle that cashed in on Lee's death. In reality, cloning by nuclear transfer yields an embryo that must develop like any other, so a clone would be a much younger genetic twin rather than a ready-made copy; no primate had been cloned from adult cells, let alone a human.

title: The Henderson Monster
text: Dr. Tom Henderson, a Nobel Prize-winning scientist, carries out genetic engineering experiments at a college in a small American town, assisted by Dr. Louise Casimir, his former girlfriend, whose husband Pete is a hard-drinking writer. Henderson is close to a major breakthrough and shows little concern for ethics. As questions arise about the safety of the work, the town's new mayor, Frank Bellona, bans the experiments and calls a public hearing, and Professor Leo Tedeschi, a former Manhattan Project scientist, arrives to bring some oversight to the research. Alongside the public dispute, the film follows the strained relationships between Henderson, Louise and Pete. Despite the title, reviewers note that no creature ever appears: the "monster" remains a theoretical possibility, and this CBS television film, directed by Waris Hussein from a script by Ernest Kinoy, is a talk-driven drama rather than a horror story. The film is a social-issue drama about the risks and regulation of recombinant DNA research. Henderson is the ambitious scientist absorbed by the prospect of a breakthrough and dismissive of possible hazards, while the mayor, the townspeople and the visiting Tedeschi stand for public oversight; bringing in a veteran of the Manhattan Project frames genetic engineering as a technology whose consequences could escape its creators. One reviewer singles out the still unsettling idea of an engineered sample being flushed into the water supply. The premise closely echoes real events: in 1976 the mayor of Cambridge, Massachusetts, Alfred Vellucci, tried to ban genetic engineering at Harvard and MIT for fear that researchers could accidentally produce hazardous organisms, which led to months of public hearings with scientists before a panel of residents rejected the ban. As reviewers point out, the techniques that alarmed the public in 1980 have since become routine laboratory tools.

title: The Leisure Hive
text: The Fourth Doctor and Romana visit the Leisure Hive on Argolis, a resort built by the Argolins after a war with the Foamasi. The Hive is near bankruptcy, and its main attraction, the Tachyon Recreation Generator, can duplicate and manipulate organic matter. The Argolin chairman Mena brings the Earth scientist Hardin, whose tachyon rejuvenation results are faked, to save her deteriorating people; a test leaves the Doctor aged. Mena's son Pangol reveals that he is the only young Argolin because he was the only successful child of a cloning experiment in the Generator. Driven by hatred of the Foamasi, he uses the machine to create an army of replicas of himself, but the Doctor has sabotaged it and the copies are only tachyon images of the Doctor. When Pangol re-enters the Generator, set to "rejuvenate", he emerges as a baby in the arms of a rejuvenated Mena. Cloning drives the second half of the serial. Pangol, the last young Argolin, is the only successful child of a cloning experiment carried out with the Tachyon Recreation Generator, and he plans to use the same machine to mass-produce copies of himself as an army for the war-forged empire he wants to build against the Foamasi. The Doctor's sabotage turns the army into harmless tachyon images, and the machine's rejuvenation setting reduces Pangol to a baby. The story frames cloning as fantasy machine technology based on tachyons rather than biology, and it uses it to show a warlike fanatic trying to multiply himself; it is defeated by trickery rather than condemned as science. The parallel rejuvenation plot is presented as tachyon physics, not genetics, and Hardin's faked results make it a story about fraud. Real cloning produces a genetically identical individual that must still develop from an embryo; it does not duplicate adults.

title: Virus
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic bioweapon post apocalyptic
text: In 1982 American agents recover MM88, a deadly virus created by accident by an American geneticist and stolen from a US laboratory, which amplifies the potency of any other microbe it meets. The plane carrying it crashes in a storm and the virus escapes, causing a pandemic disguised as the 'Italian flu'. Within seven months virtually all of humanity is dead, except 863 people at Antarctic research bases, where the cold keeps the virus inactive. The survivors form a government and begin to rebuild. Then the Japanese seismologist Yoshizumi predicts an earthquake near Washington that will trigger an automatic US nuclear retaliation system, which would in turn trigger the Soviet one, including a strike on Antarctica. Protected by an experimental vaccine, Yoshizumi and Major Carter go to Washington to stop it, but fail. In the Japanese version, Yoshizumi survives and rejoins them years later. The disaster is triggered by a laboratory virus. MM88 was created accidentally by an American geneticist and developed as a biological weapon requested by the US government; it is stolen, smuggled, lost in a plane crash and goes on to wipe out almost all of humanity. The film blames the arms race, secrecy and political cover-up more than an individual scientist: a government scientist who tries to warn the President is locked up, and a military doctrine of automated nuclear retaliation completes the catastrophe. Scientists also appear as rescuers, notably an East German scientist who wants the sample used to develop a vaccine, and Dr. Latour, whose experimental vaccine protects the heroes. The idea of a virus that boosts any other microbe is fictional, but the film's concern with bioweapons, laboratory leaks and pandemics drew renewed attention during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Per Aspera Ad Astra
text: In the 23rd century, the Earth starship Pushkin finds a derelict alien ship whose crew are identical humanoids produced by cloning. Most are dead, but one young woman survives. Professor Sergei Lebedev takes her into his home on Earth and names her Neeya. She has no memory of her past and shows telekinetic powers. A scientist, Professor Nadezhda Ivanova, discovers a neural centre in her brain that can be triggered remotely, and flashbacks reveal that Neeya comes from the planet Dessa, where a scientist named Glan created clones he could control. Neeya stows away on the Astra, which is taking a Dessan delegation home. Dessa's air and water have been poisoned by the exhaustion of its resources, and the profiteer Turanchoks, who sells gas masks from Glan's former institute, sabotages the Earth crew's clean-up and uses Glan's control device to force Neeya to plant a bomb. Neeya breaks free, helps defeat Glan's last experiment, and stays to help restore Dessa. Cloning is part of the film's premise. Neeya is one of a series of identical humanoids grown in the laboratory of the Dessan scientist Glan, who was building an army of clones fitted with a remotely triggered neural control system so they would obey orders. The story uses the cloned woman to ask whether a manufactured being can develop a free will and a human identity, and Neeya's choice to resist her programming is the moral centre of the film. Glan is portrayed as a scientist serving a plan to seize power, and his last experiment, a deadly blob-like creature, turns on the people of his own institute. The film combines this with an ecological theme, the destruction of a planet by exploitation. As in most science fiction of its time, cloning here produces adult copies with built-in control mechanisms, which goes far beyond what cloning can do.

title: Blade Runner
text: In the Los Angeles of 2019, the Tyrell Corporation manufactures replicants, bioengineered humanoids used as slave labour on off-world colonies and banned from Earth. Former police officer Rick Deckard, a "blade runner", is forced back into service to track down and "retire" four Nexus-6 replicants led by Roy Batty, who have returned to Earth illegally. Visiting Eldon Tyrell, Deckard discovers that Tyrell's assistant Rachael is an experimental replicant who believes she is human because she has been implanted with memories. Roy and his companions trace the eye designer Hannibal Chew and the genetic designer J. F. Sebastian, who suffers from a premature-ageing disorder, and through him reach Tyrell to demand a longer life. When Tyrell says it is impossible, Roy kills him. Deckard kills the remaining replicants except Roy, who, dying as his four-year lifespan ends, spares Deckard's life. Deckard then leaves with Rachael. Genetic engineering underlies the whole premise. Replicants are not robots but bioengineered beings, designed by a corporation as disposable labour (Pris is a "basic pleasure model"), and given a built-in four-year lifespan as a safeguard. The film shows biotechnology as an industry: Tyrell, the creator, is a remote corporate magnate, while the designers who make eyes and bodies are craftsmen working to order, with no say over how their products are used. The question of what separates a manufactured being from a human, and whether it may be owned and killed, drives the story; Roy's confrontation with Tyrell, a creature demanding more life from its maker, has been linked by critics to Frankenstein, and the film is described as exploring the moral implications of human mastery of genetic engineering. Nothing close to designing a complete human-like organism is possible today. The film is a founding work of cyberpunk and influenced biopunk, the subgenre built around biotechnology and genetic engineering.

title: Forbidden World
text: On Xarbia, a remote desert planet, scientists at a genetic research station have created an experimental life form, Subject 20, from a synthetic DNA strain called Proto B, intended to end a galaxy-wide food crisis. The organism mutates rapidly, kills the laboratory animals and encloses itself in a cocoon. Troubleshooter Mike Colby arrives with his robot SAM-104 and wants to destroy it, but the research staff resist. Once hatched, the creature kills most of the crew one by one, and the scientists' secret comes out: Subject 20 incorporates human DNA, and it kills by injecting Proto B into its victims, turning their bodies into a mass of pure protein that it eats. In its final form, a large insect-like monster, it is destroyed when it eats the cancer-ridden liver of the station's doctor, Cal, and its body breaks down from within. Colby and lab assistant Tracy are the only survivors. Forbidden World is a low-budget Roger Corman production in the vein of Alien, and genetic engineering supplies its monster. Subject 20 is a designed organism made from a synthetic DNA strain and, it turns out, human DNA, created by a research team with the benevolent aim of solving a food shortage. The scientists are shown as secretive and reckless: they hide the creature's human origin and resist destroying it, and their creation kills almost everyone on the station. The film's genetics is pure invention, with DNA working as a kind of acid or contagion: Proto B erases the genetic differences between cells in its victims' cells and reduces them to edible protein, and cancer cells act as a poison that makes the creature self-destruct. As in many films of the period, the story mainly serves as a warning about creating new life forms without controls rather than as an exploration of real science.

title: Piranha II: The Spawning
alt: Piraña II: los vampiros del mar
text: At the Hotel Elysium, a Caribbean resort, divers and bathers are killed near a sunken shipwreck. Diving instructor Anne Kimbrough, who studied marine biology, realizes the wounds were not made by sharks or barracudas, but her estranged husband Steve, the local police chief, and the hotel manager Raoul dismiss her warnings. Tourist Tyler Sherman, with whom Anne has an affair, reveals that he is a biochemist from a government team that developed piranhas able to fly and live out of water as a weapon; a cylinder of them was lost and they now breed in the wreck. During a night-time fish party the piranhas fly out of the sea and attack the guests, killing the fisherman Gabby among others. Anne and Tyler dive to blow up the wreck with time bombs; Tyler is eaten by the fish, while Anne escapes and is reunited with Steve and their son. The monsters are a product of military genetic engineering. Tyler Sherman's government team created a strain of piranha that can fly and survive out of water, described as genetically modified and, in the Spanish source, as a hybrid of piranha with mummichog and flying fish; the fish were meant as an "ultimate weapon". After a cylinder of them is lost in the sea, they breed in a shipwreck and kill tourists and locals. Tyler is a remorseful insider who helps the heroine destroy the nest, but the army is said to consider him unstable and he ends up eaten by his own creations, a cliché the Moria review notes. The authorities and the profit-minded hotel manager who ignore the danger share the blame. As in the first Piranha, a covert weapons programme unleashes engineered animals on civilians; hybridizing fish into fliers is pure fantasy.

title: Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan
alt: Star Trek II, la ira de Khan
text: In 2285, Admiral James T. Kirk is restless behind a desk. The starship Reliant, searching for a lifeless planet on which to test the Genesis Device, a technology that turns dead matter into habitable worlds, lands by mistake on Ceti Alpha V. There Captain Terrell and Chekov are captured by Khan Noonien Singh, a genetically engineered tyrant whom Kirk exiled fifteen years earlier and whose followers, including his wife, died when the planet became a wasteland. Using mind-controlling eels, Khan seizes Reliant, attacks the Regula I station where Kirk's former lover Carol Marcus and their son David developed Genesis, and steals the device. Kirk lures him into the Mutara Nebula, where his inexperience in three-dimensional combat costs him the battle. Mortally wounded, Khan activates Genesis. To save the crippled Enterprise from the blast, Spock repairs the warp drive in the irradiated engine room and dies of radiation poisoning; his coffin lands on the newly formed Genesis planet. Genetics defines the villain rather than the plot. Khan, introduced in the 1967 episode "Space Seed" to which the film is a sequel, is one of a group of genetically engineered superhumans bred to be free of ordinary mental and physical limitations, who in Star Trek's history controlled more than a quarter of the Earth during the "Eugenics Wars" of the 1990s before being overthrown. The film relies on that backstory: Khan's strength, intellect and arrogance are presented as products of his design, and his pride and obsession with revenge are his downfall, as Kirk exploits his lack of experience. Behind the space opera lies a warning about eugenics: engineered superiority produces not better people but would-be rulers. The scientists in the film, Carol and David Marcus, work on the Genesis Device, not on genetics. The history imagined by the franchise did not come true: there was no genetic enhancement of humans in the 1990s, and the first gene-edited babies, born in China in 2018, led to the scientist responsible being sentenced to prison.

title: Swamp Thing
text: In the Louisiana swamps, government agent Alice Cable joins a secret bioengineering project led by Dr. Alec Holland and his sister Linda, who are developing a plant-animal hybrid able to survive in hostile environments. When Linda's formula proves to trigger explosive plant growth, the lab is raided by the paramilitary forces of Anton Arcane, who wants the formula for himself. Linda is shot, and Alec, doused in the chemicals and set on fire, plunges into the swamp. He re-emerges as the Swamp Thing, a powerful plant creature that protects Alice from Arcane's men. Arcane recovers Alec's notebooks, recreates the formula and tests it on his henchman Bruno, who shrinks into a small, misshapen man, because the formula only amplifies what a person already is. Arcane takes it himself, turns into a beast, and is killed by the Swamp Thing in the swamp. Genetics is present as the scientific premise of a comic-book horror story. The Hollands' research aims to combine plant and animal traits in a hybrid organism able to withstand extreme conditions, and Alec becomes, accidentally, the subject of his own experiment, fused with the swamp's vegetation. The film's notion of the formula is vague: it regenerates tissue, makes plants grow explosively and, on people, "amplifies what is already there", turning the timid Bruno into a dwarf and the cruel Arcane into a monster. Alec and Linda are idealistic researchers working for the government, while the villain is a wealthy outsider who seeks the formula for power and immortality, a familiar contrast between well-meaning science and its misuse. There is no attempt at scientific realism: the transformations are instant and the mechanism is never explained. Real transgenic organisms combining genes from distant species exist, but they gain specific traits, not wholesale changes in body form.

title: Anna to the Infinite Power
themes: cloning nature nurture human experimentation nazi
text: Anna Hart, a twelve-year-old genius at a school for gifted children in New Jersey, is also a kleptomaniac who suffers headaches and strange prophetic dreams. When she sees her exact double, Anna Smithson, on the television news, she starts investigating and discovers that she is one of several clones of Anna Zimmerman, a scientist who died twenty years earlier. Her dreams turn out to be Zimmerman's memories of growing up as a Jewish child prodigy in Nazi Germany. Taken to a facility on Albacore Island for "re-evaluation", Anna finds other Annas kept there and learns that the project's director, Dr. Jelliff, plans to eliminate the failed clones while grooming another girl to become the new Zimmerman. Her neighbour and piano teacher, Michaela, reveals herself as Anna Parkhurst, the first clone, and forces Jelliff to spare all the Annas in exchange for the plans of Zimmerman's "replicator". Human cloning is the core of this television film, based on Mildred Ames's 1981 novel. A dead scientist's genome is reproduced in several girls who are placed with chosen families, each a scientist married to a musician, to recreate the conditions of her childhood and see whether she will turn into the same person. The story is therefore an experiment in nature versus nurture: Anna discovers she is expected to become Zimmerman, but chooses to be herself. The scientists who continue the project see the girls as experimental material and are prepared to kill the ones who do not turn out as planned, and the backstory links the research to Nazi plans for human genetic engineering. The film shares the 1970s and 1980s fascination with cloning seen in The Boys from Brazil. Real clones are genetically identical but develop differently, and inherited memories, as suggested by Anna's dreams, have no basis in biology.

title: Terrahawks
text: In this puppet series by Gerry Anderson, set in 2020, an alien force destroys NASA's base on Mars, and a small secret organisation, the Terrahawks, is formed to defend Earth from its base, Hawknest, in South America. The team is led by Doctor "Tiger" Ninestein, a somewhat bloodthirsty commander who is the ninth of nine clones created by Dr. Gerhard Stein and can be replaced by another clone if killed. His crew includes his second-in-command Mary Falconer, the pop star and pilot Kate Kestrel, the gunner Hawkeye, whose eyes were replaced with microcomputers, and Lieutenant Hiro, who commands an orbital battle station, helped by spherical robots called Zeroids. Their enemies are androids from the planet Guk led by the scheming Zelda, with her "children" Cy-Star and Yung-Star, who send monsters kept in cryogenic storage against Earth. The 39 episodes mix tongue-in-cheek humour with action. Genetics is a passing element of the premise. The leader of the Terrahawks, Doctor Tiger Ninestein, is the ninth of nine clones made by a scientist, Dr. Gerhard Stein, which explains his name and the fact that he can be replaced within 24 hours if he is killed. The series does not explore the cloning, who Stein was or what happened to the other clones; it is a comic touch in a puppet adventure about defending Earth from alien androids and monsters, where most of the science is technological. Real clones would be born as babies and could not replace an adult within a day.

title: Trading Places
text: In Philadelphia, the elderly brothers Randolph and Mortimer Duke own the commodities brokerage Duke & Duke. Holding opposing views on nature versus nurture, they make a bet: they will swap the lives of their refined managing director, Louis Winthorpe III, and a poor street hustler, Billy Ray Valentine. Winthorpe is framed as a thief and drug dealer, loses his job, home and fiancée, and is helped only by a prostitute, Ophelia. Valentine, meanwhile, is installed in Winthorpe's job and house and proves a natural at the business. When Valentine overhears the Dukes settling their wager for one dollar and planning to throw him back onto the street, he joins Winthorpe, Ophelia and the butler Coleman. Learning that the Dukes plan to corner the frozen orange juice market with a stolen crop report, the four swap the report for a forgery and, on the trading floor, ruin the brothers while making a fortune. Genetics appears only as an idea, but it drives the plot. The Dukes' wager is an informal experiment on nature versus nurture: one brother believes that a person's character and abilities are inherited, the other that environment determines how anyone behaves. Swapping the lives of a privileged white broker and a poor Black hustler turns this old argument, which has long been used to justify class and racial hierarchies, into comedy. The outcome favours nurture: Valentine thrives once given opportunity, and Winthorpe quickly falls apart when he loses his status. There are no scientists in the film; the experimenters are two wealthy, cynical businessmen who treat people as subjects for a one-dollar bet, and who end up ruined by their own subjects. Research on twins and adoptees has found that heredity and environment both contribute substantially to most behavioural traits, often inextricably, a far subtler answer than the Dukes' all-or-nothing wager.

title: Bagi, the Monster of Mighty Nature
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering gmo bioweapon
text: In the South American jungle, the Japanese hunter Ryosuke "Ryo" Ishigami tracks a monster with the help of a local boy, Chico, and recalls how he knows it. As a child he rescued a kitten and raised it as a pet, until the animal, Bagi, grew into an intelligent cat-woman and had to flee. Nine years later Bagi reappears and saves the teenage Ryo from his motorcycle gang. Together they discover that she was created at the SuperLife Center by Ryo's mother, the geneticist Professor Yoko Ishigami. They follow her to the republic of Monica, where a laboratory is developing a genetically engineered rice capable of destroying humanity, which the country's president wants to use against his opponents. The professor refuses to cooperate and is killed, and Ryo wrongly blames Bagi. In the end he stabs Bagi, then finds his mother's remorseful letter in her locket; Bagi's body disappears, and her silhouette is last seen running towards distant mountains. Genetic engineering drives the whole story. Bagi is a human–mountain lion hybrid created at the SuperLife Center by combining human and puma cells, part of a programme in which Professor Ishigami and the centre's ambitious chief had produced other similar creatures. A second thread involves an engineered rice that a dictator plans to use as a weapon, turning agricultural biotechnology into an instrument of political repression. The geneticist mother is a conflicted figure: she refuses to help build the weapon and dies for it, and her last letter expresses remorse for her failures both as a scientist and as a mother. Bagi, intelligent but rejected by humans and increasingly feral, is a Frankenstein-like creation abandoned by its makers, and the film sides with her rather than with the institutions that produced her. Written and directed by Osamu Tezuka for Nippon TV, the film combines environmental themes with a warning about biotechnology placed at the service of profit and power.

title: Dune
text: In the year 10,191, the emperor Shaddam IV hands control of the desert planet Arrakis, the only source of the life-extending spice melange, to House Atreides, while secretly plotting with the rival House Harkonnen to destroy it. Lady Jessica, concubine of Duke Leto Atreides, belongs to the Bene Gesserit, a sisterhood with extraordinary powers that has spent centuries on a breeding programme to produce the Kwisatz Haderach, a male "superbeing". Ordered to bear a daughter, Jessica instead bore a son, Paul. After the Harkonnens attack and Leto dies, Paul and Jessica take refuge with the desert people, the Fremen, who see Paul as their prophesied messiah. Paul leads them in raids that halt spice production, drinks the poisonous Water of Life and gains psychic powers. He defeats the emperor's troops, kills the Harkonnen heir Feyd-Rautha in a duel and is declared the Kwisatz Haderach. Genetics enters Dune through the Bene Gesserit breeding programme, a long-term scheme of selective breeding in which the sisterhood arranges unions between noble bloodlines to produce a being with superhuman mental powers. Paul is the product of that programme, and he exists only because Jessica disobeyed the order to bear a daughter. The programme is a form of eugenics carried out over many generations by a secretive religious and political order, not by scientists, and it is presented as a tool of power. The film does not use the vocabulary of genes or DNA, and much of Paul's transformation comes from the spice and the Water of Life rather than from heredity alone. Genetics is therefore an important background element of the story rather than its main subject.

title: Greystoke: The Legend of Tarzan, Lord of the Apes
alt: Greystoke, la leyenda de Tarzán, el rey de los monos
text: In 1886 John Clayton, heir to the Earl of Greystoke, and his pregnant wife are shipwrecked on the African coast. Their son is born, his mother dies of malaria and his father is killed by apes, and a female ape who has lost her own infant adopts the baby. The boy grows up as a member of the ape troop, discovers at his parents' treehouse that he looks different from his family, and becomes a strong, resourceful young man. Years later he nurses a wounded Belgian explorer, Phillippe d'Arnot, who teaches him English, works out who he is and takes him to the Greystoke estate in Scotland. His grandfather welcomes him and the American ward Jane falls in love with him, but John cannot fit into aristocratic society, and after his ape father is shot in London he returns to the jungle. There is no genetic science in the film; it qualifies as a nature versus nurture story, and its director, Hugh Hudson, framed it explicitly as 'the battle of nature and nurture, nature and culture'. John is human by birth and ape by upbringing. His human nature shows when he recognises his difference in a mirror and when he picks up language as a natural mimic; his upbringing shows in his ape behaviour, his loyalty to his ape family and his revulsion at how Victorian society treats animals. The film gives weight to both: he can become an earl, but he chooses to go back to the jungle. Hudson described the theme as a balance between two forces that 'shouldn't be opposing at all'. Real cases of children raised in isolation suggest that early deprivation, especially of language, is very hard to make up, so a feral child adapting this well is a romantic fiction.

title: Resurrection of the Daleks
text: In 1984 London, policemen led by the mercenary Lytton, who works for the Daleks, gun down escapees from a time corridor; one, Stien, gets away. In the future the Daleks free their creator Davros from a prison station, because they lost their war against the Movellans to a virus that attacks Dalek tissue and need him to find a cure. The Fifth Doctor, Tegan and Turlough are dragged down the time corridor to the London Docklands. Stien turns out to be a Dalek agent, and the Daleks plan to duplicate the Doctor and his companions to assassinate the Gallifrey High Council, but Stien breaks his conditioning and stops the process. Davros turns against the Daleks and uses the Movellan virus on those who come to kill him; the Doctor releases the virus against the Daleks on Earth. Davros is infected, Stien destroys the station and ship, and Tegan stays on Earth. Two biological elements drive the story. The Daleks have been defeated by the Movellan virus, a biological weapon that attacks Dalek tissue; they free Davros to find a cure, but he and the Doctor both end up releasing it to kill Daleks, and it finally infects Davros himself. The second is the Daleks' plan to duplicate the Doctor and his companions in a "duplication chamber" and send the copies to assassinate the Time Lords' High Council; the process, which also copies minds, is stopped when Stien breaks his conditioning. Both are weapons in the hands of villains in a grim, violent story, and the Doctor turns the bioweapon against the Daleks as a last resort. The duplicates are fantasy rather than cloning in the biological sense, and a reviewer noted that "the whole duplicates business makes little sense". The virus fits the familiar image of a pathogen tailored to one species.

title: Creator
text: Dr. Harry Wolper, an eccentric medical professor at a Southern California college, has spent thirty years trying to clone his wife Lucy, who died in childbirth, from cells he has kept. He hires Boris Lafkin, a struggling pre-med student, as his lab assistant and in exchange coaches him in his courtship of a fellow student, Barbara. To obtain eggs for the experiment, Harry recruits Meli, an uninhibited young woman who moves in with him and gradually falls in love with him. A rival professor, Sid Kuhlenbeck, tries to have Harry sidelined and take over his lab, but the plan backfires when Harry wins a large research grant. When Barbara suffers an aneurysm and falls into a coma, Harry helps Boris keep her alive until she wakes. Having found new love, Harry pours Lucy's cells into the sea and marries Meli. Cloning is the central scientific idea of this romantic comedy, though it is handled lightly. Harry wants to recreate his dead wife from her preserved cells, using an egg donated by Meli, and the film treats this as an expression of grief and devotion rather than as a menace. The portrait of the scientist is affectionate: Harry is brilliant, irreverent and humane, contrasted with an ambitious, petty rival who is more interested in his lab space than in research. The story ultimately rejects the cloning project, not on ethical grounds but because Harry realises that he must love the living instead of trying to recover the past, and he discards Lucy's cells. The film predates the cloning of Dolly the sheep by more than a decade. Even a successful reproductive clone would be a new individual who merely shares the donor's genome and must be born and grow up, so cloning could not truly bring a person back.

title: The Bad Seed
text: In this television remake, nine-year-old Rachel Penmark loses a penmanship medal to her classmate Mark Daigler, who is found dead near a pier after a school trip to the beach. Her widowed mother Christine notices that Rachel seems untouched by the death and later finds the medal hidden in a locket. A neighbour, Emory, is writing a book about female serial killers and mentions the case of Bessie Danker, which Christine's father Richard Bravo once investigated. Haunted by a recurring nightmare, Christine learns from Richard that it is a real memory: she is Danker's child, adopted after the killer's arrest. The janitor Leroy taunts Rachel about the boy's death, and she locks him in a shed and sets it on fire. Christine gives Rachel an overdose of sleeping pills and shoots herself, but Rachel survives and goes to live with Richard. As in the 1956 film, the genetic theme is inherited evil. Christine openly wonders whether a lack of morality can be hereditary, discovers that her biological mother was a serial killer, and fears that Rachel has inherited her psychopathy. The neighbours first explain Rachel's coldness as a normal defence mechanism, but the story proves them wrong and sides with nature: a child raised in a comfortable, caring home is born to kill. Unlike the 1956 version, the ending does not punish the child: Rachel survives her mother's attempt to kill her, implying that the bad seed lives on. No geneticist or test appears; the heredity is a matter of family history. Real behavioural genetics finds that antisocial traits are only partly heritable, depend on many genes and on the environment, and are not passed down as a fixed compulsion to kill.

title: The Two Doctors
themes: hybrids chimeras human experimentation genetic engineering
text: On Space Station Camera the Second Doctor and Jamie tell Dastari, the station's head of projects, that the Time Lords want his time experiments stopped. The gluttonous Androgums, allied with the Sontarans, drug the crew and capture the Second Doctor. The Sixth Doctor, Peri and Jamie follow the captors to a hacienda near Seville. There Dastari plans to dissect the Second Doctor's cell structure to isolate his "symbiotic nuclei", which would give the secret of time travel to Chessene, an Androgum technologically augmented to genius level; Chessene asks him instead to turn the Doctor into an Androgum who can operate a time module. Dastari gives the Second Doctor a "50 per cent Androgum inheritance" using the blood of the cook Shockeye, who breaks him out before the change becomes permanent. After Shockeye murders a restaurant owner, the Sixth Doctor kills him, Chessene shoots Dastari, and Chessene dies in the sabotaged module. The villain is Dastari, a biogeneticist who wants to extract the knowledge of time travel from the Second Doctor's genetic make-up. His plan first involves dissecting the Doctor's cells to isolate the "symbiotic nuclei" that let Time Lords travel in time; then, at Chessene's request, he implants the Doctor with a "50 per cent Androgum inheritance" from another person's blood, a forced transformation into a hybrid that would let the augmented Androgum use a time machine. The procedure is done without consent, both from the captive Doctor and from Shockeye, whose blood is used, and the Doctor gradually reverts once freed. Dastari, who serves the augmented Chessene, realises too late that she remains a predator and is killed by her. The serial treats biogenetics as a tool of power-seeking villains; writer Robert Holmes framed the whole story as an allegory of meat-eating. The idea that time travel is encoded in genes is pure fantasy.

title: Warning Sign
text: BioTek, which presents itself as a pesticide manufacturer, is a secret military laboratory. When a sealed tube breaks, a virulent bacterium developed as a biological weapon escapes, and security officer Joanie Morse seals the building with everyone inside. Her husband, Sheriff Cal Morse, enlists Dr. Dan Fairchild, an alcoholic former employee who developed an antidote, while a government containment team under Major Connelly quarantines the site and tells the public a cover story. Inside, the workers take the antidote, but it fails: the infected turn into homicidal maniacs, kill a rescue team and hunt the others, and the government decides to let everyone inside die. Cal and Fairchild go in to save Joanie, who is unaffected. A blood test shows that her pregnancy protects her, and Fairchild, before succumbing himself, designs a new antidote that works. Joanie releases it through the decontamination system, curing the survivors. The threat is a lab-made pathogen. A secret military programme hidden behind a pesticide company has developed a virulent bacterium as a biological weapon, one that drives its victims to homicidal madness, and its accidental release turns the laboratory into a death trap. The head of the laboratory team, Dr. Nielsen, puts secrecy before lives and kills himself when he fails, and the government containment team is ready to sacrifice the workers to cover up the accident. Against them, the former employee Dr. Dan Fairchild, an alcoholic but sympathetic scientist, designs a working antidote after the first one fails, using what protects the pregnant Joanie. The film warns about secret bioweapons research and official cover-ups. Its explanation, that pregnancy hormones and antibodies protect against the agent, is not grounded in real immunology, and bacteria do not cause madness in the way shown.

title: The Fly
text: Seth Brundle, a brilliant and eccentric scientist, shows science journalist Veronica "Ronnie" Quaife his invention: a pair of "telepods" that teleport objects from one to the other. Living tissue comes out mutilated until Seth reprograms the computer to understand flesh, and a baboon is transported successfully. Jealous and drunk, Seth teleports himself without noticing that a housefly has entered the pod with him. At first he feels stronger and more energetic, but he grows arrogant and violent, and his body begins to fall apart. Reviewing the computer's records, he discovers that it fused him with the fly at the molecular-genetic level. As he turns into the creature he calls "Brundlefly", Ronnie learns that she is pregnant by him and fears the child. Seth tries to fuse himself with Ronnie and their unborn child to recover his humanity, but the attempt merges him with the telepod instead, and Ronnie ends his suffering with a shotgun. Genetics enters the story through an accident rather than a design: the teleporter, unable to handle two organisms at once, splices the genes of a man and a fly, producing a gradual hybrid whose transformation is the film's body horror. Seth Brundle is an independent researcher, funded by a company but working alone, driven by curiosity, ambition and pride; he refuses to heed the warning signs and tries to repair his body with the same machine that ruined it. The film also raises fears about heredity, as Ronnie does not know whether her child was conceived before or after Seth's genes were altered and dreams of giving birth to a giant maggot. The science is fantasy: teleportation of matter does not exist, and combining two genomes would not gradually turn an adult animal into a mixture of both. The interest of the film lies in its portrait of a scientist's hubris and of the anxiety about losing one's humanity, which Cronenberg intended as a metaphor for disease and ageing and some critics read as a metaphor for AIDS.

title: American Ninja 2: The Confrontation
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement human experimentation
text: US Army Rangers Joe Armstrong and Curtis Jackson are sent to a remote Caribbean island to investigate the disappearance of several Marines. They find that the kidnappings are the work of a drug lord known as "The Lion", who has also abducted a local scientist and is using his research to create a private army of "super-ninjas" from the genetic material of the captured Marines, turning them into brainwashed killing machines. Joe and Curtis team up with Alicia Sanborn, the kidnapped scientist's daughter, and infiltrate the Lion's base on Blackbeard Island. While Joe fights the Lion's chief ninja, Curtis leads an assault with the local Marines. Genetics plays a small role in this martial-arts action film. The villain's plan is to breed an army of genetically engineered "super-ninjas" from the genetic material of kidnapped soldiers, using research forced out of an abducted scientist. The genetic engineering is never explained and serves only as a pretext for the fight scenes; the scientist is a victim coerced by a drug lord rather than a central character. The idea that soldiers' genes could be harvested to produce obedient super-fighters has no scientific basis. The film is a minor example of the "genetically engineered super-soldier" motif common in 1980s and 1990s action and science fiction.

title: Life Story
text: This BBC drama, made for the Horizon science series, follows the race to determine the structure of DNA in the early 1950s. In Cambridge, the young American James Watson and the British physicist Francis Crick try to guess the structure by building models, reasoning from what the molecule must do. At King's College London, Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin work with X-ray diffraction, but their partnership is soured by mutual mistrust, and Franklin insists on patient measurement before theorising. Both teams also fear being beaten by the American chemist Linus Pauling. The film portrays the rivalries, the institutional turf wars and the sexism that Franklin faces, and ends with Watson and Crick building the double-helix model. It was written by William Nicholson, based on Watson's memoir The Double Helix, and stars Jeff Goldblum, Tim Pigott-Smith, Juliet Stevenson and Alan Howard. Life Story is a historical drama about the founding discovery of molecular genetics, the 1953 double-helix model of DNA, and its scientists are real people. It contrasts two styles of research: Watson and Crick's intuitive leaps and model building, and Franklin's careful experimental work, against a background of competition, personal friction and the marginalisation of a woman scientist. It shows how Watson and Crick won partly by reasoning from DNA's genetic function to predict its chemical structure. The film follows the record closely; Crick wrote that it had a few inaccuracies, such as making Watson too manic, but called it a success overall. Historically, Franklin and Raymond Gosling's X-ray image known as Photo 51 was shown to Watson by Wilkins without their knowledge and was key evidence for the helix. In 1962 Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize; Franklin had died in 1958, and the prize is not awarded posthumously.

title: Light Years
text: The peaceful land of Gandahar is attacked by the Men of Metal, an army of automata that turn villagers to stone and carry them away. The Council of Women sends the young Sylvain to investigate. On his way he meets the Deformed, a community of mutant beings created by accident in genetic experiments by Gandahar's scientists and then abandoned. With Airelle, a woman he rescues, he finds the robots' base and is taken to Metamorphis, a giant brain living in the ocean, another failed creation of the same scientists. Metamorphis reveals that the Men of Metal come from the future through a portal and asks Sylvain to kill him a thousand years later. When Sylvain wakes from stasis, he learns that the aged Metamorphis has sent his robots back in time to absorb the Gandaharians' cells and prolong his life. With the Deformed's help, Sylvain kills him with a special syringe. Genetic engineering appears as the original sin of a seemingly idyllic society. Gandahar's scientists created both the Deformed, mutants born of failed experiments and pushed out of sight, and Metamorphis, a giant brain they abandoned in the sea when it grew too fast and became violent. The threat that falls on Gandahar is therefore the delayed consequence of its own research. The scientists themselves are seen only through these results: they act for the state, experiment without responsibility and discard what does not please them. The film is sympathetic to the outcasts, since the Deformed, despised as undesirable, end up saving the population. Metamorphis's need to absorb other people's cells because his own can no longer regenerate is pure fantasy, but René Laloux's animated film, based on a 1969 novel by Jean-Pierre Andrevon, uses it as a fable about scientific hubris and the treatment of those judged imperfect.

title: Superman IV: The Quest for Peace
text: Superman decides to rid the world of nuclear weapons after a boy writes to him, announces his plan at the United Nations and hurls the world's warheads into the Sun. Meanwhile Lex Luthor, freed from prison by his nephew Lenny, steals a strand of Superman's hair from a museum and uses it to make a 'genetic matrix'. Backed by arms dealers who want the arms race to continue, he attaches it to a nuclear missile; when Superman throws the missile into the Sun, the matrix gives rise to Nuclear Man, a solar-powered super-being loyal to Luthor. Nuclear Man wounds Superman with radioactive claws; Superman heals himself with a Kryptonian energy module, defeats him by cutting off his sunlight and feeds him into a nuclear reactor. A subplot follows the tabloid takeover of the Daily Planet. Superman returns the Luthors to custody. Genetics provides the villain. Lex Luthor uses Superman's hair to build a 'genetic matrix', a vaguely described piece of genetic engineering that, combined with a nuclear explosion and solar energy, produces Nuclear Man, a hostile double of the hero made from his genetic material. Luthor is a criminal, not a scientist, and he deploys the creation for revenge on Superman and for profit, in league with black-market arms dealers. Genetics plays no other role; the film's message is about nuclear disarmament, and the genetic creation of Nuclear Man is a comic-book device with no scientific plausibility (the idea that a person can be grown from a strand of hair inside a missile thrown into the Sun). It does echo the popular notion of cloning from a single hair or cell.

title: Terminus
text: In 2037, a televised sport sends truck drivers across a hostile country toward a destination called Terminus. The leading vehicle, a high-tech truck with an artificial intelligence called Monster, was designed by a boy genius, Mati, who follows the race by satellite. When the truck's AI fails, its driver, Gus, strays into uncharted territory, where she is captured and tortured by hooded gangs; before dying she gives the truck's access codes to a fellow prisoner, Stump, a former soldier. Stump takes the wheel and rescues a young slave girl, Princess, who turns out to be Mati's sister. The race is in fact a decoy that collects human blood for the cloning experiments of the masters of Terminus, and Mati himself is a clone, watched and evaluated by the sinister Doctor who created him on behalf of Sir, who plans to take over the world with artificial people. Cloning lies behind the film's deliberately vague plot. The rulers of Terminus run a deadly race that secretly harvests human blood for cloning experiments, and the boy genius Mati turns out to be an artificial creation, cloned by a mad scientist who works for Sir, a megalomaniac who wants to rule the world with artificial people. Both villains are played, campily, by Jürgen Prochnow. The genetic plot is a dystopian backdrop more than a subject: critics found the film's details wilfully obscure, and the sources do not explain how the cloning works or how the plan ends. The film never explains what the blood is used for; real cloning transfers a cell nucleus into an egg and produces a baby, not a ready-made person.

title: The Kindred
alt: Trans-Gen, los genes de la muerte
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human experimentation
text: Dr. Amanda Hollins, a renowned geneticist, is dying and makes her son John promise to destroy the laboratory notes of her last experiment; she also tells him that he has a brother, Anthony. John is sceptical. After the funeral, where he meets Melissa Leftridge, who claims to be Amanda's greatest admirer, and Dr. Phillip Lloyd, who understands what Amanda meant but keeps quiet, John goes with Melissa and some friends to his mother's house, which served as her laboratory. There they find that her experiments have produced monsters that are now out of control, among them Anthony, a tentacled creature, while Lloyd, a scientist who kidnaps people for his own experiments, wants Amanda's work for himself. Melissa turns into a gilled fish-like creature, and in the climax Lloyd raves about science before a giant tentacle drags him into the cellar. Genetic experimentation drives the whole story. Amanda Hollins, presented as a great geneticist, pursued what the film calls an advancement in human evolution in her home laboratory, creating monstrous beings including John's tentacled 'brother' Anthony; her dying wish to destroy her notes signals that she regrets the work. Dr. Phillip Lloyd is a classic mad scientist who wants her results and runs his own experiments on kidnapped people, feeding an accomplice to modified mutants. The genetics is not explained in any detail: it serves as the source of creature effects in a mid-1980s horror film in the vein of Re-Animator, and the human-animal hybrids it shows have no basis in real science.

title: Appleseed
themes: genetic engineering dna identification post apocalyptic
text: After a third world war, the survivors have built Olympus, a utopian city run by the supercomputer Gaia and inhabited by humans, cyborgs and bioroids, genetically engineered beings who make up most of the population and run the administration. Police officer Charon, embittered after his wife's suicide in what he sees as a golden cage, joins the terrorist cyborg A. J. Sebastian to bring the system down. They raid the facility where bioroids are made in order to steal data on Hitomi, a bioroid whose DNA is a genetic key able to shut Gaia down. The ESWAT officers Deunan Knute and Briareos try to stop them. Charon is killed and Gaia goes offline, but Deunan restarts it with a last shot and Sebastian dies. Genetic engineering underpins the world of the film. Olympus's managers have created bioroids, engineered humanoids who serve humankind and run the city's government, and some sources describe the whole society as bio-engineered for harmony. The plot turns on DNA as a key: Hitomi's genome carries an override code for the supercomputer that runs the city, which makes her the target of the terrorists. The film is ambivalent about this engineered utopia. The heroes defend it and the terrorists are defeated, yet the story gives weight to Charon's view that it is a stifling cage, and reviewers found the film unsure whether to see its genetically managed order as good or bad. The authorities who created the bioroids are not shown as villains. The bioroids, like the replicants of Blade Runner, are fictional; nothing like them exists.

title: Big Business
text: In 1948 a wealthy businessman's wife and a poor local woman both give birth to identical twin girls in a small West Virginia hospital, and an elderly nurse mixes up the babies, so that each family raises one of its own twins and one of the other couple's. Both pairs are named Rose and Sadie. Forty years later, the Shelton sisters run a New York conglomerate: Sadie is a ruthless executive, while Rose longs for a simpler life in the country. In rural Jupiter Hollow, Rose Ratliff is the forewoman of the furniture factory the Sheltons' company owns, and Sadie Ratliff dreams of big-city glamour. When Sadie Shelton plans to sell the factory to a buyer who will strip-mine the valley, the Ratliffs travel to New York to stop the sale. At the Plaza Hotel the two sets of twins are repeatedly mistaken for each other before they meet and block the deal together. The film is described as a 'nature versus nurture farce'. Its premise is the classic comparison of twins separated at birth: two pairs of identical twins are split, and one of each pair grows up rich in New York while the other grows up poor in the country. The comedy leans towards nature. The twins resemble each other in temperament and wishes, not only in looks: Sadie Ratliff, raised in the country, dreams of city glamour like her sister, and Rose Shelton, raised in luxury, longs for the rural life her sister leads. Upbringing shapes manners and accents, but not desires. No genetics is discussed or tested; the twins discover the mix-up by meeting face to face. Real studies of twins reared apart do find striking similarities in personality and interests, though far less complete than the comedy suggests.

title: First Born
text: A three-part BBC serial adapted from Maureen Duffy's novel Gor Saga. Edward Forester works at a government institute officially trying to cross orangutans and gorillas; secretly, he is attempting a human-gorilla hybrid, using his own sperm. A gorilla named Mary gives birth to a seemingly human boy, Gor. When the government orders all hybrid research stopped and the embryos destroyed, Forester falsifies the records and has Gor fostered, later adopting him after surgery in Switzerland allows the boy, whose vocal cords are fused like a gorilla's, to speak. As a young man, Gor falls in love with Forester's daughter Nell, unaware she is his half-sister. Digging into his past, he learns the truth about his origins and his father. He enters Mary's cage and is killed by her. Months later, Nell's newborn son makes the same sounds Gor made as a baby. The serial is built entirely around a genetic experiment: the creation of a human-gorilla hybrid by artificial insemination and its consequences. Forester is a classic overreaching scientist in the Frankenstein mould. He works for a state institute under military oversight, hides his true goal from his superiors, uses his own sperm, and falsifies records when ordered to destroy the child. Yet he also loves Gor and protects him, and the story weighs ambition, secrecy and paternal feeling. Gor looks entirely human and shows few gorilla traits beyond his strength and his fused vocal cords, which keeps the drama grounded until the ending, in which the hybrid is killed and his son reveals that the gorilla inheritance continues. Science fiction historian Brian Stableford dismissed it as a "knee-jerk hymn of hate against scientists". No human-ape hybrid has ever been verified; humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes and the other great apes 24, and Soviet attempts in the 1920s to cross humans with chimpanzees failed to produce a pregnancy.

title: Life Is a Long Quiet River
alt: La vie est un long fleuve tranquille La vida es un largo río tranquilo
text: On Christmas Eve, a nurse furious at her lover, the obstetrician Dr. Mavial, swaps two newborns in a hospital in northern France: a girl born to the Groseilles, a poor family living on benefits and petty crime, and a boy born to the Le Quesnoys, a wealthy Catholic family. Twelve years later, rejected by the doctor after his wife's death, the nurse reveals the swap to both families. The Le Quesnoys keep their daughter Bernadette without telling her, and take in their biological son Maurice, known as Momo, paying the Groseilles for him. Momo appears to fit in but secretly sells the family's silver to help the Groseilles and introduces his new brothers and sisters to his old family's way of life. Bernadette learns the truth and is horrified by her biological family. The Le Quesnoys' order falls apart, while the nurse ends up caring for the doctor, now paralysed by a stroke, and has him to herself at last. There is no genetic science in this satirical comedy, but the story is built on a classic nature versus nurture situation: two babies of different social classes swapped at birth. The film comes down on the side of upbringing. Momo, born to the wealthy Le Quesnoys but raised by the poor Groseilles, remains as resourceful and light-fingered as the family that raised him, while Bernadette, a Groseille by birth, has the tastes and prejudices of her bourgeois upbringing and is horrified by her biological family. The swap is used to mock class pretensions and bourgeois hypocrisy rather than to say anything about heredity, and blood ties count for less than the habits each child has learned.

title: Primal Rage
text: In Miami, Frank Duffy, a reporter for a local newspaper, sneaks into a research laboratory that carries out experiments on animals. There he is bitten by a rabid monkey and falls prey to an uncontrollable fury. He spreads the infection to the nearby college, where a carefree Halloween party turns into a bloodbath. The available sources give only this brief outline and do not describe how the outbreak ends or who survives. The film's horror starts in a research laboratory that experiments on animals: a monkey there carries an infection that drives people into a murderous rage, and a reporter who sneaks in is bitten and spreads it to a college campus. The available plot summaries describe the monkey only as 'rabid' and do not say what the laboratory was doing or whether the agent was created or modified there; the film counts as genetics only because the contagion comes out of a research laboratory. The scientists are not characterised in the sources. Reviewers saw the film mainly as a showcase for gore effects by Carlo Rambaldi and his son, the director, and as a borrowing from George A. Romero's The Crazies. According to the writer Umberto Lenzi, an earlier script he worked on concerned a scientist genetically mutated into a tiger, but it is unclear whether anything of it survived.

title: Ten Zan: The Ultimate Mission
text: In the Far East, a group of scientists abducts young girls from local villages and holds them in a heavily guarded facility known as the Center, where they are used in experiments with a substance that penetrates human cells and changes their chromosomes and genes. The scientists are led by Professor Larson, a Lithuanian biologist from the University of Vilna who dreams of breeding a master race to rule the world. Scientific organizations in Asia and Europe learn of the illegal experiments, and the mercenary Lou Mamet is hired through FSR, an organization that takes on jobs too delicate for governments, to end the trafficking of women. Confusingly, it is Larson himself who commissions the mission, and he is later revealed to be the head of the operation the heroes are sent to destroy, a plot hole the director blamed on script changes made without his knowledge. Genetics drives the villain's scheme. Professor Larson and his scientists use a substance that penetrates human cells and alters chromosomes and genes, testing it on abducted village girls, with the aim of breeding a master race to rule the world. This combines genetic engineering with a eugenic breeding project and with human experimentation on unwilling subjects. Larson is a stock villain, opposed by legitimate scientific organizations who send commandos to stop him. The available sources say little about what the treatment actually does to the girls or how the story ends. The idea of a single substance that rewrites a person's genes is fantasy; it serves the familiar action-film figure of the eugenicist scientist bent on world domination. The film is better known for being shot in North Korea, which it portrays as a futuristic utopia.

title: The Blob
text: A "meteorite" falls near the Californian ski town of Arborville, releasing a gelatinous organism that dissolves an old vagrant and, at the hospital, Paul, the football star who brought him in with the cheerleader Meg Penny and the local rebel Brian Flagg. The police do not believe Meg and Brian as the growing Blob kills a diner's staff and the sheriff. At the crash site they find a military operation led by Dr. Meddows, a government scientist who quarantines the town. Brian escapes and overhears that the Blob is a Cold War biological weapon, sent into orbit as too dangerous, that grew in space and brought its satellite down; Meddows means to recapture it, using townspeople as bait. Brian exposes him in front of the town before the Blob devours him, and the creature overruns the town until Meg and Brian freeze it with liquid nitrogen. A fragment survives in the jar of a deranged preacher. This remake turns the 1958 alien into a man-made threat. The Blob is a biological warfare experiment from the Cold War, created by a secret government programme and launched into space because it was too dangerous to keep; there, according to Wikipedia, it fed on bacteria mutated by radiation and grew into a predatory mass. The sources do not describe how it was made, only that it is a government bioweapon. Its keeper, Dr. Meddows, poses as a scientist preparing for first contact but is ready to sacrifice the town to recover the weapon, and is consumed by it. As Wikipedia notes, the film is a post-Watergate conspiracy story in which rebellious teenagers oppose sinister government agents, and it ends ominously with a surviving fragment. The organism has no real biological counterpart.

title: The Child
alt: Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 2, episode 1
text: As the Enterprise takes on its new chief medical officer, Dr. Katherine Pulaski, it prepares to carry samples of a deadly plasma plague to a research station working on a cure. An energy being enters the ship and impregnates Counselor Deanna Troi as she sleeps. The fetus, a male Human-Betazoid hybrid with no genetic material but Troi's, develops in 36 hours. Worf argues that it is a security threat and should be aborted, Data that it is an opportunity to study a new life form, and Troi decides to keep it. She gives birth to a boy, Ian Andrew, who grows to the size of an eight-year-old in a day. Meanwhile one of the plague strains in the containment module starts to grow, and Pulaski traces it to Eichner radiation. Ian realizes that he is the source, and dies in Troi's arms, returning to energy form; he had wanted to learn what it was like to be human. Wesley Crusher stays aboard. Two genetic elements frame the episode's mystery. The first is Ian himself: Dr. Pulaski finds that the fetus is a Human-Betazoid hybrid that contains no genetic material other than Troi's, a puzzle the episode does not explain, since the father is an energy being who wanted to experience human life. The second is the cargo: samples of a deadly plague carried to a research station for work on a cure, a significant number of which, Pulaski notes, are genetically engineered, an excessive amount of engineering that she warns Picard about. The episode's tension comes from the combination: radiation emitted by the alien child makes one strain grow in its containment, and Ian chooses to leave and die to protect the crew. Starfleet's handling of the pathogens is presented as routine, careful and aimed at a cure. Critics disliked the episode, especially its treatment of Troi's non-consensual pregnancy. A child with genes from one parent alone would be a clone-like parthenogenote, not a hybrid.

title: Twins
themes: eugenics genetic engineering nature nurture human experimentation donor conception
text: A secret genetic experiment tries to create the perfect child by combining the DNA of several distinguished individuals, but the embryo splits into twins. The mother, Mary Ann Benedict, is told that her baby died. Julius is raised by one of the scientists on a remote island and grows into a strong, highly educated but naïve man, while Vincent is left in a Los Angeles orphanage and becomes a short, cynical small-time crook. On his 35th birthday Julius learns of his brother and finds him in Los Angeles. Vincent, deep in debt, steals a car carrying a prototype fuel injector worth five million dollars, and the brothers set off to deliver it while searching for their mother, pursued by a hitman. In the end the twins defeat the hitman, reunite with their mother and marry two sisters, each later having twins of his own. Genetics provides the comedy's premise. Scientists in a secret programme try to engineer an ideal human by mixing the DNA of several exceptional donors; when the embryo splits, the joke is that one twin received all the desirable traits and the other the "leftovers", so that Arnold Schwarzenegger and Danny DeVito can play identical twins. The scientists are cold experimenters who deceive the mother about her children and abandon one of them, and one of them still calls Vincent a genetic failure decades later; the film sides with the brothers and suggests that loyalty and family matter more than pedigree. It also adds an element of nurture, as the twins grow up in opposite circumstances. Biologically the premise is impossible: identical (monozygotic) twins form when a single zygote splits into two embryos, so they carry essentially the same genome, and a split cannot sort good and bad genes between them.

title: Watchers
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras animal experimentation human enhancement
text: An explosion at a secret research laboratory lets two experimental animals escape: a highly intelligent golden retriever and the OXCOM, a monstrous killing machine that hunts the dog. Teenager Travis Cornell finds the dog, keeps it and discovers a 'GH3' tattoo in its ear marking it as a research animal. The OXCOM kills everyone in its path, including Travis's friends and police officers, while Lem Johnson, an agent of the National Security Organization, tracks the dog and silences witnesses, even murdering the sheriff. Travis and his mother Nora go on the run with the dog. At a cabin in the woods Johnson, holding Nora and Travis's girlfriend Tracey hostage, reveals that he is himself the laboratory's third experiment, a genetically engineered assassin without a conscience; Nora shoots him. Travis then kills the wounded, sobbing OXCOM, and the survivors leave with the dog. Genetic engineering creates the film's whole cast of non-human or not-quite-human characters. A classified laboratory has produced a golden retriever with near-human intelligence, an 'Outside Experimental Combat Mammal' bred as a killing machine and drawn to the dog, and, as the climax reveals, the government agent Lem Johnson, an engineered assassin with no conscience. The scientists themselves are barely seen; the research is represented by the cover-up, in which agents kidnap witnesses and murder a sheriff to keep it secret. The story contrasts the lovable dog, the heart of a boy-and-his-dog tale, with the monster and the assassin, and presents the laboratory's work as reckless and amoral, though the dying OXCOM is given a moment of pity. Based on Dean Koontz's novel, the film was widely panned, and reviewers found its creature and the dog's feats of intelligence preposterous; real animals cannot be engineered to reason or type.

title: American Ninja 3: Blood Hunt
themes: engineered pathogens human experimentation cloning bioweapon
text: Sean Davidson, whose father was murdered by gangsters in 1979 and who was raised and trained in ninjutsu in Japan, travels to a karate tournament on the Caribbean island of Triana with his friends Curtis Jackson and Dexter. The tournament's host, General Andreas, is his father's killer. Andreas is working with Dr. Saxon, a terrorist known as "The Cobra", who has developed a deadly virus as a biological weapon and wants to test it on the best fighter. Saxon's agent, the female ninja Chan Lee, lures Sean into a trap; he is captured at Saxon's laboratories, which claim to make medicines, and injected with the virus. His friends rescue him, Sean kills Andreas, and in a final assault on the lab Chan Lee, who has switched sides, is killed. Sean overcomes the virus and kills Saxon, and the army storms the laboratory. The genetic element is a biological weapon: Dr. Saxon develops a deadly virus in his laboratories, uses Sean as a human test subject and plans to sell or deploy it. The English plot summary also says Saxon commands an army of genetically engineered ninja clones led by Chan Lee, although the German summary describes ordinary ninjas and does not mention cloning, so how much the film makes of engineering and cloning is uncertain. Saxon is a stock terrorist scientist, a pure villain who orders the execution of his own agent and is killed by the hero. The science is perfunctory: Sean finally recovers from the virus through "mental strength" rather than the antidote, and the laboratory is mainly a setting for martial-arts fights.

title: Godzilla vs. Biollante
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras engineered pathogens gmo bioweapon
text: After Godzilla's attack on Tokyo, samples of its cells are smuggled to a research institute in the fictional Middle Eastern country of Saradia, to be merged with genetically modified plants that could turn the desert into farmland. A terrorist bombing destroys the laboratory and kills Erika, the daughter of the geneticist Genshiro Shiragami. Five years later, in Japan, Shiragami has merged Erika's cells with those of a rose to preserve her soul, while the scientist Kazuhito Kirishima and the army are using Godzilla cells to develop an "anti-nuclear energy bacteria" as a weapon against the monster. Saradian agents and the American company Bio-Major fight over the cells. Shiragami secretly adds Godzilla cells to one of his roses, which grows into the giant plant monster Biollante. When Godzilla is freed, it fights Biollante twice; the bacteria and an artificial lightning storm weaken Godzilla, and Biollante dissolves into spores that rise to the sky in the image of Erika. Genetic engineering is at the heart of the film. Godzilla's cells are treated as a valuable biological resource, and governments, a company and spies compete for them, foreshadowing later stories about corporate control of genetic material. Biollante is a hybrid of plant, human and Godzilla cells, created by a grieving geneticist who wants to keep his dead daughter's soul alive; his motive is personal rather than commercial, but his experiment produces a monster that he cannot control. Other scientists work for the army on a bacterial weapon derived from Godzilla's cells. The story came from a public contest won by a dentist whose entry focused on the dilemmas of biotechnology, and director Kazuki Ōmori drew on his own background in biology to make the genetic engineering plot more plausible. Scholars of kaiju cinema have noted that the film criticised genetic engineering and biotechnology several years before Jurassic Park brought the subject to mainstream Hollywood. Merging whole cells of different species to transfer a person's identity is, of course, fantasy.

title: Polymorph
text: A shape-changing creature escapes from a waste pod drifting in space and boards the mining ship Red Dwarf. Rimmer dismisses Holly's alert, and the creature attacks Lister at dinner. Kryten and Holly explain that it is a Polymorph, a man-made genetic mutant that feeds on its victims' negative emotions; it has drained Lister's fear, leaving him reckless. While trying to escape, the others are tricked one by one: the Cat loses his vanity, Kryten his guilt and Rimmer his anger, each becoming a changed and weakened person. The crew finally corner the Polymorph in the cargo decks and kill it by luck, thanks to a heat-seeking bazookoid shot, and recover their emotions. Unknown to them, a second Polymorph has come aboard and follows them disguised as Lister; in the 1998 remastered version a caption says it hid in Lister's underpants drawer and died of old age. Genetics is a one-line explanation for the monster: Kryten and Holly identify the Polymorph as a man-made genetic mutant, designed to leech off negative emotions and able to take any shape. Nobody explains who made it or why, and no scientist appears; the creature simply arrives from a space waste pod. The story uses the premise to play with the crew's personalities, showing what Lister, the Cat, Kryten and Rimmer become without their fear, vanity, guilt and anger, and suggesting that these emotions are part of who they are. The engineered creature is a pure threat that attacks the crew until it is destroyed, and the original broadcast ends with a second one at large. Shape-shifting, emotion-eating organisms are comic science fiction with no basis in real genetics; the episode is often ranked among the series' best.

title: The Fly II
themes: heredity hybrids chimeras genetic engineering human experimentation animal experimentation
text: Months after scientist Seth Brundle became a human-fly hybrid, Veronica Quaife dies giving birth to a larval sac from which a seemingly normal boy emerges. Anton Bartok, owner of the company that financed Brundle's teleportation experiments, adopts the child, Martin, and raises him in a laboratory. Martin ages very fast, has a genius intellect and needs no sleep. At five, with the body of a 25-year-old, he is asked to repair his father's Telepods, which have failed to teleport living creatures. He succeeds, falls in love with an employee, Beth Logan, and begins to show signs of becoming a hybrid himself. He discovers that Bartok knew his fate and plans to exploit his body and the Telepods' power of genetic manipulation for profit. Fully transformed, Martin forces Bartok into a Telepod and uses it to swap his insect genes for Bartok's healthy human genes, regaining human form while Bartok becomes a deformed creature. The film turns the first film's teleportation accident into a story about inheritance. Martin carries the fly genes his father acquired in the Telepod, and his accelerated growth and eventual metamorphosis are presented as a hereditary condition waiting to "awaken". The cure he devises is a crude form of gene therapy: the Telepods exchange his mutated genes for healthy human ones taken from another person, who then suffers the disfigurement. The scientist figure is a corporate one: Bartok raises Martin as an experimental subject, spies on him and wants to use his body and the machines' capacity for genetic manipulation for profit. Laboratory animal experimentation, shown through a deformed dog kept alive for study, is another theme. Scientifically, acquired changes in an adult's body are not passed to children in this way, and genes cannot be swapped between whole organisms like parts, but the film uses these ideas as body horror.

title: The Vengeance Factor
alt: Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 3, episode 9
themes: engineered pathogens genetic engineering human enhancement bioweapon
text: In this Star Trek: The Next Generation episode, the Enterprise traces raids on Federation outposts to the Gatherers, Acamarian nomads who split from their society a century earlier. Captain Picard persuades Sovereign Marouk, the Acamarian leader, to negotiate a reunification, and she brings her assistant Yuta aboard. During the talks Yuta touches an old Gatherer, Volnoth, who dies of an apparent heart attack. Dr. Crusher finds that he was killed by a fast-acting micro-virus engineered to attack one DNA profile. Data finds that another member of the same clan, the Lornak, died the same way 53 years earlier, with Yuta present and unaged. Riker realises that Yuta is the last survivor of the Tralesta clan, wiped out by the Lornaks, and that her next target is the Gatherer leader Chorgan. When she refuses to stop, Riker kills her with his phaser, and the two Acamarian groups agree a truce. The weapon in this murder mystery is a genetically targeted virus. Dr. Crusher determines that the micro-virus that killed Volnoth was purposely engineered to attack a specific Acamarian DNA profile, that of the Lornak clan, and to be harmless to everyone else; Yuta reveals that she was genetically altered to carry it, transmitting it by touch, and to stop her own ageing so that she could hunt the clan for decades. The alterations also make her resistant to low phaser settings. Who engineered her is never shown; the genetics serves her clan's vendetta, and the episode presents her as a tragic avenger whose revenge has to be stopped for peace to be possible. Crusher's genetic analysis is what exposes the murders. A weapon that kills only people of one lineage echoes real concerns about ethnically targeted bioweapons, although no real pathogen can discriminate between clans of one population this way.

title: Unnatural Selection
alt: Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 2, episode 7
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement evolution gene therapy
text: The Enterprise finds the supply ship USS Lantree adrift, its entire crew dead of old age although many were young. The ship's last stop was the Darwin Genetic Research Station on Gagarin IV, whose scientists are now ageing rapidly too and beg Captain Picard to evacuate the station's genetically engineered children, who have been kept in isolation. Dr. Pulaski examines one of the children, a telepathic teenager, aboard a shuttle piloted by Data, and catches the disease. She discovers that the children were engineered with aggressive immune systems that fight pathogens by genetically altering them, even outside their bodies; reacting to a harmless flu carried by a Lantree officer, they produced airborne antibodies that rewrite the DNA of ordinary humans and make them age. Using a strand of Pulaski's hair as a genetic template, the crew restores her through the transporter, then treats the station's staff. The children must remain isolated. Genetic engineering is the core of the episode. Scientists at a Federation research station have designed children with enhanced abilities, including telepathy and a super-immune system, and Dr. Pulaski first greets them as "the next step in human evolution". The improvement backfires: the children's immune defence, which alters pathogens genetically, becomes a weapon that rewrites the DNA of everyone around them and kills by accelerated ageing. The researchers are well-meaning but have failed to foresee the consequences of their designs, and the children end up condemned to permanent isolation, unintended victims of the experiment. The episode is a cautionary tale about human enhancement. Scientifically, antibodies are proteins that bind targets but do not alter DNA, and restoring someone's genome from a hair sample through a "transporter" is pure fiction; the link between DNA damage and ageing, however, is a real field of research.

title: Up the Long Ladder
alt: Que entren los clones Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 2, episode 18
