text: The Enterprise answers a distress call from Bringloid V, a colony threatened by solar flares and founded centuries earlier by the crew of the SS Mariposa. Its inhabitants, led by Danilo Odell and his daughter Brenna, live a pre-industrial Irish rural life and are evacuated aboard the ship. Odell mentions a second Mariposa colony, and Riker, Worf and Dr. Pulaski visit it. Pulaski discovers that all its people are clones: only five scientists survived the original landing, too few for a viable population, so they reproduced by cloning alone. After almost three centuries, accumulated copying errors are about to make further clones nonviable. Prime Minister Granger asks for the crew's DNA, and when Riker refuses, the Mariposans abduct him and Pulaski and grow copies of them, which Riker destroys. Pulaski proposes instead that the two colonies merge to create a viable gene pool. Cloning and population genetics are central. A colony founded by only five people chooses cloning over sexual reproduction, and after generations of copies faces "replicative fading", an accumulation of small errors in the genetic code that will soon make new clones nonviable. The solution is not more technology but genetic diversity: Dr. Pulaski persuades the Mariposans to mix with the Bringloidi so that a varied gene pool can sustain the colony. The Mariposan scientists are polite but willing to take DNA without consent, and the episode frames bodily integrity and individual uniqueness as reasons to refuse being copied. The idea loosely echoes a real concern: very small founding populations suffer from inbreeding and loss of genetic diversity, although "replicative fading" itself is a fictional device. The episode drew criticism because Riker's destruction of his clones was read as a stance on abortion.

title: Gremlins 2: The New Batch
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras animal experimentation
text: After the death of his owner, Mr. Wing, the mogwai Gizmo is captured by scientists from Splice O' Life, a genetic engineering laboratory in the Clamp Centre, a Manhattan skyscraper owned by the eccentric billionaire Daniel Clamp. Billy Peltzer and Kate Beringer, who now work in the building, rescue him, but Gizmo gets wet and spawns new mogwai, which eat after midnight and turn into gremlins. The gremlins overrun the tower, and in the laboratory they drink Dr. Catheter's experimental serums: one becomes a talking, intelligent Brain Gremlin, others turn into a spider-like creature, a bat, a vegetable gremlin, a female gremlin and an electric gremlin, which kills Catheter. As the gremlins prepare to break out into the city, Billy traps the electric gremlin and uses it, together with the building's sprinklers and fire hoses, to destroy the rest, while Gizmo kills the spider gremlin with a flaming arrow. Genetic engineering is the film's main satirical target. Splice O' Life is a corporate laboratory inside Clamp's tower, a building that parodies late-1980s commercial excess (Clamp was modelled on Donald Trump and Ted Turner), and its head, Dr. Catheter, is played by Christopher Lee as an openly sinister scientist, at director Joe Dante's request. His shelves of gene-altering serums give the second half of the film its set pieces: each gremlin that drinks one instantly takes on new traits, such as a bat's wings, a spider's body, plant tissue, pure electricity or human-level intelligence, producing comic hybrids of gremlin with animal, vegetable or even a female identity. The science is deliberately cartoonish: real genetic modification acts on cells or embryos and takes effect over generations or long treatments, not as a drink that transforms an adult animal in seconds. The film uses the idea to mock both corporate biotechnology and the monster-movie trope of the mad scientist.

title: Robot Jox
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement post apocalyptic
text: Fifty years after a nuclear war, the two remaining superpowers, the Market and the Confederation, settle territorial disputes through duels between giant robots piloted by 'jox'. The Market's champion Achilles faces the Confederation's undefeated Alexander for control of Alaska, but the fight goes wrong and Achilles' robot falls on the spectators, killing hundreds. Branded a coward, he retires. The Market replaces him with Athena, a genetically engineered 'gen jox' and the first female pilot. Drawn to her and worried for her, Achilles agrees to fight again, angering her. Meanwhile the strategist Tex Conway, the real Confederation spy, murders the robot designer Matsumoto, and later kills himself when a recording exposes him. On the day of the match Athena drugs Achilles and pilots the robot herself, but is defeated; Achilles takes over, wins, and persuades Alexander that the duel need not end in death. Genetic engineering appears in the 'gen jox' programme, which the Market runs to produce a new generation of pilots; German Wikipedia attributes it to a Professor Laplace. Athena, one of these engineered 'tubies', is the film's second lead and the pilot meant to replace Achilles, and her determination to prove herself drives the final match. The film says little about how the gen jox are made and passes no explicit judgement on the programme, which stays in the background as part of the military-technological world; the story is about the robot duels, espionage and the futility of the conflict, and academic critics read it as wary of the attractions of technology. Breeding pilots in vitro with engineered traits is speculative science fiction.

title: Suddenly Human
alt: Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 4, episode 4
text: The Enterprise answers a distress call from a damaged Talarian ship and rescues four Talarian youths and a human teenager, Jono. Dr. Crusher finds old fractures that suggest abuse, and records show that Jono is Jeremiah Rossa, grandson of a Starfleet admiral, whose parents were killed in a Talarian attack on a Federation colony. He was raised by the Talarian captain Endar, who adopted him to replace a son lost in battle, and he responds only to male authority. Picard reluctantly takes Jono into his quarters to help him rediscover his human side, while Endar arrives and threatens war unless his son is returned. Torn between the two, Jono stabs the sleeping Picard, expecting to be executed. Picard realises that the boy's home is with Endar and lets him go back. No genetic science appears; the episode is a nature versus nurture story about adoption across species. Producer Michael Piller described it as the story of 'someone who was Human who had been raised in a totally alien environment. Is he Human any longer?'. Jono is human by birth, and memories of his parents' death surface when Picard shows him their pictures, but his values, loyalties and habits are Talarian. The episode favours nurture: Picard's attempt to restore Jono's human identity fails, and the boy returns to the father who raised him. Some critics found the crew ethnocentric for assuming that Jono should want to be human, and some viewers objected to sending a possibly abused child back. The premise fits what is known about human development: culture, language and attachments are learned, not inherited.

title: The Rift
text: Submarine designer Wick Hayes is blamed for the loss of the experimental submarine Siren I in the Dannekin Rift, a deep trench off Norway, and insists that modifications made by the Contek corporation are to blame. Contek sends him down in the Siren II under the tough Captain Phillips with a NATO crew to find the missing sub's black box. Trapped in a field of toxic weed at a depth where plant life should be impossible, Hayes frees the ship by electrifying the hull, but some of the weed gets inside. Following the black box signal into an underwater cave, the crew discovers that Contek has been running illegal genetic engineering experiments there, which have produced a range of mutant creatures that attack them. The climax brings a fight with a company double agent and the destruction of the submarine. Genetics appears as the hidden secret at the bottom of the rift: the Contek corporation has been conducting illegal genetic engineering experiments in an undersea cave, producing mutant creatures that turn on the crew. The sources give no details of the methods or aims; the Moria review notes that it is never clear what the sinister corporation is up to, and the toxic weed is not explicitly linked to the experiments. The film is a low-budget underwater monster movie in the wake of Aliens, and genetic engineering serves mainly to explain its monsters and to cast a corporation as the villain. The scientific content is minimal and implausible.

title: Watchers II
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras animal experimentation
text: At Anodyne Laboratories, a secret genetics facility in the California desert, animal psychologist Barbara White works with Einstein, a golden retriever whose intelligence has been raised by experiments. Facing closure, the lab's director secretly lets animal-rights activists in to free the animals, and they also release the Outsider, a hybrid monster bred as a military assassin and psychically linked to the dog. Einstein escapes and causes the crash of a jeep carrying Marine captain Paul Ferguson to prison. Paul flees with the dog, discovers its intelligence and, with Barbara's help, tries to evade both the authorities and the Outsider, which leaves a trail of bodies as it tracks Einstein. This loose remake of Watchers, based on Dean Koontz's novel, was released straight to video. Genetic manipulation drives the whole plot. In a secret laboratory, scientists have produced a super-intelligent dog and, for military purposes, the Outsider, a hybrid creature designed as an assassin and linked to the dog so that it hunts it down. The animal experiments are presented sympathetically through Barbara and the dog, but the military programme and the lab director's recklessness unleash a killing machine, and the film treats this kind of research as dangerous. The genetic background is sketchy: the sources describe the lab only in general terms, and the psychic link between dog and monster is pure fantasy. Raising an animal's intelligence to human-like levels through genetic engineering is far beyond current science.

title: Camille
text: Lister tries to teach the mechanoid Kryten how to lie, but Kryten cannot do it in front of others. Sent to pilot Starbug, Kryten answers a distress call and rescues the only survivor of a doomed ship, Camille. Each crew member sees her differently: to Kryten she is a mechanoid, to Rimmer a hologram, to Lister a woman who shares his interests, and to the Cat a copy of himself. Lister notices that Camille gives different answers to each of them and reveals that she is a pleasure GELF, whose true form is a green blob with tentacles. Hurt but undeterred, Kryten compliments her real appearance and dates her, and they watch Casablanca together. When Camille's husband arrives to take her back, Kryten, in a parody of the film's ending, tells her to leave with him, lying to spare her feelings and proving he has learned his lesson. The genetic element is Camille herself, a pleasure GELF (genetically engineered life form), a type of being created in the Red Dwarf universe by genetic engineering. She was designed to appear to each person as the object of their desire, which drives the comedy and the episode's reflection on appearance and love: Kryten chooses to accept her true form, a green blob. Her makers never appear and nothing is said about who engineered her or why; the engineering is simply part of the setting, and it is treated with light humour rather than as a warning. A creature that projects a different appearance to each observer is pure fantasy and has no basis in real genetics.

title: Chimera
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering human experimentation animal experimentation
text: Nurse Tracy Pickford leaves London for a job at the Jenner Clinic, a private fertility clinic in rural Cumbria, where a locked outbuilding and secret meetings make her suspicious. One night an unseen creature kills the clinic's staff, including its founder Dr. Jenner, and Tracy too. Her boyfriend, the journalist Peter Carson, arrives to find the police sidelined by a government official, Hennessey, who hands the manhunt to the army. With Alison Wells, a researcher who survived, Peter learns from Jenner's former colleague Dr. Liawski that Jenner, funded by Hennessey, created a human-chimpanzee hybrid as the first of a new species for slave labour, military use and medical experiments. The hybrid, Chad, had been kept caged for years and killed the staff when Jenner ordered him dissected. Hiding on a farm, Chad befriends two children. Peter and Alison try to expose him to the public, but he is shot dead. In the final scene, a facility holds dozens of infant hybrids. Genetic engineering is the core of this ITV miniseries, adapted by Stephen Gallagher from his 1982 novel. A fertility clinic serves as cover for a secret, state-funded project to create human-chimpanzee hybrids, using patients as surrogate mothers, with the aim of producing a slave species for labour, war and medical research. Dr. Jenner is a scientist serving government interests with no regard for his creation, whom he keeps caged, mutilates and finally orders to be dissected; his colleague Liawski is ashamed but silenced, and another colleague is fascinated and carries on the work. Chad, the hybrid, is the tragic figure of the story, and the drama focuses on the cruelty and the official cover-up rather than the science. Human-chimpanzee hybrids have never been produced, and such experiments are banned on ethical grounds. In the United States the series was re-edited and released as Monkey Boy.

title: DNA
text: The crew of Red Dwarf board a drifting spacecraft. Rimmer and Kryten find the remains of a mutated human with three heads, while Cat accidentally activates a machine that turns Lister into a chicken. Kryten works out that the ship's crew were researching DNA modification and that the machine can rewrite the DNA of anything organic. Lister is turned into a hamster before Cat repeats his steps and restores him, but Kryten, whose brain is partly organic, is transformed into a human. Back on Red Dwarf, Kryten is delighted at first, but finds he cannot do what he did as a mechanoid and soon wants to change back. As a test, Lister has the machine modify the meat in his vindaloo, which becomes an indestructible curry monster. Lister turns himself into a one-foot-tall cyborg "Man Plus" and kills the creature by exploiting its weakness for lager. The episode is built around a DNA-rewriting machine, and its official full title is "Do Not Alter". The machine can reshape any organic being by rewriting its DNA, turning Lister into a chicken, a hamster and a tiny super-human, a robot with an organic brain into a man, and a curry into a monster. The premise draws on the popular idea of DNA as a code that defines what an organism is, and the story plays it entirely for comedy, raising light questions about identity and what it means to be human through Kryten's brief life as a person. The scientists who built the machine never appear; the three-headed corpse aboard their ship hints that their experiments went wrong. Real genetic modification works on cells and embryos and cannot transform a living adult into another species, still less convert machinery or cooked meat, so the episode is a farce on genetic engineering rather than a portrayal of it.

title: Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah
text: In 1992 a UFO lands near Mount Fuji carrying 'Futurians' from the year 2204, who say that Godzilla will destroy Japan in their time. They propose travelling back to 1944 to remove from Lagos Island the dinosaur that nuclear tests later turned into Godzilla. Writer Kenichiro Terasawa, psychic Miki Saegusa and Professor Mazaki join them. In 1944 the dinosaur is teleported to the Bering Strait, but the Futurians secretly leave behind three small creatures, the Dorats, which radiation fuses into the three-headed King Ghidorah. Back in 1992 they use Ghidorah to attack Japan, whose future economic dominance they want to prevent. Futurian Emmy Kano turns against them. Godzilla, recreated by radiation from a sunken submarine, defeats Ghidorah and destroys the Futurians' ship, and Emmy returns from the future with the cyborg Mecha-King Ghidorah to stop Godzilla. Genetic engineering creates the film's second monster. The Futurians plant three genetically engineered creatures, the Dorats, on Lagos Island in 1944; the 1954 hydrogen-bomb test turns them into King Ghidorah, a monster the visitors control and use to bring Japan to its knees. Godzilla's own origin is radiation-induced mutation of a surviving dinosaur rather than deliberate engineering. The engineers are villains with a political aim: they want to destroy present-day Japan to stop it from becoming a 23rd-century superpower, and they die when their ship is destroyed; only Emmy, who betrays them, is sympathetic. Genetics here is a tool of conquest that produces an uncontrollable weapon, as in much of the kaiju genre, and the radiation-fusion of engineered animals into a giant three-headed dragon is pure fantasy.

title: Identity Crisis
alt: Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 4, episode 18
text: Lieutenant Commander Susanna Leijten visits the Enterprise because members of an away team she and Geordi La Forge served on five years earlier, on the planet Tarchannen III, have been deserting and stealing shuttles to return there. One shuttle burns up in the atmosphere. On the planet the new away team finds an empty shuttle and strange footprints; Leijten falls ill and begins to transform, her veins turning blue and her fingers fusing into claws. Reconstructing the old mission on the holodeck, La Forge discovers the shadow of an invisible humanoid creature, and then changes into one himself and slips down to the surface. Dr. Crusher finds that a parasite in Leijten's body is rewriting her DNA and removes it. Using ultraviolet light, Leijten finds La Forge among the creatures and talks him back aboard to be cured; the others are too far changed and are left on the protected planet. The episode's horror rests on a genetic idea: an alien parasite from Tarchannen III reproduces by overwriting its host's DNA, turning humanoids, gradually and irreversibly, into members of its own invisible species. Dr. Crusher orders a full genetic analysis, finds the organism (in the thymus, according to Memory Alpha) and removes it surgically, which reverses the change in Leijten and La Forge in time; the earlier victims cannot be saved. The only scientist is the ship's doctor, shown as competent and caring, and no one engineers anything: the threat is a natural alien life cycle, and Picard has the planet quarantined to protect both visitors and creatures. Rewriting an adult's whole genome into another species is fiction, though it loosely echoes real viruses and parasites that insert their genetic material into host cells.

title: Switched at Birth
text: This two-part television miniseries dramatises a real case from Florida. In late 1978 Regina and Ernest Twigg take home a baby girl, Arlena, who soon turns out to have a serious heart condition. Blood tests show that Arlena cannot be their biological daughter. After she dies at the age of nine, the Twiggs search for their own child and find her being raised as Kimberly Mays by Bob Mays, a man who believes he is her father: the two babies had been switched in the hospital where both were born. Mays at first lets the Twiggs visit Kimberly but later cuts off contact, and the story follows the bitter dispute between the girl's biological parents and the man who raised her. The miniseries was broadcast in 1991, while the real legal battle was still going on. The genetics is parentage testing. In the real case, Arlena's blood group B could not come from two group-O parents, and immunogenetic tests at Johns Hopkins confirmed that she was not the Twiggs' child; later tests on Kimberly, which Bob Mays first refused, showed that she was. These tests are the plot's turning points, but the drama is about what they cannot settle: whether a child belongs to the parents who share her genes or to the father who raised her. The miniseries gives real weight to both claims. It aired before the case was resolved: in 1993 a Florida court allowed the real Kimberly to cut off contact with her biological family and recognised Bob Mays as her psychological father, though she later moved in with the Twiggs for a time. Blood typing can exclude parentage, as here, but only DNA testing can confirm it with near certainty.

title: The Guyver
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human experimentation mutants regeneration
text: Dr. Tetsu Segawa, a researcher for the Chronos corporation, steals an alien device called the Guyver unit and is killed by Lisker, a Chronos henchman who can transform into a monstrous Zoanoid. Before dying, Segawa hides the unit, and it is found by Sean Barker, the boyfriend of Segawa's daughter Mizuki. The unit fuses with Sean and covers him in a powerful biomechanical armour. With the help of CIA agent Max Reed, Sean fights the Zoanoids, who kidnap Mizuki to recover the device. In one battle the armour's control metal is ripped off and Sean dies, but the metal regenerates in Chronos's laboratories and, after it is accidentally swallowed by Dr. East, the head of genetics research, it brings Sean back to life. Sean defeats Lisker and the Chronos president, Fulton Balcus, who reveals himself as the Zoalord. Genetic engineering is the business of the villains. The Chronos corporation turns human beings into Zoanoids, genetically engineered monsters that look human but can transform into combat creatures, and its laboratories, run by a head of genetics research, keep a gallery of these forms and experiment on captives; the CIA agent Max Reed is forcibly mutated into a cockroach-like Zoanoid and dies when his body rejects the new form. The Guyver itself is alien biotechnology that bonds permanently with its host, regenerating both itself and the person wearing it. The scientists are portrayed as corporate servants of a hidden, non-human leader seeking power, and their work is shown only as a source of weapons and suffering. The film is a low-budget adaptation of a Japanese manga and does not attempt any scientific realism; genetics serves as a pretext for transformations, monsters and fights.

title: The Unborn
text: Virginia Marshall, a children's book author, and her husband Brad have been unable to conceive. They join an experimental in vitro fertilisation programme run by Dr. Richard Meyerling, and Virginia quickly becomes pregnant. The pregnancy goes badly: the regimen Meyerling prescribes makes her ill, and she becomes increasingly unstable and paranoid. She learns that other women treated at the clinic had terrible outcomes, including children who grew up cold and psychopathic, and she comes to believe that Meyerling is secretly carrying out unauthorised genetic experiments on the embryos he implants, aiming to create superior children. Her fears prove justified, and the pregnancy ends with the birth of a monstrous baby. The film was directed by Rodman Flender. The Unborn is a horror film in the tradition of Rosemary's Baby and It's Alive, with genetic engineering in place of the devil. Its fear is of reproductive medicine: in vitro fertilisation, still relatively new when the film was made, becomes the route by which a doctor secretly manipulates embryos in the hope of creating superior children, and the results are psychopathic or monstrous offspring. Dr. Meyerling is a classic mad scientist, running a private fertility clinic and deceiving his patients for his own eugenic project. Reviewers have noted that the film draws on the Human Genome Project, launched in 1990 and much in the news at the time, and a montage pairs a headline about cracking the DNA code with tabloid stories. The film's genetics is vague and never explained. In reality, in vitro fertilisation and genetic modification of embryos are very different things. Editing human embryos for reproduction became a real controversy only in 2018, when He Jiankui announced the birth of gene-edited twins, work widely condemned as a breach of accepted ethical norms.

title: Alien 3
text: An alien egg on board the spaceship Sulaco releases a facehugger, and a fire forces the ship to jettison the escape pod carrying Ellen Ripley, the girl Newt, Corporal Hicks and the android Bishop. The pod crashes on Fiorina 161, a foundry planet used as a maximum-security prison for violent male inmates. Ripley is the only survivor. An alien bursts from the prison dog and begins killing inmates, while the prison has no weapons. Ripley discovers that she carries an alien queen embryo, and that the Weyland-Yutani Corporation is sending a team to capture it for its biological weapons programme. With the inmates led by their spiritual leader Dillon, she lures the adult alien into the foundry and destroys it. When the company team arrives, led by a man identical to Bishop who claims to be his creator, Ripley throws herself into the furnace as the queen bursts from her chest. Genetics appears only in passing. The prison's inmates are described as men with a 'genetic predisposition for antisocial behaviour'; in the longer Assembly Cut they are said to carry a 'double-Y' chromosome pattern, an allusion to the once-popular and since discredited idea that men with an extra Y chromosome are prone to violence. The label explains why such men have been sent to a remote penal colony but plays no part in the plot, in which the inmates become Ripley's allies. The story's central biological threat is the alien, which the Weyland-Yutani Corporation wants for its bioweapons division, but no genetic work is done in the film. Studies in the 1960s found more XYY men in prisons than expected, but later research showed no strong link between the karyotype and violent crime.

title: Killer Tomatoes Eat France
alt: Los tomates asesinos se comen Francia
text: In the fourth and last film of the Killer Tomatoes series, released direct to video, the mad scientist Dr. Mortimer Gangreen escapes from prison and sets up base in his assistant Igor's castle outside Paris, still bent on world domination. An old prophecy foretells that the king of France, Louis XVII, will return to claim the throne, and since Igor closely resembles the only known image of the lost king, Gangreen plans to use his army of killer tomatoes to stage a second French Revolution and crown Igor as a puppet monarch. To build his army, he kidnaps FT, a friendly, intelligent tomato. Michael, an American has-been actor, and Marie, a French woman he falls in love with, try to stop him while the tomatoes, including a giant fire-breathing one, attack France. The real Louis returns and triumphs over Igor, and Gangreen flees in a tomato-shaped hot-air balloon, swearing revenge. Genetics is little more than a running gag in this parody. Earlier films in the series established that the killer tomatoes were the product of Professor Gangreen's experiments, and here he wants the DNA of FT, a benign tomato, to build a new tomato army; one review summarises his plan in exactly those terms. Gangreen is the classic cartoon mad scientist: an escaped convict who uses his creations for a ludicrous political scheme, with no interest in science for its own sake. The film is inconsistent even with its own franchise, as it shows fruit and vegetables that are sentient without his intervention, and the tomatoes now speak English. Its jokes are aimed at horror clichés and French stereotypes rather than at biology, and the "genetic" element makes no statement about real plant breeding or genetic modification.

title: Lorenzo's Oil
text: Based on a true story, the film follows Augusto and Michaela Odone, whose young son Lorenzo begins to show neurological problems after the family moves from the Comoro Islands to the United States. He is diagnosed with adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD), a degenerative disease expected to kill him within two years. Finding that doctors can offer no treatment, the parents, who have no scientific training, study medical libraries and animal research, badger researchers, clash with a sceptical support group and organise an international symposium on the disease. They learn that oleic acid lowers the very long chain fatty acids that accumulate in ALD, and later add erucic acid, eventually persuading an elderly British chemist to produce a purified mixture of the two. The oil normalises Lorenzo's blood levels and halts the progression of his disease, although the damage already done recovers only very slowly. The film ends with boys treated early with the oil. The film is a medical drama about an inherited disease. ALD is an X-linked disorder: women who carry the faulty gene often develop milder symptoms later in life, while their sons can develop the severe childhood form. The film shows Michaela learning that she passed the disease on to Lorenzo, and her guilt is part of the drama. The genetics is in the background, however; the story is about biochemistry and about lay parents confronting a slow and cautious medical establishment, represented by a well-meaning but hesitant specialist, Professor Nikolais. Hugo Moser, the real researcher on whom Nikolais was based, called the portrayal "an abomination", and the film was criticised for suggesting a miracle cure. Later research has not clearly shown that Lorenzo's oil helps once neurological symptoms have started, although it appeared to prevent onset in many boys treated before symptoms appeared. Lorenzo Odone died in 2008 at the age of 30, two decades longer than doctors had predicted.

title: On Leather Wings
alt: Alas de Piel Batman: The Animated Series, season 1, episode 2
text: A giant bat-like creature attacks a guard during a raid on Phoenix Pharmaceuticals, and Batman is blamed. Against Commissioner Gordon's advice, the mayor authorises Detective Bullock to form a squad to catch him. Batman finds that other pharmaceutical companies have been robbed in the same way, and narrowly escapes Bullock's squad with two clues: a recording of the attack and a sample of fur. As Bruce Wayne he takes them to Dr. Robert March, a bat expert at the Gotham Zoo, whose daughter Francine and her husband, Dr. Kirk Langstrom, offer to analyse them; March reports a mix of starlings and brown bats. Returning to the zoo at night, Batman finds Kirk, who confesses that he and March developed a formula to create a new species, "neither man nor bat", tested it on himself and became addicted. Kirk turns into the Man-Bat; Batman subdues him and brews an antidote, warning Francine that the Man-Bat may not be gone for good. The episode introduces the Man-Bat, a classic Batman story of self-experimentation. Kirk Langstrom and his father-in-law, the zoo's bat expert Dr. March, have developed a formula meant to create a new species, part human and part bat; Kirk tests it on himself, becomes addicted and turns into a creature that raids pharmaceutical companies for the chemicals he needs. The sources describe the formula as creating a new species but do not say whether the episode explains it in genetic or purely chemical terms, and Batman reverses it with a chemical antidote. Kirk is presented as a sympathetic scientist undone by his own ambition rather than a villain, and the closing warning that the Man-Bat may return leaves the experiment's danger hanging. Turning a human into a human-bat hybrid with a drink is pure comic-book science.

title: The Hand That Rocks the Cradle
alt: La mano que mece la cuna
text: Claire Bartel, a Seattle housewife pregnant with her second child, is sexually assaulted by her new obstetrician, Dr. Victor Mott, during a check-up. Encouraged by her husband Michael, she reports him, other women come forward, and Mott kills himself. His pregnant widow loses her home and her baby, and has to have a hysterectomy; she blames Claire. Six months later, under the name Peyton Flanders, she is hired as the Bartels' nanny and sets out to destroy the family from within. She secretly breastfeeds the baby, turns the daughter against her mother, gets the loyal handyman Solomon fired, sabotages Michael's work, and plants evidence of an affair. When a family friend discovers her identity, Peyton kills her with a trap in Claire's greenhouse and empties Claire's asthma inhalers. Once unmasked, Peyton attacks the family to take the children, but Claire, helped by Solomon, defeats her, and Peyton dies in a fall. Genetics plays no real part in this psychological thriller. Its only link to the field is Michael Bartel, Claire's husband, whom Spanish- and German-language plot summaries describe as a biotechnology engineer or genetic engineer; English-language sources do not state his profession. His work appears only as background: Peyton's destruction of a funding proposal he has to submit is one of her many attacks on the Bartels. The film shows nothing of his research and does not use genetics as a theme; no scientific work is seen on screen, and nothing in the plot depends on his field. He is portrayed as a decent, supportive husband, and it is he who encourages Claire to report the abuse. If those summaries are right, the title is an example of a scientist appearing in a mainstream film in a purely incidental role, as an ordinary professional whose occupation signals the family's social standing. The story's real concerns are motherhood, trust and revenge.

title: The Masterpiece Society
alt: La obra de arte social Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 5, episode 13
text: The Enterprise tracks a stellar core fragment from a disintegrated neutron star that will pass close to Moab IV, home of a human colony founded about two centuries earlier. Its leader, Aaron Conor, refuses evacuation, because the colonists were genetically engineered and selectively bred so that each person fits a role in a perfectly balanced society, and leaving would destroy it. The colony's scientist, Hannah Bates, works with Geordi La Forge on a tractor beam to deflect the fragment, and La Forge adapts the technology of his VISOR to make it work, noting that the colony's planners would never have allowed someone born blind like him to exist. Meanwhile Troi and Conor become attracted to each other. The colony is saved, but Bates and 22 other colonists ask to leave with the Enterprise. Picard accepts their request as a matter of free will, and reflects that the Federation's contact may have harmed the society as much as the fragment would have. The episode is an extended argument about genetic perfectionism. The colony of Moab IV is a planned society built through genetic engineering and selective breeding, in which every person is designed from conception for a particular function, and its leaders see any outside contact as a threat to a carefully tuned order. The script undercuts this ideal from two directions. Geordi La Forge, blind from birth, points out that such a society would have screened him out, yet it is the technology built around his disability that saves the colony. And the colonists who leave show that being engineered for a role does not mean accepting it: their departure, framed by Picard as a matter of free will, suggests that a society fixed in advance by design leaves no room for individual choice. Bates, the colony's own scientist, is portrayed sympathetically. The themes anticipate later debates on embryo selection and on whether choosing traits before birth narrows a person's future, as explored in films such as GATTACA.

title: Universal Soldier
text: In Vietnam in 1969, Private Luc Deveraux refuses to take part in atrocities committed by his deranged sergeant, Andrew Scott, and the two kill each other. Their bodies are secretly frozen. Decades later they are revived, with other dead soldiers, as 'Universal Soldiers' (UniSols), an elite counter-terrorism unit whose memories are suppressed with a neural serum. When Deveraux begins to recover memories of his past, he rescues the television reporter Veronica Roberts, who has sneaked onto the base and discovered the project, and the two go on the run. Scott, whose madness returns, kills the unit's commander and leads the other UniSols in pursuit. Dr. Christopher Gregor, a scientist from the programme, explains to them its origins and flaws. The chase ends at Deveraux's family farm in Louisiana, where Deveraux, after injecting himself with muscle enhancers, kills Scott in a hay harvester. The UniSols are presented as genetically augmented soldiers, reanimated corpses with enhanced healing and strength, created in a secret military programme begun in the 1960s to produce the perfect soldier. The film's science mixes genetics with cryonics, reanimation, a neural serum that suppresses memory and keeps the soldiers obedient, and injectable muscle enhancers; the genetic element is a label more than a mechanism. The programme has serious flaws: the soldiers overheat and need ice baths, and their last memories return amplified, so that Scott relives his Vietnam madness. The project and its leaders are portrayed as unethical and secretive, turning dead men into weapons, covering up the project and trying to kill a journalist; the scientist Dr. Gregor helps the heroes in the theatrical version but is a manipulative villain in an alternative ending. The film belongs to the early-1990s wave of super-soldier action films; nothing in it resembles a real genetic technique.

title: Babel
alt: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, season 1, episode 5
text: In this Star Trek: Deep Space Nine episode, an overworked Chief O'Brien, repairing a faulty food replicator, unknowingly activates a hidden device. Soon he speaks only gibberish and cannot understand language, and Dax shows the same aphasia. Dr. Bashir finds a virus in food from the command-level replicators, which causes dangerous fevers; Quark has been selling food from an unused replicator, spreading it, and the virus mutates to become airborne. With the station quarantined and most of the crew stricken, Major Kira finds that the virus was engineered by a Bajoran resistance fighter, Dekon Elig, during the Cardassian occupation, to be released through the station's replicators. Elig is dead, so Kira abducts his former assistant, Surmak Ren, now a medical administrator on Bajor, who refuses to help until he learns that he too is infected. Meanwhile, Odo and Quark eject a freighter whose damaged core threatens the station. Using Bashir's notes, Ren creates an antidote that cures the crew. The threat is an engineered virus left over from a past war. During the Cardassian occupation of Bajor, a resistance scientist designed a synthetic virus that attacks the brain's language centres and causes fatal fevers, and hid a device in the station's replicators to write it into food; triggered years later by accident, it infects nearly everyone aboard and mutates to spread through the air. Dr. Bashir identifies the agent, and by analysing its DNA and construction determines that it is synthetic and of Bajoran rather than Cardassian origin, which leads to the creator's former assistant. The resolution depends on the expertise of the people who made the weapon: Surmak Ren, reluctant and abducted, uses Bashir's research to make the antidote. The episode presents the weapon as a dangerous legacy of terrorism rather than dwelling on the ethics of its makers, and the doctors as competent heroes. A virus that selectively scrambles language is fictional, although some infections can cause aphasia.

title: Born Bad
text: Teenager Chris Pollit, who lives in a foster home, beats a fellow resident, Johnny Lasky, to death. His lawyer, Helen Brolin, seeks a verdict of not guilty by reason of genetic defect: she argues that Pollit is genetically predisposed to violence because he has an extra Y chromosome, so that the prosecution must answer a defence based on his genes rather than on his actions. The episode was later adapted by Law & Order: UK as 'Unloved'. The only available source is a short synopsis, which does not describe the investigation, the trial or the verdict in more detail. The episode turns on the 'XYY defence'. In the 1960s, surveys found men with an extra Y chromosome (47,XYY) overrepresented in high-security institutions, and the idea of a 'criminal chromosome' spread to the press and to some courtrooms. Later, larger studies showed that most XYY men are never diagnosed and are not violent; the condition is associated mainly with greater height and a higher rate of learning and behavioural difficulties, and the modest excess of convictions largely reflects these and social factors rather than aggression. The defence therefore rests on a discredited idea. The episode sets this genetic excuse in the case of a boy raised in foster care, so upbringing is implicitly part of the question. The available synopsis does not say how the court rules or how the episode frames the argument.

title: Cardassians
alt: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, season 2, episode 5
text: On Deep Space Nine, a Cardassian boy, Rugal, bites the tailor Garak. Rugal is a war orphan left behind when Cardassia withdrew from Bajor, and he has been raised by a Bajoran, Proka, who loves him but has taught him to hate Cardassians. Gul Dukat, the former Cardassian prefect of Bajor, takes up the cause of the orphans and then reports that the boy's DNA has identified him as the son of Kotan Pa'Dar, a prominent Cardassian politician who believed him dead. Pa'Dar comes to claim him, Rugal rejects him as a 'Cardassian butcher', and Commander Sisko presides over a custody hearing. Meanwhile Dr. Bashir and Garak visit a Bajoran resettlement centre and uncover Dukat's plot: he had the boy left behind deliberately to disgrace his rival. Sisko gives custody to the biological father. The genetic element is DNA identification: a DNA test reveals that the supposed orphan is the son of a living Cardassian official, which turns a story about war orphans into a custody dispute and leads to a political conspiracy. The episode is mainly about biological versus social parenthood. Rugal is Cardassian by birth but Bajoran by upbringing, and he has absorbed his adoptive people's hatred of his own species. The story gives weight to both sides: it presents Proka's love as genuine but questions an upbringing built on hatred, and it sends Rugal back to his biological father, a decision driven as much by the exposure of Dukat's plot as by blood ties, with the boy going reluctantly. Using DNA to identify a missing child's parents is a standard forensic technique today.

title: Carnosaur
themes: genetic engineering engineered pathogens de extinction hybrids chimeras bioweapon
text: Dr. Jane Tiptree carries out secret research for the Eunice Corporation in a laboratory near the small town of Climax, Nevada, where she works with genetically modified chickens. One of her eggs hatches a Deinonychus, which escapes and begins killing people, while the townspeople fall ill with a mysterious flu-like disease. Doc Smith, the night watchman at a nearby quarry, and Ann Thrush, an environmental activist, survive the creature's attacks and trace it back to the laboratory. There Tiptree reveals her plan: infected chicken eggs spread an airborne virus that makes women pregnant with dinosaur embryos, so that dinosaurs can replace the human race. The government quarantines the town and orders civilians shot on sight. Tiptree herself dies giving birth to a dinosaur, and Doc kills her Tyrannosaurus rex and injects Thrush with a cure, but soldiers kill them both and burn their bodies, destroying the serum. Genetic engineering is the engine of the plot. Tiptree recreates dinosaurs by modifying chickens, the living relatives of dinosaurs, and engineers a virus that makes human women carry dinosaur embryos, so genetics becomes a weapon for exterminating humanity. She is a pure mad-scientist figure, working in secret for a corporation that funds her research while the defence agency DARPA watches but cannot legally intervene; her motive is misanthropic, a wish to give the Earth back to the dinosaurs. The authorities respond with quarantine, killing and, in a satirical subplot, plans for a new social order based on controlled fertilisation and artificial wombs. The premise is not plausible: birds descend from dinosaurs, but genuine dinosaur DNA has never been recovered, and early reports of it were later traced to contamination. The oldest DNA known is around two million years old, while non-avian dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. The film, produced by Roger Corman, was released just before Jurassic Park.

title: Emohawk: Polymorph II
text: Charged with looting derelict ships by a computer-controlled Space Corps enforcement vessel and sentenced to death, the crew of Starbug escape but crash-land on a moon inhabited by GELFs. Needing a new oxygen generator, they bargain with the Kinitawowi tribe, but the price turns out to be Lister's marriage to the chief's daughter. Lister flees, the crew escape with the parts, and the angry chief sends his pet Emohawk, a domesticated polymorph, after them. While Lister and Kryten install the new parts, the creature drains the others of personality traits: the Cat loses his cool and becomes the hapless Duane Dibbley, and Rimmer loses his bitterness and becomes the heroic Ace Rimmer. After Rimmer proposes ejecting himself and the Cat through an airlock, the crew agree instead to track down and freeze the creature. Rimmer asks to stay Ace for another day, while the Cat asks to be changed back at once, but as Duane he accidentally freezes the others. Genetics is only in the background of this episode. The Emohawk is a domesticated polymorph, a shape-changing creature that feeds on emotions, kept as a pet by the chief of a GELF tribe; it brings back the creature type from the Series III episode 'Polymorph'. This episode does not explain where the creature comes from or how it works, and no one in the story does any genetic work. The polymorph serves as a comic device for draining the crew's character traits and reviving two alternative personas from earlier episodes, Duane Dibbley and Ace Rimmer. Critics considered it one of the weaker episodes of the sixth series. Creatures that drain personality traits are pure fantasy.

title: Eve
themes: cloning eugenics human enhancement human experimentation nature nurture
text: Two men are killed at the same moment on opposite sides of the United States, one in Connecticut and one in California, each drained of blood through incisions in the neck. FBI agents Mulder and Scully find that each victim had a young daughter, Teena and Cindy, who look identical. Both girls were conceived by in vitro fertilization at a San Francisco clinic, where Dr. Sally Kendrick had been fired for eugenics experiments with patients' eggs. Deep Throat tells Mulder about a Cold War programme that produced genetically engineered clones called "Adams" and "Eves". In a psychiatric hospital the agents meet Eve 6, who looks exactly like Kendrick and explains that the clones had extra chromosomes that gave them superhuman intelligence and strength but also homicidal psychosis. Kendrick, really Eve 7, cloned the girls from herself. The girls poison her, then try to poison the agents. They are locked up alongside Eve 6, where Eve 8 comes to visit them. Cloning and genetic engineering are central to the episode. A secret government programme created clones with enhanced abilities, and one of them, posing as a fertility doctor, secretly uses patients' IVF treatment to produce new copies of herself, so the parents unknowingly raise her clones. The episode links the scientists to eugenics and military research and shows the results as monstrous: the clones are brilliant and strong but psychopathic, and the girls kill their fathers. The idea that "extra chromosomes" produce superhuman traits has no basis; in reality, an extra chromosome is a cause of genetic disorders such as Down syndrome, and most extra autosomes are lethal to the embryo. The episode also plays on the fear, common in the 1990s, that reproductive technology could be secretly misused, and uses identical twins separated at birth as the hook of the mystery.

title: Jurassic Park
text: Industrialist John Hammond has built a theme park of cloned dinosaurs on Isla Nublar, off Costa Rica. After a worker is killed, his investors demand a safety review, and Hammond invites palaeontologist Alan Grant, palaeobotanist Ellie Sattler and mathematician Ian Malcolm, along with the investors' lawyer and his own grandchildren, Lex and Tim. The visitors learn how the animals were made and debate the ethics of the park. During a tropical storm, the computer programmer Dennis Nedry shuts down the security system to steal frozen embryos for a rival company, and the electric fences fail. A Tyrannosaurus escapes and attacks the tour, Nedry is killed, and Grant and the children must cross the park on foot, discovering on the way that the dinosaurs are breeding. Attempts to restart the power release the Velociraptors, which kill several staff. The survivors are rescued by helicopter after Grant and Hammond agree not to endorse the park. Genetic engineering is the premise of the film. Hammond's scientists, led by chief geneticist Henry Wu, recovered dinosaur DNA from the blood in mosquitoes preserved in amber, filled the gaps in the genomes with frog DNA and made all the animals female to prevent breeding. The plan fails because of that frog DNA: like some amphibians, the dinosaurs change sex in a single-sex population, so life finds a way. Through Malcolm the film argues that genetic power was obtained without discipline or humility, and the geneticists serve a commercial project, although Hammond himself is a sympathetic showman rather than a villain. Real ancient DNA cannot do this. DNA breaks down over time, and even under the best conditions the upper limit for sequencing is thought to be roughly one to two million years, while the last non-avian dinosaurs died about 66 million years ago.

title: Made in America
themes: nature nurture dna identification donor conception
text: Zora Mathews, a gifted African American high-school student, discovers from a blood test that her blood group could not have come from her late father and her mother Sarah, who runs an African American bookshop. Sarah admits that she conceived Zora with donor sperm, having asked for a tall Black donor. With her friend Tea Cake, Zora sneaks into the sperm bank's records and finds her donor's name: Hal Jackson, a loud white car dealer known for his outlandish television commercials. After a rough start, Hal grows fond of Zora and falls for Sarah. When Sarah is badly injured in a bicycle accident, a hospital blood test reveals that Hal cannot be Zora's father after all. By then he has become one: at her graduation, Zora, who has won a scholarship to MIT, thanks both Sarah and Hal as her parents. The film's genetics consists of two blood-group tests that work as simple paternity tests. The first, showing that Zora's blood group is incompatible with her parents', reveals that she was conceived by donor insemination; the second, after Sarah's accident, shows that Hal, the donor named in the sperm bank's records, cannot be her biological father. The story uses these revelations to ask what makes a parent, and it favours nurture: Zora gives her mother the credit for who she is, and Hal becomes a father to her through affection rather than biology. The racial mix-up, a white donor for a Black mother who asked for a Black one, is played for comedy. Blood groups follow simple Mendelian inheritance, so they can rule a man out as the father, though they cannot prove that he is; today DNA tests do both.

title: Man's Best Friend
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras animal experimentation
text: Television reporter and animal activist Lori Tanner breaks into the laboratories of EMAX, a genetic research company run by the scientist Dr. Jarret, and frees a Tibetan Mastiff named Max. She adopts him without knowing that he is the product of genetic engineering, spliced with DNA from big cats, snakes, chameleons and birds of prey, and that he needs a drug to keep his violent rages in check. Max is loyal and affectionate with Lori and can understand human speech, but when she is away he kills a mugger, a cat, a parakeet and a mailman, and sabotages the car of her boyfriend, Perry. When Lori gives him away, he kills the junkyard owner who abuses him and returns home to find he has been replaced by a puppy. The police hunt him, and Jarret kidnaps Lori to lure Max back to the lab, where the scientist shoots him and is himself electrocuted. Months later, a neighbour's collie gives birth to a puppy that looks like Max. Genetic engineering is the source of the threat. Max is a transgenic animal combining the DNA of several species, and each borrowed trait gives him a new ability, such as his strength, speed, senses and acidic urine, in the style of a monster film rather than real biology. His violent instability is the side effect the company tries to manage with drugs, and the final shot of a puppy he has fathered suggests that his engineered traits may now spread through breeding. The scientist, Dr. Jarret, is presented as an animal experimenter whose laboratory is exposed as a place of cruelty; he reports Max stolen instead of warning about the danger, and dies in his own facility. The film reflects early-1990s public unease about genetic engineering and animal experimentation. Real transgenic animals carry one or a few added genes, and nothing like a mixture of mammal, reptile and bird traits has been produced.

title: Psirens
text: In this Red Dwarf episode, Lister wakes with amnesia aboard the small ship Starbug, and Kryten explains that the crew has spent 200 years chasing their stolen mother ship, Red Dwarf. Taking a shortcut through an asteroid belt, they find it is a graveyard of ships haunted by Psirens, shape-changing creatures that lure travellers with telepathic illusions to feast on their brains. Starbug crashes, and Lister has to go outside to free it; a Psiren tries to seduce him with an illusion, and another, disguised as Kryten, gives itself away by calling him Dave. Back on board, there are two Listers, and the crew identifies the impostor by asking both to play the guitar: the real Lister is terrible, while the Psiren copied his own flattering self-image. The wounded Psiren traps Kryten in the waste compactor, but Kryten, crushed into a cube, kills it, and the crew continues the chase. The monsters of the episode are genetically engineered life forms, or GELFs, a category of creatures in the Red Dwarf universe. The Psirens are shape-changing predators that use psychic illusions, based on what their victims believe about themselves, to lure space travellers to their deaths, like the sirens of the Odyssey. The episode does not say who engineered them or why; genetic engineering is simply the origin of a menace, and the story is a comic horror adventure built around the crew's attempts to tell friends from impostors. The idea that engineered organisms could change shape or project telepathic illusions is fantasy.

title: Rightful Heir
alt: Heredero legítimo Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 6, episode 23
text: Going through a crisis of faith, Worf travels to the Klingon monastery on Boreth, where the faithful await the return of Kahless, the legendary warrior who founded the Klingon Empire. After days of ritual, a man appearing to be Kahless materialises before him, and Worf brings him aboard the Enterprise, though he is troubled by gaps in Kahless's memory. Chancellor Gowron, suspecting an impostor planted by the priests to gain power, brings an ancient dagger stained with Kahless's blood and asks for a genetic comparison; the DNA matches. Gowron then defeats Kahless in a duel, and the high priest Koroth admits that this Kahless is a clone of the original. Worf persuades Gowron to install the clone as a ceremonial emperor who can unite the Klingon people while real power stays with the council. Cloning and DNA identification drive the plot, but the episode's real subject is faith and political legitimacy. The priests of Boreth use ancient blood preserved on a dagger to clone their messiah, and the deception survives a genetic test precisely because a clone carries the same DNA as the original: the test proves genetic identity, not that the man is the historical Kahless. The scientists here are religious leaders who use the technology to revive belief and strengthen their own influence, and the episode leaves open whether their manipulation is harmful or beneficial for the Klingon people. It also makes the point, familiar from real discussions of cloning, that a clone is a new individual who shares a genome with the donor but not his memories or experience; this Kahless lacks the memories the real one would have had. Recovering an intact genome from centuries-old blood and cloning from it remains well beyond current science.

title: The Chase
alt: Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 6, episode 20
text: In this Star Trek: The Next Generation episode, Captain Picard's old archaeology mentor, Professor Richard Galen, asks him to join an expedition of enormous importance; Picard declines, and soon afterwards Galen is fatally wounded in an attack on his shuttle. In Galen's files the crew finds blocks of numbers that turn out to be DNA fragments from nineteen species on different worlds. Combined, they form an algorithm coded at the molecular level some four billion years ago, still incomplete. Following Galen's trail, the Enterprise competes with Cardassian and Klingon ships, which expect a weapon or a power source, and with a hidden Romulan vessel. On Vilmor II, Dr. Crusher completes the program with DNA from surviving lichens, and it projects a hologram: an ancient humanoid species, alone in the galaxy, seeded many planets with its genetic code so that humanoid life would arise. The Klingons and Cardassians are disgusted by their common ancestry, while the Romulan commander hints at a shared future. The whole mystery is genetic. Professor Galen, an archaeologist, has been collecting DNA from life forms on many planets; Dr. Crusher combines the fragments by protein-link compatibility, Geordi recognises in them an algorithm rather than a natural sequence, and the program is completed with DNA from the races competing for it and from lichens on the last planet. The answer is a message written into the genomes of the galaxy by an ancient humanoid species that seeded worlds with its genetic material to steer evolution towards humanoids like itself. The episode thus uses directed panspermia as an in-universe explanation of why most Star Trek aliens look human, and treats the discovery of a common ancestry as a call for unity, which the Klingons and Cardassians reject. The ancient engineers are presented as benevolent creators, and the scientists who decipher their work as heroes. Hiding a readable message in genomes for billions of years of mutation and evolution is not plausible, and the episode was inspired by Carl Sagan's Contact.

title: Tomcat: Dangerous Desires
themes: gene therapy hybrids chimeras genetic disease human experimentation
text: Tom, a young modern dancer, suffers from a rare degenerative condition of the nervous system. Jacki, a scientist in genetic research who becomes his lover, treats him with an experimental therapy based on genetic material from a cat. The treatment restores his health, but it has side effects: Tom gradually takes on feline traits and becomes devious and dangerous. As he grows attached to Imogen, a fellow dancer, Jacki becomes jealous, fearing she will lose both her patient and her lover. Tom turns on the people around him, killing Jacki and then those who stand between him and Imogen, until a final pursuit in a lumberyard. The premise is an inter-species genetic treatment: a geneticist cures a man's degenerative disease with feline DNA, and the cure slowly turns him into a predatory, cat-like killer. The film combines this idea with an erotic thriller in the style of Basic Instinct, and the scientist's motives are personal as much as professional, since her patient is also her lover. Sources differ slightly on the treatment itself, which Wikipedia describes as injections of feline brain material and other summaries as a genetic implant of cat DNA. According to the Moria review, the genetic angle is barely explored and its main visible effect is Tom's sudden fear of water, a trait the reviewer notes is not genetically determined in cats. As science, the idea that animal genes would transfer behaviour and personality to a human is fantasy; it belongs to a long line of "hybrid monster" stories rather than to real gene therapy.

title: Armageddon Game
alt: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, season 2, episode 13
text: Chief O'Brien and Dr. Bashir help the T'Lani and the Kellerun, former enemies, destroy their stockpiles of Harvesters, deadly biogenic weapons from their long war; Bashir finds that a particular radiation frequency disrupts the weapons' genetic structure, and O'Brien erases all the technical data. As the last Harvesters are destroyed, Kellerun soldiers burst in and kill the scientists; in the struggle a drop of Harvester liquid falls on O'Brien's skin. O'Brien and Bashir beam down to the planet and hide while O'Brien, increasingly ill from the infection, guides Bashir through repairing an old transmitter. On Deep Space Nine, the two ambassadors tell Commander Sisko that both men died in an accident and provide a recording. Keiko notices that it shows O'Brien drinking coffee in the afternoon, which she is sure he never does, and Sisko and Dax find evidence they survived. The ambassadors reveal that they planned to kill everyone who knew how to make Harvesters, but Sisko rescues the pair. The episode revolves around a genetic weapon. The Harvesters are biomechanical 'gene disruptors' that both sides used in their war; Bashir neutralises them with a radiation frequency that destroys their genetic integrity, and O'Brien, infected by a single drop, rapidly loses his sight and ability to walk before being treated. The episode's moral twist is that destroying the weapons is not enough for the two governments: to make sure the Harvesters can never be rebuilt, they decide to kill everyone who knows how they work, their own scientists and the Federation officers included. Bashir is presented as a capable, heroic scientist using his knowledge to dismantle the weapons, while the knowledge itself becomes a death sentence. An early pitch, abandoned, had the weapon encoded in O'Brien's DNA.

title: Dragon Ball Z: Bio-Broly
alt: Doragon Bōru Zetto: Chō Senshi Gekiha!! Katsu no wa Ore da Dragon Ball Z: Los guerreros de plástico
text: Mr. Jaguar, a rich man who was Mr. Satan's rival at summer camp, invites the martial arts champion to his island laboratory to fight his "bio-warriors", humanoids created by the scientist Dr. Collie, threatening otherwise to expose an embarrassing secret. Android 18 goes along to make sure Mr. Satan pays her a debt, and the boys Goten and Trunks stow away. During the tournament the boys discover a tank holding what looks like Broly, the Legendary Super Saiyan they had killed. A shaman explains that he took a sample of Broly's blood to Jaguar, who had a clone created. The clone breaks out, and the fight ruptures tanks of a bio-fluid that devours matter. Drenched in it, the clone becomes the deformed Bio-Broly and later merges with the fluid. The heroes discover that seawater turns the fluid to stone, flood the island and destroy the petrified giant. Cloning drives the plot. Jaguar and his scientist, Dr. Collie, grow artificial bio-warriors in tanks and create a clone of the dead Broly from a blood sample, intending to use these fighters to humiliate Mr. Satan. Their motives are petty and personal rather than scientific, and the experiment escapes their control: the culture fluid used in the laboratory proves more dangerous than the clone itself, kills the bio-warriors and most of the scientists and threatens to cover the whole Earth. The film treats cloning as a way of bringing back a dead fighter with his powers intact, a common idea in fiction that does not match real cloning, which produces a genetically identical individual who must still develop from an embryo and would not share the original's memories or abilities. The genetics is a premise for a martial arts adventure and is not explored further.

title: Felidae
text: In the late 1980s, Francis, an intelligent house cat, moves with his owner into a run-down house and finds a cat killed by a bite to the neck. With the help of the one-eyed Bluebeard, he investigates a series of feline murders and discovers a sect of cats that worships a figure called Claudandus. A video recording reveals that the top floor of his house was once a laboratory where stray cats were used to test a tissue glue, until the only survivor, Claudandus, killed the deranged lead researcher, Dr. Preterius. Haunted by nightmares of the geneticist Gregor Mendel, Francis finally learns that the killer is Pascal, the elderly, computer-literate cat who is Claudandus himself. Pascal has spent years breeding a new race of cats and killing those who refused to cooperate. Francis deletes his records, and in the fight that follows Claudandus dies as the house burns. The film is an animated adaptation of Akif Pirinçci's 1989 novel. Genetics enters through classical heredity rather than genetic engineering. Claudandus, the survivor of cruel animal experiments, was taken in by a former laboratory assistant and learned Mendel's laws of inheritance. He uses them to run a eugenic breeding programme, selecting mates over generations to bring back the traits of an imagined ancestor of all domestic cats, a superior breed meant eventually to wipe out humanity. Cats who refuse to take part are murdered. The villain is thus both a victim of science and a self-taught geneticist who turns its methods into a racial project, with clear echoes of human eugenics; Mendel himself appears in Francis's nightmares. The scientists of the original laboratory are portrayed as cruel and, in Preterius's case, unhinged. The approach Claudandus uses is real in principle: domestic animal breeds are produced by selective breeding, and Mendel's experiments on pea plants established how traits are passed on. Recreating an ancestral species this way, however, is far beyond what breeding can achieve.

title: Genesis
alt: Génesis Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 7, episode 19
text: While Captain Picard and Data leave the Enterprise in a shuttle to recover a stray photon torpedo, Dr. Crusher treats Lieutenant Barclay for a mild flu by injecting a synthetic T-cell that activates a dormant immune gene. Soon crew members behave strangely: Troi feels cold and thirsty, Riker cannot concentrate, and Worf turns hot and aggressive, bites Troi and spits venom that injures Crusher, who is put in stasis. When Picard and Data return three days later, the ship is adrift and most of the crew have regressed into earlier life forms: Troi into an amphibian, Riker into a caveman, Barclay into a spider. Data finds that the T-cell has mutated into a contagious agent that activates dormant genes at random. As Picard himself begins to change, Data uses antibodies from the amniotic fluid of a pregnant nurse to make a retrovirus that restores everyone. The episode is built on a genetic premise. A routine gene-activating treatment, a synthetic T-cell meant to switch on one dormant immunity gene in Barclay, mutates because of an anomaly in his genes, becomes transmissible and switches on all the dormant genes of whoever it infects; Data explains that these introns preserve sequences from millions of years of evolution, so the crew 'de-evolve' into ancestral forms. Genetic medicine also provides the solution, as Data designs a retrovirus that restores each person's genetic pattern, and Crusher closes the episode by naming the condition 'Barclay's protomorphosis syndrome' and admitting the fault was hers. The doctors are well-meaning professionals and the tone mixes horror with comedy. The science is fanciful: writer Brannon Braga used introns because their function was then poorly understood, but they do not contain dormant ancestral bodies, and evolution cannot be run backwards in an individual.

title: Guyver: Dark Hero
text: A year after bonding with the Guyver, an alien bio-booster armour, and destroying the Los Angeles branch of the Cronos Corporation, Sean Barker fights crime but is worn down by the unit's urge to kill. Drawn by cave paintings in Utah that match his dreams, he travels to an archaeological dig led by Marcus Edwards, whose daughter Cori guides him there. The dig uncovers an ancient alien ship. Arlen Crane, the dig's funder, turns out to work for Cronos, which is still active, and is himself a Zoanoid, one of the monstrous transformed humans that serve the corporation. Through the ship, Sean learns that in prehistoric times aliens created the Guyvers and Zoanoids in a failed attempt to turn early humans into soldiers. Crane fuses with a damaged Guyver unit, but Sean kills him, sends the ship home and refuses a government offer to fight Cronos. Genetics is only a light background element. The Guyver armour and the Zoanoids are the products of alien biological engineering: in the backstory, aliens tried to turn primitive humans into living weapons, and the Cronos Corporation now uses Zoanoids, humans transformed into monsters, as its henchmen. The film presents the armour as an alien bio-booster unit bonded to its host rather than in explicit genetic terms, and the sources do not say how the Zoanoids are made, so the genetic framing is thin. The idea of humans engineered into soldiers by outsiders, and of a corporation exploiting the technology, is a familiar theme of the Japanese manga on which the film is based.

title: Junior
text: Austrian research geneticist Dr. Alex Hesse and obstetrician Dr. Larry Arbogast have developed Expectane, a drug to reduce the risk of miscarriage, but the FDA will not let them test it on humans. With a pharmaceutical company willing to fund the trial if they find a volunteer, Larry persuades Alex to test it on himself: an egg codenamed "Junior" is fertilised and implanted in his abdomen. Alex suffers morning sickness and mood swings, and when the trial should end he decides to carry the pregnancy to term. He falls for Dr. Diana Reddin, a scientist from the egg-freezing department, who is furious to learn the egg was hers but comes to accept that she is the mother and he the father. Alex hides in a retreat for expectant mothers disguised as a woman, the lab director tries to claim credit, and Alex finally gives birth by caesarean to a healthy girl. Genetics plays a modest role in this comedy; its real subject is reproduction and gender roles. The protagonist is a research geneticist and the heroine a scientist who works on egg freezing, but the science involves a fertility drug, in vitro fertilisation and the implantation of an embryo in a man's abdomen. The scientists are ambitious and break the rules: they bypass the FDA, keep the trial secret and use an egg without its donor's consent, which the film treats as a romantic complication rather than an ethical breach. A greedy lab director who tries to take the credit serves as the villain. The film's interest lies in Alex learning empathy and the emotional side of parenthood. Male pregnancy by implanting an embryo in the abdomen has never been attempted; specialists consider it theoretically conceivable but so dangerous for parent and child that it is unlikely ever to be studied in humans. The title fits the database mainly through its geneticist protagonist.

title: Street Fighter
themes: human enhancement human experimentation genetic engineering
text: In the Asian country of Shadaloo, the warlord General M. Bison holds dozens of Allied Nations relief workers hostage and demands a $20 billion ransom. Colonel William Guile refuses to pay and sets out to find Bison's base, recruiting the con artists Ryu and Ken, who infiltrate the organisation of Bison's arms supplier Sagat. Reporter Chun-Li and her crew pursue their own revenge. Meanwhile Bison has Guile's captured friend Charlie Blanka taken to his laboratory, where the scientist Dr. Dhalsim turns him into the first of Bison's 'genetic supersoldiers'. Charlie is horribly disfigured, but Dhalsim secretly preserves his humanity. Guile's forces storm the base and free the hostages, and Guile defeats Bison. Dhalsim and Charlie stay behind as the base explodes, Dhalsim wishing to atone for what he did. Genetic engineering is a secondary but recurring thread in this campy adaptation of the video game. Bison wants an army of 'genetic supersoldiers' to conquer the world and uses the captured soldier Charlie as his first guinea pig. The scientist who carries out the procedure, Dr. Dhalsim, works for the dictator but is shown sympathetically: he secretly alters Charlie's mental programming so that he keeps his humanity, protects him, and finally chooses to stay with him to atone. The genetic transformation itself is presented as monstrous, leaving Charlie a green-skinned, disfigured creature (the game's Blanka), and as a tool of military domination. Turning an adult into a super-strong being overnight is pure fantasy; the film uses 'genetic' as a label for a comic-book transformation.

title: The Abandoned
alt: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, season 3, episode 6
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement nature nurture
text: Quark buys salvage from a wrecked ship and finds a baby inside. In the infirmary Dr. Bashir measures an extraordinary metabolism: within hours the infant grows into a boy and then a teenager, though he is biologically only weeks old, which Bashir can explain only by advanced genetic engineering. The aggressive youth turns out to be a Jem'Hadar, one of the Dominion's engineered soldiers, and he instinctively reveres Odo as one of the Founders, the shapeshifters who rule the Dominion. Starfleet wants him sent away for study, but Odo, once a research subject himself, takes charge of him and tries to teach him to think for himself and control his aggression. They learn that the Jem'Hadar depend on a substance only the Founders supply. When the boy threatens Sisko with a phaser, Odo takes him through the wormhole and lets him return to his people. The Jem'Hadar are genetically engineered soldiers, and this episode, which introduces them in detail, is a test of nature against nurture. Bashir deduces the engineering from the boy's accelerated growth, and the crew discover that the Founders have built in a dependence on a substance that only they supply, a way of guaranteeing loyalty. Odo's attempt to give the boy free will through patient upbringing fails, because his aggression and his reverence for the Founders are presented as part of his genetic design. The story sides firmly with nature: Odo admits to Kira that she was right and the boy could not be changed. The Founders appear only through their creation, but they come across as cynical engineers of obedience. Real genetics offers nothing like this: behaviour is influenced by many genes and by experience, and there is no known way to engineer loyalty or a fixed drive to kill.

title: The Erlenmeyer Flask
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering human experimentation
text: After a car chase in Maryland, a fugitive, Dr. William Secare, is shot and escapes into the water; the police find that his blood is green. Deep Throat steers Mulder to the case, which leads to Dr. Terrance Berube, a geneticist who worked on the Human Genome Project and who is soon murdered by a government operative. In Berube's laboratory Mulder finds a flask labelled "Purity Control", whose contents a Georgetown microbiologist identifies as containing DNA of extraterrestrial origin; she and her family are then killed. Mulder discovers a storage facility with men suspended in tanks. Deep Throat explains that Berube had been experimenting on six terminally ill volunteers with alien material and had created alien–human hybrids, and that the project worked better than expected. To rescue the captured Mulder, Scully obtains an alien foetus from a high-security facility; Deep Throat exchanges it and is shot dead. The X-Files are closed. This season-one finale introduces one of the central ideas of The X-Files mythology: secret government experiments that combine human and alien DNA to create hybrids. The scientist at its centre, Dr. Berube, is presented as a genome researcher working covertly for the government; the experiments on terminally ill volunteers appear to cure them, and he is killed when he tries to protect one of his subjects. Genetics provides both the evidence (DNA in the flask that cannot come from any earthly organism) and the conspiracy itself, and later episodes develop the themes of hybrids, toxic alien blood and alien foetuses introduced here. Genome sequencing and experimental gene transfer were real and topical when the episode aired in 1994, during the Human Genome Project, but alien–human hybridisation and the "extraterrestrial" DNA signature are fiction.

title: The Killing Machine
text: Harlin Garrett, a mafia hitman left for dead by his employers, wakes with amnesia in a secret facility run by a covert government agency under the menacing Mr. Green, who tells him he died in a fire and was brought back to life. Given the choice of working for the agency or being disposed of, Garrett is trained to kill again. His missions target people connected to HIV research and the gay community: a gay rights activist, whom he is to kill while posing as his chauffeur, and a journalist, both to be made to look like accidents. His key target is Dr. Ann Kendall, an MIT scientist who has found proof that the AIDS virus was artificially manufactured and that the government enabled its spread; he is to seduce her to learn what she knows and then kill her. Instead Garrett falls for Ann, deals with her jealous boyfriend, and turns against Green and the agency to protect her. The film's conspiracy rests on an engineered pathogen: an MIT scientist, Dr. Ann Kendall, has found proof that the AIDS virus was artificially manufactured and that a government agency enabled its spread, and the agency kills activists, journalists and researchers to bury the evidence. The idea echoes conspiracy theories about the man-made origin of HIV that circulated in the 1980s and 1990s, which have no scientific basis; HIV arose by natural transmission from primates. The film does not say who made the virus, how or why, a gap the Moria review criticises. Science is represented by Kendall, a lonely but principled researcher who becomes the moral centre of the story, set against a sinister state agency that also 'resurrects' and reprograms a hitman by unexplained means.

title: The Stand
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic bioweapon post apocalyptic
