His obnoxious alter ego, Buddy Love, still takes over his body at the worst moments, so Sherman uses Denise's method to isolate and remove the DNA in which Buddy has manifested, ignoring his assistant's warnings. A dog hair falls into the extracted material and Buddy grows into an independent being, who tries to sell the youth formula to Phleer Pharmaceuticals. Meanwhile the extraction makes Sherman steadily lose his intelligence. Sherman's father secretly drinks the formula, Buddy sabotages a demonstration in which a hamster grows to giant size, and Sherman is fired. Finally the formula reduces Buddy to a glowing mass of genetic material, Sherman drinks it to restore his mind, and he marries Denise. DNA is the comic engine of this sequel. Sherman treats his personality as something written in his genes: with his girlfriend's DNA-isolation technique he cuts 'Buddy Love' out of his genome, and the extracted material, mixed with a basset hound's hair, grows into a separate person with dog-like habits. Removing it turns out to damage Sherman's brain, so the cure is to take the DNA back, by drinking it. The youth formula, presented in some sources as a genetic modification, rejuvenates his father and, once tampered with, turns a hamster into a giant. The scientists are sympathetic: Sherman is a well-meaning hero whose rash experiment backfires, and Denise is a capable researcher. A college dean and a drug company that want to profit from the formula are the cynics. None of it is meant seriously: personality traits are not stored in a removable stretch of DNA, and drinking DNA does not change one's genome.

title: Seeds of Destruction
alt: Las semillas de la destrucción The Outer Limits, season 6, episode 7
text: The biotechnology company Macroseed chooses the farming town of Hobson to test TX-40, a fast-growing genetically engineered corn that promises bigger harvests. The local veterinarian, Dr. Linda Andrews, grows suspicious when a farmer brings in a dead cat from his field with a tumour that sprouts a fifth leg. Aggressive tumours then appear in people, including teenagers and her own nephew. Her husband Rex and her lover Harold Zimmer, both Macroseed employees, insist the corn is safe and that her inquiries could ruin the town's new prosperity. Reading the company's test data, the town doctor explains that crops are modified either with a particle gun or with the tumour-inducing bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens, and he and Linda notice that the safety tests used DNA only from middle-aged white men, while the victims all have high levels of growth hormone. TX-40 has crossed from the corn to milkweed and from there to people. Harold admits he knew, shoots the doctor and tries to kill Linda, but Rex stops him. Workers burn the crops, but a crow carries off a piece of contaminated plant. Genetically modified crops are the subject. The episode imagines an engineered corn whose trait escapes into a wild plant and then into animals and humans, causing tumours in those with high growth-hormone levels, and it ends on a warning that the contamination cannot be contained. It names real techniques of plant transformation, the particle gun and the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens, and criticises safety testing done only on DNA from middle-aged white men, which misses the people at risk. The scientist-executives of Macroseed are driven by profit, conceal what they know and are ready to kill to protect the product, while the investigator is a local veterinarian. The episode aired amid public controversy over genetically modified crops, including the StarLink corn recall of 2000. Gene flow from crops to related plants is a real subject of study, but a transgene jumping from corn to an unrelated weed and then into people, where it causes tumours, has no basis in science. The episode is best read as an expression of the era's anxieties about agricultural biotechnology.

title: Sole Survivor
themes: genetic engineering cloning human enhancement human experimentation
text: A year after his wife and young daughter died in a plane crash, the reporter Joe Carpenter meets Rose Tucker at their grave. Rose was on the passenger list but claims to have survived. She explains that she was a researcher on a secret project of the Quartermass organization, which created children with paranormal powers, and that she fled with one of them, a girl known as 21-21 who can heal people and let them see the afterlife, because the project's leaders wanted controllable children for military use. The girl saved them both from the crash by briefly moving them into another dimension. Rose is hunted by Victor Yates, a former CIA agent turned mercenary who has been killing scientists and witnesses. Rose is shot and dies. Another child from the project, the mind-controlling boy 89-58, forces Yates to shoot himself and dies too. Joe rescues the girl, names her Nina and starts a new life with her. Genetic engineering is behind the plot. The secret Quartermass project genetically engineers children, described in one summary as clones, to give them paranormal powers such as healing and mind control, with the aim of producing children who can be used and controlled as weapons. The leaders of the project and their hired killers are the villains: the plane crash that killed Joe's family and the murders of witnesses all follow from the hunt for the children. The only sympathetic scientist is Rose Tucker, a former researcher who betrays the project to save one of the children and dies for it. The film, based on a novel by Dean Koontz, uses genetic engineering as a source of supernatural powers, which has no basis in real science, and its message is a warning about experimenting on children for military ends.

title: The 6th Day
text: In the near future, animal cloning is commonplace, but human cloning is banned by "Sixth Day" laws. Charter pilot Adam Gibson is hired by Michael Drucker, billionaire owner of the cloning company Replacement Technologies, and undergoes what seem to be routine tests. That day, his partner Hank takes his place on the flight, and Drucker and Hank are killed by an anti-cloning assassin. Believing Adam was killed too, Drucker's people clone him, and Adam comes home to find a copy of himself living with his family. Hunted by Drucker's security team, he learns from the company's chief scientist, Dr. Griffin Weir, that his DNA and memories were recorded during the tests, that Drucker himself is a clone, and that Weir has repeatedly cloned his own wife, who is dying of cystic fibrosis. Adam and his clone join forces, destroy the facility and save the family; the clone starts a new life in Argentina. Human cloning drives the whole plot. The film imagines a mature cloning industry built on pet cloning ("RePet") and a secret capacity to clone adult humans in hours, complete with their memories. Its scientist, Dr. Weir, is a sympathetic but compromised figure: he serves Drucker's illegal programme because he hopes to save his wife, whom he keeps recreating as she dies of cystic fibrosis. Drucker, the businessman, is the true villain: he uses cloning to cheat death and keep control of his fortune, and has his clones engineered with deliberately shortened lifespans as insurance against betrayal. The film raises questions about identity, legal personhood and ownership of clones, which have no legal rights in its world. The science is fictional: real cloning produces an embryo that must develop and grow like any other, so an adult copy with the original's memories is impossible. Pet cloning, however, has been offered as a service since the 2010s, so the film's opening premise is less far-fetched than it seemed in 2000.

title: The Crimson Rivers
alt: Les Rivières pourpres Los ríos de color púrpura
themes: eugenics heredity genetic disease human experimentation
text: In Guernon, an isolated university town in the French Alps, Superintendent Pierre Niémans investigates the brutal murder of a professor and librarian whose eyes have been removed. Elsewhere, Inspector Max Kerkerian looks into the desecration of the grave of Judith Hérault, a girl who died in 1982. The two cases converge. Niémans learns that the town's academic elite has spent generations trying to breed a race of superior intellect, and that inbreeding has left the faculty with serious hereditary disorders. To keep the programme going, doctors at the university hospital have been secretly swapping healthy babies from the village for the faculty's own. Judith was the identical twin of Fanny Ferreira, who was swapped as a baby; their mother faked Judith's death after the family was pursued. The detectives trace the murders to the twins and confront them on a mountain, where a gunfight triggers an avalanche. The mystery rests on a eugenic breeding programme. The founders of Guernon's university, intellectuals rather than geneticists, set out to create a "super-race" defined by intellect by marrying within their own closed community. The film shows the classic consequence: generations of inbreeding produce serious genetic disorders, as an ophthalmologist explains to Niémans. Rather than abandon the project, the faculty and the hospital doctors replace their affected children with healthy babies taken from local families, keeping one of a pair of twins with her birth family as a control. The programme thus survives on stolen children and ends in murder. Its organisers act out of elitism and the belief that they are improving the species, and the film presents them as secretive and ruthless. The genetic premise is sound: related parents are more likely to carry the same harmful recessive variants, so their children more often inherit two copies and develop recessive disease.

title: The Other Me
text: Will Browning, a struggling high-school student, is threatened with being sent to a strict summer camp unless his grades improve. He orders a science kit for a school project, but the kit has been contaminated with a cloning formula belonging to two greedy scientists, and Will accidentally creates a copy of himself, whom he names Twoie. Twoie is more confident than Will and takes his place at school, where he becomes popular, makes peace with Will's rival, asks out the girl Will likes and draws Will's reclusive grandfather out of his shell. Will grows jealous, and Twoie decides to leave town after a school dance. Will then learns from the scientists that Twoie will weaken and die without a stabilising formula. He steals it, the scientists capture Will by mistake, and Twoie rescues him. The scientists are arrested, Will tells his family the truth, and they welcome Twoie into the household. This Disney Channel comedy, based on Mary C. Ryan's novel Me Two, uses cloning as a vehicle for a story about self-confidence. Will's clone appears as a teenager identical to him, and the differences in personality between the two boys make the point that identical genes do not mean identical people. The scientists who developed the cloning formula are cartoonish, greedy villains, and the dependence of the clone on a stabilising formula adds a note of fragility to artificial life. The ending, in which the family adopts the clone as a second son, treats him as a full person. Real cloning bears no resemblance to the film's: it cannot be done with a home science kit and does not produce a grown copy, but a new embryo that develops and ages normally. Genetics here is a playful premise rather than a subject the film examines.

title: What Lies Beneath
text: Claire Spencer, a former cellist, lives in a lakeside house in Vermont with her husband Norman, a research scientist at the local university. After her daughter leaves for college, Claire begins to experience strange events: doors open by themselves, the bathtub fills with water and she sees a woman's face reflected in it. She first suspects that her neighbour has murdered his wife, but the wife turns up alive. Claire then finds that the ghost is Madison Elizabeth Frank, a young woman who disappeared a year earlier, and she recovers the repressed memory that Norman had an affair with Madison, one of his students. Norman first claims that Madison killed herself, then confesses that he murdered her when she threatened to expose the affair, and tries to kill Claire by paralysing her with a drug and drowning her in the bath. Claire escapes, and in the lake Madison's body seems to drag Norman to his death. Genetics is only the professional background of the villain in this ghost story. Norman Spencer is described by reviewers as a brilliant geneticist who has taken a prestigious chair at the university where his late father taught, and he does laboratory research; one critic calls him a "brilliant (i.e. unstable) geneticist". His science plays no part in the plot apart from his access to laboratory chemicals: he paralyses Claire with an anaesthetic. The film draws on an old association between scientific brilliance and moral coldness. Norman is ambitious and outwardly charming, has an affair with a student and kills her to protect his career, and then tries to kill his wife. Nothing in the story concerns heredity, DNA or genetic research, so the title belongs in the database mainly as an example of how a scientist, and specifically a geneticist, is portrayed on screen.

title: X-Men
text: In a world where some people are born as mutants with superhuman powers, US Senator Robert Kelly campaigns for a Mutant Registration Act. The telepath Charles Xavier, who runs a school for young mutants, fears the response of his old friend Erik Lehnsherr, known as Magneto, a Holocaust survivor who can control magnetic fields. Rogue, a teenager whose touch absorbs other people's life force and powers, runs away from home and meets Logan, or Wolverine, a mutant with metal claws and accelerated healing. After the members of Magneto's Brotherhood attack them, both are taken to Xavier's school, home of the X-Men. Magneto has built a machine that generates radiation able to induce mutations in normal humans; tested on Senator Kelly, it eventually kills him. Magneto plans to use it on the world leaders gathered at a summit on Ellis Island, powering it through Rogue at the cost of her life, but the X-Men defeat the Brotherhood on the Statue of Liberty and destroy the machine, and Logan saves Rogue by transferring his healing power to her. Genetics is present as the premise rather than as science. Mutants are people born with mutations that give them extraordinary powers, usually emerging in adolescence; the plot is about how society treats them, from the registration law proposed by Senator Kelly to Magneto's plan to force mutation on world leaders with radiation. No geneticist appears: the leading characters are mutants themselves, and Magneto's machine is the only experiment in the story, one that kills its first human subject. The film works as an allegory of discrimination against minorities. It opens in Auschwitz, linking the registration of mutants with Nazi persecution, and director Bryan Singer described the mutants as outsiders whose difference appears at puberty, an allegory that actor Ian McKellen read as being about gay people. Real mutations do not produce abilities of this kind, and radiation causes random DNA damage rather than useful new traits.

title: Geneshaft
text: In the late 23rd century, genetic engineering defines human society. A totalitarian world government has kept peace for 200 years by controlling all births and designing each person's genes for their role in society; lifespan is limited to 45 years, family structures have been abolished and love and lust removed. Women outnumber men nine to one, since men are thought to carry irreducibly destructive tendencies, and each man is watched by an emotionless female "Register". Five years after a giant ring-shaped object appears near Earth and devastates a space station and much of the planet's surface, a crew of genetically engineered men and women aboard the spaceship Bilkis sets out to investigate the ring and the alien technology found on Ganymede. Fighting the ring's machines with the giant robot Shaft, the crew meet people and situations that lead them to doubt whether they are as superior as they believe, and how perfect their society really is. This anime series is built around a society organised entirely by genetic engineering, and it explores the consequences of that technology dominating human life. The state controls reproduction and designs every individual for a function, people are ranked by the quality of their DNA, and those of supposedly inferior gene types, such as the main character Mika, are openly mocked. Emotions and family ties are engineered away, and the sex ratio is set by policy on the belief that male genes carry aggression. Some characters are defined by their pride in their "perfect" DNA, while a rebel faction wants to restore humanity's natural order. The series is therefore a dystopia about eugenics and genetic determinism, in which the crew's journey leads them to question the system. The idea that complex traits such as leadership, personality or emotional life could be precisely designed into people goes far beyond real genetics, in which such traits depend on many genes and on environment.

title: Jurassic Park III
text: Palaeontologist Alan Grant is struggling to fund his research on the intelligence of Velociraptors when Paul and Amanda Kirby, apparently a wealthy couple, offer him money in exchange for guiding an aerial tour of Isla Sorna, the island where the company InGen bred its dinosaurs. Once there, the Kirbys force the plane to land; they are in fact a divorced couple searching for their son Eric, who went missing near the island while parasailing. After a Spinosaurus destroys their plane, the group crosses the island, chased by the Spinosaurus, by Pteranodons in a giant aviary and by a pack of Velociraptors. The raptors are pursuing them because Grant's assistant Billy has stolen two of their eggs, hoping to sell them to fund the excavation. They find Eric alive, return the eggs to the raptors, and are finally rescued by the US Navy and Marines, summoned by Grant's former colleague Ellie Sattler. Genetics is the background rather than the subject of this sequel. The dinosaurs on Isla Sorna were created by InGen using the franchise's premise of cloning dinosaurs from DNA preserved in blood-filled mosquitoes trapped in amber, filling the gaps with frog DNA. No geneticist appears on screen; the film's scientist is a palaeontologist who distrusts the whole project. In an early scene Grant tells his students that real scientists make real discoveries in the rocks, and that what John Hammond and InGen created were "genetically engineered theme park monsters, nothing more and nothing less". Consistent with research at the time, the film's Velociraptors were given feather-like quills. Cloning dinosaurs is not possible: claims of recovering dinosaur DNA were later attributed to contamination, and the oldest DNA ever recovered is about two million years old, far younger than the dinosaurs.

title: Lineage
alt: Linaje Star Trek: Voyager, season 7, episode 12
themes: genetic engineering gene therapy genetic discrimination hybrids chimeras genetic disease
text: B'Elanna Torres, Voyager's half-Klingon chief engineer, discovers that she is pregnant by her husband, Tom Paris. The Doctor finds that the seven-week-old fetus has a genetic defect that causes an abnormal curvature of the spine in Klingon females, the same condition B'Elanna had surgically corrected as a child, and proposes to fix it by genetic resequencing. When a holographic projection shows that her daughter will have Klingon forehead ridges, B'Elanna, haunted by memories of being teased as a child and of her human father leaving the family, asks the Doctor to remove the baby's Klingon traits as well. Tom and the Doctor object, and Captain Janeway treats it as a matter for the couple. The Doctor suddenly changes his mind and declares the procedure medically necessary; Icheb finds an error in his assessment, Seven discovers that his program has been tampered with, and Tom stops the operation in time. B'Elanna admits her fear that Tom will leave her, the alterations are undone, and she asks the Doctor to be the child's godfather. The episode is built around the difference between treating a disease and changing who a child will be. Correcting the inherited spinal defect is presented as uncontroversial medicine, but B'Elanna's wish to erase her daughter's Klingon features, so that she will not be rejected as she was, turns gene editing into a way of avoiding discrimination by changing the child rather than the society. Tom and the Doctor stand for acceptance of the child as she is, and the Doctor's integrity is tested when his program is secretly altered. B'Elanna's motives are shown with sympathy, rooted in childhood pain and fear of abandonment, and she finally accepts her daughter's heritage. The distinction between therapy and enhancement or cosmetic selection is central to real bioethical debates on germline editing, and the episode also touches on hybrid ancestry, since the child is a quarter Klingon.

title: Lion's Den
text: Peter Shotwell once dreamed of the Olympics but blew out his knee, while his best friend Jon went on to become an international athletics star. Peter is now the coach of the Lewisborough Lions, his old high school's wrestling team, which sits at the bottom of the league, and his son Morris, a member of the team, resents his failures. Jon offers him Nuriflex 500, a new performance-enhancing drug he says contains scientifically balanced nutrients. Under pressure from the principal and his own son, Peter agrees to a trial. The team soon rises to the top, but the drug has horrific side effects: the wrestlers become aggressive and their eyes and teeth turn animal-like, and they kill a rival coach who threatens to expose them. When Peter tries to take them off the drug, the team, including his son, kills him. Genetics plays a secondary role in this episode about doping in school sports. The drug Nuriflex 500 is said to be spliced with animal DNA, big cat DNA according to the episode summary on Wikipedia, and the Outer Limits fan wiki describes it as based on animal hormones; the young wrestlers gradually take on animal features and predatory behaviour. The story uses this as a Jekyll-and-Hyde metaphor for steroids and the pressure to win, and its moral concerns parents and coaches rather than scientists, who never appear: the drug comes through Jon, a former champion turned promoter. The idea that taking DNA in a pill transfers animal traits has no basis in biology, since ingested DNA is digested like any other food. The episode's real-life counterpart is the fear of gene doping in sport, the misuse of gene therapy to enhance performance, which the World Anti-Doping Agency added to its list of banned practices in 2003.

title: Mimic 2
text: Four years after the events of Mimic, three men are found mutilated in New York, their faces removed. Detective Klaski discovers that all of them knew Remi Panos, an entomologist teaching at an inner-city high school. Klaski first suspects Remi, until he sees the creature that has been stalking her: an intelligent mutant insect that can take the face of its last victim and wants to mate with her. Remi, Klaski and two students are trapped inside the school as the creature hunts them, while a special forces unit led by a man called Darksuit prepares to gas the building. Remi escapes, but the creature has killed Klaski and taken his form, and it follows her home. Remi decapitates it in her apartment, yet the creature is not dead, leaving her and a student wondering what to do next. Genetics appears here only as backstory. The creature belongs to the "Judas breed", the insect created by genetic engineering in the first film to wipe out disease-carrying cockroaches, which survived and evolved into a predator able to mimic human appearance. Mimic 2 itself focuses on a horror chase in a school and does not show the creation of the creatures, a geneticist or any laboratory work; its scientist character, Remi, is an entomologist and the creature's target, not its maker. The premise implicitly warns about the unintended consequences of releasing engineered organisms, but the film does not develop the idea. Its connection to genetics is weak, and it may not merit inclusion in the database.

title: Mutant X
themes: genetic engineering mutants human experimentation hybrids chimeras genetic discrimination
text: Mutant X follows a team of "new mutants", people with extraordinary powers who were used as test subjects in covert genetic experiments run by Genomex. Their leader, Adam Kane, was the chief bio-geneticist behind those experiments and formed Mutant X to atone for his mistakes; he uses a stolen database to find other new mutants, protect them and help them control their powers. The original team includes Jesse Kilmartin, who can change his body's density; Shalimar Fox, a "feline feral" with combined human and animal DNA; the empath Emma DeLauro; and Brennan Mulwray, who generates electricity. Their main enemy is Mason Eckhart, Genomex's former security chief, who heads the Genetic Security Agency and hunts new mutants to control them. Another adversary is Gabriel Ashlocke, the psychopathic "patient zero" of the experiments. The series ran for three seasons, from 2001 to 2004, and was cancelled abruptly, ending on a cliffhanger. Genetic engineering is the premise of the series: every new mutant owes his or her powers to the experiments of Genomex, described as covert and government-backed, and categories such as "feral", "molecular" or "elemental" mutants reflect the different kinds of genetic manipulation they received. Some carry recombined human and animal DNA, and the new mutants live with medical problems derived from the procedures; Jesse is said to be the only one to have outlived his "expiration date". The show offers two contrasting portraits of geneticists. Adam Kane is a repentant creator who turns his knowledge to caring for his creations, looking for treatments for their conditions; Eckhart and the Genetic Security Agency represent the institution that wants to keep them under control, and other scientists, such as a biogeneticist recruited to make a mind-controlling toxin, serve those aims. The series is action-adventure in the mould of X-Men, and its genetics is fantasy, but its theme of people harmed by secret medical experiments and then treated as a threat gives the show its moral frame.

title: No Ordinary Baby
text: Also known as After Amy, this television film follows Linda Sinclair, an ambitious reporter who gets the scoop on the birth of the first human clone. As the story breaks, a media and public furore develops around the pregnancy and the unborn child, and Dr. Amanda Gordon, the physician responsible for the cloning, sees her reputation and career put at risk. The film follows the consequences of the coverage for everyone involved, including the baby, and the reporter's growing ethical doubts about her role. It is based on "Carbon Copy: Meet the First Human Clone", a 1998 short story by Richard Kadrey published in Wired magazine. Human reproductive cloning is the subject of the film, approached through its social reception rather than its science. The story imagines the announcement of the first cloned human baby and focuses on the media frenzy, public outrage and professional backlash that follow, and on the damage they do to the doctor who performed the procedure and to the child. The scientist is a physician presented as the target of controversy rather than as a villain. Made in 2001, a few years after the cloning of Dolly the sheep, when claims of imminent human cloning were in the news, it reflects the debate of its time. Monkeys were first cloned by the Dolly method in 2018, but human reproductive cloning is prohibited in many countries, including Australia and Canada. Detailed plot information on this film is scarce, so this description relies on short synopses.

title: Replica
text: Zach and Nora Griffiths, scientists played by Peter Outerbridge and Sherilyn Fenn, run a biotech firm with a business partner that is close to producing cloned human organs. Nora has developed a "neuro-mapper" that can copy a mind into a cloned brain, and when their partner orders the program shut down she tests the untried device on herself and suffers a seizure. A year later she lies in a coma, which Zach blames on a drowning accident. Pressed to withdraw life support, he illegally clones her as an adult, with the reluctant help of a colleague, using the company's organ replicator, archived body scans and her stored memories. The clone, who believes she is Nora, grows jealous of the comatose original, and then Nora unexpectedly wakes up. Both women share the same memories and both claim Zach; the couple plan to erase the clone's memory, and the two Noras fight in the lab. Zach's solution is to clone himself: in the final scene the two couples share a skiing holiday and toast "to science". The episode is built around human reproductive cloning, used here to replace a loved one rather than to create a new person. The scientist is a grieving husband who misuses his company's technology and breaks the law for personal reasons, after his wife's own reckless self-experiment caused her coma, and the story turns on the consequences of treating a clone as a substitute: once the original wife wakes up, the copy has her own claim to the life she was given. In this way the episode raises the question, common in Outer Limits stories, of whether a duplicate is a person with her own rights, although its almost comic ending, in which the husband clones himself so that each Nora has a partner, sidesteps the dilemma. Its science is speculative: real cloning would produce a genetically identical embryo that would have to develop and grow up, not an adult double, and the episode instead assembles the body from old scans and supplies the mind by uploading recorded memories, which is not genetics at all.

title: Replicant
text: Edward "the Torch" Garrotte is a serial killer who murders mothers and sets them on fire. Seattle detective Jake Riley has hunted him for three years without success. Shortly after Jake retires, a secret government agency recruits him for a special project: it has cloned Garrotte from DNA found at a crime scene. The clone, the Replicant, has the body of a forty-year-old but the mind of a child, together with fragments of Garrotte's memories and a telepathic link to him. Jake must train him to track the killer down. Jake treats him roughly, but the Replicant sees Jake as family and gradually learns about the world. He refuses Garrotte's invitation to join him and discovers that he is not a killer. In the final fight in a hospital furnace room, Jake shoots Garrotte. The Replicant seems to die in an explosion, but weeks later Jake finds he is alive and leading a normal life. Cloning and the question of nature versus nurture are central to this action film. A government agency creates an adult clone of a serial killer from crime-scene DNA, hoping that his genetic identity will give him access to the murderer's memories and help catch him. The film plays on the fear that a clone of a killer will inherit his violence, but argues the opposite: brought up, however harshly, by a policeman who becomes his only family, the clone develops a gentle personality and rejects his original. A flashback shows that Garrotte's violence comes from childhood abuse, reinforcing the idea that environment shaped him. The scientists are faceless government operatives who use the clone as a tool. Real clones are born as babies and grow up normally; they cannot be produced as adults, and memories are not stored in DNA or shared telepathically between genetically identical people.

title: Rite of Passage
themes: genetic engineering human experimentation human enhancement
text: On the fourth anniversary of her arrival on Earth, Cassandra collapses and asks to be taken to a forest; Dr. Janet Fraiser finds that a retrovirus is transforming her DNA. Footage from an earlier mission to Cassandra's home planet, Hanka, shows that its young people used to collapse at sixteen, go to a forest and return cured. SG-1 visits the forest and finds a hidden Goa'uld laboratory and a tablet reading 'Hok'tar', 'advanced human'. As Cassandra develops telekinetic powers, Daniel Jackson links the case to the System Lord Nirrti, who experimented on Hanka's people for generations to create a perfect Goa'uld host and wiped them out to hide her success. Nirrti, who has followed the team to Earth while invisible, is captured. Under Fraiser's threat she cures Cassandra in exchange for her freedom, warning that she will not abandon her research. The episode turns on a multi-generational genetic experiment. The Goa'uld Nirrti has been engineering the people of Hanka to produce the 'Hok'tar', an advanced human who would make a perfect host for a Goa'uld. A retrovirus rewrites the DNA of adolescents, who are taken to her hidden laboratory, studied and returned; Cassandra, the last survivor of Hanka, is the culmination, and her transformation brings collapse and telekinetic powers. Nirrti is a clear villain, experimenting on a whole population without consent and exterminating it to protect her secret; she cures Cassandra only under threat and promises to continue. On the other side, the base physician, Dr. Fraiser, diagnoses the retrovirus and fights for her adopted daughter. Retroviruses do insert genes into host cells, which makes them real tools of gene therapy, but genes that confer telekinesis are science fiction.

title: Tail Sting
text: A low-budget creature feature. After a scheduled flight is cancelled, a group of passengers boards a charter from Melbourne, Australia, to Los Angeles. In the hold is a cargo of genetically engineered scorpion hybrids that a team of scientists is taking to the United States to find funding for their research. A double-dealing scientist on the team, working for a rival company, sneaks into the hold to steal the samples, and turbulence smashes the jars. The scorpions, grown to giant size, attack passengers and crew, kill most of the flight crew and chew through vital wiring. The surviving passengers, led by the pilot and one of the scientists, must fight off the creatures and bring the crippled plane down safely, while the traitor tries to protect the scorpions so that he can sell them. Genetic engineering is little more than the pretext for the monsters. The scorpions are hybrids created by a research team, and one scientist explains that they were crossed with DNA from prehistoric giant scorpions, a choice reviewers note the film never justifies. Scientists appear in several roles: an older scientist who mostly delivers exposition, a female researcher who is one of the heroes, and a treacherous colleague who sells out to a rival corporation and endangers everyone to save the creatures. The film thus repeats the familiar pattern of the genetic monster unleashed by commercial greed rather than by research itself. Scientifically it is implausible: DNA from extinct arthropods has not been recovered, and giant body size in insects and scorpions is constrained by how they breathe and by their exoskeletons, not just by their genes.

title: The Accidental Spy
alt: 特務迷城 Espía por accidente
text: Buck Yuen, a Hong Kong exercise-equipment salesman and orphan, becomes a local celebrity after foiling a bank robbery. A man named Manny Liu tells him that a dying Korean, Park Won-sung, is searching for his long-lost son, and Yuen travels to Seoul, where Park offers him his estate if he can win a game of clues. Following the clues to Istanbul, Yuen is attacked by thugs demanding 'the thing'. Two CIA agents, Carmen and Philip, explain that it is Anthrax II, a biological weapon deadlier than anthrax that has already killed many people in Anatolia, and that the crime lord Lee Sang Zen wants to buy it. Yuen finds two vials in a church basement and trades them for Yong, a woman enslaved by Zen, but Zen kills her. Yuen recovers the weapon in a road chase in which Zen dies, and learns that the whole adventure was a CIA test to recruit him as a spy. A stolen bioweapon is the object everyone in this Jackie Chan action comedy is chasing. In the original Hong Kong version, 'the thing' is Anthrax II, a biological weapon deadlier than anthrax that has already killed many villagers in Anatolia; the film opens with scientists looking for a cure for the apparent pneumonia outbreak and being murdered by terrorists. A crime lord wants to buy the agent and the CIA wants to secure it, and the hero ends up retrieving it for the agency. Nobody in the film is shown making the weapon, and the story treats it purely as a deadly MacGuffin. In the international version distributed by Dimension Films the bioweapon was replaced by 'Opio Maxa', a super-potent opium, which removes the film's only connection with biology.

title: The Clone
text: In the early 1980s, Jade, a young Muslim woman raised in Rio de Janeiro, moves to Fez, Morocco, to live with her strict uncle Ali after her mother's death. There she falls in love with Lucas Ferraz, a wealthy Brazilian visiting with his identical twin Diogo, their father Leônidas and the twins' godfather, the geneticist Augusto Albieri. Their romance defies her family and religion. When Diogo dies in a helicopter crash, Lucas abandons his plan to run away with Jade, who marries Said. The grieving Albieri secretly uses Lucas's cells to create the first human clone and implants the embryo in Deusa, a patient who believes she is receiving ordinary artificial insemination. Twenty years later, Lucas and Jade, both unhappily married, meet again, while the clone, Léo, has grown into the image of the young Lucas and falls for Jade. When the cloning is discovered, Leônidas and Deusa fight in court over Léo, who struggles to find his place in the world. Human cloning is one of the telenovela's main storylines, alongside a cross-cultural romance between Brazil and the Muslim world. The geneticist Augusto Albieri is a sympathetic but tragic figure: grief at the death of his godson, combined with the ambition to be the first to clone a human, leads him to create a clone in secret and to implant the embryo in a woman without her knowledge, a serious violation of consent. The story then explores the consequences for the clone himself, who shares Lucas's genome but not his life, and for the families who claim him, including a legal fight over parenthood. Writer Glória Perez said she was inspired by Dolly the sheep and wanted to contrast a Muslim world submissive to God with a West that installed geneticists as new creators of life. Human reproductive cloning remains unachieved and widely opposed, but the telenovela's central point holds: a clone would be a much younger genetic twin with a life of his own, as Léo is.

title: Towelie
text: Stan's mother buys the boys an Okama Gamesphere console, and they plan to play all weekend, but they are pestered by Towelie, a talking towel who appears whenever water is mentioned, reminds them to bring a towel and asks if they want to get high. The console is stolen, and a ransom call demands that they hand Towelie over at a gas station at night. There an old man from Tynacorp, the company that made Towelie, receives him, and the United States military ambushes the meeting. For the rest of the episode the boys shuttle between a secret military base and Tynacorp, caring only about their console while a conspiracy unfolds in which aliens plan to take over the Earth with genetically modified towels. The Tynacorp building is blown up, Kenny falls into molten metal, and Towelie defeats the evil prototype towel GS-401 and saves the boys. Genetics is the label on the episode's parody conspiracy. Towelie is a genetically modified towel made by the company Tynacorp, aliens plan to conquer the Earth with genetically modified towels, and, according to the Russian Wikipedia summary, the military wants to capture Towelie to copy his DNA for weapons of mass destruction. Corporation, military and aliens are all shown as scheming and violent, and the episode resolves the plot by blowing up the building. The science is never more than a phrase: the point is to spoof conspiracy thrillers and, as Wikipedia notes, to mock South Park's own merchandising through a deliberately shallow character who exists to sell products. The boys' total indifference to the plot is the main joke.

title: WXIII: Patlabor the Movie 3
alt: WXIII 機動警察パトレイバー WXIII: Patlabor la película 3
text: In 2000, after a military transport plane crashes into Tokyo Bay, Labors (giant work robots) and people around the bay start being attacked. Two police detectives, the veteran Shinichiro Hata and the young Takeshi Kusumi, investigate with the help of Captain Goto's Special Vehicles Section 2. Clues lead them to suspicious cargo from the crashed plane and, after a couple is killed near the Babylon industrial zone, to a huge creature that hides in the bay and is drawn to the ultrasonic hum of Labor motors. The trail points to a biological weapons project backed by a Japanese Self-Defense Forces general and a US Army colonel, and to Saeko Misaki, a researcher at the Tokyo Biomedical Research Institute whose six-year-old daughter died of cancer. Misaki has grown the monster, called WXIII, from her daughter's cancer cells and calls it 'that child'. In the final battle SV2's Labors strip the creature's armour and Isao Ota kills it with a single virus-warhead round. The monster is an artificial organism created in the laboratory. Saeko Misaki, a chief researcher at a biomedical institute, synthesizes WXIII from the cancer cells of her dead daughter combined with the 'Nishiwaki Cell' discovered by her father; the creature keeps mammalian and human traits, which the film uses to suggest it is in some sense her child. Her motive is grief: an obsessive attempt to bring her daughter back. The project is funded by a Japanese general and a US colonel as part of a weapons series, and the military conspirators intend to use it to attack strategic targets and spread panic. The film thus pairs a tragic, transgressive experiment with the military exploitation of biological research, and the creature's killings drive the story. Growing a giant intelligent animal from human tumour cells is fantasy; the cell line recalls immortal cancer lines such as HeLa, but the film does not make that link explicit.

title: 28 Days Later
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic animal experimentation post apocalyptic
text: Animal rights activists break into a laboratory in Cambridge where chimpanzees are kept in an abnormally aggressive state. Despite a scientist's warning that the animals are infected with "rage", they free one, which attacks them; within seconds the infected become violent, and the virus spreads across Britain. Twenty-eight days later, Jim, a bicycle courier, wakes from a coma in a deserted London hospital. Rescued from the infected by the survivors Selena and Mark, he finds that his parents have killed themselves, and after Mark is infected, he and Selena join the taxi driver Frank and his daughter Hannah. A radio broadcast leads them to a military blockade near Manchester, where Frank is infected and shot. The soldiers who take in the others turn out to be planning to keep the women as sex slaves. Jim escapes, releases an infected soldier to attack the troops, and rescues Selena and Hannah; weeks later, the three wave a giant "HELLO" banner at a passing jet from a remote cottage, where the infected are dying of starvation. Genetics plays a minor role. The film's starting point is a pathogen kept in a research laboratory, where scientists hold chimpanzees infected with an aggression-inducing "rage" virus; its accidental release by activists who do not believe the scientists' warning causes the catastrophe. The film does not explain how the virus was created or what the research was for, and the scientists appear only briefly; the rest of the story deals with survival and with the violence of the survivors themselves, especially the soldiers. Rather than supernatural zombies, the infected were conceived as victims of a biological contagion: Danny Boyle drew on real diseases, especially Ebola and aspects of rabies, and on the British outbreaks of BSE and foot-and-mouth disease of the time. An abandoned ending showed the laboratory that created the virus. The rage virus is fictional, and its near-instant effect is a dramatic device.

title: Black Mask 2: City of Masks
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human enhancement human experimentation
text: Kan Fung, a former super-soldier who escaped from the organisation that gave him his abilities, fights crime in a futuristic city as Black Mask while looking for a geneticist who can cure him. A wrestling promoter's stars, Iguana, Chameleon, Snake, Wolf and others, turn out to have been injected with animal DNA by Dr. Moloch, which lets them transform into human-animal hybrids. After Iguana dies in a fight with Black Mask, the others seek revenge. Black Mask contacts the geneticist Dr. Marco Leung, but is himself injected with animal DNA and becomes a tiger hybrid until Leung finds a chemical that reverses the change. In the climax, his old enemy Lang, who has overpowered Moloch, plants a bomb capable of altering the DNA of everyone in the city. The hybrid wrestlers are killed one by one, the invisible Chameleon sacrificing herself to hand Black Mask the bomb, and he defeats Lang and defuses it. Leung finally rides off with Kan, implying she has cured him. Genetics is the source of the film's monsters and its central threat. The villain scientist, Dr. Moloch, injects wrestlers with animal DNA to improve their performance, and they gain the power to turn into human-animal hybrids, at the cost of losing control of their bodies. The climax revolves around a "DNA bomb" designed to mutate the population of a whole city. Scientists appear on both sides: Moloch works for profit and for a criminal organisation, while the geneticist Dr. Leung is the one who can undo the damage and cure the hero, so genetics is shown both as a weapon and as a cure. The genetics is pure comic-book fantasy. Real gene therapy modifies genes in some of a patient's cells to treat a disease, and its effects are limited to the cells it reaches; adding animal DNA to an adult cannot make a body take on another species' shape or abilities, let alone switch between forms at will.

title: Blade II
themes: eugenics genetic engineering engineered pathogens mutants human experimentation
text: In Prague, the half-vampire hunter Blade rescues his mentor Whistler, who had been turned into a vampire, and cures him. A pandemic is turning vampires into "Reapers", ravenous mutant creatures whose infectious bite transforms both vampires and humans, spread by the first carrier, Jared Nomak. The vampire overlord Eli Damaskinos proposes a truce, and Blade joins the Bloodpack, an elite vampire squad trained to kill him. They discover that Reapers are immune to most vampire weaknesses except ultraviolet light and destroy their nest, but most of the team die. Damaskinos then captures Blade and reveals that the Reapers are the result of his own attempts to engineer a stronger breed of vampire without its natural weaknesses; Nomak, the first Reaper, is his son, whom he regards as a failure. He plans to use Blade's blood to create vampires immune to sunlight. Blade escapes, Nomak kills his father, and Blade defeats Nomak. Genetics plays a background role. The Reapers are presented as the product of a vampire lord's experiments to breed a superior race free of vampires' weaknesses, a eugenic project that fails and produces an uncontrollable plague. Damaskinos is a ruthless creator who experiments on his own son and dismisses him as a failure, and his daughter Nyssa, who dissects a Reaper to study its anatomy, turns against him when she sees how he treats his children. Blade himself is a human–vampire hybrid whose blood Damaskinos wants in order to create vampires that can walk in daylight. The Reaper condition spreads like an infectious disease, so the film mixes ideas of engineering, mutation and contagion without explaining any of them in genetic terms. It is mainly an action-horror film, and its relevance to genetics is limited to this "engineered master race" motif.

title: Clone High
text: This animated sitcom is set in a high school in the fictional town of Exclamation, USA, populated by teenage clones of famous historical figures created in the 1980s. Officially the school is a military experiment run by the Secret Board of Shadowy Figures, which plans to harness the clones' talents for the US military, while the principal, mad scientist Cinnamon J. Scudworth, secretly wants to use them for a clone-themed amusement park. The show follows the clones of Abe Lincoln, Joan of Arc, Cleopatra, JFK and Gandhi through teenage crushes, exams and parties, centred on Abe's choice between the vain Cleopatra and Joan, who loves him. The first season (2002–2003) ended with the clones abducted on prom night. In the 2023 revival on HBO Max, they are unfrozen twenty years later and return to Clone High, where they meet a new generation of clones, including Harriet Tubman and Frida Kahlo. Human cloning is the comic premise of the series rather than its subject. Each clone has the genome of a historical figure, and much of the humour comes from the gap between the "clonefathers" and their teenage copies: Gandhi is a party animal, JFK a narcissistic womaniser, Abe Lincoln an insecure romantic. The characters' struggle to live up to, or rebel against, their genetic originals is a running joke about the limits of genetic determinism; personality, the show suggests, is not written in DNA. The scientists are cartoon villains: a government board that wants to use the clones as military assets and a principal who sees them as amusement-park attractions, a satire of the idea of breeding people for a purpose. The series is mainly a parody of teen dramas such as Dawson's Creek. Its Gandhi character provoked protests in India in 2003, and he was left out of the revival.

title: Die Another Day
text: In the twentieth James Bond film, Bond infiltrates a North Korean base to stop Colonel Tan-Sun Moon from trading weapons for African conflict diamonds. Moon appears to die, and Bond is captured and tortured for fourteen months before being exchanged for the terrorist Zao. Suspended by M, Bond escapes and follows Zao to a clinic in Cuba that uses DNA restructuring to give clients new appearances; with the NSA agent Jinx he finds Zao in mid-treatment, and diamonds that lead to the British billionaire Gustav Graves. In Iceland, Graves unveils Icarus, an orbital mirror that focuses sunlight into a weapon, and Bond discovers that Graves is Colonel Moon, transformed at the Cuban clinic, and that MI6 agent Miranda Frost is the traitor who betrayed him. Graves plans to use Icarus to clear a path through the Korean Demilitarized Zone for an invasion of the South. Bond and Jinx stop him aboard his plane, where Graves and Frost are killed. The genetic element is a fictional gene therapy for disguise. The Clínica Álvarez in Cuba, run by Dr. Alvarez, offers wanted people a permanent new identity through DNA restructuring, which changes their physical features. The North Korean Colonel Moon has used it to become the British billionaire Gustav Graves, which is the central twist of the plot, and his henchman Zao, whose face was studded with diamonds by Bond's bomb, is found in the middle of his own treatment. The clinic is a service for criminals and terrorists, and its director is killed when the heroes raid it; the technology appears only as a tool of villainy. Critics counted the gene therapy among the film's outlandish quasi-science-fiction elements, alongside an invisible car and a solar weapon. Real gene therapy cannot rebuild an adult's face or change his ethnicity, so the idea is pure fantasy.

title: Godzilla Against Mechagodzilla
alt: ゴジラ×メカゴジラ Godzilla x Mechagodzilla
text: Forty-five years after the first Godzilla was killed in 1954, a new Godzilla attacks Japan, and Lieutenant Akane Yashiro of the Anti-Megalosaurus Force panics during the battle, causing the deaths of her comrades. The government assembles scientists, including Dr. Tokumitsu Yuhara, a single father who specialises in building robots from animal DNA, to build a cyborg weapon, Kiryu, around the skeleton of the original Godzilla. Akane becomes its pilot despite the resentment of Lieutenant Hayama, whose brother died in the earlier attack. When Godzilla attacks Yokohama, its roar awakens memories in Kiryu's bones and the machine runs berserk through the city. Akane grows close to Yuhara and his daughter Sara. In a final battle at Shinagawa, with the remote control knocked out, Akane pilots Kiryu from inside, pushes Godzilla out to sea and fires the Absolute Zero Cannon; Godzilla retreats wounded and Kiryu, badly damaged, is repaired. Genetics enters through the construction of Kiryu, the 'Mechagodzilla' of the title. Dr. Yuhara, an expert in building robots from animal DNA, uses the skeleton of the original Godzilla as the frame of a cyborg weapon for Japan's defence, and the film states that Kiryu shares Godzilla's DNA. This genetic link gives the machine a will of its own: when the new Godzilla roars, Kiryu recovers memories of its past life and goes on a rampage, destroying the city it was built to protect. Yuhara is a sympathetic scientist working for the state, and the weapon ultimately drives Godzilla back. Critics read the film as a reflection on the limits of technology and bio-engineering and on losing control of one's creations. The idea that memories or will survive in the DNA of bones is pure fantasy.

title: Jurassic Bark
text: At a museum exhibit, Fry is shocked to find a fossilised dog that he recognises as Seymour, the pet he had in the 20th century before he was frozen. After he protests outside the museum for three days, he is given the fossil. Professor Farnsworth explains that, because the dog fossilised unusually fast, a DNA sample can be used to produce a clone, and even to restore Seymour's personality and memories. Bender, jealous of the attention Fry gives the dog, throws the fossil into a pit of lava, then regrets it and dives in to recover it. As the cloning begins, the computer reports that Seymour died at the age of 15, twelve years after Fry was frozen. Believing the dog moved on and forgot him, Fry stops the process. A closing flashback shows that Seymour in fact spent the rest of his life waiting faithfully outside Panucci's Pizza for Fry to return. Cloning from ancient DNA is the device of the plot. The Professor proposes to recover DNA from a fossil and grow a new Seymour, and adds that the clone would also have the dog's personality and memories, which is the science-fiction part: a clone shares its donor's genes, not its experiences. The computer's ability to read Seymour's age at death from the sample is another comic liberty. The episode uses the idea not to explore science but to raise an emotional question, whether bringing back a lost companion would be for the dog's sake or Fry's. The Professor is the series' usual eccentric scientist, here a helpful one. Pets have been cloned in real life, but mammalian cloning requires intact, viable cell nuclei rather than DNA alone, so a fossil could not serve; the episode itself presents Seymour's rapid fossilisation as a special case.

title: Lilo & Stitch
text: On the planet Turo, the scientist Dr. Jumba Jookiba is convicted by the United Galactic Federation of illegal genetic experimentation. His creation, Experiment 626, an aggressive, almost indestructible creature built for destruction, is sentenced to exile but escapes and crash-lands on Kauaʻi, Hawaii, where it poses as a dog at an animal shelter. Lilo, a lonely girl being raised by her older sister Nani after their parents' death, adopts him and names him Stitch. Stitch's destructive behaviour costs Nani her job and strengthens the doubts of the social worker Cobra Bubbles about her ability to care for Lilo. Jumba and the agent Pleakley are sent to recapture him, and their fights destroy the family's house. When Captain Gantu captures Lilo, Stitch, who has learned from her the Hawaiian idea of ʻohana, or family, asks for help, and Jumba joins in the rescue. The Grand Councilwoman lets Stitch stay on Earth with Lilo, and Jumba and Pleakley join the family. Genetic engineering explains Stitch's existence and his nature. Jumba Jookiba is a stock mad scientist made comic: an alien geneticist convicted for illegal experiments who designed Experiment 626 as a weapon, with great strength, near-indestructibility and an urge to destroy. The film then sets up a contest between design and upbringing: Stitch was engineered to destroy, but Lilo's affection and the idea of ʻohana gradually change his behaviour, and by the end his creator, too, has become part of the family. The message is that a creature's genetic programming does not fix its destiny, a light-hearted version of the nature-versus-nurture debate. The film does not dwell on the science, and Stitch's abilities are pure fantasy. According to the filmmakers, the relationship of creator and creation was not part of the original concept: Stitch began as the leader of an intergalactic gang with Jumba as a former crony, and the two were recast as scientist and experiment after test screenings.

title: Minority Report
text: In 2054, Washington, D.C.'s experimental Precrime unit arrests murderers before they act, using the visions of three "precogs" who foresee homicides. Its chief, John Anderton, still grieving the abduction of his son, is himself predicted to kill a man he has never met, Leo Crow. On the run, he visits Dr. Iris Hineman, the geneticist whose research made Precrime possible. She tells him that the precogs' abilities arose in children born to mothers addicted to the drug neuroin, and that the precogs sometimes disagree: the dissenting vision, a "minority report", is deleted. Anderton kidnaps the strongest precog, Agatha, to search her memories, and uncovers a murder covered up by Precrime's director, Lamar Burgess: the killing of Agatha's own mother, Anne Lively, who had tried to reclaim her. Exposed, Burgess kills himself, Precrime is shut down and its prisoners are released. Genetics plays a modest but important role in the film's backstory. The precogs' clairvoyance is a side effect of damage caused in the womb by their mothers' addiction to neuroin, and Dr. Iris Hineman, a geneticist, studied these children and developed the research on which Precrime is based. She is portrayed as an ambiguous, reclusive figure living apart from the system her work made possible, and it is she who reveals that its supposed infallibility depends on deleting dissenting visions. The film is less about heredity than about determinism: whether a person can be punished for a predicted act and whether the future is fixed. In that sense it touches the same concerns raised by genetic prediction of behaviour and disease risk, though the film's mechanism is psychic rather than genetic. The precogs themselves are treated as tools of the state and are only freed, to live in anonymity, at the end.

title: Mobile Suit Gundam SEED
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering genetic discrimination cloning
text: In the Cosmic Era, humanity is divided between Naturals and Coordinators, people genetically enhanced before birth. Persecuted on Earth, most Coordinators have emigrated to space colonies called the PLANTs, and the two sides are at war. When the PLANTs' forces, ZAFT, attack the neutral space colony Heliopolis to seize prototype mobile suits built for the Earth Alliance, Kira Yamato, a young Coordinator student, pilots one of them to protect his friends, and finds himself fighting his childhood friend Athrun Zala, now a ZAFT pilot. Kira joins the crew of the warship Archangel and later, with the singer Lacus Clyne and other defectors, forms a third force that tries to stop both sides from destroying each other. Along the way he learns that he is the "Ultimate Coordinator", the product of a secret research project, and that the masked ZAFT commander Rau Le Creuset is a clone. The 50-episode series aired in Japan in 2002–2003. Genetic enhancement is the foundation of the series' world. The war between Naturals and Coordinators is a conflict born of genetic inequality: Coordinators are engineered to be stronger and more intelligent, Naturals resent them, and the natural-human supremacist group Blue Cosmos campaigns, with the slogan "for the preservation of our blue and pure world", for their destruction, while radicals on the PLANTs plan genocide in return. Behind the story is GARM R&D, a research company on the Mendel colony. Its chief researcher, Dr. Ulen Hibiki, developed Kira as the Ultimate Coordinator, a foetus grown outside the womb with enhancements intended to surpass all other Coordinators; Kira was the only one to survive the process. Hibiki also cloned the wealthy Al Da Flaga, and the clone, Rau Le Creuset, has short telomeres that make him age rapidly, which feeds his hatred of humanity. The series uses these ideas to explore prejudice and the ethics of designing people; its sequel, Gundam SEED Destiny, extends them to a plan to assign everyone's role in life by their genes.

title: Reign in Darkness
themes: engineered pathogens human experimentation hybrids chimeras genetic engineering
text: In this low-budget Australian action-horror film, Michael Dorn is a virologist researching a virus called RKV-17 for a mysterious group known as the Council, which tells him that it might lead to a cure for HIV. His experiments use homeless people as subjects. When one of them struggles, Michael accidentally injects himself with the viral serum. The project's hired gun, the bounty hunter Lance Bates, tries to shoot him, but Michael escapes and discovers that he is turning into a vampire with a constant need for blood. While he tries to understand his condition, the Council sends Lance and Gage, a human-vampire crossbreed, to eliminate him. Part of the background is that vampires are trying to develop a genetically engineered cure for themselves because their lungs cannot cope with pollution. The film ends with Michael still on the run from his hunters. The premise combines vampire mythology with biomedical research. Michael Dorn, a virologist working for a secret organisation that turns out to be part of a vampire conspiracy, experiments with the virus RKV-17 on homeless people, believing that it could cure HIV; an accidental injection turns him into a vampire. In the background, vampires are trying to develop a genetically engineered cure for their inability to cope with pollution, and the Council's enforcers include a genetically engineered human-vampire crossbreed. The film thus links vampirism to a virus and presents the research as unethical experimentation on vulnerable people, controlled by a sinister cabal that hunts down its own scientist. The only available source is a short review, which treats these ideas as clichés of modern vampire films and gives few details of how they develop, so the summary is limited.

title: Repli-Kate
text: Max Fleming, a graduate student, has built a cloning machine for the egotistical Dr. Jonas, who takes all the credit. Kate Carson, a magazine reporter, comes to interview Max about the research and accidentally cuts herself, letting a few drops of her blood fall into a cloning sample. That night Max runs the machine and creates an adult replica of Kate, whom he calls Repli-Kate. She has none of Kate's knowledge, so Max and his roommate Henry set out to educate her as their ideal woman: beer-drinking, sports-loving and sexually forward. Max soon realises that the woman he really wants is the original Kate. Jonas learns of the clone, kidnaps both women and plans to present "his" cloning breakthrough to scientists from around the world, but Max and Henry rescue them with the help of a clone of Jonas. Max takes over the lab and becomes famous, Max ends up with Kate and Henry with Repli-Kate. Cloning is the comic premise of this National Lampoon sex comedy. A machine produces an instant adult copy of a woman from a few drops of blood, and the clone is a blank slate that two young men try to shape into their fantasy partner. The scientists are a credit-stealing professor and an awkward student inventor, played for laughs rather than as a comment on research. The film is not interested in the science, and its depiction of cloning is pure fantasy: real cloning, as with Dolly the sheep in 1996, requires nuclear transfer into an egg and a pregnancy, and produces a baby rather than an adult. The film's only link to real debates is the idea, also common in more serious works, that a clone shares the original's appearance but not her memories or personality.

title: Resident Evil
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic human experimentation bioweapon
text: Beneath Raccoon City lies the Hive, a secret genetic research facility owned by the Umbrella Corporation. When a thief steals the genetically engineered T-virus and releases it inside, the facility's artificial intelligence, the Red Queen, seals the Hive and kills everyone in it. Alice wakes up with amnesia in a mansion above the facility and is taken down into the Hive by a team of Umbrella commandos, together with a police officer, Matt, and another amnesiac, Spence. Once they shut down the Red Queen, the infected staff rise as zombies, together with Lickers, creatures created through experiments with the virus. As the group fights its way out, Alice remembers that she was helping Matt's sister, an activist, to expose Umbrella's illegal experiments, and Spence turns out to be the thief. Only Alice and Matt survive, but Umbrella scientists take them; Matt is assigned to the Nemesis programme, and Alice later wakes up to find Raccoon City devastated. Genetic engineering appears as the activity of a ruthless corporation. The Umbrella Corporation runs a hidden underground laboratory where it develops the T-virus, a genetically engineered virus that reanimates the dead and that has been used to create monsters, as well as an antivirus to counter it. The research is illegal and secret, and the scientists remain faceless employees of the corporation: when the virus escapes, the company's response is to seal the laboratory with its staff inside and later to reopen it for study, while turning the survivors into new experimental subjects. The film reflects a common fear about biotechnology: that commercial research on dangerous pathogens, kept away from public scrutiny, could cause a catastrophe. The T-virus itself is fantasy, as no virus can bring the dead back to life.

title: Smallpox 2002
text: Presented as a documentary looking back on events, with mock interviews and stock footage, this BBC docudrama imagines a smallpox attack in 2002. In New York a young woman is first sent home with a flu diagnosis; when she returns covered in pustules, a bioterrorism specialist recognises smallpox and finds more cases, but a proposal for a lockdown and mass vaccination is rejected. A traveller carries the disease to London, and the CDC identifies a strain from Soviet bioweapons laboratories, probably sold abroad by unemployed scientists. The infection spreads worldwide; vaccine shortages, hidden by the British government, lead to strikes, riots, forced quarantine and the breakdown of supplies, and in the developing world hundreds of thousands die each week. Investigators trace the attack to a man who infected himself and spread the virus in New York's transit system, and whose body is found in a subway tunnel. The pandemic is finally defeated after killing 60 million people. The film is a warning about bioterrorism rather than a story about genetics. Its weapon is the smallpox virus, eradicated in nature: the CDC traces the outbreak to a strain held in Soviet biological weapons laboratories, and the Dutch Wikipedia summary adds that unemployed Soviet scientists probably sold samples to the highest bidder. The English Wikipedia describes the premise as one man who creates the virus himself and infects himself to spread it, and the sources do not say whether any genetic engineering is involved. Laboratory stocks are the danger; scientists and doctors also appear as the experts who recognise the disease, identify the strain and fight it, often unheeded by officials. Mixing real epidemiology with fiction, the docudrama shows how a lab-held pathogen could overwhelm public health and social order.

title: Spider-Man
text: On a school trip to a Columbia University genetics laboratory, shy teenager Peter Parker is bitten by a genetically engineered spider. The next day he has spider-like abilities: strength, agility, heightened senses, the ability to cling to walls and organic webbing produced in his wrists. Meanwhile Norman Osborn, head of the company Oscorp and father of Peter's friend Harry, tests a performance-enhancing chemical on himself to win a military contract; it gives him superhuman strength but drives him insane. After Peter lets a thief escape and the same man kills his Uncle Ben, he becomes the masked crime-fighter Spider-Man and sells photos of himself to the Daily Bugle. Osborn, as the Green Goblin, kills Oscorp's board, deduces Peter's identity and targets the people he loves, finally forcing him to choose between saving Mary Jane and a cable car full of children. Peter saves both, and Osborn dies impaled by his own glider. Peter then hides his feelings for Mary Jane to protect her. Genetic engineering is the origin story. Peter gains his powers from the bite of a genetically modified spider exhibited in a university genetics laboratory, and the film presents the result as a lasting change to his body: overnight his strength and senses are enhanced and he begins to produce web from his own wrists. The film does not explain how a bite could do this, and it works purely as a superhero device. The villain's origin is chemical rather than genetic: Norman Osborn is an industrialist-scientist who tests an untried enhancer on himself under pressure to secure a military contract, and its side effects turn him into a murderous split personality. The two transformations offer a contrast familiar in the genre, between an accidental gift used responsibly and a reckless self-experiment in the service of corporate and military interests. In reality no animal bite can rewrite the genome of an adult's cells, and it is the film's moral, "with great power comes great responsibility", rather than its science that has endured.

title: Star Trek: Nemesis
text: After the Romulan Senate is wiped out by a weapon planted during a debate, the Reman rebel leader Shinzon seizes power. The Enterprise, carrying Captain Picard and his crew, recovers B-4, a prototype android resembling Data, and is sent to Romulus because Shinzon claims to want peace with the Federation. There Picard learns that Shinzon is his clone, created by the Romulans to replace him as a spy within Starfleet. The plan was abandoned and the child was sent to the mines of Remus to die, but he rose to lead the Remans and built the warship Scimitar, armed with thalaron radiation. Dr. Crusher discovers that Shinzon is dying because of the way he was cloned and that only a transfusion of Picard's blood can save him. Shinzon kidnaps Picard and plans to use his weapon against Earth. Picard kills Shinzon aboard the Scimitar, and Data sacrifices himself to destroy it. Cloning is the film's central device. Shinzon is a genetic copy of Picard grown by the Romulans for espionage, and the story uses him to explore nature against nurture: sharing Picard's genome, he was shaped by abandonment and slavery into a very different man, and much of the drama turns on whether Picard, in his place, would have become the same. The cloners themselves are an unseen Romulan intelligence programme that treats the boy as a disposable tool. A further plot point is that Shinzon's cloning was flawed, leaving him with a fatal degeneration that only Picard's blood can stop. In real terms, a clone is simply a delayed identical twin, and the film's attention to the role of upbringing reflects that well.

title: Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones
alt: Star Wars. Episodio II: El ataque de los clones
text: Ten years after the events of The Phantom Menace, the Galactic Republic is threatened by a Separatist movement led by Count Dooku. After two attempts on the life of Senator Padmé Amidala, Obi-Wan Kenobi follows the trail of the assassin's employer to the ocean planet Kamino, where he finds a clone army being produced for the Republic, supposedly ordered by a dead Jedi Master. Its genetic template is the bounty hunter Jango Fett, who also keeps an unaltered clone as his son, Boba. Obi-Wan follows Jango to Geonosis and discovers the Separatists' droid army, but is captured. Meanwhile Anakin Skywalker, guarding Padmé, falls in love with her and massacres the Tusken Raiders who killed his mother. When Obi-Wan, Anakin and Padmé are about to be executed, Yoda arrives with the clone troopers, beginning the Clone Wars, and Anakin and Padmé marry in secret. Cloning is the plot device that gives the film its title. On Kamino, the Kaminoans, a species of expert cloners, have produced an army of soldiers from the DNA of Jango Fett, a bounty hunter recruited by Count Dooku. The clones are genetically altered so that they age at twice the normal rate and are more obedient and easier to command, while Jango asked for one unaltered clone to raise as his son, Boba. The Kaminoans are presented as detached, courteous technicians who treat the clones as a product, and the army is later revealed to be part of the Sith plan to seize power: in the following film the clones turn on the Jedi. Real reproductive cloning produces a genetically identical twin that must develop at the normal pace and does not copy memories or skills; accelerated growth and engineered obedience are fiction.

title: Tamala 2010: A Punk Cat in Space
alt: TAMALA2010 a punk cat in space Tamala 2010
text: On 'Cat Earth', a Tokyo ruled by advertising and corporations, the foul-mouthed kitten Tamala runs away from her human foster mother in a spaceship, heading for her birthplace in Orion. She is shot down by the immortal Mysterious Postcat, an agent of the conglomerate CATTY & Co., and crash-lands near Hate City on Planet Q, a violent city of cats and dogs. She falls for the cultured cat Michelangelo and discovers a mural of the ancient Minerva cult and a statue of a cat named Tatla, before being eaten by Kentauros, a sadistic dog dressed as a police biker. In a lecture, Professor Nominos, apparently an older Michelangelo, reveals that CATTY & Co. grew out of the Minerva cult and that Tamala has been its mascot since 1869, a recurring reincarnation of Tatla whose ritual sacrifice feeds the cult's power. Tamala revives and leaves for Orion while CATTY & Co. takes over Hate City. Genetics is a small but telling element of this avant-garde animated satire. According to the English Wikipedia, Tamala was genetically engineered in 1869 to remain forever about a year and a half old, so that she could serve as the immortal mascot of the conglomerate CATTY & Co., an offshoot of the Minerva religion whose power depends on her repeated sacrifice. Genetic engineering is thus one of the tools by which a corporate cult manufactures and owns a cute brand character. The film, which borrows from Thomas Pynchon's The Crying of Lot 49, is a satire of consumerism and corporate power rather than a story about science, and its genetics is never explained; reviewers found the second half close to incomprehensible.

title: Teknolust
text: Bio-geneticist Rosetta Stone, a lonely scientist who works on the artificial production of organs, uses her own DNA to create three female clones, Ruby, Olive and Marinne, self-replicating automatons who live in a cyberspace inside her computer and whom she calls her family. To survive they need a constant supply of the Y chromosome, that is, semen. Ruby, who has learned how men and women behave from classic romance films, goes out at night, seduces men and brings their sperm back for her sisters. The men become impotent, a barcode appears on their foreheads and their computers crash, and FBI agent Hopper investigates. Rosetta loses control of her rebellious creations and is arrested by mistake. In the end the clones gain their independence, Marinne makes new clones, Rosetta finds love with Hopper, and Ruby falls for her shy neighbour Sandy and becomes pregnant. Cloning is the premise of this playful feminist science fiction comedy by Lynn Hershman Leeson. A scientist creates copies of herself by injecting her DNA into artificial beings, for companionship and to do chores, and finds she cannot control them. The clones' need for the Y chromosome, which they obtain by collecting sperm, is a satirical conceit rather than biology, and the story mixes genetics with computer viruses: the men they sleep with are infected by a virus that also crashes their computers. Rosetta is an awkward, lonely but sympathetic scientist, neither villain nor hero, and the clones are presented as a family seeking autonomy. German critics saw it as a playful contribution to the cloning debate. Real cloning does not produce adult copies, and nothing in genetics requires a supply of Y chromosomes.

title: The Adventures of Pluto Nash
text: In 2080, on the lunar colony of Little America, the reformed smuggler Pluto Nash buys a nightclub from his friend Tony Francis to save him from mobsters, and with his friend Miguel and the android Bruno turns it into a success. Seven years later he hires Dina Lake, a young woman stranded on the Moon. When he refuses to sell the club to the mysterious entrepreneur Rex Crater, Crater's henchmen blow it up. Helped by Dina, Bruno, the retired detective Rowland and the smuggler Felix Laranga, Pluto learns that Crater has links to human cloning and to the mobster Mike Marucci, and he infiltrates Crater's casino at Moon Beach. There Crater reveals that he is Pluto's clone and that he has disposed of his creators by shooting them into orbit. After a fight, Pluto throws Crater out of a window to his death and later reopens the rebuilt Club Pluto. The villain is a clone of the hero. Rex Crater was made by the geneticist Dr. Runa Pendankin for the mobster Mike Marucci, who wanted a public face for his operations, from DNA taken from Pluto's appendix, removed while he was in prison. The clone turns against his makers, shoots them both into orbit and builds his own criminal empire, which brings him into conflict with Pluto; the plot twist allows Eddie Murphy to play both hero and villain. Cloning also appears as a running gag: Tony Francis has two cloned wives and does not care which is the original. Genetics is treated as a comic device rather than a serious subject, and the scientist is a minor figure. Real cloning would produce a much younger twin, not an adult copy who looks like the original at the same age.
