title: Accelerate
text: Lana Lang believes she is seeing the ghost of Emily Dinsmore, a childhood friend who drowned six years earlier, and who appears to her still ten years old. Clark discovers that Emily is real and that she seems to vanish and walk through walls because she can move at super-speed. Searching her father's house, Clark and Lana find a hidden laboratory with two more copies of Emily asleep in glass tanks. Lex learns that Emily's father, Pete Dinsmore, had been working on accelerating cell growth and could bring a rabbit embryo to adulthood in days. Emily is a clone whose growth was accelerated with green meteor rock, and her father warns that she has no moral conscience. Angry at Lana for not saving her years ago, Emily pushes her off the bridge where she died, and Clark rescues her. Lex discovers that his father, Lionel Luthor, is funding the cloning research, and Lionel takes Emily away to a new lab. Human cloning is at the centre of this episode. A grieving father uses his research on accelerated cell growth, boosted by kryptonite, to recreate his dead daughter as a ten-year-old clone, and keeps spare copies in tanks. The episode plays on the "replacement child" theme: the clone has the girl's appearance and childhood attachments, but lacks a moral conscience and turns violent. The scientist is driven by grief rather than ambition, but his work is financed by Lionel Luthor's LuthorCorp, which takes over the clone at the end; Lex accuses his father of continuing the secret Level Three projects he believed had been abandoned. Real cloning produces a genetically identical baby who must grow at a normal rate, so a clone could not be made at the age of the original or inherit her memories. Like many science-fiction clones, Emily also embodies the misconception that a copy will be a defective version of the person it replaces.

title: Blueprint
text: Iris Sellin, a celebrated concert pianist, learns that she has multiple sclerosis. Fearing that her talent will die with her, she persuades the reproductive medicine specialist Martin Fischer to clone her, and gives birth to Siri, her genetic copy and her daughter. When Siri is thirteen, Fischer makes the cloning public, and she learns what she is. The bond between them breaks, and for years mother and daughter make each other's lives miserable. Seeking to escape her mother's shadow, Siri moves to the Canadian wilderness, where she lives alone and works as a wildlife photographer. There she meets Greg, an architect, whose love helps her build a life of her own and ease the conflict with Iris. Franka Potente plays both Iris and Siri; the film is based on Charlotte Kerner's prize-winning young-adult novel. Human reproductive cloning is the premise, but the film is mainly a psychological drama about identity and a mother-daughter relationship. Iris has herself cloned to preserve her musical gift, treating her daughter as a copy rather than as a new person, and Siri struggles to find out whether anything in her is her own. Fischer, the doctor who performs the cloning, breaks the secret when Siri is thirteen, exposing her to stigma; at a Mother's Day concert, Siri wears a Star of David bearing the word "Klon" (clone), an image that recalls the persecution of Jews in Nazi Germany. The German film magazine film-dienst noted that the ethics of gene technology serves mainly as a backdrop. The film's central idea fits genetics well: a clone is in effect a delayed identical twin, and twin studies show that sharing a genome does not mean sharing talents, personality or fate. No cloned human has ever been verified, and reproductive cloning is banned in many countries, including Germany under its Embryo Protection Act.

title: Code 46
themes: cloning genetic testing genetic discrimination engineered pathogens
text: In 2077, people live either "inside" in tightly controlled cities or "outside" in the desert as an underclass, and movement is regulated by "papeles", travel documents issued as insurance cover. William Geld, an investigator from Seattle, is sent to Shanghai to find who is forging papeles at the company that issues them. Helped by an engineered empathy virus, he identifies Maria Gonzalez as the forger, but he is drawn to her, blames someone else and begins an affair with her. When he returns, Maria has been taken to a clinic: she was pregnant, and the pregnancy was terminated as a breach of Code 46, which forbids reproduction between genetically related people. Her memory of him has been erased. William tests her DNA and discovers that she is a clone of his mother. He takes her to Jebel Ali, where they flee together, but they are caught after a car crash. William's memories are erased and he returns to his family, while Maria is exiled outside. Genetics shapes both the society and the love story. In this world, widespread use of in vitro fertilisation, embryo splitting and cloning means that people cannot know who they are related to, so the law called Code 46 forbids reproduction between any two people who share 25% or more of their genetic identity; violations are detected through genetic tests, pregnancies are terminated, memories erased, and viruses are used to make offenders physically averse to their partners. Genetic and health information is also used to decide who may live and travel inside the cities. William's discovery that Maria is a clone of his mother turns the affair into a form of incest. The film does not focus on scientists but on the state and corporate apparatus that applies genetics, and critics noted that it explains its biotechnology through opening text rather than exploring it. The 25% threshold corresponds to the relatedness between, for example, a grandparent and grandchild. As a clone of his mother, Maria would share about half of William's genome, as a mother does.

title: Fragile Balance
text: An intruder caught using Colonel Jack O'Neill's ID badge at Stargate Command turns out to be a fifteen-year-old boy who claims to be O'Neill and knows everything O'Neill knows. Dr. Janet Fraiser's genetic tests show that he is genetically O'Neill, apart from a small abnormality, and later that he is dying. Remembering a vision of an Asgard and floating lights, the boy suspects an alien abduction; Daniel and Teal'c find eight other people with similar stories, and the Tok'ra Selmak and Fraiser establish that the boy is a clone. SG-1 waits for the abductor to return, and the young O'Neill gets them aboard his ship, where they capture Loki, a renegade Asgard scientist who has been experimenting on humans. Thor arrives, returns the real O'Neill and punishes Loki. He also repairs the clone's genetic defect, and the young O'Neill goes back to high school. Cloning drives the episode and DNA testing unlocks it. A medical DNA test confirms that the teenage intruder really is O'Neill, genetically, and the small anomaly it reveals is later recognised as the mark of a clone. The cloner is Loki, a renegade Asgard scientist: his species, which reproduces only by cloning, suffers from cellular degeneration, and he abducts humans and makes short-lived, deliberately defective clones of them to study human DNA in search of a cure, returning the originals so that no one notices. Loki is a villain, condemned by his own people for unsanctioned experiments on humans, while the base physician Dr. Fraiser and the Asgard Thor, who repairs the clone's genetic defect so that he can live, are positive figures. The episode then treats the clone as a person in his own right, with a second chance at youth. Real cloning produces a genetic twin born as a baby, not a teenage copy with its original's memories.

title: Hulk
themes: heredity genetic engineering mutants human enhancement regeneration
text: In the 1960s, David Banner, a government genetics researcher trying to improve human DNA, experiments on himself after his superior, Thaddeus Ross, forbids tests on humans. His son Bruce inherits his altered DNA. When Ross shuts down his research, David sabotages a gamma reactor and accidentally kills his wife; he is sent to a mental hospital, and Bruce is adopted and represses the memory. As an adult, Bruce works on regenerative "nanomeds" at Berkeley with Ross's daughter Betty. Shielding a colleague in an accident, he absorbs a massive dose of gamma radiation that merges with his altered DNA, and from then on rage turns him into the Hulk, a giant green creature. David, now a lab janitor, uses Bruce's DNA to mutate dogs that attack Betty. The military, now led by General Ross, and the corporate opportunist Talbot try to capture the Hulk. David gains the power to absorb energy and matter and fights his son until a bomb destroys him; Bruce is presumed dead. Ang Lee's film changes the Hulk's origin to make heredity central. Bruce's condition begins with his father's self-experimentation: David Banner, a researcher for the military, alters his own DNA in pursuit of human improvement, passes the change to his son, and the gamma accident decades later only activates what Bruce inherited. Much of the film is a family drama about what children inherit from their parents, biologically and emotionally, with Bruce's repressed childhood trauma acting as the trigger for each transformation. Scientists are shown at their worst through David, whose ambition turns to megalomania and who uses his son's DNA to create monstrous dogs, while military and corporate interests, represented by Ross and Talbot, want to exploit the Hulk for regenerating soldiers. The genetics is fictional, but the film touches on a real distinction: changes to a person's germline, unlike those to other body cells, can be passed to the next generation, which is why editing the genomes of human embryos is so tightly restricted today.

title: It's All About Love
alt: It's All About Love (Todo es por amor)
text: In 2021, as the world's climate goes haywire and snow falls in summer, John, a Polish university lecturer, stops in New York to sign divorce papers with his wife Elena, a world-famous figure-skating champion surrounded by a managing entourage. At her hotel he meets a woman identical to Elena, and Elena, frightened, begs him to stay. He learns that her management has had three clones of her made, officially to relieve her of an exhausting career, though she fears they will dispose of her once the clones are trained. Her brother Michael tells John that the clones are to keep the business going while Elena, who has a heart defect, disappears into a new life with him. With Michael's help the couple escape; the clones are shot dead on the ice, and Michael freezes to death. John and Elena die in each other's arms in the cold, while John's brother Marciello, flying over a frozen world, narrates the end. Cloning is the engine of this apocalyptic romance by Thomas Vinterberg. Elena's managers have three exact copies of her made so that the skating star, and the investments built on her, can carry on without her, and the original may be pushed aside once the copies are trained. The film never shows how the clones were made or who made them; it treats cloning as a business operation run by a faceless entourage, and the copies end up shot dead when they are no longer needed. The sources describe the cloning as a metaphor for the commodification of people, part of the film's wider picture of an emotionally frozen world in which people die of broken hearts. Fully grown, instantly trained adult clones are pure fiction; the film is not interested in the science.

title: Lilith Needs a Favor
text: On a flight to Seattle, Frasier's ex-wife Lilith meets Albert, a pale, awkward fellow passenger, and tells him she is going to ask an old friend for a favour. In Seattle she asks Frasier to donate sperm so that she can have another child, appealing to their memories of raising their son Frederick. The two go to a sperm bank, where they talk the matter through and part on good terms. Meanwhile, Daphne takes her mother, Roz and Roz's daughter Alice to a theme park in Canada, leaving Niles with a set of photographs; he and Frasier puzzle over the last one, which Niles mistakes for a picture of Daphne until she reveals that it shows Martin. On the flight back to Boston, Lilith meets Albert again, learns that he is a divorced scientist, and the two discover that they have much in common. Genetics enters through the choice of a biological father. Lilith wants another child and turns to her former husband as a sperm donor, hoping in effect for another child like their son Frederick, a comic take on choosing a donor for his traits. The episode treats assisted reproduction, sperm banking and donor choice as ordinary parts of modern family planning, mining them for awkward humour rather than ethical debate. No scientist plays a role in the procedure, although Lilith's new acquaintance, Albert, turns out to be one. Its relevance to genetics is therefore light: it reflects the idea, common in real donor selection, that prospective parents look for desirable traits in a donor, though the heredity of complex traits such as intelligence or temperament is far less predictable than such choices assume.

title: Lilo & Stitch: The Series
text: Continuing from Stitch! The Movie, Lilo Pelekai and Stitch, Experiment 626, set out to find the 623 other experiments created by the alien scientist Jumba Jookiba, which are scattered across Kauai as dormant pods. In each episode, an experiment is activated and causes trouble with its special power, such as generating electricity, causing earthquakes or turning good experiments bad with a song. Lilo and Stitch, helped by Jumba and Pleakley, catch it, tame its destructive programming and find its 'one true place', a role where its ability can do good. They compete with Captain Gantu and his lazy sidekick, Experiment 625, who try to capture the experiments for Jumba's former partner, the imprisoned Dr. Jacques von Hämsterviel, who wants to use them to conquer the Galactic Federation. The series ends with the film Leroy & Stitch, in which Lilo, Stitch and the reformed experiments defeat Hämsterviel and Lilo and Stitch become official experiment hunters. Genetic engineering provides the whole premise. Each of the 600-odd 'cousins' is a genetic experiment made by the alien scientist Jumba Jookiba, many of them designed for destruction, and in most episodes Jumba explains the engineered ability of the creature at hand before Lilo and Stitch capture and rehabilitate it. The series' message is that an engineered creature is not bound by its design: given acceptance and a purpose, a being built for mischief can find a place where its traits do good, in keeping with the theme of 'ohana (family). Jumba is a self-described evil genius turned lovable uncle, who still occasionally builds a new experiment for personal reasons, while his former partner and financier, Hämsterviel, wants the experiments as weapons to conquer the galaxy. The creatures and their powers are cartoon fantasy with no basis in real genetics.

title: Memories of Murder
alt: 살인의 추억 Crónica de un asesino en serie
text: In 1986, two women are found raped and murdered in the countryside near a small South Korean town. The poorly equipped local police, led by detectives Park Doo-man and Cho Yong-koo, beat suspects and fabricate evidence to extract confessions, first from Baek Kwang-ho, a young man with an intellectual disability. Seo Tae-yoon, a methodical detective from Seoul, joins them; he finds a third victim and deduces that the killer strikes on rainy nights against women wearing red, while a female officer notices that the same song is requested on the local radio before each murder. The trail leads to Hyeon-gyu, a clerk at the local mine with soft hands, who sent in the requests. With no hard evidence, the police send semen from a new victim to the United States for DNA comparison, since Korea cannot yet do the test. After another girl is murdered, Seo is about to shoot Hyeon-gyu when the results arrive: inconclusive. In 2003, Park, now a salesman, returns to the first crime scene, where a girl tells him an ordinary-looking man recently stood reminiscing about something he once did. Genetics enters Bong Joon-ho's film as forensic DNA analysis at the moment it was becoming available. After months of beatings, false confessions and failed stakeouts, the detectives obtain a semen sample from a victim, and because South Korea cannot yet perform DNA tests, they send it to the United States for comparison with their prime suspect. The test is the investigation's last hope, and its inconclusive result is the turning point: it neither convicts nor clears Hyeon-gyu, the detectives' certainty collapses, and Seo, the scientific detective, is reduced to holding a gun to the suspect's head. The film presents DNA science neutrally, as a powerful tool that the police of the 1980s could neither command nor interpret, against a background of brutal and incompetent policing. The film is based on the Hwaseong serial murders, in which evidence was actually sent to Japan; the real killer, Lee Choon-jae, was identified by DNA in 2019, sixteen years after the film.

title: Metamorphosis
text: In this Stargate SG-1 episode, a Russian team brings a Jaffa, Alebran, back to Stargate Command; he says the Goa'uld Nirrti has been experimenting on his people, and then dissolves into water. SG-1 and the Russian team led by Colonel Evanov travel to Nirrti's fortress, where they find deformed people who have developed powers such as telekinesis and telepathy. They believe that their goddess Nirrti is curing them with a machine, a DNA resequencer. The telepath Eggar uncovers the team's plan to kill Nirrti, and the mutant Wodan, Alebran's brother, imprisons them. Nirrti captures the team, uses the resequencer on Carter and Evanov, and finds that Jonas Quinn's DNA is unusual. Evanov dies like Alebran and Carter's condition worsens. Finally Eggar reads Nirrti's mind and confirms she has deceived them; Wodan kills her, and Eggar, using knowledge taken from her mind, reverses Carter's changes and promises to cure his people and destroy the machine. The episode is built around a machine that rewrites DNA. The Goa'uld Nirrti uses her DNA resequencer on the people of a planet, who believe she is a goddess healing them; in fact her experiments leave them deformed, give some of them psychic powers such as telekinesis and telepathy, and kill others, who dissolve into water. She also uses the machine on captured team members, altering Carter's DNA and analysing that of Jonas Quinn, whose genome she finds unusual. The available source does not say what Nirrti hopes to achieve, only that she experiments on people without their informed consent and that the episode presents her as a deceitful villain. Her victims finally turn against her, and the knowledge taken from her mind is used to reverse the changes. Rewriting an adult's genome with a machine, let alone producing psychic powers, is science fiction.

title: Seeing Double
text: The pop group S Club are finishing a tour in Barcelona when their manager Alistair is abducted. The next day they see an S Club performing on television that they do not recognise: perfect copies of themselves, managed by Alistair. Arrested for running out on their hotel bill and for allegedly impersonating S Club, they escape and make their way to Los Angeles. Swapping places with some of their doubles, they discover that the clones have no belly buttons, live by strict rituals and are brainwashed at night. They learn that the clones were made by Victor Gaghan, a former genetics professor fired for illegal cloning experiments, who plans to take over the world through music, since celebrities attract more attention than politicians. At his Hollywood castle, Eagle Peak, the band find Gaghan's other cloned stars, from Elvis Presley to Madonna. Clones and originals join forces, Gaghan is arrested, and the clones end up standing in for the band when it wants a holiday. Cloning is the comic premise of this musical. The villain, Victor Gaghan, is a stock mad scientist, a disgraced genetics professor who clones pop stars from memorabilia he buys online, including their underwear, and uses the copies to pursue world domination through pop music. The clones are adults made to order with implanted, programmed memories and a telltale lack of belly buttons, and they have to learn simple pleasures for the first time once they rebel. The film plays the idea entirely for laughs, and its sympathy lies with the clones, who are treated as people in their own right and are freed rather than destroyed. Its science is pure fantasy: a real clone would start life as an embryo and would grow into a much younger twin, without the memories or skills of the original.

title: Similitude
text: During the Enterprise's mission against the Xindi, Chief Engineer Trip Tucker falls into a coma after an engine accident. Doctor Phlox proposes a controversial procedure: growing a "mimetic symbiote" from Tucker's blood to serve as a source of neural tissue. Captain Archer approves it for the sake of the mission. The symbiote, named Sim, ages from baby to adult in days, has a natural lifespan of about two weeks, and develops Tucker's memories and personality, including his love of engineering and his attraction to T'Pol. Sim learns that the transplant will kill him and that an experimental procedure might extend his life, which Phlox had kept quiet. He asks to live out his life, and Archer tells him he would rather Sim agree than be forced. Thinking of his sister, killed in the Xindi attack, Sim accepts the procedure. Tucker recovers, and the crew hold a funeral for Sim. The episode is an ethical drama about creating a person for spare parts. Sim is effectively a short-lived clone grown from Tucker's blood, and the story asks whether a being created to save someone else has a right to his own life. Phlox, the ship's doctor, is portrayed as caring, acting as Sim's father, but he withholds information about a possible way to extend Sim's life; Captain Archer puts the mission first and is willing to sacrifice Sim. Reviewers have singled out the episode as one of the most thought-provoking in the series for this dilemma. The science is invented: the clone ages to adulthood in days and inherits Tucker's memories, neither of which is possible with real cloning. The premise echoes real debates about creating embryos or "saviour siblings" as sources of tissue for others.

title: Star Wars: Clone Wars
text: This animated series is set between the films Attack of the Clones and Revenge of the Sith and follows the Galactic Republic and the Jedi in their war against the Separatists and the Sith. Its first volume covers Obi-Wan Kenobi's assault on Muunilinst, home of the Banking Clan that funds the Separatists and hires the bounty hunter Durge; Count Dooku's new apprentice Asajj Ventress, sent to kill Anakin Skywalker, who defeats her on Yavin 4; and battles fought by Mace Windu, Yoda, Kit Fisto and others, including the first encounter with General Grievous. The second volume sees Anakin knighted and jumps to the end of the war, when Anakin and Obi-Wan free the Nelvaanians, who had been enslaved and mutated by the Separatist Techno Union, and Anakin has a vision of becoming Darth Vader. Grievous attacks Coruscant and kidnaps Chancellor Palpatine, leading into Revenge of the Sith. Genetics is a passing element. The Republic's army consists of clone troopers, clones of the bounty hunter Jango Fett, who fight alongside the Jedi throughout the series, but the series does not deal with how they were made or what being a clone means. In the second volume, the Separatist Techno Union is shown to have enslaved and mutated the Nelvaanians, whom Anakin and Obi-Wan free; the sources do not say how the mutation was done. The series is about battles and Anakin's path towards the dark side, not about genetics.

title: Stitch! The Movie
themes: genetic engineering cloning hybrids chimeras bioweapon
text: Stitch, alien Experiment 626, struggles to fit in with Lilo in Hawaii and longs for 'cousins' like himself. The mercenary Gantu, working for Dr. Jacques von Hämsterviel, the former partner and backer of Stitch's creator Jumba, kidnaps Jumba to obtain his other experiments, stored as dehydrated pods. Lilo and Stitch find the hidden container and, against Pleakley's warning, rehydrate Experiment 221, an electrical creature they befriend as Sparky. Hämsterviel trades Jumba for the container, escapes with Sparky's help, and the pods scatter across Hawaii during a struggle aboard his ship. Hämsterviel captures Lilo and Stitch and prepares to clone Stitch a thousand times, but Sparky sabotages the machine. The heroes free themselves, Hämsterviel is arrested, and the Grand Councilwoman lets Lilo and Stitch track down and rehabilitate the scattered experiments instead of destroying them, setting up the television series. Genetic engineering is the premise. Stitch and the 625 earlier experiments are illegal genetic creations of the alien scientist Jumba Jookiba, funded by Dr. Hämsterviel, and the plot turns on who controls them. Jumba, once a mad scientist, is now a sympathetic captive protecting his creations, while Hämsterviel is the villain who claims the experiments as his property and plans to clone Stitch a thousand times, presumably to build an army. The film's message, carried by Lilo, is that the engineered creatures are not weapons but family ('ohana') who deserve rehabilitation rather than destruction, and the dangerous Sparky becomes a friend. The genetics is cartoon fantasy (creatures stored as dehydrated pods and revived with water), used to set up the series about collecting the experiments.

title: Teenage Mutant Leela's Hurdles
text: Fed up with Professor Farnsworth's senility, the Planet Express crew takes him to a rejuvenating spa in Florida, where he is bathed in anti-aging tar; when Bender works the pump too hard, the whole crew falls in. The Professor becomes a man in his fifties, the others turn into teenagers and Dr. Zoidberg reverts to his larval stage. Leela, who never had a normal adolescence, moves in with her parents in the sewers and dates the teenage Fry. Finding that time-altering chronitons have stuck to the crew's DNA, the Professor concocts a genetically modified bacterium to clear them, but Leela refuses the treatment. It backfires: everyone else keeps getting younger, heading for 'pre-life'. Leela finds the mythical Fountain of Aging in a storybook and takes the shrinking crew there; she dives into its current to save them, giving up her teenage life, and Farnsworth's escaped gargoyle Pazuzu rescues the Professor. Everyone returns to normal. Genetics is played for comedy. The de-aging tar works by sticking time-altering 'chronitons' to the crew's DNA (and to the robot Bender's 'RNA', robonucleic acid), and Professor Farnsworth's attempt to fix this with a genetically modified bacterium that clears their DNA backfires, making them regress towards foetuses and non-existence. The Professor is the series' archetypal senile mad scientist, well-meaning but reckless, and the cure comes from a mythical fountain rather than from his science. A passing joke involves Zoidberg's clone siblings. The episode, a pastiche of rejuvenation myths, uses genetic vocabulary as technobabble, with no attempt at plausibility.

title: Underworld
text: A centuries-old secret war divides vampires and Lycans (werewolves). Selene, a vampire assassin, discovers that the Lycans are hunting Michael Corvin, a young American doctor. Michael is bitten by Lucian, the Lycan leader believed dead, and Selene hides him while suspecting that the vampire Kraven is conspiring with the enemy. She awakens the vampire elder Viktor prematurely. The captured Lycan scientist Singe reveals that vampires and Lycans share a common ancestor, Alexander Corvinus, and that Michael, his descendant, carries a unique genetic strain that can produce a vampire–Lycan hybrid free of both species' weaknesses. Lucian also tells of Viktor's murder of his own daughter for loving a Lycan. Selene bites the dying Michael, who becomes a hybrid; she learns that Viktor killed her family and beheads him. In the final scene the elder Marcus awakens as a hybrid. Underworld gives the vampire and werewolf myths a pseudo-genetic explanation. The two species descend from a common ancestor, Alexander Corvinus, whose descendant Michael carries a unique genetic strain; with his blood, the Lycan scientist Singe plans to create a hybrid without the weaknesses of either species. The creators conceived the conditions as a viral mutagen and a 'genetic anomaly transmitted by blood'. The hybrid project, backed by the Lycan leader Lucian, is the reason Michael is hunted, and the vampire elder Viktor opposes it as an abomination, to the point of having killed his own pregnant daughter. Singe is a minor, villainous figure killed by Viktor, while Michael becomes the sympathetic hybrid hero. The genetics is decorative: bloodlines, bites and transfusions stand in for real inheritance, and nothing like a cross between two 'species' through a bite exists.

title: Appleseed
themes: genetic engineering cloning engineered pathogens genetic discrimination eugenics post apocalyptic
text: In 2131, after a world war, the soldier Deunan Knute is still fighting in a ruined city when she is rescued by Hitomi, a bioroid, and her former lover Briareos, now a cyborg. They take her to Olympus, a utopian city ruled by the supercomputer Gaia, Prime Minister Athena, General Uranus and a Council of Elders, where half the population are bioroids, engineered beings made from the DNA of Deunan's late father. Deunan joins the ESWAT counter-terrorism unit and learns that bioroids cannot reproduce and depend on life-extension facilities, which a rogue army faction led by Colonel Hades destroys. She also learns that she carries the Appleseed data, left by her mother Gilliam, the creator of the bioroids, which can restore their ability to reproduce. The Elders reveal that they plan to use a virus in the D-Tank to sterilize humanity and leave the Earth to bioroids. Deunan and Briareos stop them, and Deunan uses the data to restore the bioroids' reproductive functions. Genetic engineering is at the centre of the world and the plot. The bioroids, half of Olympus's population, are engineered clones made from the DNA of Carl Knute, designed without harmful emotions to keep the peace and with their reproduction suppressed, which shortens their lives. Their creator, Dr. Gilliam Knute, also developed the D-Tank, which holds a virus able to sterilize humans, and the Appleseed data, which can restore bioroid reproduction; she hid the data with her daughter before she was killed. The conflict pits anti-bioroid soldiers, who hate them partly because they all share one man's DNA, against the Council of Elders, who want to use the virus to replace humanity with bioroids. Gilliam and her daughter are sympathetic and their genetics is used to secure coexistence, while the Elders show how the same science could be turned into a tool for wiping out humanity. The film raises questions about prejudice and the right to life of engineered people.

title: Blade: Trinity
text: In the third Blade film, vampires led by Danica Talos revive Drake, the first vampire, better known as Dracula, from a tomb in the Syrian desert, hoping his powers will free their race from its weaknesses. To keep Blade out of the way, they frame him for murder; the FBI raids his hideout, his mentor Whistler dies, and Blade is arrested, then rescued by Hannibal King and Abigail Whistler, leaders of a band of human vampire hunters, the Nightstalkers. Their blind scientist, Sommerfield, has created Daystar, a virus designed to kill vampires at the genetic level, but it needs the pure blood of Drake to work. Drake, who despises both humans and modern vampires, tests Blade, while Abigail uncovers vampire blood farms of brain-dead humans. The vampires massacre the Nightstalkers and take King and Sommerfield's daughter Zoe. In the final fight, Blade stabs Drake with the Daystar arrow, releasing the completed virus, which kills Drake and the vampires around them. Drake takes Blade's form in death, letting Blade escape. The heroes' weapon is genetic. Sommerfield, the Nightstalkers' scientist, has engineered Daystar, an experimental viral bioweapon designed to kill vampires at the genetic level; to work against the whole species it needs blood from Drake, the first vampire, whose DNA is pure and uncontaminated, which is also why he can walk in sunlight. Her recorded warning that the virus could kill Blade, a human-vampire hybrid, too, adds risk to the final confrontation. Unlike most films with engineered viruses, the bioweapon here is the instrument of salvation: it is created by a sympathetic scientist on the side of humanity and, once completed with Drake's blood, wipes out the vampire leadership, while the vampires' own plan is to farm humans for blood. The idea of genetic purity in an ancestral lineage is borrowed loosely from biology, and a virus that recognises one species' genome and kills it on contact is fantasy.

title: Borderland
text: In 2154, genetically enhanced humans known as Augments seize a Klingon Bird-of-Prey after killing its crew. Starfleet sends the Enterprise to stop them, and Captain Archer collects Dr. Arik Soong from prison, where he is serving a sentence for stealing the embryos from which the Augments were raised. Soong, who regards them as his children, promises to persuade them to stand down. In the Borderland, a lawless region between Klingon and Orion space, Orion slavers attack the Enterprise and capture several crew members, including T'Pol, and Archer needs Soong's help to rescue them from a slave market. Soong tries to escape during the rescue and then refuses to lead Archer to the Augments. Aboard the Klingon ship, Persis manipulates the Augment leader Raakin, who is killed by Malik. The Bird-of-Prey docks with the disabled Enterprise, Malik forces Archer to release Soong, and Soong announces that they will now go after the remaining Augment embryos. The episode opens a three-part arc about human genetic enhancement. The Augments were raised by Soong from embryos preserved from the time of the Eugenics Wars, the conflict that in Star Trek's history produced Khan Noonien Singh, and their strength and intelligence are matched by arrogance and violence. Soong is a brilliant but irresponsible geneticist who sees himself as their father, steals the embryos and refuses to accept that his project has gone wrong; later in the arc he tries to remove aggressive behaviour from the remaining embryos, and he ends it doubting that engineering humans is feasible. He is the ancestor of Noonien Soong, creator of the android Data. The arc reflects Star Trek's long-standing suspicion of human genetic enhancement, while letting Soong argue for its potential, and its "Augments" echo real concerns that enhancing traits could create a privileged class.

title: Cold Station 12
themes: eugenics human enhancement genetic engineering genetic discrimination
text: In the middle episode of a three-part story, Captain Archer and his crew pursue Dr. Arik Soong and the Augments, genetically enhanced humans Soong raised from embryos stolen after the Eugenics Wars. On the planet Trialis IV they find the building where the young Augments were raised and capture Udar, nicknamed "Smike", an Augment cast out by his siblings because he lacks their enhanced abilities except for his hearing. Meanwhile Soong and the Augments seize a Denobulan medical ship and use it to enter Cold Station 12, a secret Starfleet medical facility that stores pathogens and 1,800 frozen augmented embryos. They take the staff hostage, including Dr. Lucas, a friend of Enterprise's Dr. Phlox. Tension grows between Soong and the ruthless Augment Malik, who tortures Lucas and threatens other scientists with deadly pathogens. Malik finally forces Lucas to give up the security codes. The Augments escape with the embryos, but not before Malik kills Smike, steals pathogens and sabotages the station's containment systems. The episode deals directly with human genetic enhancement and its legacy. Soong raised the Augments as his "children", and they themselves show the dangers his critics feared: they are stronger and smarter than ordinary humans but also arrogant and increasingly violent, and Malik's ruthlessness strains his relationship with Soong. Smike, born with the Augments' genome but without their abilities, shows that genetic design does not guarantee the intended result, and his rejection and murder by his siblings shows how they value people by their traits. Starfleet, for its part, keeps the embryos from the Eugenics Wars in storage instead of destroying them. The arc revives the genetically engineered Augments who appeared alongside Khan Noonian Singh in the original series and is a cautionary tale about eugenic ambitions. Its enhancements are fictional; nothing comparable can be engineered into human embryos.

title: Corn
text: Emily Rasmussen, a young woman who is pregnant and has dropped out of college, returns to the rural sheep ranch of her family to rebuild her life; the father of her child, a politician, refuses to help her for fear of scandal. She notices that the sheep are behaving strangely: they fight viciously, and even injure themselves on the fence wire, to reach a weed that grows from the neighbouring farm's corn. The neighbour has planted a new genetically engineered corn supplied by a large company. After a lamb is born with only two legs and the newborn baby of a friend who regularly eats lamb dies, Emily investigates and discovers that the corn is an experiment in genetic engineering. She tries to warn people about the contaminated meat, but few listen, and she ends up confronting the company testing the corn, her employers and her own family. The film is a cautionary drama about genetically modified crops. A biotechnology company tests a new corn variety in an ordinary farming community; the crop spreads an unexpected weed, the sheep that eat it become aggressive and addicted to it, and the effects appear to pass through the food chain to the people who eat the meat, causing birth defects and deaths. The scientists behind the corn appear only occasionally and grow worried as the problems emerge, while the company is portrayed as a powerful interest that local people are reluctant to challenge. Sources differ on the details of the modification: one synopsis describes a corn engineered to resist pesticides and grow with little water, while a review mentions a gene from a cold-water fish. The film was made on a very small budget and reviewers found its treatment of the theme thin. The harms it depicts are fictional: there is a scientific consensus that food from currently available GM crops poses no greater risk to health than conventional food, although each new crop must be assessed case by case.

title: Elfen Lied
themes: mutants human experimentation genetic discrimination nature nurture
text: This anime series, adapted from Lynn Okamoto's manga, follows the Diclonii, a newly mutated species that looks human apart from two small horns but has "vectors", invisible telekinetic arms that can cut through anything within reach. Lucy, a teenage Diclonius held in a secret research facility off the coast of Kamakura, escapes in a massacre but is wounded in the head and develops a second, childlike personality called Nyu, who can say little more than her name. She is taken in by two students, Kouta and his cousin Yuka, who know nothing of her past. The facility repeatedly tries to recapture her, sending a special assault team and other Diclonii, including Mariko, the daughter of one of its researchers. Flashbacks gradually reveal how Lucy was rejected by humans as a child, and that her meeting with Kouta, who has lost his childhood memories, is not a coincidence. The 13-episode anime ended while the manga was still running, so its ending differs from the manga's. Elfen Lied uses a mutation as the basis of its conflict between two species. The Diclonii are a new branch of humanity that could replace their parent species: a Diclonius's vectors can transmit a "vector virus" to human men, whose children are then born as Diclonii, so the mutation spreads by infection rather than ordinary inheritance. The scientists who run the research facility hold Diclonii captive, experiment on them and treat them as a threat to be contained, and they take drastic measures against the virus's spread: one researcher, Kurama, whose daughter Mariko was born a Diclonius after he was touched by a Diclonius's vectors, urges a colleague to be sterilised. A central question of the series is whether the Diclonii's violence is part of their genetic code or the result of abuse by humans, and the anime's director, Mamoru Kanbe, said he intended it to show how atrocities are shaped by the way people are treated. In the manga, the Diclonii are kept in a cave named after the Nazi Lebensborn programme. A virus that turns a man's future children into another species has no real counterpart.

title: Frankenfish
text: In the Louisiana bayou, a fisherman is killed by an unseen animal. Medical examiner Sam Rivers and biologist Mary Callahan go to investigate and reach a small community of houseboats and stilt houses, where residents say a strange boat washed upriver after a hurricane three months earlier. Sam and Mary find the boat with its crew dead in the hold and accidentally trigger a homing signal. That night, huge fish that can breathe air and move on land begin attacking the residents, killing several people and sinking their homes. Jeff, a wealthy hunter whose team was tracking the signal, arrives and explains that the fish are genetically engineered snakeheads. Sam and the survivors are forced to join his hunt; a third, much larger fish kills Jeff and his men. Sam kills it by luring it into the fan of his airboat, but the film ends with dozens of young fish attacking a survivor stuck in the mud. Genetic engineering explains the monsters but is barely explored. The fish are snakeheads modified to grow to the size of a man, and they escape when the boat carrying them is wrecked by a hurricane; the people responsible are never seen, and the only figure linked to them is a wealthy bounty hunter tracking the boat's signal. The film thus treats genetic modification as a commercial product released through negligence, with ordinary bayou residents paying the price. Its real inspiration was ecological rather than genetic: in 2002 a northern snakehead, an invasive East Asian fish that can breathe air and wriggle between bodies of water, was found in a pond in Crofton, Maryland, an incident that also inspired two other films. Real genetically engineered fish do exist; AquAdvantage salmon, which grow to market size faster thanks to an added growth hormone gene, became the first genetically engineered animal approved as food in the United States and Canada, but they are not larger at maturity and pose nothing like the film's threat.

title: Godsend
text: The day after his eighth birthday, Adam, the only son of Paul and Jessie Duncan, is killed by a car. Soon after, Dr. Richard Wells, a former professor of Jessie's, offers to clone the boy, an illegal procedure that requires the family to move and change identity. The new Adam grows up normally until he passes the age at which his predecessor died; then he begins to have nightmares and waking visions of a boy named Zachary, of a school on fire and of a woman killed with a hammer, and he becomes cruel and violent. Paul discovers that Zachary Clark was a disturbed boy who set fire to his school, killed his mother and died in a house fire, and that his father was a geneticist: Wells, living under a new name. Wells had mixed Zachary's DNA into Adam's clone in the hope of bringing his own son back. The family flees, but the ending suggests that Zachary has taken over. Godsend is a supernatural thriller built on human reproductive cloning, presented as a way to replace a dead child. Its geneticist, Richard Wells, works illegally and deceives the grieving parents: he secretly uses their son's cloning to resurrect his own dead son, whose fire-damaged DNA he mixes with Adam's. The film treats the clone as a kind of reincarnation in which personality, memories and even violent tendencies return with the DNA, and it raises the ethical questions of grief-driven cloning and of a doctor playing God with families. Biologically, a clone is a genetic copy, a later-born identical twin, not a copy of a person's mind or memories, and DNA from two individuals cannot simply be blended to bring one of them back. Mammalian cloning from an adult cell was achieved with Dolly the sheep in 1996, but human reproductive cloning has never been demonstrated.

title: Hide and Seek
text: In Atlantis, Dr. Rodney McKay volunteers for Dr. Carson Beckett's gene therapy, which gives him the ATA gene that people need to operate the technology of the Ancients. It works: he activates a personal shield that protects him from a fall, a gunshot and a blow, but he cannot switch it off and can no longer eat or drink. Meanwhile, the Athosian boy Jinto, playing hide-and-seek, accidentally opens a containment device in which the Ancients had trapped an energy-eating entity. The 'shadow' drains the city's generators, burns Lieutenant Ford and grows more dangerous. Attempts to recapture it fail, and Teyla suggests letting it leave through the Stargate. When the creature starts feeding on the gate, McKay, whose shield has dropped, reactivates it, walks into the entity and throws a generator through the gate; the creature follows, and McKay survives. Gene therapy opens the episode and shapes its subplot. In the Stargate universe, the Ancients' technology responds only to people who carry a particular gene, the ATA gene, and the Atlantis expedition's physician, Dr. Carson Beckett, has developed a gene therapy to give it to those who lack it. McKay is a willing volunteer, and the therapy works, but with an unforeseen side effect: he cannot turn off the personal shield he activates. Beckett wonders whether the 'artificial gene' is to blame, while the team suspects McKay's own fear is keeping it on. The treatment is presented as a legitimate, useful medical innovation by a well-meaning doctor, its mishap is mostly played for comedy, and the shield finally lets McKay save the city. Real gene therapy is used to correct inherited diseases rather than to add new abilities, and no gene lets anyone control machines by thought.

title: Mobile Suit Gundam SEED Destiny
alt: 機動戦士ガンダムSEED DESTINY Gundam SEED Destiny
themes: eugenics human enhancement genetic discrimination genetic engineering
text: Two years after the war of Mobile Suit Gundam SEED, in Cosmic Era 73, an uneasy peace holds between the Earth Alliance of ordinary humans (Naturals) and the PLANTs, space colonies of genetically enhanced humans (Coordinators). The theft of three new ZAFT mobile suits by Phantom Pain, a unit of the anti-Coordinator movement Blue Cosmos, and the crash of the colony Junius Seven onto Earth by ZAFT extremists reignite the war. The young Coordinator pilot Shinn Asuka, who lost his family in the last war, fights for ZAFT aboard the Minerva, while the veterans Kira Yamato and Athrun Zala are drawn back in. After Blue Cosmos leader Lord Djibril fires the superweapon Requiem at the PLANTs and is killed, PLANT chairman Gilbert Durandal unveils his Destiny Plan, a world order assigning everyone's role by their genes. Kira and Athrun defeat his forces, Durandal is killed by his follower Rey, and the extended finale ends in peace talks. Genetics is the setting and, in the end, the stake of this mecha war drama. Society is split between Coordinators, humans genetically enhanced before birth, and unmodified Naturals, and the war is driven by resentment and bigotry on both sides, embodied by the anti-Coordinator movement Blue Cosmos. The Earth Alliance also fields "Extended" pilots like Stella Loussier, Naturals raised to Coordinator level by experiments and conditioning that the sources do not describe as genetic. The final arc turns to eugenics: Durandal's Destiny Plan would decide each person's job and place in society by their genes and enforce this with the Requiem superweapon against anyone who resists. The heroes, themselves Coordinators, reject it in the name of free choice, and the series presents genetic determinism imposed from above as the last villainy of the war rather than as a path to peace.

title: ReGenesis
text: This Canadian series, which ran for four seasons from 2004 to 2008, follows the scientists of NorBAC, the North American Biotechnology Advisory Commission, a fictional agency based in Toronto that investigates scientific threats across North America, such as bioterrorism, mysterious diseases and sudden environmental changes. The team is led by David Sandström, a molecular biologist and the agency's chief scientist, and includes the geneticist and physician Carlos Serrano, the biochemist Bob Melnikov, virologists and bioinformaticians, together with the agency's executive directors, who handle its political pressures. Episodes combine scientific detective work with personal storylines. In the first season, for example, Sandström befriends Mick, a teenage boy who believes he is a clone: he was in fact a frozen embryo whose DNA his father, a doctor, manipulated to remove a cancer-causing gene, with unintended changes that left him ill. Genetics and biotechnology are the subject of the series, and its central characters are working scientists. NorBAC's cases range from bioterrorism and outbreaks of unknown diseases to embryo manipulation and mad cow disease, and the show often uses them to address social, political and ethical questions. The scientists are portrayed as skilled but fallible professionals who work for a public agency rather than for a corporation or a villain, and are as likely to solve a crisis as to be drawn into its ethics. The Mick storyline illustrates the show's approach: a father's attempt to correct a disease gene in an embryo has unintended effects elsewhere in the genome, a concern that still applies to real embryo editing. The series' scientific consultant was Aled Edwards, a Canadian molecular biologist and director of the Structural Genomics Consortium, and the first-season DVD included white papers by the Ontario Genomics Institute on the facts behind the fiction.

title: Resident Evil: Apocalypse
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic human enhancement human experimentation genetic disease bioweapon
text: After escaping the Hive, the Umbrella Corporation's underground genetic research facility, Alice wakes in a deserted hospital to find the zombie outbreak spreading through Raccoon City. Umbrella seals the city, leaving survivors such as the police officer Jill Valentine and Umbrella soldier Carlos Olivera to fend for themselves, and unleashes Nemesis, a mutated super-soldier. Umbrella scientist Dr. Charles Ashford, trapped in the quarantine, offers to arrange the survivors' escape if they rescue his daughter Angela, warning that Umbrella plans to destroy the city with a nuclear bomb. Angela reveals that her father created the T-virus to treat her genetic disease, and she carries an antiviral serum. At the extraction point, Umbrella's Major Cain kills Ashford and forces Alice, herself enhanced by the T-virus, to fight Nemesis, who turns out to be her former ally Matt. The survivors escape as the city is destroyed; Alice is gravely injured and wakes in an Umbrella laboratory, from which she escapes in a move Umbrella has planned. The second Resident Evil film reveals the origin of its zombies. The T-virus was created by Dr. Charles Ashford, an Umbrella researcher, to treat his daughter Angela's genetic disease; Umbrella appropriated it, and its release in the Hive turned people into zombies. Ashford is shown as a desperate father who also holds the antiviral serum, while the corporation is the villain: it experiments on captives, turning the activist Matt into the mutated super-soldier Nemesis and enhancing Alice with the T-virus, and it covers up the outbreak by destroying Raccoon City with a nuclear bomb and blaming a power-plant meltdown. The film thus combines a well-meant gene therapy gone catastrophically wrong with a corporation that sees human beings as experimental material. Reviewers read the cover-up as an allegory of corporate and state lies. A virus that both corrects a genetic disease and reanimates the dead belongs to the video-game mythology, not to real virology.

title: Resurrection
text: In this Stargate SG-1 episode, written by cast member Michael Shanks and directed by Amanda Tapping, an NID agent, Malcolm Barrett, calls SG-1 to a facility in Los Angeles where 32 members of a rogue NID unit have been massacred. Security footage shows that the killer is Anna, a young woman now held in a glass cell; the other survivor is Dr. Keffler, an older German scientist and the son of a Nazi war criminal. The facility holds Goa'uld artefacts that belonged to Sekhmet and were first recovered by the Germans. Anna tells Daniel that Keffler created her, and Carter's research shows that she is a human and Goa'uld hybrid. Anna's drawings reveal the combination of a Goa'uld ark, which turns out to contain a naquadah bomb. Keffler admits he made her to tap the Goa'uld genetic memory, and she has a second personality, Sekhmet. While the team works on the bomb, Anna escapes; she and Keffler are found dead. The episode is about a human made from alien DNA. Dr. Keffler, working for a rogue unit of the NID, an American intelligence agency, combined a human egg with Goa'uld DNA from a symbiote kept in an ancient jar to create Anna, a hybrid grown to adulthood within a short time (with nanites, according to one source). His aim is to use her as a conduit to the Goa'uld's genetic memory, which in the series passes knowledge from one generation to the next. He treats Anna as an instrument: she is kept in a cell, forced to draw her visions and, according to the Spanish source, switched between her own personality and that of the Goa'uld Sekhmet with electric shocks. Keffler, the son of a Nazi war criminal, is presented as a villain; reviewers saw no redeeming features in him, although the actor saw him as believing he could save millions. The experiment ends in a massacre and the deaths of both creator and creation. Genetic memory, the inheritance of acquired knowledge, has no basis in real biology.

title: Species III
text: Eve, a clone of the alien hybrid Sil, gives birth to a daughter before being killed by Portus, a half-breed son of the astronaut Patrick Ross. Dr. Bruce Abbot, a biochemistry professor, takes the baby, names her Sara and raises her in secret, while a government agent, Wasach, destroys the evidence. Sara grows rapidly, and the dying Portus reveals that other half-breeds suffer from fatal illnesses. Abbot recruits his student Dean to help perfect the alien DNA and save the species. After pupating into an adult, Sara kills Abbot's superior when he tries to rape her and goes in search of a mate; a sick half-breed, Yosef, mortally wounds Abbot. Another hybrid, Amelia, kidnaps Dean's roommate Hastings to force him to refine the DNA. At Dean's experimental power plant, Sara throws Amelia into the core. Dean later uses the refined DNA to create a mate for Sara, making sure he is sterile. Genetics drives this third Species film. Its creatures are human-alien hybrids descended from a government project, Project Athena, that combined human DNA with alien DNA and produced Sil and her clone Eve, and from an astronaut infected with alien DNA on Mars. Most of the resulting half-breeds are genetically defective and dying, while Sara is the most perfect combination. Dr. Abbot, a biochemistry professor, kidnaps and raises Sara to perfect the alien DNA and save the species, arguing that it is wrong to decide whether a species should live or die; his student Dean continues the work, falls for Sara and finally engineers a sterile mate for her so she will not be alone without endangering humanity. The film treats extinction and species rescue as an ethical question, but its science, from cross-species alien hybrids to pupation, is pure fantasy.

title: The Augments
text: Concluding a three-part story, Dr. Arik Soong and the "Augments", genetically enhanced humans he raised from embryos, escape Cold Station 12 with 1,800 frozen Augment embryos from the time of the Eugenics Wars and pathogen samples. Captain Archer pursues them into Klingon space in the Enterprise. Soong wants to hide in a remote region and raise the embryos, but Malik, the Augments' leader, plans to fire a pathogen-filled torpedo at a Klingon colony to start a war between the Klingons and Starfleet. When Soong tries to remove aggressive traits from the embryos, Malik mutinies; Soong escapes and helps Archer. The Enterprise destroys the torpedo, Malik scuttles his ship, killing the other Augments and the embryos, and Archer kills Malik when he tries to murder Soong. Back in custody, Soong begins to doubt that humans can be improved through genetic engineering and turns his thoughts to artificial life. Human genetic enhancement is the subject of the episode, which ends the Enterprise arc about the Augments, descendants of the engineered supermen of Star Trek's Eugenics Wars, and links the series to Khan in the original series. Dr. Arik Soong is an idealistic scientist who sees himself as the Augments' father and believes they represent the future, yet the episode shows his creations as arrogant, aggressive and willing to commit genocide. Soong's attempt to edit aggression out of the embryos provokes the mutiny, and his final conclusion is that genetic engineering of humans may be a dead end, and he turns instead to artificial life, foreshadowing the android Data. The episode repeats Star Trek's recurring message that enhancement brings ambition and violence along with superior abilities. Genetic enhancement of human traits, as opposed to the treatment of disease, remains hypothetical.

title: A.T.O.M.
text: In Landmark City, five teenagers, Axel Manning, Catalina Leone, Crey Kingston, Zack Hawkes and Ollie Sharker, win a television contest that is really a front through which Janus Lee, head of Lee Industries, recruits talented adolescents. As the team A.T.O.M. (Alpha Teens On Machines), they receive prototype weapons, gadgets and transforming vehicles to fight the crime boss Alexander Paine, who killed Axel's father, and his henchmen. At the end of the first season they defeat Paine, but learn that Lee's true aim was to harvest their DNA and use it to create clones enhanced with animal DNA. In the second season the teens unite against their former benefactor and his 'Mu-Team', an army of animal-powered mutant clones, while also facing other villains, until they stop Lee. Genetics drives the second season of this animated superhero series. The teens' patron, the industrialist Janus Lee, turns out to have recruited them in order to take their DNA without their knowledge, and he uses it to create clones powered by animal genes, the 'Mu-Team', which he turns against the original team. Genetic engineering (cloning and the mixing of human and animal DNA) is thus presented as a tool of betrayal and exploitation in the hands of a corporate villain seeking power. The sources mention a character called Dr. Recombo but do not describe any role. The science is cartoon fantasy, in line with many children's action shows of the period that use animal-human hybrids as villains.

title: Affliction
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering engineered pathogens pandemic
text: As Enterprise returns to Earth and Trip Tucker transfers to the new starship Columbia, Doctor Phlox is kidnapped in San Francisco. Following clues that point to Rigelian attackers, Enterprise gives chase, while Lieutenant Reed is secretly given orders by an agent of a covert organisation he seems to know. Enterprise is attacked and boarded, and a captured intruder who looks human turns out to be a Klingon; saboteurs force the ship to flee at record speed to avoid a warp core breach. Meanwhile, Phlox is taken to a Klingon colony, where General K'Vagh and Doctor Antaak demand that he cure a plague. Examining a victim, Phlox finds that his DNA has been combined with that of genetically augmented humans: the Klingons had experimented with Augment DNA, but it mutated and spread as a plague. Given five days to stop the outbreak, Antaak proposes creating stable augmented Klingons, but Phlox refuses to help. The story continues in "Divergence". Genetic engineering drives the episode, the first part of a two-part story. The Klingon Empire, alarmed by the genetically enhanced human "Augments" seen earlier in the season, has tried to create its own super-soldiers using Augment DNA, and the experiment has turned into a plague. Phlox, a doctor kidnapped to fix the problem, refuses to help produce more augmented Klingons, while the Klingon scientist Antaak is a reluctant participant in a military programme. The plague's symptoms include the loss of the Klingons' forehead ridges, and the story was designed to explain in-universe why Klingons looked human in the original series of the 1960s and had ridges from the 1979 film onwards. Critics welcomed the link to the Augments. Scientifically, the idea of a virus spreading another species' engineered genes and reshaping the anatomy of adults is fantasy, although viral vectors are used in real gene therapy to deliver genes into cells.

title: Ben 10
text: Ten-year-old Ben Tennyson is spending his summer holidays travelling across the United States in a motorhome with his cousin Gwen and their grandfather Max. On their first night camping, Ben finds an alien pod containing the Omnitrix, a prototype device shaped like a watch that attaches itself to his wrist and lets him transform into a range of alien creatures, each with its own powers. As he learns to use it responsibly, the trio face a series of extraterrestrial and supernatural enemies, above all the alien warlord Vilgax, who wants the Omnitrix for himself. Other recurring villains include Dr. Animo, a scientist who mutates animals, and Kevin 11, a delinquent who absorbs energy and eventually turns into a permanent hybrid of Ben's alien forms. Genetics provides the series' central gadget. The Omnitrix contains the DNA of many alien species, and by using it Ben temporarily rewrites his body into one of those species, an idea that presents DNA as a code that fully determines an organism's form and abilities and can be swapped at will. The device can also scan new species, as happens by accident with the alien Zs'Skayr, so DNA acts almost as a collectable resource. The clearest scientist figure is the villain Dr. Animo, a veterinary scientist whose career ended when he was discovered carrying out twisted genetic experiments on animals, and who keeps creating mutant creatures to defeat Ben and rule the world. Kevin 11's transformation into an irreversible hybrid of Ben's aliens shows the risks of such power. The series is aimed at children and does not attempt realism: an adult body cannot be transformed by changing its DNA, since DNA directs development and cell function rather than reshaping an existing organism instantly.

title: Carl²
text: Carl², or Carl Squared, is a Canadian animated sitcom that ran for four seasons on Teletoon from 2005 to 2011. Carl Crashman is a lazy 14-year-old whose only talent is slacking. After a bad day, while complaining about his life online, he accidentally orders a clone from a spam e-mail, supplying his fingerprint, a yearbook photo and a scabby bandage. An online cloning company sends him an exact copy of himself in a box, whom he names C2. C2 looks, talks and walks like Carl, though with a higher-pitched voice, but he is ambitious, hard-working and charming. Carl uses him to slack off even more, but C2 often does the opposite of what Carl wants. Carl keeps the clone secret from everyone except his best friend, Jamie James, and the episodes follow the comic complications of sharing one identity. Cloning is the series' premise, played for comedy and aimed at children and young teenagers. The clone is ordered online from a company advertising through spam, made from a fingerprint and a scab, and delivered fully grown in a box, a parody of consumer biotechnology rather than a depiction of real science. The series explores identity through the contrast between two genetically identical boys with opposite personalities: the original is lazy, while the clone is diligent and likeable, implying that sharing a genome does not mean sharing a character. No scientists play a significant role. In reality a clone would be an embryo that develops and grows up like any child, making it a much younger identical twin rather than an instant double of the same age.

title: Conversion
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras engineered pathogens bioweapon
text: In this second-season episode of Stargate Atlantis, Major John Sheppard has been injected with the Wraith retrovirus, the experimental agent that the expedition hopes can turn Wraith into humans. Instead it begins transforming him into a hybrid of human and Iratus bug, an insect species. The Atlantis team races against time to find a way to reverse the transformation before it becomes complete. As the change progresses Sheppard becomes increasingly difficult to deal with, yet he may also hold the key to his own salvation. The episode is built on the season's central project: Dr. Carson Beckett's retrovirus, designed to turn a Wraith into a human, which the expedition sees as a weapon against its enemies. Here the retrovirus has the opposite effect on a human: once injected into Sheppard, it starts to turn him into an Iratus bug hybrid, and the expedition's doctors and scientists must undo the transformation. The episode thus shows a genetic weapon whose effects its makers cannot fully control, with the medical team presented as the heroes trying to save their colleague. The source gives only a short summary and does not describe how the cure is found. The idea of a retrovirus rewriting a whole organism into another species in days is fiction, although real retroviruses do insert their genes into host DNA, which is why they are used as vectors in gene therapy.

title: Dalek
text: A distress signal draws the Ninth Doctor and Rose Tyler to an underground bunker in Utah in 2012, owned by Henry van Statten, a billionaire who collects alien artefacts and exploits their technology. His prize specimen, chained and tortured to make it speak, turns out to be a Dalek, the last survivor of the Time War in which the Doctor believed he had destroyed its whole race. Van Statten also has the Doctor chained and scanned, planning to patent his alien physiology. Moved by the creature's suffering, Rose touches it; the Dalek absorbs her DNA, uses the biomass of a time traveller to regenerate, breaks free and massacres the staff. But Rose's DNA has changed it: it cannot bring itself to kill her and begins to feel fear and new emotions. Calling its mutation a sickness, the Dalek asks Rose to order it to die and destroys itself. Genetics enters this acclaimed episode through DNA absorption. By touching the Dalek, Rose lets it take her DNA, which it uses to rebuild itself, but the human genetic material also 'mutates' it, giving it fear and other emotions no Dalek should have; unable to bear being a mutant, it chooses to die. The episode thus treats DNA as carrying not just bodily traits but feelings, an idea that serves the drama of a monster made sympathetic. Its real target is the abuse of science by private wealth: van Statten tortures alien prisoners for information and wants to patent the Doctor's physiology, which links the story to debates on patenting biological material. No real organism can repair itself or acquire emotions by absorbing someone else's DNA through touch.

title: Divergence
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering engineered pathogens pandemic human experimentation
text: In this second part of a two-part story, Doctor Phlox is a prisoner at a Klingon colony, forced to work with the Klingon physician Antaak on a cure for a plague. The disease began as an attempt to create Klingon "Augments" using the DNA of genetically enhanced humans; the altered DNA mutated, spread as a virus and is killing its victims after stripping them of their cranial ridges. Meanwhile, Commander Tucker joins Enterprise from Columbia to purge the sabotage that keeps the ship at dangerous speed, and Captain Archer learns that Lieutenant Reed has been working for Section 31. As a Klingon admiral prepares to destroy the colony to contain the outbreak, Enterprise and Columbia arrive. Phlox infects Archer to obtain the human antibodies needed for the cure, and Antaak beams the virus onto the admiral's ship, forcing him to accept the cure. The Klingon High Council distributes it, but the cured keep their human-like appearance. The episode concludes an arc about the Augments, genetically enhanced humans in Star Trek's history. Klingon scientists tried to create their own super-soldiers by adding Augment DNA to Klingons, but the modified genome turned into a contagious virus that threatens the whole species. Phlox, who refuses to build "living weapons", works to switch off the virus rather than perfect the Augments, and the cure leaves the survivors with smooth foreheads. The episodes were written to explain why Klingons look human in the original 1960s series but have ridged foreheads in later productions. Scientists appear on both sides: Antaak, who blames himself for the outbreak, and Phlox, a doctor with firm ethics; the experiment itself was ordered by the military and tested on prisoners and on a unit of soldiers. A virus that spreads a genetic modification evokes real viral vectors used in gene therapy, but the idea that such changes could sweep through a population as an epidemic is fiction.

title: Doom
themes: genetic engineering human experimentation mutants human enhancement
text: Loosely based on the video game series. In 2046, the Union Aerospace Corporation (UAC) runs a research station on Mars, reached through the Ark, a portal discovered under the Nevada desert. After an attack on the facility, a squad of marines led by Sarge is sent to retrieve the company's research data, accompanied by the scientist Samantha Grimm, sister of the marine John "Reaper" Grimm. They find that the scientists had uncovered the remains of an ancient humanoid race with an artificial extra pair of chromosomes, the 24th, and had been injecting this "C24" into humans. Most of those injected turn into monsters, which spread through the station and through the Ark to Earth. Samantha suggests that C24 transforms people according to their nature. When Reaper is gravely wounded, she injects him with it: he gains superhuman abilities, kills the infected Sarge and carries his sister home. Genetics provides the film's horror premise. The UAC's anthropology and genetics research has found that an extinct Martian race was genetically enhanced with an artificial 24th chromosome pair, and the company has been testing this "Martian chromosome" on people, without regard for the consequences. Samantha Grimm explains the results in moralistic terms: C24 grants superhuman abilities to some but turns those with violent or psychotic tendencies into monsters, as she believes happened to the Martians. The scientists are mostly victims of their own experiments, while the corporation is the real culprit, valuing the data above the lives of its staff. Genetically, the premise does not hold up. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, so a 24th pair would be a new, artificial addition, and a single injection could not insert it into the trillions of cells of an adult body. Behaviour is shaped by many genes and the environment, not by a switch that sorts good people from bad.

title: Get Ed
text: This animated series is set in the futuristic Progress City. Ed is a genetically engineered teenager who works as a courier for Dojo Deliveries, together with Burn, Deets, Fizz and Loogie, under their mentor Ol' Skool. Ol' Skool created Ed from instructions in an ancient alien artefact, secretly supplied by the Caretaker, a guardian of alien machines who believes Ed is destined to save both Earth and her own planet. Besides delivering packages, the team fights identity theft and data crime, while Ed uncovers his origins and finds alien artefacts that bond with him and give him new abilities. Their enemy is Mr. Bedlam, Ol' Skool's treacherous former partner, a greedy industrialist who wants to control the city, sends armies of regenerating clone couriers and robots after the team, and tries to capture Ed to copy his genetic signature or make his own Ed. Genetic engineering defines the hero and drives much of the conflict. Ed is an 'electro-genetically' enhanced teenager, built by his kindly mentor from alien instructions, whose engineered body lets him bond with alien technology. The villain, Bedlam, covets that genetic design: he wants to collect Ed's DNA to change his own genetic signature or produce his own Ed, and his company, DNA Deliveries, fields armies of unstable, regenerating clone couriers that dissolve into slime when beaten. The series thus sets a benevolent creator, whose creation protects the city, against a corporate villain who wants to exploit genetics for power and profit. Its genetics is cartoon science: clones that regenerate and melt, and a genome that can be 'matched' by stealing someone else's DNA, are pure fantasy.

title: Guyver: The Bioboosted Armor
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement human experimentation hybrids chimeras
text: The secret Chronos Corporation, which has plans for the world, has biologically engineered employees and soldiers who can turn into powerful monsters called Zoanoids. A test-type Zoanoid escapes with three alien devices that Chronos was studying, the Guyver units, and blows himself up, scattering them. High school student Shō Fukamachi finds one and accidentally activates it; it merges with him as a living armour that gives him great strength and weapons. Chronos sends Zoanoids to recover the unit or cut it from his body, endangering his friend Tetsurō and Tetsurō's sister Mizuki, whom Shō loves. As the battles escalate, hidden from the public by Chronos's influence over politics and the media, Shō meets other Guyver hosts, including the ambiguous Agito Makishima, son of the former head of Chronos Japan, and the journalist Masaki Murakami, used as a test subject by Chronos, and he uncovers the origins of the Guyvers, the Zoanoids and Chronos. The series' monsters are products of biological engineering. The Chronos Corporation turns its own employees and soldiers into Zoanoids, people who can transform into powerful creatures, refines them through an optimization process, and uses those who fail it, the Lost Numbers, as expendable test subjects for genetic research. It also experiments on captured people, such as the journalist Masaki Murakami, in programmes to create more powerful beings. The Guyver units themselves are a living alien armour that bonds with its host. Chronos is the villain throughout: a corporation that pursues world domination through human experimentation and hides its secret war from the public. The source used here is brief and does not explain the biology or the final revelations about the origins of Chronos and the Guyvers. Turning people into transforming monsters is fantasy with no basis in real genetic engineering.

title: Identity
alt: Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, season 6, episode 12
themes: nature nurture dna identification human experimentation
text: Detectives Benson and Stabler investigate a gang member who fell from a building after the person he tried to rape bit him in self-defence. They believe they have found the victim, a teenage boy, but his twin sister says that she was the one who bit the attacker, even though analysis of the bite shows that it came from someone chromosomally male. The twins are shocked to learn the truth: after a botched circumcision, their parents raised one of the boys as a girl. The investigation then uncovers the ulterior motive of a doctor who wanted to use the twins to prove that nurture overrides nature. The episode is partly inspired by the real case of David Reimer. Two genetic elements drive the episode. Forensic analysis of the bite shows that the biter was chromosomally male, which exposes the secret of the twin raised as a girl. The deeper theme is nature against nurture in gender identity: a doctor with an ulterior motive used the twins to prove that upbringing could override biology. The story sides with nature, presenting the experiment as a deception that harmed the twins. The real case behind it was that of David Reimer, a Canadian twin raised as a girl after a botched circumcision on the advice of the psychologist John Money, who claimed for years that the reassignment had succeeded; in fact Reimer rejected the female identity and later lived as a man, and the case is now cited as evidence that gender identity is not simply learned. The only available source is a short synopsis, so details of the resolution are unknown.

title: Instinct
text: In this second-season episode of Stargate Atlantis, the Atlantis team investigating a planet comes across a young Wraith girl who survived the crash of a Wraith ship years earlier. She has been raised in secret by a human man, who hides her from the people of the nearby village because he fears for her life. The girl longs to be human and takes an incomplete version of a drug developed by Dr. Carson Beckett to turn Wraith into humans, without considering the consequences. Meanwhile, the team learns that another Wraith who survived the crash is killing villagers. The genetic element is Dr. Carson Beckett's experimental retrovirus, the season's central project, meant to turn a Wraith into a human. In this episode a Wraith girl raised by a human takes an unfinished version of the drug in the hope of becoming human herself, without considering the consequences. The source summary does not say how the drug affects her, but the episode sets up the dangers of the retrovirus that the following episode, Conversion, develops when it turns a human into an Iratus bug hybrid. Beckett's unfinished work is thus used before it is ready. Turning one species into another with a drug remains pure fiction.

title: Larva
text: In Host, Missouri, a town dominated by the Tender Meats processing plant, new veterinarian Eli Rudkus finds strange larvae in the stool of a cow belonging to farmer Jacob Long. He traces them to a special feed that the company's CEO, Fletcher Odermatt, has sold to local farmers: it is genetically engineered to make the meat taste better, and it has mutated fluke-like parasites. When Eli tries to warn the town at a public meeting, the company's lawyer, Haley Anderson, shuts him down. The larvae grow fast inside animals and people, burst out of their hosts and turn into large bat-like creatures that devour everything in their path.
