Eli and Haley are forced to work together, the survivors are chased into the sewers, and Jacob's stockpile of weapons helps save the day before the parasites are destroyed in a huge explosion. The monsters are an unintended product of agricultural genetic engineering. A meat-processing company sells farmers a genetically engineered cattle feed meant to make beef tastier; parasites in the animals mutate after eating it and become fast-growing, flesh-eating creatures that burst out of their hosts. The practitioner is the corporation, represented by its CEO and its lawyer, who silence the vet who raises the alarm: a standard 'sinister corporation' plot in which profit-driven tampering with the food chain unleashes horror. Reviewers noted that the film's genetic explanation is vague and that the story borrows heavily from Arachnophobia. The idea that a feed could make parasites mutate into large predators is pure monster-movie invention, though the fear of genetically modified food it plays on was a live public concern.

title: Lilo & Stitch 2: Stitch Has a Glitch
text: On Kauai, Lilo prepares an original hula for the May Day competition her late mother once won, while her alien friend Stitch, an illegal genetic experiment, has nightmares about reverting to his destructive programming. Soon he starts having seizures and turning violent against his will. His creator, Dr. Jumba Jookiba, finds that his molecular structure was never fully charged because his creation was interrupted by Jumba's arrest; unless fixed, Stitch will die. Lilo, absorbed by the competition, thinks Stitch is misbehaving on purpose and grows angry with him, while Jumba builds a recharging machine from household objects. When a seizure makes Stitch scratch Lilo's face, he flees in Jumba's spaceship and crashes. Lilo abandons the contest to find him; placed in the machine, Stitch seems to die, but Lilo's declaration that he is her family revives him, and the family performs the hula together that night. Stitch is a creature made in a laboratory, an "illegal genetic experiment" built by Jumba, a former evil genius, as a weapon of destruction. This sequel turns the premise into a medical drama: because his creation was cut short when Jumba was arrested, Stitch has a built-in defect that triggers seizures, brings back his destructive programming and will eventually kill him. Jumba, now a member of the family, is shown as a caring if eccentric scientist who works frantically to save his creation, improvising a machine from household appliances after the first one explodes. In the end, though, it is Lilo's love rather than the machine that revives Stitch, as Jumba himself concludes; the film's message is that family and acceptance matter more than how one was made. The "molecular charge" is cartoon science, not genetics.

title: Locusts
text: At a Department of Agriculture laboratory in Virginia, Dr. Maddy Rierdon, an agriculture official specializing in pests, discovers that her former professor and boss, Dr. Peter Axelrod, has bred a hybrid of the Australian plague locust and the desert locust that shrugs off DDT. She orders the insects destroyed and fires him, but a few escape, some through a sink and others when samples taken by the military are dropped in California. Within weeks, swarms are stripping farms in California and attacking people in the East, putting Peter's daughter in a coma, and the eastern swarm turns carnivorous. Peter, arrested by the FBI, warns Maddy that the authorities plan to use VX nerve gas, and Maddy wrecks the military's test run. Sheltering in a grain silo, Peter dies fetching fuel so that the others can electrify it. Finally the national power grid is rerouted into two giant electric traps that destroy the swarms. Genetic engineering creates the disaster. Dr. Peter Axelrod, a government agricultural scientist, has engineered a hybrid super-locust by crossing the Australian plague locust with the desert locust, producing insects that resist pesticides such as DDT; once a few escape, the swarms devour crops across the United States and even turn on people. The film follows the familiar formula of genetic tinkering with a harmless creature, accidental release, and scientists racing to find a solution before the military takes drastic action. Axelrod is responsible for the catastrophe, but he admits it, tries to help and dies saving the others, while the heroine, a government pest scientist, stops the military's plan to use nerve gas. Real locust species cannot be crossed to produce pesticide-proof, carnivorous swarms.

title: Mansquito
text: In Baltimore, Dr. Jennifer Allen is looking for a cure for the deadly Gillen virus by working with infected mosquitoes, which she treats with small doses of radiation. Ray Erikson, a convict who joins her programme in exchange for a commuted sentence, takes a hostage and forces his way into the experiment room; in the shoot-out an explosion drenches him and Allen with chemicals and genetically altered mosquitoes. Ray turns into a giant human-mosquito monster, kills his ex-girlfriend and goes on a killing spree, pursued by Allen's boyfriend, police lieutenant Tom Randall, who finds that a stun gun hurts it. Allen begins to transform too, and believes the creature wants her as a mate. She releases the last, perfected batch of altered mosquitoes, and when the monster attacks her at the lab she electrocutes it, dying herself. The altered mosquitoes wipe out the Gillen virus. This made-for-television monster film, in the vein of The Fly, turns a well-meant medical experiment into a human-insect hybrid. Dr. Jennifer Allen works with mosquitoes infected with the Gillen virus, which she irradiates and genetically alters in search of a cure. An accident caused by an escaping convict showers him and Allen with chemicals and altered mosquitoes, and both begin to transform into mosquito-human creatures. Allen is a sympathetic scientist who sacrifices herself to destroy the monster, and her final batch of mosquitoes does wipe out the virus, so the film ends with the research vindicated at a terrible cost. The underlying idea loosely echoes real proposals to release modified mosquitoes against disease, but the transformation of people by exposure to irradiated insects is pure B-movie fantasy. The source gives little detail on the science.

title: Painkiller Jane
themes: engineered pathogens human enhancement genetic engineering human experimentation bioweapon
text: During a mission in Chechnya, a special forces unit is exposed to a biochemical weapon and then executed by men in hazmat suits. Captain Jane Browning survives both the execution and the infection, and develops rapid healing, increased speed and strength, heightened senses and a photographic memory. Questioned by a psychiatrist, Dr. Graham Knight, and tested by the military, she escapes with the help of a thief, Nick Pierce, when her superior, Colonel Ian Watts, plans to move her to Alaska. Searching for answers, she learns that the virus she was exposed to was designed to alter people's DNA and enhance them, and that its creator, Peter Erfan, is the man who posed as Dr. Knight. Erfan calls her the "new Eve": her body altered the virus, which in turn changed her. He kidnaps her to use her for his project, but she escapes. In the final scene Erfan, who has apparently injected himself, meets Asian business partners to create an army of superhumans. The film's premise is a virus engineered to modify human DNA. The geneticist Peter Erfan creates it as a way of enhancing people, but it is used as a weapon and kills an entire special forces unit; only Jane survives, because something in her body changes the virus, which then gives her healing and other enhanced abilities. The scientist is a villain who conceals his identity, uses the military and plans to sell the enhancement to foreign business partners to build an army of superhumans, so genetic modification is shown as a weapon and a commodity rather than a medical advance. Using viruses to carry genes into human cells is a real technique in gene therapy, where modified viruses act as "vectors". In reality, however, they deliver genes to some cells to treat specific diseases, and the risks include immune reactions; nothing like the instant, body-wide transformation in the film is possible.

title: Prototype
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras evolution human enhancement
text: Investigating a gravitational disturbance near the planet P3X-584, SG-1 finds an underground laboratory containing a DNA manipulation device, records written in the language of the Ancients, and a man in a stasis pod. They bring him to Earth, where he calls himself Khalek and claims to have been a prisoner of a Goa'uld. By translating the laboratory's records, Daniel Jackson learns the truth: Khalek was created by the Goa'uld Anubis, who combined human and Goa'uld DNA, gave him the genetic memory of the Goa'uld and accelerated his evolution, but was defeated before finishing this "prototype". Khalek has superhuman abilities, including telekinesis, and is close to being able to ascend to a higher plane of existence. Daniel argues that he must be killed, but an oversight committee sends Richard Woolsey to ensure he is kept alive for study. Khalek escapes his confinement and SG-1 must stop him. Khalek is a product of genetic engineering by a villain. Anubis built him in a laboratory by combining human and Goa'uld DNA and artificially accelerating his evolution, producing a being with the inherited memories of the Goa'uld, the series' parasitic villains, who is close to ascension. The episode uses the series' concept of "genetic memory", inherited knowledge passed through DNA, which is fictional; real DNA does not store memories, and evolution is not a ladder that an individual can be pushed up. The scientist, Anubis, is absent and malicious, and the episode's dilemma is about what to do with his creation: whether a being made as a weapon can be held responsible, killed preventively, or kept for research. The oversight committee's wish to study him despite the danger adds the familiar temptation to exploit a dangerous discovery.

title: The Fugitives
themes: cloning eugenics hybrids chimeras human experimentation
text: In this British children's science-fiction series, twelve-year-old Jay Keaton, a gifted boy, overhears his father, Marshall, talking about him with agents of the corrupt cloning company EmbroGen. Afraid that he is the subject of its experiments, Jay steals files from his father's office and runs away, joined by his friend Mel Banks. Pursued by EmbroGen's operatives Lomas and Boyer, the two discover a laboratory full of Jay's clones, are helped by an eccentric former professor, Maggie Wych, and learn from Jay's uncle Harry that Jay is a chimera with two complete sets of DNA, before finding that Harry works for EmbroGen too. Marshall, forced back to work by the company's head, Salko, is made to help with Eden II, a project to create perfect children, and secretly sabotages it. When Jay's sister Fleecey is badly injured, one of the clones, J2, donates a kidney to her. In the finale, Jay and Mel expose the clones to backers and press, and Salko's arrest turns out to be staged by his own operatives. Genetics drives the whole series. EmbroGen, a sinister company led by Salko, has cloned Jay several times, keeps the clones in an underground laboratory, tests their intelligence and uses one of them to impersonate him; its Eden II project aims to correct the errors of earlier work and create a world of perfect children, a eugenic goal that gives its head the future of the human race in his hands. Jay himself is revealed to be a chimera with two complete sets of DNA, created by his father, Marshall, a company scientist whom the story first presents as part of the plan and then redeems as he sabotages Eden II. Another scientist, Salko's former professor Maggie Wych, works to stop him. The clones are shown as innocent children who want a family, and one of them gives a kidney to Jay's sister. Human chimeras with two cell lineages do exist naturally, but a chimera does not have twice the number of genes.

title: The Gift
text: In this first-season episode of Stargate Atlantis, Teyla Emmagan is plagued by terrifying nightmares. To understand them she looks into her past offworld and finds an abandoned Wraith laboratory. She brings its findings back to Atlantis, where Dr. Carson Beckett, the expedition's doctor, analyses them and makes a surprising discovery about Teyla's DNA. The discovery opens a possible way for the expedition to gather information about its enemy, the Wraith, whose fleet is approaching the city, setting up the season finale. The episode turns on a genetic analysis: Dr. Carson Beckett studies Teyla's DNA, using findings from an abandoned Wraith laboratory linked to her past, and makes a surprising discovery about her genetic make-up that offers a way to gather intelligence about them. Genetics is presented as a useful diagnostic tool in the hands of a sympathetic doctor, and the discovery becomes a strategic advantage for the expedition. The source summary does not specify what Beckett finds in her DNA or what was done in the Wraith laboratory, so the episode's genetics can only be described in general terms. Real DNA analysis can reveal a person's ancestry and inherited traits, although the episode's use of it belongs to science fiction.

title: The Island
text: In 2019, Lincoln Six Echo and Jordan Two Delta live in a sealed compound whose residents believe that the outside world has been contaminated and that their only hope is to win a lottery to go to "the Island", the last uncontaminated place on Earth. Lincoln, troubled by dreams of things he has never experienced, discovers that the residents are clones of wealthy sponsors, and that the lottery winners are killed to harvest their organs or used as surrogate mothers. He escapes with Jordan, who has just been selected, pursued by mercenaries hired by Dr. Merrick, the scientist who runs the institute. In Los Angeles they meet Lincoln's sponsor, Tom Lincoln, who betrays them because he needs a new liver. Lincoln tricks the mercenaries into killing Tom and takes his identity. Learning that Merrick plans to exterminate the latest clone generations, Lincoln and Jordan return to the compound, kill Merrick and free the other clones. The Island is an action film about reproductive cloning used to supply spare parts. Rich clients pay the Merrick Institute to keep a clone of themselves as an insurance policy for organ transplants, or as a surrogate to bear their children. They are told that the clones are kept in a vegetative state, but Dr. Merrick has found that the organs only survive if the clones are conscious, so he raises them as people kept in ignorance. Merrick is the archetype of the scientist who has abandoned ethics for profit and power. The film raises the question of whether clones have the same rights as other people, and its answer is that they are fully human. It also uses a familiar fictional device: Lincoln inherits some of his sponsor's memories, attributed to a cloning defect, which has no basis in biology. The film's premise closely resembles Parts: The Clonus Horror (1979), whose creators sued for copyright infringement. Human reproductive cloning has not been achieved, and research on producing tissues for transplants focuses on therapeutic cloning and stem cells rather than whole cloned people.

title: Æon Flux
themes: cloning human experimentation pandemic post apocalyptic
text: In 2011 a virus kills 99 percent of humanity. Four centuries later, the last five million people live in Bregna, a walled city-state ruled by a congress of scientists, where people regularly disappear and are plagued by nightmares. Æon Flux, an agent of the Monican rebels, is sent to kill the city's leader, Trevor Goodchild, after her sister Una is killed. She discovers that she is being manipulated by council members plotting a coup, and that every inhabitant of Bregna is a clone grown from recycled DNA, because the cure for the virus left humans infertile. Æon is the first clone in 400 years of Katherine, the original Trevor's wife. Trevor has been trying to reverse the infertility, and Una was pregnant as part of his experiments, but his brother Oren had the fertile women killed to keep the Goodchild clone dynasty in power. Æon turns against Oren and destroys the Relical, the airship storing the DNA, and its crash breaks open the city wall. Cloning is the hidden foundation of the society in which the film is set. After the cure for a pandemic left humanity infertile, Bregna's rulers sustain the population by cloning the dead from DNA stored in an airship, so that people are reborn again and again with fragments of their previous lives surfacing as nightmares. Genetics thus serves as a tool of political control: the Goodchild dynasty has ruled for four centuries through its own clones, and when nature begins to restore fertility, Oren kills the pregnant women to preserve its power. Trevor, the scientist-ruler, is more ambiguous, a well-meaning researcher trying to cure infertility within a system built on deception. The film ends with a rejection of endless cloning in favour of natural reproduction and mortality. As science, it is speculative: cloning produces a genetic copy, not a continuation of the same person, and the idea of inherited memories reflects the story's themes of identity rather than biology.

title: Black Sheep
text: Henry Oldfield, who grew up on a New Zealand sheep farm, developed a crippling fear of sheep after his older brother Angus played a cruel prank on him. Fifteen years later, he returns to sell his share of the farm to Angus, unaware that Angus has been running secret genetic experiments on the flock with the scientist Dr. Astrid Rush. Two environmental activists break into the lab and accidentally release a mutant lamb, which bites one of them and then other sheep. The bite spreads quickly: the docile flock becomes a horde of carnivorous killers, and bitten humans begin to turn into monstrous human-sheep hybrids. Angus presses on with a presentation of his new breed to international investors, who are devoured. Henry, the activist Experience and their friend Tucker discover that amniotic fluid from the mutant lambs reverses the transformation, destroy the flock and save the bitten humans, while Angus is eaten by his own sheep. Genetic engineering is the source of the horror in this comedy, which plays on New Zealand's sheep-farming identity. Angus, the farmer, wants to breed the perfect sheep and present it to investors, while the scientist Dr. Rush carries out the work in a farm laboratory; both are driven by ambition and commercial interest, and their creation goes disastrously wrong. The environmental activists, who want to expose the experiments, unwittingly trigger the outbreak, so the film satirises both biotech enthusiasm and protest culture. Genetics behaves here like a virus: a bite transmits the mutation and turns humans into sheep-hybrids, and the cure is amniotic fluid. None of this resembles real genetic modification: engineered changes are inherited by offspring but cannot be passed on by a bite, and the film makes no attempt at plausibility, using the premise for gore and satire.

title: Heroes
themes: mutants human enhancement engineered pathogens pandemic heredity bioweapon regeneration
text: Heroes follows ordinary people around the world who discover that they have superhuman abilities and must work together to prevent catastrophic futures. In the first season, the geneticist Mohinder Suresh continues his late father's research into the biological source of the abilities, including a list of people who have them, while Noah Bennet works for "the Company", a secret organisation that tracks, controls and, if necessary, eliminates people with powers. The second season deals with the Company's research on the Shanti virus, whose strains affect both people with abilities and ordinary humans, and the threat of a global pandemic from a weaponised strain. In the third, Arthur Petrelli and his rival company Pinehearst seek a formula that would give ordinary people abilities, and Mohinder injects himself with an early version. The fourth season introduces a carnival whose leader gathers people with abilities to increase his own power. The series ran on NBC for four seasons, from 2006 to 2010. Genetics provides the scientific frame of the series. The abilities are treated as a biological phenomenon, and a research geneticist, Mohinder Suresh, is one of the main characters; he follows his father's work, studies the source of the powers and later develops a cure for a new strain of the Shanti virus using the blood of Claire, a girl who can regenerate. Scientists are shown in several roles: as independent researchers, as employees of the secretive Company, which studies and contains people with abilities and weaponises the Shanti virus, and as part of Pinehearst's project to create a formula that gives powers to anyone. Mohinder's self-experiment with an incomplete formula gives him strength but also makes his body mutate, a classic warning about scientists who test on themselves. Arthur Petrelli presents the formula as a way to improve the world, while it is pursued for power. Like most superhero fiction, the series uses the language of genes and evolution loosely; no real genetic variant confers anything like these abilities.

title: Idiocracy
text: In 2005 Joe Bauers, an army librarian chosen for being the most average man in the armed forces, and Rita, a prostitute, take part in a one-year military hibernation experiment that is forgotten when its officer is arrested. Over the next five centuries, the narrator explains, intelligent people choose not to have children while the least intelligent reproduce freely, and intelligence and civilisation decline. Joe and Rita wake in 2505 in an anti-intellectual, hyper-commercial America where crops are failing. Arrested for lacking a bar code tattoo, Joe takes an IQ test that reveals him as the most intelligent person alive, and President Camacho, a former wrestler, appoints him Secretary of the Interior. Joe finds that the crops are being irrigated with a sports drink, Brawndo, and replaces it with water; the economic collapse that follows leads to his death sentence, but when the crops sprout he is pardoned. He later becomes president and marries Rita. The film's premise is a satirical version of dysgenics, the idea that a population can deteriorate genetically when people with less desirable traits have more children. In the film, the most intelligent people choose not to have children while the least intelligent reproduce freely, and five hundred years later society is too dim to run its own technology. No scientists or genetic technologies are involved: the mechanism is simply who has children. The film is mainly a satire of anti-intellectualism, commercialism and consumerism, but its premise echoes the worries of nineteenth- and twentieth-century eugenicists about the 'wrong' people having children. The real evidence points the other way: genetic studies have found no sign of dysgenic effects in human populations, and intelligence test scores rose substantially across much of the world during the twentieth century, a trend known as the Flynn effect.

title: Jaane Hoga Kya
text: Siddharth Sardesai is a scientist working on human cloning, two years after his friend and colleague Sanjay died in a failed experiment. When his boss, Dr. Krishnan, and the police officer Rathore discourage the project, his girlfriend Aditi's father agrees to fund it, and Siddharth sets up a secret laboratory in an abandoned factory. After repeated failures he clones a rat, which turns out aggressive. Pursued by the police, he jumps off a cliff and is thought dead, but survives and clones himself. The clone is more violent: he assaults a woman and frames Siddharth, seduces Krishnan's daughter Suchitra, kills Krishnan to steal the research and has Siddharth committed to an asylum. Aditi, who blames Siddharth for her brother Sanjay's death, has been helping the clone, but she dies protecting Siddharth. With Rathore's help, Siddharth destroys a warehouse full of clones and kills his double. Human cloning is the core of this Hindi science-fiction thriller. Siddharth, a scientist who believes in cloning despite a colleague's death in an earlier experiment and his superiors' warnings, pursues it in a secret privately funded laboratory, first with rats and then on himself. The film presents the result as a dark double: the clone is more violent than the original (the source notes he is also darker-skinned), commits crimes in Siddharth's name, steals the research and plans to release an army of clones. Siddharth is a sympathetic scientist undone by his own creation, and the film frames cloning as dangerous and easily misused, ending on uncertainty about the child the clone has fathered. In reality a clone would be a genetically identical but younger individual, not an adult copy with a different temperament.

title: Kyle XY
themes: cloning human enhancement human experimentation nature nurture
text: Kyle XY is an American science fiction series broadcast on ABC Family from 2006 to 2009. A teenage boy wakes up naked in a forest near Seattle with no memory and no navel. He is taken in by a therapist, Nicole Trager, and her family, who name him Kyle. Kyle must learn everyday life from scratch but has extraordinary mental abilities. In the first season he searches for his origins and finds a link to Adam Baylin, a brilliant student who disappeared twenty years earlier. In the second season he learns that he was created by scientists in an experiment in artificial gestation at a facility called Zzyzx, and meets Jessi, a female counterpart created by a rival programme and controlled by the company Madacorp. The third season centres on the secret society Latnok, whose director, Michael Cassidy, killed Jessi's mother. In the series finale Kyle learns that Latnok plans to produce multiple clones of him and that Cassidy is his half-brother. Human cloning and artificial gestation are at the core of the series' mythology, though the show is mainly a family and teen drama. Kyle, codenamed "781227" or "XY", was cloned from the scientist Adam Baylin and grown at Zzyzx, Baylin's facility for experiments in artificial gestation; Jessi, "781228" or "XX", was cloned from Baylin's former girlfriend Sarah Emerson in a competing experiment. The scientists and organisations around them are mostly portrayed as treating the clones as assets: corporations and a secret society seek to control or copy Kyle, while Baylin is shown more sympathetically as his mentor. The series suggests that Kyle's abilities come from his engineered development, but it also stresses that his identity is shaped by the family that raises him. Real clones would be born as babies, not as teenagers without memories or navels, and cloning would not create superhuman mental powers.

title: Leroy & Stitch
text: After capturing and rehabilitating all of Jumba's alien experiments, Lilo, Stitch, Jumba and Pleakley are honoured by the Galactic Alliance; Jumba returns to his laboratory, Pleakley takes a teaching post and Stitch becomes captain of the Galactic Armada, leaving Lilo behind in Hawaii. Gantu frees the villain Dr. Hämsterviel from prison, and Hämsterviel forces Jumba to create a new experiment from Stitch's template: Leroy, a red near-twin of Stitch. Hämsterviel defeats Stitch, sends him, Jumba and Pleakley towards a black hole, and clones Leroy into an army to conquer the galaxy and destroy the other 624 experiments. Lilo, helped by Experiment 625, Reuben, and a reformed Gantu, rejoins her friends after they escape, and in the final battle at Aloha Stadium they disable the Leroys with a shutdown command Jumba secretly built in: Elvis Presley's version of "Aloha ʻOe". Genetic engineering is part of the premise of the whole Lilo & Stitch franchise: Stitch and the other experiments are artificial creatures designed by the alien mad scientist Jumba Jookiba, and this film's antagonists are a new engineered creature, Leroy, built from Stitch's template, and an army of his clones. The film treats these ideas as cartoon devices rather than science; Leroy is created under duress, and a song acts as a built-in kill switch. Jumba is a comic, ultimately benevolent scientist, coerced into working for the villain, and the story's message is that engineered beings can find a family and a place in the world. For younger audiences it presents genetic creation and cloning as tools of good or evil depending on who uses them. There is no attempt at scientific plausibility.

title: Michael
themes: human experimentation gene therapy hybrids chimeras
text: A man wakes up in the Atlantis infirmary with no memory and is told that he is Lieutenant Michael Kenmore, an expedition member rescued from the Wraith. Dr. Carson Beckett gives him regular injections, and he notices that people treat him with suspicion: he can read Wraith writing, Ronon attacks him, and he dreams of seeing himself as a Wraith. Only Teyla shows him friendship. Searching Beckett's office, he finds recordings showing that he was a captured Wraith, transformed into a human by Beckett's experimental retrovirus, which also erased his memories. Feeling betrayed, Michael argues that he has been changed for humans' benefit, not his own. He escapes, killing a guard, and is recaptured. While being moved to another planet for a stronger dose, he takes Teyla hostage and flees through the Stargate as his Wraith body returns. Sheppard and Ronon rescue Teyla, and Michael rejoins the Wraith. The episode centres on a genetic experiment on a sentient being. Dr. Beckett's retrovirus suppresses the Wraith's Iratus bug DNA so that their otherwise suppressed human traits are expressed, turning a Wraith into a human, with the side effect of wiping his memory. The Atlantis team, who are the protagonists, are shown in an uncomfortable light: they experiment on a prisoner without consent, invent a false identity for him and debate wiping his mind again when he learns the truth. Michael's question, whether he was "cured" for his own sake or for theirs, is the moral core of the episode, and Teyla and Beckett are shown doubting what they have done. The idea of reversing a species by switching off its non-human genes is fiction, though it loosely echoes real gene therapy using modified viruses to deliver genes. Michael later becomes a recurring villain who conducts his own genetic experiments.

title: New Earth
alt: Nueva Tierra Doctor Who, season 2, episode 1
text: The Doctor takes Rose to New Earth in the year five billion and twenty-three, where a telepathic message summons him to a hospital run by the Sisters of Plenitude, an order of cat-like nuns who can cure almost any disease. There he finds the ancient Face of Boe, dying of old age. Meanwhile, Rose is lured to the basement by Chip, a cloned servant of Lady Cassandra, who transfers her mind into Rose's body. Cassandra and the Doctor discover the hospital's secret: thousands of artificially grown humans kept in pods and deliberately infected with every known disease so that the Sisters can find cures. Cassandra releases the infected people to escape, and they kill several Sisters. The Doctor cures them all with a mixture of every medicine sprayed through a disinfectant shower, and the Sisters are arrested. Cassandra finally leaves Rose for Chip's failing body and dies in the arms of her younger self. The episode's central genetic element is a 'human farm': the Sisters of Plenitude grow artificial humans in pods and infect them with every disease in the galaxy to develop cures for their paying patients, claiming the subjects are just flesh and killing any that become healthy enough to speak or move. The story treats this as an atrocity of medical experimentation behind a façade of compassionate healing; the Doctor is outraged, the victims are shown as lonely people who have never been touched, and the Sisters end up under arrest. A second genetic element is Chip, a force-grown clone created to serve Cassandra, whose body fails when she takes it over. The episode, a mix of comedy and pathos, echoes real debates about using human tissue and clones as research material, without any scientific detail.

title: Perfect Creature
themes: engineered pathogens mutants human experimentation religion genetic engineering
text: In an alternative, steampunk New Zealand, a genetic mutation that appeared three centuries earlier causes some boys to be born vampires. They form the Brotherhood, a church that protects humans in exchange for blood, but no female vampire has ever been born and no new vampire has been born for seventy years. When women are found killed by bites, detective Lilly Squires works with Brother Silus, who reveals that the killer is his brother Edgar. Edgar had worked on the Brotherhood's secret research to create a female vampire with a virus injected into pregnant women; the virus mutated, turning the women into violent psychopaths and killing them, and it drove Edgar mad. Edgar escapes and contaminates the slum's water supply with his blood. Defying the Brotherhood, Silus saves Lilly, who kills Edgar, and they find the baby girl the virus produced, the first female vampire. Genetics is central to this vampire film. Vampirism is presented as a natural mutation, and the plot hinges on the Brotherhood's secret genetic research to save its kind from extinction by creating a female vampire. While the church publicly bans genetic research and blames it for influenza outbreaks, its scientists inject an engineered virus into pregnant women; the virus mutates, kills the subjects and turns the researcher Edgar into an insane killer who tries to infect a whole district. The scientist is a villain and the institution behind him is hypocritical and ruthless, ready to burn the slum for the greater good, so research in secret, human experimentation and a man-made epidemic all appear as dangers. The ending is ambiguous: the experiment has produced the first female vampire, a 'perfect creature' that the hero hides from the Brotherhood. Real viruses can carry genes into cells, but not turn a fetus into another kind of being.

title: Ultraviolet
themes: engineered pathogens human enhancement cloning mutants pandemic bioweapon
text: In the 21st century, a failed attempt to create super-soldiers in an illegal laboratory releases a virus that turns part of the population into hemophages, vampire-like people who are stronger, faster and smarter than humans but die young. Humanity wages war on them under the ArchMinistry, a fascist world government led by Vice-Cardinal Ferdinand Daxus. Violet, a hemophage in the resistance, steals what is said to be a weapon against her kind and finds it is a nine-year-old boy, Six, a clone of Daxus said to carry a deadly virus. Refusing to let him be killed, she goes on the run with him, pursued by Daxus's forces and by the hemophage leader Nerva. She learns that Daxus plans to release a toxin and sell the antidote in order to control the population, and that he is a hemophage himself who deliberately caused the original accident. Violet kills Daxus, and Six, who had died, is revived. The world of the film is created by a genetic catastrophe. An illegal laboratory trying to create super-soldiers releases a virus that overwrites human DNA, turning people into hemophages, vampire-like beings whose genes eventually unravel and kill them. Daxus, who as a laboratory assistant deliberately caused the accident to gain power, rules a genocidal regime against the hemophages, has made eight clones of himself, and plans to use one of them, Six, to carry a new pathogen whose antidote he would sell to keep everyone in his power. The sympathetic scientist Garth helps Violet, but genetic and viral science otherwise serves military ambition and tyranny. The sources disagree on details: in one summary the boy carries a virus against hemophages, and in another a toxin against humans. A virus that rewrites the genome of an adult and gives superhuman abilities is far beyond any real gene therapy.

title: X-Men: The Last Stand
text: Worthington Labs announces a "cure" for mutants: an injection that suppresses the X-gene responsible for their powers, made from the genome of a young mutant, Jimmy, who neutralises the powers of mutants near him. The cure attracts some mutants, such as Rogue, who cannot touch anyone without harming them, while Magneto warns that it will be used as a weapon and rebuilds his Brotherhood to destroy it. Meanwhile Jean Grey, believed dead, returns as the destructive Phoenix, kills Cyclops and Professor Xavier and joins Magneto. The cure is soon turned into a weapon, fired in darts. Magneto's army attacks Alcatraz, where the cure is produced, to kill Jimmy; the X-Men defend the island, Magneto is injected with the cure and loses his powers, and Wolverine is forced to kill Jean to stop her. In the aftermath, Rogue takes the cure, and Magneto shows a hint that his powers may be returning. The mutant cure is the film's central idea. In the X-Men world, mutants owe their powers to an X-gene, and Worthington Labs, founded by an industrialist whose son is a mutant, develops a treatment from Jimmy's genome that permanently suppresses it. The science is presented through Dr. Kavita Rao, a researcher at the company, and the film is ambivalent about the scientists' intentions: the cure is offered as voluntary, but it is soon used as a weapon, fired at mutants in darts. The story asks whether a genetic difference is a disease to be treated or an identity to be protected. Some mutants, such as Rogue, want the cure because their powers keep them from normal lives, while others, led by Magneto, see it as an attempt to eliminate their kind, and the film leaves Rogue's choice to take it as a legitimate personal decision. The ending suggests that the cure may not even be permanent. The X-gene itself is a fictional device of the comics, not a real gene.

title: 28 Weeks Later
text: During the first outbreak of the Rage virus in Britain, Don abandons his wife Alice to the Infected in a farmhouse and escapes. Twenty-eight weeks later, the Infected have starved, and US-led NATO forces under Brigadier General Stone are resettling London through a guarded safe zone on the Isle of Dogs. Don is reunited with his children, Tammy and Andy, and tells them their mother is dead. The children sneak out to their old home and find Alice alive. The army medical officer, Major Scarlet Levy, discovers that Alice is an infected but symptomless carrier and urges that she be kept alive to develop a vaccine; Stone orders her killed. Don visits Alice, is infected by her kiss, kills her and starts a new outbreak. Stone orders everyone in the zone killed and London firebombed. Scarlet and the sniper Doyle protect the children, believing their genes could hold a cure, but both die; Andy becomes a carrier, and the children are flown to France, where the virus soon appears. Genetics enters as the hope for a cure. Major Scarlet Levy, the army medical officer and the film's sympathetic scientist, finds that Alice carries the Rage virus without symptoms because of a genetic anomaly, and argues that her body could yield a vaccine; she also notes that Andy has inherited his mother's heterochromia and concludes that the children's genetic makeup may be the key to a cure, so she risks her life to save them. The military command, embodied by General Stone, rejects this and orders the carrier killed and then the whole zone exterminated. The genetic hope is destroyed: Alice and Scarlet die, Andy becomes a carrier himself, and the final scene shows the virus reaching Paris. Critics read the film as an allegory of militarised crisis management. Asymptomatic carriers and inherited resistance to infection are real phenomena, though not in this fictional form.

title: Daleks in Manhattan
alt: Daleks en Manhattan Doctor Who, season 3, episode 4
text: In November 1930 the Doctor and Martha Jones arrive in New York, where people are vanishing from Hooverville, the Central Park shantytown of those ruined by the Depression. With the community's leader, Solomon, and a young man, Frank, they take sewer work offered by the businessman Mr. Diagoras. Underground they find alien organic matter and are attacked by Pig Slaves, half-human, half-pig creatures; Frank is captured. At the Majestic Theatre the showgirl Tallulah is searching for her missing boyfriend Laszlo, whom the Doctor finds half-transformed into a Pig Slave. Laszlo explains that the Daleks sort their captives: those of low intelligence become Pig Slaves, the clever ones are kept for an experiment. In the unfinished Empire State Building, the four surviving Daleks of the Cult of Skaro reveal their plan to merge humans and Daleks, and Dalek Sec fuses with Diagoras to become a human Dalek. The first part of a two-part story, the episode is built around an alien eugenic and hybridisation project. Reduced to four survivors, the Daleks of the Cult of Skaro conclude that their obsession with purity has driven them to near-extinction and that their race must evolve by merging with humans. They abduct the poor of Depression-era New York, scan their brains to sort them by intelligence, turn the 'low intelligence' ones into half-pig slaves and keep the clever ones for the 'Final Experiment', which Dalek Sec begins on himself by fusing with a human with the help of a 'chromatid solution'. The Doctor, for his part, identifies the organic matter as Dalek tissue from its DNA. The episode draws on Universal horror and The Island of Doctor Moreau, and its hybrid-makers are monsters, though Sec's break with Dalek dogma hints at the ambivalence explored in the second part. The biology is fantasy.

title: Evolution of the Daleks
alt: La evolución de los Daleks Doctor Who, season 3, episode 5
themes: hybrids chimeras human experimentation evolution genetic engineering
text: In New York in 1930, concluding the story begun in "Daleks in Manhattan", the Doctor confronts the Cult of Skaro, whose leader Dalek Sec has merged with a human to become a Dalek-human hybrid. In their laboratory in the Empire State Building, Sec plans a new race by combining Dalek and human DNA in brain-dead human bodies, powered by gamma radiation from a solar flare channelled through the building's mast. The Doctor agrees to help, since the subjects cannot otherwise be saved, and offers to take the new race to another planet. But Daleks Caan, Jast and Thay mutiny, chain Sec as a traitor and switch the gene solution to pure Dalek DNA. The Doctor clings to the mast as the lightning strikes and the hybrids awaken. Sec dies shielding the Doctor; the hybrids, who have absorbed the Doctor's Time Lord DNA, question their orders and kill Jast and Thay, before Caan kills them all and escapes. The episode is built around genetic hybridisation. Dalek Sec, already fused with a human body, wants to save his dying species by blending Dalek and human DNA into a new race with Dalek intelligence and human emotions, freed from the obsession with supremacy. His fellow Daleks see this as a betrayal of Dalek purity and turn the project into an army of pure Dalek minds in human bodies, but the Doctor's Time Lord DNA, transferred by the lightning strike, gives the hybrids free will. The story also shows the cost of Dalek experimentation on humans, the subjects are brain-dead and the "pig-slave" Laszlo can only be stabilised, and it ends with Caan exterminating the hybrids, which the Doctor calls genocide. Sec is a tragic figure who evolves towards compassion, while the purists are villains; the genetics is entirely fantastical.

title: Frankenstein
text: In this present-day British television version of Mary Shelley's novel, Dr. Victoria Frankenstein works on the Universal Xenograft Project, growing replacement organs from stem cells, in the hope of saving her terminally ill eight-year-old son, William. She secretly adds William's blood to the stem-cell mixture, and an organism begins to grow in the tank; the team, which calls it 'the UX', lets it live for the sake of science. After William dies, a power cut lets the humanoid creature escape: it kills a girl in the sewers and then a guard and Victoria's colleagues Ed Gore and Andrew Waldman. Captured and moved to a secret laboratory run by Victoria's ex-husband, Henry Clerval, the creature behaves like William, and Victoria comes to see it as her son. She frees it with Henry's help, but armed men kill Henry and seize them both. Her boss, Professor Jane Pretorius, wants the creature as a model for soldiers; the film ends with Victoria teaching it in captivity. The film moves the Frankenstein story into stem-cell and genetic research. Victoria Frankenstein, a geneticist growing organs in the laboratory, adds her dying son's blood, and with it his DNA, to a stem-cell culture, which grows into a humanoid creature carrying William's DNA. The work is driven by a mother's love: she first wants a cure and a donor for William, and later sees the creature as her son and tries to show it love. Unlike Shelley's creator she is presented as humane, but her secret experiment produces a creature that kills four people. The darker figures are Henry Clerval and Professor Jane Pretorius, who want to exploit the creature for weapons research and soldiers, and the ambiguous ending leaves Victoria in captivity under their control. Growing organs from stem cells is a real research goal; a culture turning into a child-like creature with a dead boy's identity is fiction.

title: I Am Legend
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic genetic engineering human experimentation post apocalyptic
text: In 2009, a genetically engineered measles virus developed as a cure for cancer mutates, kills 90% of humanity and turns most survivors into Darkseekers, aggressive nocturnal creatures that cannot bear sunlight. Three years later, US Army virologist Robert Neville, who is immune, lives alone with his dog Sam in deserted Manhattan. He scavenges by day, broadcasts radio messages to find survivors and works in his home laboratory on a cure, testing it on rats and on a Darkseeker woman he captures. After Sam is bitten by infected dogs and he has to kill her, Neville recklessly attacks the Darkseekers and is rescued by two survivors, Anna and the boy Ethan. When the Darkseekers besiege his house, Neville finds that his latest treatment is curing the captured woman. In the theatrical ending he hands a sample of her blood to Anna, hides her and Ethan, and kills himself and the attackers with a grenade. In an alternate ending, Neville returns the woman to the Darkseekers and leaves for Vermont with Anna and Ethan. Genetic engineering causes the apocalypse. Dr. Alice Krippin, seen in a television interview at the start of the film, announces a cancer cure based on a genetically engineered measles virus; the modified virus mutates and becomes a lethal pandemic. The film thus contrasts two scientists: the researcher whose well-meaning medical innovation backfires on a global scale, and Neville, a military virologist who sacrifices everything to find a cure, experimenting on animals and on captured infected people. His work finally produces a cure. The premise draws on real research: viruses that selectively destroy cancer cells, known as oncolytic viruses, are an active field, measles virus has been tested in clinical trials, and a genetically modified herpes virus was approved in the United States in 2015 for melanoma. Nothing in this research suggests the risk of a virus turning into one that transforms people as shown, and experts consulted by Popular Mechanics questioned the film's depiction of the virus's mutation.

title: I Am Omega
text: In a post-apocalyptic Los Angeles overrun by cannibalistic, zombie-like humans, Renchard struggles to survive alone and has planted time bombs around the city to destroy it. Brianna, a survivor stranded on her way to Antioch, a community of survivors, contacts him by webcam and asks for help, but he refuses. Two men, Vincent and Mike, arrive claiming to come from Antioch and insist that Brianna carries the cure in her blood; at gunpoint, Renchard leads them into the city, with 24 hours before the bombs go off. Mike is killed in the sewers. After they rescue Brianna, Vincent shoots Renchard and takes her, saying he 'liked the world the way it was'. Renchard recovers, kills Vincent as he tries to rape and kill Brianna, and the bombs destroy the city. Renchard and Brianna set out for Antioch to make a cure, but a single zombie has survived. Genetics is mentioned only as the cause of the apocalypse. The people of Los Angeles have degenerated into a feral, cannibalistic subspecies because of a 'genetic infection', a virus whose origin the film does not explain, and a survivor is said to carry a cure in her blood. The film, an Asylum mockbuster released to cash in on I Am Legend, uses this premise only to set up a survival thriller; no scientists appear, and the cure remains a hope for the future. The idea that an infection could turn humans into a different subspecies is pure fiction.

title: Ice Spiders
text: In a secret laboratory on a Utah mountain, Dr. April Sommers and other scientists are working for the army on a new breed of giant spiders. When the spiders escape, they kill most of the lab staff and head for the ski resort on the other side of the mountain, where a team of teenage skiers is training. Sommers teams up with Dash, a former Olympic skier who works at the resort, as the spiders kill hunters, a park ranger and guests at the lodge. Reading the experiment's records, Sommers realises that Professor Marks deliberately accelerated the spiders' growth, making them larger and stronger, insatiably hungry and resistant to the cold. With the help of an army captain, Dash lures the spiders into a snowboard half-pipe, where they are blown up with an avalanche cannon; Marks, who tried to protect them, is killed by the last one. The government then covers up the incident. Ice Spiders is a low-budget creature feature in which genetic experimentation by the military supplies the monsters. Dr. Sommers' original aim is to obtain large amounts of spider silk for new types of armour, a project that is presented as legitimate, but Professor Marks secretly pushes the experiment further, accelerating the spiders' growth to make them bigger and stronger. The result is a breed of giant, cold-resistant black widows that escape and kill, and the film follows the familiar pattern of an ambitious scientist working with the military who refuses to destroy his creation and is killed by it, while the government covers everything up. The biology is not explained. The film does start from a real line of research: spider silk is exceptionally strong, and because spiders cannot be farmed like silkworms, scientists have produced silk proteins in genetically modified organisms, such as goats that secrete them in their milk, with applications that include ballistic armour.

title: Mr. Brooks
text: Earl Brooks, a respected Portland businessman just named Man of the Year, is secretly the 'Thumbprint Killer', a serial murderer urged on by his imaginary alter ego, Marshall. After two years without killing, he murders a couple in their bedroom but leaves the curtains open, and a neighbour who calls himself Mr. Smith photographs him and blackmails him into taking him along on his next murder. Meanwhile Brooks's daughter Jane drops out of college pregnant, and Brooks realises that she has killed someone on her campus; to shield her, he commits a copycat murder there. Detective Tracy Atwood hunts the Thumbprint Killer while being pursued by another escaped killer. Brooks kills Smith, whose urine, left at the last crime scene, gives the police DNA that points to Smith as the killer, and Brooks remains free and unable to stop. Two genetic elements appear. The main one is inherited character: Brooks treats his compulsion to kill as an addiction, and when he discovers that Jane has killed, he blames himself because his evil seems hereditary and fears it has passed to her. The story favours nature: Jane, raised in a wealthy and loving family, appears to become a killer like her father, and the film ends with Brooks dreaming that she murders him. The second is DNA forensics: the urine Smith leaves at a crime scene gives the police DNA that steers suspicion away from Brooks. As for plausibility, family studies show that antisocial behaviour runs in families partly through genes, but the effect is spread over many genes and depends heavily on the environment; there is no inherited compulsion to murder that a father can pass to his daughter.

title: Planet Terror
text: In rural Texas, a rogue military unit under Lt. Muldoon tries to buy large quantities of DC2, a deadly biochemical agent, from the chemical engineer Abby; when Muldoon tries to take him hostage, Abby releases the gas, turning most of the townspeople into deformed, zombie-like creatures. Go-go dancer Cherry Darling loses a leg in an attack and is rescued by her ex-boyfriend El Wray, who fits her with a table leg. At the hospital, Dr. William Block cripples the hands of his wife Dakota, an anaesthetist, out of jealousy, before he is infected. The survivors gather at the Bone Shack restaurant and are captured by Muldoon's men; Abby reveals that the soldiers, already infected, need the gas to delay their own mutation, and that some people are immune, hinting at a cure. The group fights back, Cherry gets a machine-gun leg, many die, and the survivors found a peaceful community on a Mexican beach as the outbreak spreads worldwide. The outbreak comes from DC2, a biochemical weapon developed by the engineer Abby and coveted by a rogue army unit: released as a gas, it makes people mutate into zombie-like creatures, and infected soldiers inhale it to hold off their own transformation. By this database's criteria it counts as a weaponised, man-made agent, although the film never describes it in genetic terms beyond 'mutation'. Abby, its creator, ends up helping the survivors and points to immune people as a source of a cure, while the military is shown as demented and predatory. Robert Rodriguez's half of the Grindhouse double feature is an over-the-top homage to 1970s exploitation films, and its science is deliberately absurd.

title: Power Rangers Operation Overdrive
text: In this season of the Power Rangers franchise, the billionaire explorer Andrew Hartford discovers the Corona Aurora, a powerful crown whose five jewels were scattered across the Earth by its guardian, the Sentinel Knight. The discovery frees two villainous brothers, Flurious and Moltor, who were turned into monsters and banished after trying to steal the crown long ago. To find the jewels before them, Hartford recruits five young adventurers, Mack (his son), Will, Dax, Ronny and Rose, gives them genetic enhancements and high-tech equipment, and makes them the Overdrive Rangers. Travelling around the world, they also face other villains, such as Kamdor and the Fearcats, and are joined by Tyzonn, an alien who can turn his body into mercury. An anniversary episode brings back veteran Rangers. Late in the series Mack learns that he is a robot built by his father with implanted memories; he sacrifices himself to destroy Flurious and is made truly human by the crown. Genetic enhancement is the origin of the heroes' powers. Andrew Hartford, the team's wealthy mentor, modifies the DNA of the five recruits to give each of them a superpower: super strength for Mack, super hearing and telescopic vision for Will, super agility for Dax, super speed for Ronny and invisibility for Rose. The enhancement is presented as a benevolent gift that equips the team to protect the world, alongside Hartford's technology and the magic of the crown, and it has no harmful consequences in the story. Hartford is a father figure and a positive practitioner, although he also built his son as a robot with false memories, a revelation the series uses to explore identity rather than genetics. As in most superhero fiction, the idea that editing DNA in adults could produce such powers has no basis in real science.

title: Resident Evil: Extinction
themes: cloning engineered pathogens pandemic human experimentation bioweapon post apocalyptic
text: Five years after the T-virus escaped from Raccoon City, the infection has spread worldwide and turned most of the planet into desert. Alice, who has acquired telekinetic powers, wanders the wasteland and joins a convoy of survivors led by Claire Redfield, persuading them to head for a reportedly uninfected area in Alaska. In an underground Umbrella Corporation facility, Dr. Isaacs breeds clones of Alice, which die one after another in tests, and experiments on zombies to make them more intelligent and docile, creating faster and stronger "Super Undead". Against orders from his superior, Albert Wesker, he ambushes the convoy to recapture Alice and is bitten. The survivors escape by helicopter, while Alice enters the facility and learns from an artificial intelligence that her blood can cure the virus. Helped by one of her clones, she kills the mutated Isaacs and later warns Wesker that she and her clones are coming for him. The film combines two genetic motifs: a virus engineered by a corporation and human cloning. The T-virus has turned humanity into the undead, and Umbrella's scientists continue experimenting rather than containing the disaster. Dr. Isaacs, the chief scientist, works on dozens of clones of Alice and uses blood taken from them to create the "Super Undead"; he is ambitious, defies his superiors and ends up infected and mutated by his own work. The clones are treated as disposable: their bodies are dumped in a pit after each failed test, an image the film uses to underline the company's disregard for human life. Alice's immunity, which makes her blood a potential cure, echoes the real use of survivors' antibodies to develop treatments. The film draws on the Resident Evil video games, where the corporation's bioweapons research is a constant theme; scientific plausibility is not a concern.

title: Species: The Awakening
alt: Species – The Awakening Species IV: The Awakening
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering human experimentation
text: Miranda Hollander, a young university lecturer in classics and biology who can read books by touching them, lives with her 'uncle' Tom and believes her parents died when she was a baby. After collapsing, she is taken to hospital, where she turns into an alien creature and kills several staff. Tom sedates her with human hormones and drives her to Mexico, revealing on the way that she is the product of an experiment combining human and alien DNA that he carried out with his college friend Forbes McGuire, and that he has suppressed her alien nature with hormones since childhood. In Mexico, Forbes, who lives with another hybrid, Azura, and earns money making half-alien copies of clients' dead pets and relatives, finds that Miranda is dying. Only fresh human DNA can save her, so they abduct a mugger as a donor. The botched treatment lets Miranda's alien side take over: she seeks mates, kills Forbes and becomes pregnant. Azura fatally wounds her, Tom kills Azura and blows up the lab. The film, the fourth in the Species series, rests on a genetic experiment: Miranda was created by two college friends who combined human and alien DNA, and her human side has been maintained only by regular hormone injections. One creator, Tom, became her protective guardian; the other, Forbes McGuire, carried on alone in Mexico, creating further hybrids and selling half-alien copies of dead pets and relatives, and the film presents him as a vulgar, unethical scientist. When Miranda begins to fail, the cure is an infusion of DNA or stem cells taken from an abducted human donor, a procedure the film equates with human sacrifice, and its botched execution unleashes her alien instincts. The hybrids end up dead and the lab destroyed. The science, from hormones that suppress alien genes to adult DNA infusions that rescue a dying hybrid, is pure B-movie fantasy.

title: Tao of Rodney
text: In this third-season episode of Stargate Atlantis, an Ancient device inside the city of Atlantis alters Dr. Rodney McKay's DNA and gives him superhuman powers. McKay at first takes his new abilities as a blessing, as his already formidable intellect grows even sharper. But the change comes at a price: his enhanced brilliance is checked by his impending death, and the only way to escape it is to overcome his ego and ascend. The episode's premise is a genetic change: a device built by the Ancients rewrites Rodney McKay's DNA and gives him superhuman powers and enhanced intelligence. The story treats this enhancement as a double-edged gift. What McKay welcomes as a blessing becomes a death sentence, and the only escape is a spiritual one, ascension, which requires him to overcome his ego. The genetics is therefore a vehicle for a moral about arrogance and humility rather than a study of science, and no scientist is responsible for the change, which comes from ancient alien technology. The source summary does not detail his powers or how the episode ends. Real genetic modification cannot transform an adult's abilities in this way; changes to the DNA of a few cells would not alter the brain of a grown person so quickly.

title: The Gene Generation
themes: genetic engineering gene therapy genetic discrimination post apocalyptic
text: In the decaying future city of Olympia, Michelle is an assassin who hunts 'DNA hackers', criminals who use genetic technology to get inside people's bodies and kill them. She is saving money to buy travel papers for herself and her younger brother Jackie to Demeter, a city that admits only the genetically pure. Years earlier, her neighbour Christian, a scientist at Hayden Technologies, invented the Transcoder, a device that instantly reprograms DNA and was meant to eliminate all illness; its unpredictable side effects turned the company's CEO, Dr. Josephine Hayden, into a tentacled mass, destroyed the company and poisoned Olympia's air. Jackie gambles away Michelle's savings, runs up a debt to the casino owner Randall and steals the Transcoder from Christian, hoping to sell it. Michelle and Christian are drawn into a violent chase for the device, pursued by Randall's thugs and by Hayden's brother Abraham, who wants it to heal his sister. Genetic technology is the core of this biopunk thriller. The Transcoder, which reprograms DNA instantly, was created by the scientist Christian with the benevolent aim of ending all disease, but its unpredictable side effects caused a disaster: the company CEO was turned into a monster, the company exploded and the city's atmosphere was poisoned. Knock-off Transcoders now serve 'DNA hackers', criminals who kill by rewriting their victims' DNA (in one scene a tissue coated with genetic material makes a man melt). The world is also divided by genetics: the city of Demeter admits only the genetically pure, a form of genetic discrimination that motivates the heroine. The film is a noir chase after a MacGuffin and offers no scientific detail; it is a cautionary picture of gene editing as both a failed cure and a weapon.

title: The Lazarus Experiment
alt: El experimento Lazarus Doctor Who, season 3, episode 6
text: The Doctor brings Martha Jones home to London, where her sister Tish works for Professor Richard Lazarus, a 76-year-old scientist who promises to 'change what it means to be human'. At the launch party at Lazarus Laboratories, he enters a capsule that uses sound waves to rejuvenate him; the Doctor prevents an overload, and Lazarus steps out young again. Analysing a DNA sample that Martha took when Lazarus kissed her hand, the Doctor finds that the process has awakened something in his DNA that is changing him into something else. Lazarus turns into a giant scorpion-like creature and kills his partner, Lady Thaw, by draining her life energy, which he needs to stabilise his DNA. After several attacks, the Doctor traps him in Southwark Cathedral and uses the amplified sound of the organ to disrupt his DNA; Lazarus falls to his death. This episode is a classic mad-scientist story with a genetic twist. Professor Lazarus uses a machine that 'instructs' his genes with sound waves to make him young, but the treatment also unlocks dormant genes, which the Doctor calls an evolutionary throwback that humanity had rejected, and turns him into a monster that must drain other people's life energy to keep his unstable DNA in shape. The Doctor and Martha identify the problem by analysing a DNA sample, and the Doctor finally uses sound to disrupt Lazarus's DNA. Lazarus is presented as a vain, ruthless man who wants to defeat ageing for himself, funded by the sinister Mr. Saxon, and the episode frames his fate as nature punishing hubris, while also giving him a moving fear of death. The idea that genes respond to sound, or that an old genome hides a monster, has no basis in real biology.

title: The Witches Hammer
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement human experimentation
text: Rebecca is attacked in the street and wakes up in the hands of Project 571, a covert organization whose agents tell her that she cannot return to her husband and son because they have altered her into a genetically modified vampire. Promised that she might see her family again if she cooperates, she trains to become a skilled assassin. Returning from a mission, she finds everyone at Project 571 slaughtered and is rescued by the warlock Edward, who takes her to the witch Madeline, head of the rival Project 572. Madeline needs her to recover The Witches Hammer, a book of spells written by the Russian witch Katanya, because only one of its spells can kill Hugo Renoir, a vampire who has made himself invulnerable. Rebecca and Edward set out after the book, fighting rival vampires and Hugo's minions who also want it, and Hugo is finally destroyed with a spell from the book. Genetic modification creates the heroine. A covert organization, Project 571, turns Rebecca into a genetically modified vampire and coerces her into becoming its assassin by holding out the hope that she might see her family again. The film never explains how the modification works or why the project makes engineered vampires, and after the opening the story turns into a quest for a book of spells in which magic, not science, defeats the villain. The scientists or agents of Project 571 appear only briefly and are presented as a cold, coercive organization before they are massacred. Genetics here is a modern explanation for a vampire in an otherwise supernatural story; no real genetic change could produce a vampire.

title: Underdog
text: Dr. Simon Barsinister, a scientist whose proposal for genetic experiments has been rejected, sets out to prove his theory in a secret laboratory, assisted by his henchman Cad. Cad kidnaps a beagle that has been dismissed from the police bomb squad, but the dog escapes after a fire and exposure to the laboratory's chemicals alter his DNA, giving him super strength, speed, hearing, smell, the ability to fly and the power of speech. He is adopted by Dan Unger, a former police officer, and his teenage son Jack, who names him Shoeshine. Secretly, he becomes the caped hero Underdog. Unable to recreate the serum, Barsinister tries to obtain Underdog's DNA, turns his powers into "super pills" given to three German Shepherds, and plans to use a mind-control serum in a bomb to take over Capital City. Underdog rescues Molly and Polly, carries the bomb away before it explodes, and Barsinister is arrested and injected with an antidote. Genetic engineering is the source of the hero's powers and of the villain's ambitions. Barsinister is a classic frustrated scientist: his genetic research has been rejected by the establishment, and he turns to secret, unlicensed experiments to prove himself and then to seize power. The laboratory accident alters the dog's DNA, granting abilities from flight to speech, and his later plans, harvesting the hero's DNA and turning it into pills, treat genetics as a source of power to be bottled and distributed. The film is a family comedy based on the 1960s cartoon, and its science is pure fantasy: no change to DNA could give a dog flight or human speech, and real genetic modification of an adult animal would not take effect instantly. The story nevertheless follows the familiar pattern of the mad scientist undone by his own creation, with the dogs he mistreated finally turning against him.

title: Viyabari
text: Suryaprakash is an ambitious businessman who wants to become richer than Bill Gates. His obsession costs him his family and social life. Savithri, a college student researching him for a project, falls in love with him, and he marries her, though mostly because she is a good cook. Bothered by the demands of his family, Suryaprakash asks the scientist Stephen Raj to clone him, so that the clone can take care of things at home while he concentrates on his business. The clone soon realises that the problem lies not with the family but with Suryaprakash himself, and sets out to show him what his family is worth. After the death of his mother, Suryaprakash finally gives up his greed and comes to understand the value of his family. S. J. Suryah plays both the businessman and his clone in this Tamil comedy. Cloning is the comic premise. The businessman commissions a copy of himself as a way to delegate his family life, and the story turns on the contrast between the original and the clone, who turns out to be the better son and husband. As in many clone comedies, the copy is created as an adult with the original's appearance but a different character, which serves the moral of the film, that a person's choices and attention matter more than his identity. The scientist, Stephen Raj, plays a supporting role as the provider of the technology and is not the focus of the story. Real cloning creates a new embryo that would grow up as a younger, genetically identical twin, not an adult double. Genetics here is a narrative device for a family drama and comedy and is not explored.

title: Anaconda 3: Offspring
text: A giant anaconda captured in the Amazon is held at a genetic research facility in Romania owned by the company Wexel Hall, where scientists led by Dr. Amanda Hayes are developing a serum from the Blood Orchid, a plant recovered in Borneo. When the project's backer, the industrialist J.D. Murdoch, provokes the snake, it breaks free, kills many of the staff and releases a second, "queen" anaconda. Murdoch sends the hunter Stephen Hammett and his team after the snakes. As the hunters are killed one by one, Amanda admits that the queen is pregnant and will soon give birth to genetically altered offspring. Hammett turns out to be working for Murdoch, who wants a live baby snake. Amanda wounds him and blows up the factory where the queen gives birth, killing Hammett, the queen and her young. However, one of Murdoch's men finds a surviving baby snake and delivers it to him, while Amanda burns her research. Genetic research is the source of the threat, although the film is mainly a creature feature. The anacondas are kept for experiments at a corporate genetic research facility working on a serum derived from the Blood Orchid, and the danger is that the pregnant queen will give birth to more genetically "special" offspring. The scientists work for a wealthy industrialist who funds the research for profit and is willing to sacrifice everyone to obtain a live specimen; the lead researcher, Amanda, admits her responsibility only reluctantly and ends by destroying her own documentation, a gesture against the misuse of her work. The film thus repeats a familiar pattern of the genre: commercial genetic research, poor containment and an animal that turns on its creators. Its science is not developed beyond this premise. Real anacondas are among the largest snakes, but no genetic technique could produce animals of the size and abilities shown.

title: Babylon A.D.
text: In a near future of war-torn slums outside a fortified United States, the mercenary Toorop is hired by the Russian gangster Gorsky to smuggle a young woman, Aurora, from a convent of the Noelite sect in Central Asia to New York, in exchange for money and a new identity. Aurora travels with her guardian, Sister Rebeka. On the way she speaks languages she never learned, foresees attacks and takes command of a submarine. In New York, Aurora reveals that she is pregnant with twins although she is a virgin. In a battle with Gorsky's men and the Noelites, Rebeka is killed and Aurora shoots Toorop so that a missile tracking him misses. He is revived by Dr. Arthur Darquandier, Aurora's father, who explains that the Noelites commissioned her as a messiah for a staged virgin birth. The Noelite High Priestess kills Darquandier; Aurora dies after giving birth, and Toorop raises the twins. Aurora is a designed human. Her creator, Dr. Darquandier, built her to carry humanity's knowledge and abilities from birth, according to the German Wikipedia summary as a step in human evolution, implanting a computer in her brain while she was a fetus; the Noelites, a wealthy religious movement, commissioned her so that she would conceive without sex and give them a manufactured messiah. She was "designed to breed", not to live, and her death after childbirth was programmed in advance. The film presents the scientist as a sympathetic father who wants to protect his creation and dies for it, while the High Priestess uses biotechnology for power and money. The engineering is vague and mixed with cybernetics and mysticism; the Moria review finds the ending muddled.

title: Clone
text: This six-part BBC Three comedy follows Dr. Victor Blenkinsop, an arrogant scientist hungry for scientific glory, who creates the world's first human clone for the military as a prototype super-soldier meant to replace Britain's army. The clone emerges from his birthing tube as an adult with the mind of a naive, clumsy and gentle child, more likely to hug than to shoot. To avoid his ruthless paymaster, Colonel Black of MI7, Victor flees with the clone, later named Albert after Einstein, and his loyal assistant Ian to a small village, where he poses as a travel writer. There he meets Rose Bourne, the landlady of the local pub, whose photographic memory and mathematical gifts suggest that a map of her brain could unlock the clone's dormant military "memory engrams". Victor manipulates Rose to scan her brain and builds a device to "fix" Albert, while Black closes in. The series ends on a cliffhanger. Human cloning is the premise, played for comedy. The series reworks Frankenstein, with Victor as a modern Dr. Frankenstein and Ian as his Igor, and adds a military motive: the clone is designed as a weapon for the state, and the scientist is driven by vanity and the wish to join the great names of science. Albert emerges as an adult equipped with implanted "memory engrams", but he behaves like an innocent child, so the comedy rests on the gap between the scientist's design and what he has actually created. The scientific side is fantastical: a real clone would be born as a baby and grow up normally, and memories or skills cannot be programmed into a cloned brain. The series is better understood as a satire of scientific ambition and military patronage than as a story about genetics.

title: Cyborg Soldier
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering human experimentation regeneration
text: I.S.A.A.C. (Intuitive Synthetic Autonomous Assault Commando), played by mixed martial artist Rich Franklin, is the first prototype of a secret military "human weapon" programme. A former death-row inmate, he has been genetically reconstructed and trained into a deadly assassin, with a regenerating body and enhanced intellect. After escaping, he takes deputy sheriff Lindsay Rearden hostage while on the run. Both are pursued by military agents led by the robotics engineer Simon Hart, who wants his creation back, and the two end up working together to expose the group behind the programme to create such super soldiers. The film was directed by John Stead and released in 2008. Genetic engineering, combined with other modifications, is how the military programme creates its soldier: I.S.A.A.C. is described as genetically reconstructed, physically regenerative and intellectually superior, a man redesigned as a weapon. The scientists behind him serve a secret military project, use a death-row inmate as raw material and pursue him when he escapes, so the film follows the familiar pattern of the super-soldier story, in which the creation turns against its makers and the hero's task is to expose those responsible. The available sources describe the method only in vague terms, and the film, despite its title, seems to treat genetic and cybernetic enhancement interchangeably. Real research on regeneration or on enhancing human performance is nowhere near producing a soldier of this kind.

title: Day of the Dead
text: In this remake of George A. Romero's zombie film, the National Guard seals off the town of Leadville, Colorado, for a supposed 24-hour quarantine exercise. Corporal Sarah Bowman leaves her post with Private Bud Crain to visit her sick mother and finds that many townspeople have flu-like symptoms. At the overcrowded hospital, the sick suddenly turn into fast, ferociously strong zombies, and Sarah, Bud, Private Salazar and Dr. Logan of the CDC escape. Bud is bitten and turns, but keeps enough of his mind not to attack his friends. Rescuing Sarah's brother and his girlfriend from the radio station, the group reaches an underground bunker, where Logan reveals that the virus came from a government project led by Dr. Engel to create a bioweapon that would paralyse enemy soldiers, until it mutated. The zombified Engel kills Logan, Bud saves Sarah, and the survivors burn the horde and escape. The zombie outbreak is traced to a military bioweapon. Dr. Engel's government project set out to create a virus that would temporarily paralyse enemy combatants by affecting their nervous system, but the virus mutated, turned the scientists themselves into zombies and spread to the town. The CDC doctor who knows the truth is self-serving, pushing a woman into the zombies to save himself, and Engel ends as a monster, so both scientists are presented negatively. The film does not discuss genetics directly; the key ideas are a laboratory-made pathogen and its uncontrolled mutation, a common device of zombie fiction. Real viruses do mutate, but no mutation could turn a nerve agent-like infection into reanimation of the dead.

title: Glass Maiden
alt: クリスタル ブレイズ
themes: human enhancement human experimentation genetic engineering
text: In Rags Town, a slum on the edge of a prosperous near-future Asian city, former police detective Shuu runs the S&A Detective Agency with his younger brother Akira and two high-school apprentices, Manami and Ayaka. He takes in an amnesiac girl who turns out to be HW-9, an escapee from a secret programme that turns women into living weapons; she hates her designation and takes the name Sara.
