Her body runs at about 40 °C and releases powerful static electricity when a man touches her. The detectives protect her from a group of women hunting her for the programme's leader, the cruel scientist Kito, who is obsessed with recapturing her. Kito tests a new drug on Sofia, a journalist investigating the 'Glass Maiden' incidents, who turns to glass and dies in front of Shuu. The rogue weapon BW-Alpha kills Kito's bodyguard Kyrie, and in the end Sara stays in Rags Town, working at Porilyn's shop. The series centres on illegal weapons research on human beings. Sara, designated HW-9, belongs to the HW series, women genetically engineered into living weapons, a successor to the BW series, whose glass-based weapons make their targets turn to glass and burst into flames. The English Wikipedia says the programme was meant for military use. Its head, Kito, is a cruel mad scientist obsessed with recovering his escaped subject, who uses unwilling people as test subjects, as when his new drug kills the journalist Sofia. Sara, by contrast, is a sympathetic victim who rejects her number and tries to build a life with the detectives who protect her. The series frames the genetic programme as exploitation of the marginal, set in a slum where society's 'failures' are dumped. The engineered traits, a high body temperature and electrical discharges triggered by men's touch, are fantasy; the sources say little about the science.

title: Kaiba
text: In a universe where memories are stored on chips and minds can move between bodies, the rich above a barrier of electrical storms trade bodies and memories for longevity and pleasure, while the poor below sell their bodies to survive. Kaiba wakes with no memories, a hole in his chest and a locket picturing an unknown girl. Pursued by people who want his body, he flees aboard the freight ship Neuron, hiding his mind in a stuffed toy, then in the body of Chroniko, a poor girl who sold her body and was killed by a corrupt doctor; the ship's sadistic sheriff Vanilla falls in love with him and dies protecting him. Meanwhile Neiro, the girl in the locket, works as a terrorist for the Issoudan movement against the trade in bodies and memories. Kaiba discovers that he is Warp, that the Issoudan leader Dada-sama is three aged clones of Warp, and is finally reunited with Neiro. Genetics is marginal in this series, which is about memory rather than genes. Its central technology stores minds on chips and moves them between bodies, and the French Wikipedia notes that artificial bodies and advanced cloning are part of this world. Cloning matters in one plot revelation: the mysterious leader of the Issoudan movement, Dada-sama, turns out to be three aged clones of Warp, Kaiba's true identity, seeking to take his place. The series' questions about identity, the copying and editing of memories, and the exploitation of the poor's bodies by the rich are explored through memory technology, not through genetic science.

title: L: Change the World
alt: L change the World Death Note 3
text: In this spin-off of Death Note, set in the last days of the detective L's life, a deadly virus wipes out a village in Thailand, and one of L's agents rescues the only survivor, a boy with a gift for calculation. The virus, far more infectious than Ebola, was created by Dr. Kimihiko Nikaido, whose assistant Dr. Kimiko Kujo turns out to lead the terrorist group behind it. When Nikaido refuses to hand over his antidote, destroys it and injects himself with the virus, Kujo kills him. His young daughter Maki, who has also injected herself with the virus, flees to L, and Kujo's group pursues them. L takes the children to Nikaido's research partner, Dr. Kouichi Matsudo, who finds that Maki is protected for now by her low blood sugar and, with a clue from the boy and the boy's blood, recreates the antidote. L stops the terrorists' plane to the United States and cures the passengers. He leaves the boy at the orphanage where he grew up, naming him Near, before he dies. The story revolves around a laboratory-made virus that a terrorist group wants to use as a biological weapon. Dr. Kimihiko Nikaido created the virus and an antidote; according to one source he did not know he was working for people who meant to sell the weapon, and he destroys the antidote and infects himself rather than hand it over, before he is killed. His assistant, Dr. Kimiko Kujo, heads the terrorist group. Against her, Nikaido's research partner Dr. Kouichi Matsudo recreates the antidote with L's help, using the blood of the immune boy and a clue left by Nikaido. The film thus sets responsible scientists against a scientist who turns the work into a weapon. Its science is loose: the virus is said to need sugar to infect rapidly, and the immunity is not explained.

title: La Possibilité d'une île
text: A man calling himself 'the Prophet' tours Belgium lecturing on eternal life and on overcoming death through technical progress, accompanied only by his unenthusiastic son Daniel and a technician. Three years later he has many followers. His sect, the Elohimites, believes in the Elohim, extraterrestrials who will bring eternal life, and it recruits a prominent geneticist, Professor Slotan Miskiewicz, to develop a cloning technique that reproduces an adult person within minutes, complete with their memories. Daniel leaves the cult but returns years later to succeed his father. Thousands of years on, Daniel reappears as Daniel25, the latest of a line of clones called neo-humans. Living alone in a cave, he reads about humanity's past until a vague longing sends him out across a desolate world. A dog becomes his companion and brings him close to love, which the neo-humans have lost, while another clone, Marie, wanders the same wasteland. Cloning is the means by which the film's cult pursues immortality. Michel Houellebecq adapts his own novel: the Prophet's followers believe in extraterrestrial creators and fund a geneticist, Professor Miskiewicz, to perfect a technique that makes an adult copy of a person in minutes, memories included. Thousands of years later, the result is a line of 'neo-humans' who live in isolation and have lost the capacity for love; the clone Daniel25 rediscovers a hint of it only through a dog. The film thus presents cloning-based immortality as a religious promise that ends in a lonely, emotionally barren existence, though the sources say little about how it portrays the geneticist himself. Real cloning cannot make an adult copy or transfer memories; a clone is a genetic twin who starts life as a baby.

title: Os Mutantes: Caminhos do Coração
alt: The Mutants: Ways of the Heart
themes: mutants genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human experimentation genetic discrimination
text: This Brazilian telenovela, broadcast by Record in 2008–2009, is the second part of a trilogy that began with Caminhos do Coração. In the first part, Dr. Júlia Zaccarias, a physician at the biotechnology company Progênese, had created genetically modified humans with superpowers in a secret laboratory on the island of Arraial. Now, having taken a rejuvenating elixir to escape prison, she runs the laboratory under the name Juli Di Trevi. The existence of the mutants becomes public, and men and women turned into vampires, werewolves, snakes, spiders and other creatures attack São Paulo, while a government department, DEPECOM, is divided between controlling the mutants and exterminating them. Maria, heiress to the Mayer fortune, founds the League of Good to protect peaceful mutants against the villains' league, which includes her twin sister Samira, raised in Júlia's laboratory. The story expands to include aliens, reptilians, vampires and a journey to the centre of the Earth. Genetic engineering is the origin of the mutants around whom the whole telenovela revolves. Dr. Júlia, a physician at the biotech company Progênese, created superpowered humans in secret experiments and kept some of them, such as Samira, in her laboratory from birth. She is a classic mad scientist: driven by her experiments, she has people murdered to protect them, takes an elixir of youth and allies herself with alien reptilians. The series uses the mutants to stage a debate about difference and persecution, in the manner of X-Men, a model for the first part of the trilogy: the public hunts the mutants, and a government department splits between those who want to imprison only the violent and those who want to exterminate them all. As the story progresses, genetics gives way to fantasy, with references to Dracula, The Island of Dr. Moreau and Jurassic Park, Brazilian folklore and science-fiction aliens. The science is not meant to be realistic.

title: Quarantine
text: Television reporter Angela Vidal and her cameraman Scott are filming a night shift with the Los Angeles Fire Department when firefighters are called to an apartment building where an elderly resident has been screaming. The woman attacks and bites a firefighter and a police officer, and those bitten soon become feverish and violent. The authorities and the Centers for Disease Control seal the building, trapping the residents inside; a resident who is a veterinarian likens the symptoms to rabies, and an inspector reveals that a sick dog belonging to a little girl prompted the quarantine. One by one the residents are bitten and turn, while a sniper kills anyone trying to escape. Fleeing into the attic flat, Angela and Scott find laboratory equipment and clippings showing that its tenant, a doomsday-cult member, stole a mutated rabies virus from a military biological facility. In the dark, an emaciated infected figure kills Scott and drags Angela away. The American remake of the Spanish film [REC] replaces the original's religious explanation with a man-made one. The infection that turns the building's residents into violent, rabid attackers is revealed in the final minutes to be the 'Armageddon virus', a highly contagious mutated form of rabies developed as a biological weapon in a military facility and stolen by a member of a doomsday cult, who has been experimenting with it in his attic flat. The military scientists who created it are never seen, and the CDC officials who enforce the quarantine are unable to contain the outbreak. The film thus belongs to the bioterrorism strand of outbreak horror, in which the danger comes from weapons laboratories and the people who steal from them; some critics regretted the need to explain at all. Real rabies spreads mainly through bites and takes weeks to develop, not minutes.

title: Repo! The Genetic Opera
text: In 2056, after an epidemic of organ failures has killed most of humanity, the megacorporation GeneCo sells organ transplants on credit, and Repo Men hunt down clients who miss payments to "repossess" their organs. GeneCo's terminally ill founder, Rotti Largo, despises his three spoiled children and plans to leave his fortune to 17-year-old Shilo Wallace, daughter of his late former fiancée Marni. Shilo has supposedly inherited her mother's rare blood disease and is kept indoors by her father Nathan, who believes he killed Marni with a treatment he created; in fact Rotti poisoned it and blackmailed Nathan into becoming GeneCo's chief Repo Man. Shilo meets a grave robber who sells an addictive painkiller extracted from corpses, and Blind Mag, a singer whose GeneCo eyes will be repossessed when she resigns. At the opera, Mag gouges out her own eyes and is killed, Rotti reveals that Nathan has been poisoning Shilo's medicine to keep her at home, and shoots him. Shilo refuses the company and leaves. Despite its title, this rock opera is more about biotechnology and transplant medicine as business than about genetics in the strict sense. GeneCo turns the body into merchandise: organs and surgical enhancements are sold on credit, and debtors are killed to recover them, a satire of commercial medicine, debt and cosmetic surgery addiction. The corporation's scientists and surgeons serve power and profit, and its founder uses medicine to manipulate and kill. The genetic element lies mainly in Shilo's story: she believes she has inherited her mother's blood disease and is defined by it, until she discovers that her symptoms were caused by her father's "medicine". Her final song, "Genetic Emancipation", celebrates her decision that her parents' actions and her inheritance do not dictate her future, a rejection of genetic and family determinism.

title: Resident Evil: Degeneration
text: In this computer-animated Resident Evil film, set seven years after the destruction of Raccoon City, a T-virus outbreak hits Harvardville Airport, where the activist Claire Redfield meets Senator Ron Davis, a shareholder in the pharmaceutical company WilPharma. Federal agent Leon S. Kennedy leads the rescue. WilPharma's vaccine trucks are blown up, and terrorists demand that the government admit its role in the Raccoon City disaster. At WilPharma's research facility, Claire learns from its head researcher, Frederic Downing, that the company is also working on the G-virus. Curtis Miller, a Raccoon City survivor and the brother of Leon's partner Angela, bombs the facility and injects himself with the G-virus, becoming a monster that Leon eventually kills. Downing turns out to be the mastermind: a former Umbrella researcher who stole the T and G viruses and staged the attacks to sell viruses and vaccines to buyers such as General Grande. He is arrested, but the company Tricell buys WilPharma and recovers G-virus samples from Curtis's body. The film's threat is a pair of laboratory-made viruses from the Resident Evil franchise: the T-virus, which turns people into zombies, and the G-virus, which causes rapid, monstrous mutation. Both were created by the Umbrella Corporation, and here they are traded as products: the researcher Frederic Downing stole them, developed vaccines at WilPharma, and staged bioterror attacks to create demand and to sell the whole package of viruses and vaccines to an arms buyer. The activist group TerraSave accuses WilPharma of experimenting on people, and Curtis Miller, manipulated by Downing, turns himself into a mutant monster with the G-virus. The story presents pharmaceutical science as entangled with corporate greed, bioterrorism and government cover-ups; even after Downing's arrest, a new corporation, Tricell, collects samples to continue the work. As in the games, the viruses are fantasy: no virus can reanimate the dead or reshape a body within minutes.

title: Star Wars: The Clone Wars
text: This animated series, created by George Lucas, is set during the Clone Wars between Attack of the Clones and Revenge of the Sith. Jedi Knights Anakin Skywalker and Obi-Wan Kenobi, with Anakin's Padawan Ahsoka Tano, lead the Galactic Republic's army of clone troopers against the droid armies of the Separatists under Count Dooku and General Grievous. Beginning as standalone episodes and growing into multi-episode arcs, the series covers battles, political intrigue, bounty hunters and the Mandalorians, while Darth Sidious, secretly Chancellor Palpatine, manipulates both sides to destroy the Jedi and found the Galactic Empire. The clones, all grown from the bounty hunter Jango Fett, emerge as individuals such as Captain Rex, and a squad of mutated clones, the Bad Batch, is introduced. The final season, the Siege of Mandalore, runs parallel to Revenge of the Sith and ends with the fall of the Republic as the clones turn on the Jedi. Cloning is built into the premise. The Republic's army consists of clones grown on the planet Kamino from the genetic template of the bounty hunter Jango Fett and accelerated in their development, and the series gives these mass-produced soldiers names, personalities and moral agency, highlighting the human cost of a war fought with manufactured people. The Kaminoan cloners appear as cool professionals proud of their product. A squad of clones with genetic mutations that give them special abilities, the Bad Batch, is introduced and later got its own series. Ultimately the clone army is the instrument of Darth Sidious's plan: the series ends with the clones turning on the Jedi. The dossier on which this text rests gives few sourced details about the cloning itself; the series treats it as space-opera technology rather than science.

title: Star Wars: The Clone Wars
text: During the Clone Wars, Anakin Skywalker and Obi-Wan Kenobi lead clone troopers, including Captain Rex and Commander Cody, against a Separatist droid army on the planet Christophsis. Yoda sends Ahsoka Tano to be Anakin's Padawan, and she wins his respect by helping him disable an enemy shield. The Jedi then learn that Rotta, the infant son of Jabba the Hutt, has been kidnapped in a plot by Count Dooku and Jabba's uncle Ziro to frame the Jedi and turn the Hutts against the Republic. Anakin and Ahsoka rescue Rotta on Teth and escape Dooku's assassin Asajj Ventress, whom Obi-Wan later defeats. On Coruscant, Senator Padmé Amidala uncovers Ziro's conspiracy and has him arrested. On Tatooine, Anakin distracts Dooku while Ahsoka returns Rotta to Jabba, and Padmé's message convinces Jabba to grant the Republic passage through Hutt space. Genetics is only part of the setting. The Republic's soldiers are clone troopers, such as Captain Rex and Commander Cody, who fight alongside the Jedi, but the film does not show or discuss how they were created or what it means to be a clone; all of them are voiced by the same actor. The story is about the war, the rescue of Jabba's son and the political plot against the Jedi, and no other genetic element appears.

title: Stitch!
text: This Japanese anime spin-off of Disney's Lilo & Stitch is set years after Leroy & Stitch. Stitch, the destructive genetic experiment 626, flees his creator Dr. Jumba Jookiba and crash-lands on Izayoi, an island near Okinawa, where he befriends Yuna, a ten-year-old karate student. A magical spirit stone will grant his wish to become the strongest being in the universe if he performs enough good deeds, and Jumba, now living with them, builds a good-deed counter. Stitch's old enemy Dr. Hämsterviel schemes to steal the stone's power, using mind-controlled experiments. Other experiments created by Jumba appear, including Angel, Sparky, Reuben and the violent prototype Experiment Zero. In the end Stitch uses his wish to stay with Yuna. In the third arc, set in Okinawa New Town, Hämsterviel's partner Delia creates a powerful experiment, Dark End, which nearly kills Stitch before his friends revive him. As in the rest of the franchise, Stitch and his 'cousins' are genetic experiments: artificial alien creatures with special powers made by the scientist Jumba. Here they are the series' backdrop rather than its subject. Jumba, originally an 'evil genius' who designed Stitch for destruction, is now a friendly, comic mentor who reprograms experiments to find a good purpose, while the villains Hämsterviel and Delia alter experiments to make them stronger and evil and create a monster, Dark End, to defeat Stitch. Created beings are therefore not inherently bad: what matters is how they are raised and used, and Stitch's growth comes through friendship and good deeds, not science. The genetics is entirely cartoon science fiction, and the sources describe the creatures' powers rather than how they were made.

title: Survivors
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic human experimentation post apocalyptic
text: A virus called European flu kills almost everyone on Earth. In Britain, Abby Grant, searching for her missing son Peter, gathers a group of strangers: the self-reliant Greg, the shaken doctor Anya, the businessman Al, the boy Najid, the opportunist Sarah and the escaped convict Tom. They face a corrupt provisional government set up by a former minister and violent gangs. Abby and Peter are the only characters to have survived the virus without prior immunity, which makes them targets for a shadowy consortium. In the second series the group finds a secure laboratory where the biochemist Dr. James Whitaker, working for a pharmaceutical company, is developing a cure from Abby's and Peter's blood; Peter had been kidnapped and held in a slave-labour camp. The company's Mr. Landry admits the virus was engineered. Whitaker is killed by Landry's sniper, Sarah dies of a mutated strain, Al survives a trial vaccine, and the series ends on a cliffhanger. The second series reveals that the pandemic was man-made. Mr. Landry, of the pharmaceutical consortium funding the research, admits that the virus was a genetically engineered attempt to create a universal cure for influenza that failed and escaped into the population. The same company is now racing to produce a vaccine from the blood of Abby and her son, the rare survivors without prior immunity, and treats them as resources to be captured. Its lead scientist, Whitaker, is the main antagonist of the second series: he lies to his colleagues, hides his own family in the facility against protocol and keeps the stolen anti-virus for himself, and his deception lets the virus into the lab. A trial vaccine does work on Al, but the series presents corporate science as secretive, self-serving and the origin of the apocalypse.

title: The Doctor's Daughter
alt: La hija del Doctor Doctor Who, season 4, episode 6
text: The TARDIS takes the Doctor, Martha and Donna to the planet Messaline, where human soldiers force the Doctor's hand into a "progenation machine", which within moments produces a fully grown young woman from his tissue: his daughter, whom Donna names Jenny. Humans and the fish-like Hath are locked in a war, each side breeding new soldiers in the machines, and both are searching for "the Source", which the humans' General Cobb believes will let them wipe out the enemy. Donna works out from dated plaques that the colony ship landed only seven days ago: so many generations have been produced in a week that the war's origins have become myth. The Source turns out to be a terraforming device, and the Doctor releases it and declares the war over. Cobb tries to shoot the Doctor, and Jenny dies taking the bullet. After the Doctor leaves, Jenny revives and departs in a stolen rocket. Reproductive technology drives the story. The progenation machines take a tissue sample and generate a fully grown soldier within moments, so that each side can breed armies continuously. Jenny is genetically derived from the Doctor, and the episode is mostly about whether that makes her his daughter: he initially rejects her as a mere product of a machine, then comes to accept her as his child. Jenny is effectively a clone of the Doctor, and the episode turns on the difference between genetic origin and family ties. No scientists appear; the technology is used by soldiers who have forgotten why they fight. Producing an adult person from a tissue sample in moments is pure fantasy, but the episode raises the familiar question of whether shared genes make a family.

title: The Poison Sky
alt: El cielo envenenado Doctor Who, season 4, episode 5
text: In the second part of a two-part story, the Earth's atmosphere is being choked by poison gas released from the ATMOS devices fitted to 400 million cars. The Sontarans capture the TARDIS with Donna inside, while a clone of Martha Jones, working for them, stops UNIT from launching nuclear missiles at their ship. UNIT counterattacks with the aircraft carrier Valiant. In the ATMOS factory the Doctor finds the real Martha held in a cloning machine; waking her kills the clone, who reveals before dying that the gas is clone feed meant to turn Earth into a breeding world for billions of Sontaran soldiers. The young genius Luke Rattigan, who helped the Sontarans, learns they were using him. The Doctor builds a device that burns off the gas, then offers the Sontarans a chance to withdraw, but Rattigan takes his place on their ship and sacrifices himself to destroy it. Cloning is the Sontarans' plan and a key plot device. The Sontarans are a species of cloned soldiers, and losing their war with the Rutans, they want to turn Earth into a breeding world where new batches of clones can be grown; the gas pumped into the atmosphere is clone feed that would make the planet suitable for them, killing humanity in the process. They also clone Martha Jones in a machine that keeps the original unconscious and use the copy as a spy inside UNIT. The Doctor recognizes the clone because she shows no concern for her family, and she dies when the real Martha wakes. Cloning is thus presented as the method of a militaristic alien empire. Real cloning cannot produce an adult copy with the original's memories, and no gas could serve as clone feed.

title: The Sky Crawlers
text: Mamoru Oshii's animated film, based on Hiroshi Mori's novels, is set in an alternate world at peace, where two private corporations, Rostock and Lautern, stage a real air war to give the public a sense of conflict. Their pilots are the Kildren, genetically engineered humans who remain adolescents and never age. Pilot Yūichi Kannami arrives at Area 262 to replace a pilot who has died, and grows close to the base commander, Suito Kusanagi, who is also a Kildren but has a daughter who passes as her younger sister. Kannami begins to sense that he has no real past, that new pilots resemble the dead, and that his memories may belong to his predecessor. Kusanagi admits that she killed that predecessor at his own request. Kannami dies challenging the Teacher, an invincible enemy ace and an adult, and a new pilot with Kannami's mannerisms arrives, continuing the cycle. Genetic engineering underpins the film's world but is never explained on screen. The Kildren are humans designed not to age, created to serve as disposable pilots in a staged war, and the film suggests that when they die they are replaced by new individuals carrying traces of their predecessors' memories and manner. Their arrested development is the core of the story: they live in an endless adolescence with no past and no future, unable to grow up, and the film treats their condition as a metaphor for repetition and stagnation. The engineers and corporations behind them remain invisible, which makes the system seem impersonal and inescapable. Scholarly readings have discussed the film's depiction of engineered adolescence and endless war as a critique of a society that sustains conflict as a commodity. Arrested ageing has no real genetic equivalent in humans, although researchers study the genetics of ageing in model organisms.

title: The Sontaran Stratagem
alt: La estratagema Sontaran Doctor Who, season 4, episode 4
text: Fifty-two people die simultaneously in cars fitted with ATMOS, a zero-emissions system invented by the teenage prodigy Luke Rattigan, among them a reporter who had called the system dangerous. Martha Jones, now a UNIT medical officer, calls in the Doctor, who arrives with Donna Noble. UNIT raids the ATMOS factory, whose workers have never taken a sick day, and two soldiers find a cloning tank in the basement before being captured by General Staal of the Sontarans. The Doctor discovers that Rattigan is working for the Sontarans and escapes from their ship. Martha is captured, and the Sontaran Commander Skorr grows a clone of her, loaded with her memories, that takes her place in UNIT. At Donna's home, the Doctor finds that ATMOS hides a gas weapon; Staal activates all 400 million devices, and the episode ends with cars filling the world with poison while Donna's grandfather Wilfred is trapped in one. Cloning is one of the Sontarans' infiltration tools in this first half of a two-part story. Alongside mind control and the ATMOS gas devices, the invaders grow human copies in tanks; the main one is a clone of Martha Jones that receives her memories and her clothes and replaces her at UNIT as a mole. According to Wikipedia, the production originally planned for all the factory workers to be clones, but cut this back to Martha; it was the first time the revived series showed the cloning process on screen. The cloners are the Sontarans, a militaristic warrior species, and the copy is cast as an evil double who calmly reports that there is no cause for alarm as the invasion begins. The growth of an adult copy with transferred memories is pure science fiction.

title: Tokyo Gore Police
themes: engineered pathogens mutants human experimentation bioweapon
text: In a dystopian Japan whose police force has been privatised, a mad scientist known as the Key Man has created a virus that turns humans into "Engineers", mutants whose wounds sprout grotesque biomechanical weapons. The police have formed a special squad of Engineer Hunters, who maintain order through sadistic violence and street executions. Ruka, a skilled hunter, is obsessed with finding the assassin who killed her father, a police officer, years before. The Key Man infects her by inserting a key-shaped tumour into her arm. Investigating, she learns that he is a scientist, Akino Miyama, whose father was the sniper hired to kill her father and was then murdered by the police commissioner, the real mastermind; Akino turned himself into the Key Man by injecting himself with the DNA of infamous criminals. Ruka kills Akino and, as her own body begins to mutate, takes revenge on the commissioner. A post-credits scene shows that the Key Man survived. Genetics serves as the pretext for the film's extreme body horror. The Key Man, a scientist driven by revenge, spreads a virus that rewrites the bodies of infected people, and he transforms himself by injecting the DNA of notorious criminals, as if criminality could be acquired by taking up their genes. The film treats this mutation as a way to criticise a violent, privatised police state: the Engineers are hunted and executed in public, and the authorities use the crisis to justify indiscriminate killings of anyone suspected of being infected. The scientist is portrayed both as a monster and as a victim of the corrupt system he attacks. The film, written and directed by Yoshihiro Nishimura, is deliberately excessive and makes no attempt at scientific credibility: injected DNA cannot transfer behaviour, and no virus could produce such transformations.

title: Zombie Strippers
themes: engineered pathogens human enhancement human experimentation bioweapon
text: In a satirical near future, George W. Bush is serving a fourth term, Congress has been dissolved, public nudity is banned and the United States is at war with much of the world. To overcome a shortage of soldiers, a secret laboratory in Sartre, Nebraska, run by Dr. Chushfeld, develops a virus that reanimates dead Marines for combat. The virus escapes, infecting test subjects and scientists, and a Marine 'Z Squad' is sent to destroy the zombies. One bitten Marine flees into an alley, dies and comes back to life inside the Rhino, an illegal strip club run by Ian Essko. He bites the star dancer Kat, who returns to the stage as a zombie and becomes more popular than ever, so the other dancers choose to be infected too, and the zombie strippers devour customers in private dances. When the zombies break loose, the Z Squad storms the club and learns that the Bush administration let the plague escape to distract the public from its failures. The zombies come from a military bioweapon programme. In a secret laboratory, Dr. Chushfeld, working with the US military and, according to the German Wikipedia, a company called W-Industries, develops a transmissible virus to reanimate dead Marines as fearless soldiers, to overcome a shortage of troops for endless wars. The virus breaks containment, infecting test subjects and scientists, and in the German account it reacts differently with the female chromosome set, turning the infected strippers into super-strong, still-lucid dancers rather than mindless ghouls. The satire is aimed at the government and the military: at the end, the administration is revealed to have let the outbreak escape deliberately as a political distraction. The scientist is part of the conspiracy and the creation is lethal, so the film follows the familiar pattern of the lab-made zombie plague. Loosely inspired by Ionesco's Rhinoceros, it is a deliberately trashy horror comedy, and its virology is not meant seriously.

title: Avatar
text: In 2154, with Earth's resources exhausted, the Resources Development Administration (RDA) mines the mineral unobtanium on Pandora, a moon inhabited by the Na'vi, tall blue-skinned humanoids who live in harmony with nature. Scientists of the Avatar Program explore Pandora in Na'vi-human hybrid bodies controlled remotely by matched human operators. Jake Sully, a paraplegic former Marine, takes the place of his dead identical twin as an operator. In his avatar he is taken in by the Omaticaya clan and falls in love with Neytiri, while the security chief, Colonel Quaritch, promises to restore his legs in exchange for intelligence. When the RDA destroys the clan's Hometree, Jake, the program head Dr. Grace Augustine and their allies side with the Na'vi. Grace is killed, but the united clans, helped by Pandora's wildlife, defeat the RDA, which is expelled. Jake is permanently transferred into his avatar body. Genetics underpins the premise rather than the drama. The avatars are genetically engineered Na'vi-human hybrid bodies, each genetically matched to a human operator who controls it with his mind; because of this matching, Jake can take over the avatar grown for his dead identical twin. The avatars let humans breathe Pandora's air and approach the Na'vi, and Jake's life in his avatar is what turns him from corporate spy into a defender of the clan. The scientists of the Avatar Program, led by the exobiologist Dr. Grace Augustine, are portrayed sympathetically: they study the Na'vi and Pandora's ecosystem, oppose the RDA's brutality and join the rebellion. The villains are the mining corporation and its security force, whose greed concerns unobtanium, not genetics. The film's final transfer of Jake into his avatar is achieved through the Tree of Souls, presented as a spiritual and biological process rather than a genetic one.

title: District 9
text: In 1982, a huge spaceship stops over Johannesburg, carrying a population of starving insect-like aliens. They are confined to a camp, District 9, which becomes a slum, and humans despise them as "prawns". Twenty-eight years later, the private military company Multinational United (MNU) is hired to evict them to a new camp, and the operation is led by Wikus van de Merwe, a mild bureaucrat. In an alien shack, Wikus is sprayed by a fluid that the alien Christopher Johnson had spent twenty years synthesising as fuel for their ship, and he begins to turn into an alien. MNU scientists discover that his hybrid DNA lets him operate the aliens' biologically locked weapons, and his own father-in-law orders his body harvested. Wikus escapes and allies with Christopher, who reaches the mothership with his son and promises to return to cure him. Wikus, now fully transformed, stays behind. Genetics is central to the second half of the film. Exposure to the alien fluid rewrites Wikus's body, and MNU's laboratory finds that his partly alien DNA allows him to use alien weapons, which only respond to alien biology. MNU has long been carrying out vivisections and other brutal experiments on the aliens in search of this capability, and its executives treat Wikus as a source of genetic material to be harvested. The scientists are portrayed as instruments of a corporate weapons programme, indifferent to the suffering of their subjects, human or alien, in a story that uses the aliens' treatment to evoke apartheid-era forced removals in South Africa, such as those of Cape Town's District Six. The biology is not meant to be plausible: there is no reason to expect life from another world to share our genetic code, and no fluid could rebuild an adult's whole body. The film's interest lies in its picture of biological research serving discrimination and profit.

title: Futurama: Into the Wild Green Yonder
text: On Mars, Amy's father Leo Wong demolishes old Mars Vegas to build a bigger resort, and Leela rescues a Martian muck leech, the last of its kind, from the site. An eco-feminist protester's necklace lodges in Fry's brain and makes him telepathic, and a secret society of telepaths, the Legion of Mad Fellows, tells him that two species are locked in an ancient evolutionary struggle: the Encyclopods, who preserve the DNA of endangered species, and the Dark Ones, who want to destroy all life. The last Encyclopod egg is a violet dwarf star that Leo plans to implode to make way for the universe's largest miniature golf course, a project Professor Farnsworth approved after being bribed. Leela and Amy join the eco-feminists to stop it, while Fry infiltrates Leo's security staff to find the last Dark One. At the demolition ceremony the leech is revealed as the Dark One; the reborn Encyclopod kills it and preserves the DNA of Hutch, an ally it has killed, and the crew escape into a wormhole. Genetics appears as a comic cosmic myth. The Encyclopods are giant creatures that evolved to preserve the DNA of endangered species so that they can be restored, and their last egg must hatch before a developer destroys it; they are opposed by the Dark Ones, which evolved to destroy all life, in what the film calls an evolutionary arms race. Once born, the Encyclopod gathers the DNA of the dead Hutch and ignores Fry's protest that humans are not endangered, while Zoidberg eats the dead Dark One before its DNA can be saved. The film's satire targets the greedy developer Leo Wong and environmental destruction, with Farnsworth briefly corrupted by a bribe; DNA preservation is cast as the force of life. The Encyclopod is a whimsical take on gene banks and frozen zoos, which store genetic material from endangered species, though no real biobank restores species on demand.

title: Midnight
text: In this Fringe episode, a man is found dead with his spinal column severed and his spinal fluid drained, and Walter finds human bite marks and an extinct strain of syphilis in the killer's saliva. The strain leads to Lubov Pharmaceutical, which bought biological samples useful for weapons, and to its head, Nicholas Boone, who admits to working for the bioterrorist group ZFT. When he refused to cooperate, ZFT infected his wife, Valerie, with a contagion that makes her burn through spinal fluid, so that she must kill to survive; Boone has already lost the use of his legs trying to cure her with his own fluid. Boone works with Walter on a cure, an augmented penicillin, and secretly gives more of his spinal fluid than he can spare. Olivia and Peter track Valerie with thermal imaging and capture her, and the cure saves her, but Boone dies. In a recorded message, he reveals that ZFT is funded by William Bell, founder of Massive Dynamic. The episode's genetic element is a man-made contagion used as a weapon. The bioterrorist group ZFT, funded by the Massive Dynamic founder William Bell, deliberately infected Valerie Boone to force her husband, a pharmaceutical executive, to work for them; the agent, linked to an extinct strain of syphilis that his company had acquired, alters her body so that she needs other people's spinal fluid and grows fangs, turning her into a killer. The sources do not explain the contagion in genetic terms, beyond ZFT's interest in using it as a carrier to alter people. The cure is the work of two scientists: Nicholas Boone, who collaborated with terrorists but is presented sympathetically as a man who sacrifices his life for his wife, and Walter Bishop, who develops an augmented penicillin with him. The episode thus sets a cruel bioterror group against scientists who use their skills to save a victim. Spinal-fluid hunger caused by a syphilis strain is pure fiction.

title: Moon
text: Sam Bell is nearing the end of a three-year contract as the only worker at Sarang, a lunar base where the company Lunar Industries mines helium-3 for energy on Earth. With live communications apparently broken, his only company is the base's computer, GERTY, and recorded messages from his wife Tess. After a rover accident, Sam wakes up in the infirmary, goes out against orders, and finds an injured double of himself in the crashed rover. GERTY admits that both are clones of the original Sam Bell, given his implanted memories. The older Sam is already deteriorating, as earlier clones did at the end of their contracts, and the two find a vault of hundreds of sleeping clones and a jamming system that blocks contact with Earth. Calling home, the older Sam learns that Tess has died and that the original Sam lives on Earth with their teenage daughter. The dying clone stays behind while the newer one escapes to Earth, where he becomes a whistleblower. Cloning is the film's central twist and its moral subject. Lunar Industries uses clones of one employee, each given implanted memories of a wife and daughter and a three-year lifespan, to avoid the cost of training and sending new astronauts; at the end of each contract, the clone believes he is going home but is incinerated. No scientists appear: the cloning is a corporate cost-saving measure, managed remotely, and the only helper the clones have is the base's AI, GERTY. The film's focus is on identity: the two Sams share the same genes and memories but differ in age and temperament, and their humanity is never in doubt for the viewer. Its science is deliberately simplified. A real clone would start life as an embryo and would have to grow up, rather than emerge as an adult copy, and memories are not inherited or transferable with DNA. Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, was born in 1996.

title: My Sister's Keeper
text: When their young daughter Kate is diagnosed with acute promyelocytic leukaemia and no one in the family is a genetic match, Sara and Brian Fitzgerald conceive Anna through in vitro fertilisation as a "saviour sister". From her umbilical cord blood onwards, Anna donates blood and stem cells to Kate, at the cost of repeated hospitalisations and painful procedures. When Kate, now fifteen, goes into kidney failure, eleven-year-old Anna hires the lawyer Campbell Alexander to sue her parents for medical emancipation rather than give up a kidney. The case divides the family: Sara, who gave up her legal career to fight for Kate, cross-examines her own daughter in court. Flashbacks show Kate's romance with another young cancer patient, Taylor, and his death. At the hearing, Anna's brother Jesse forces her to admit that she refused at Kate's request, because Kate knows she would not survive another operation and is ready to die. Kate dies peacefully, and Anna wins the case. The film is built around a real reproductive technology: the saviour sibling. Anna is conceived by IVF so that she will be a genetic match for her sister; in practice, several embryos are created and tested by preimplantation genetic diagnosis, and only one whose tissue type (HLA) matches the sick child is transferred. No scientist is a character; the genetics is in the background, and the drama is ethical and familial. It turns on the objection most often raised against the practice, that the child is conceived as a means to an end, and extends it to a question the procedure itself does not settle: who may decide what is done to the donor's body afterwards. The first saviour sibling selected this way, Adam Nash, was born in the United States in 2000, and the practice is regulated differently from country to country; Spain authorised it in a 2006 law. Jodi Picoult's novel, on which the film is based, has a different ending, in which Anna dies and her kidney saves Kate.

title: Night of Desirable Objects
text: In Lansdale, Pennsylvania, a construction worker is dragged into a tunnel under a cornfield by an unseen creature, one of several unexplained disappearances in the area. Still recovering from a car crash, Olivia Dunham returns to work while Walter believes she travelled to a parallel universe; she begins to develop unusually sharp hearing. At the scene, Walter finds a blue paralytic substance that he suspects comes from mutated DNA. The investigation leads to local resident Andre Hughes, who says he lost his wife and baby in childbirth and refuses to give a blood sample. When the bodies are exhumed, the baby's coffin is empty, and Hughes kills himself before he can be questioned. Walter discovers that Hughes's wife had a form of lupus that made her unable to carry a child, so Hughes genetically altered the baby to survive. The child has grown into a creature that feeds on people; it is killed when its tunnel collapses. Genetic modification of an unborn child drives the case in this Fringe episode. Andre Hughes, desperate for his child to survive a pregnancy his wife's lupus made impossible, altered the baby's DNA, and the boy became a burrowing predator that secretes a paralytic substance and feeds on people. Walter identifies the substance as a product of mutated DNA. Hughes is portrayed as a parent driven by love and grief rather than a cold scientist, and his experiment shows the series' recurring theme of well-meant science with monstrous consequences. The episode reflects real anxieties about germline modification and "designer babies", but grossly exaggerates its effects: no genetic change could turn a human infant into a creature with animal traits within a few years.

title: Pandorum
themes: evolution mutants human enhancement post apocalyptic
text: With Earth exhausted by overpopulation, the ship Elysium carries 60,000 colonists in hypersleep on a 123-year voyage to Tanis, an Earth-like planet. Corporal Bower and Lieutenant Payton wake with partial amnesia in a dark, apparently abandoned section of the ship. While Payton guides him by radio, Bower crawls through the ducts towards the reactor and meets other survivors, Nadia and Manh, as they evade cannibalistic humanoid hunters. A survivor, Leland, explains that years earlier a crew member, Gallo, went mad with "pandorum", a deep-space psychosis, after learning that Earth had been destroyed, and that the hunters descend from passengers changed by an enzyme meant to help them adapt to Tanis. "Payton" turns out to be an aged Gallo. Bower restarts the reactor and learns that 923 years have passed and that the ship lies on the ocean floor of Tanis. Bower and Nadia escape in a hypersleep pod, and the remaining 1,211 pods rise to the surface. Genetics provides the film's monsters. The hunters are the descendants of colonists exposed to a treatment, described as an enzyme, that was meant to help them adapt to the new planet; after centuries in the closed environment of the ship, it has driven an accelerated evolution that produced a cannibalistic, predatory form of human. The idea combines two themes: the hubris of engineering humans in advance for an unknown environment, and the fear that evolution, once accelerated, might not lead towards anything resembling progress. The scientists who designed the treatment never appear, and the horror lies in its unintended consequences rather than in a villainous researcher. As biology the premise is fanciful: evolution acts on populations through selection over many generations, and no single treatment could steer a population towards a new form in a few hundred years, let alone within a lifetime. The film treats the mutants mainly as a horror device in a story about isolation and madness.

title: Quagmire's Baby
text: In this Family Guy episode, Glenn Quagmire finds a newborn girl on his doorstep, with a note from her mother telling him she is his daughter. A paternity test confirms it, and he names her Anna Lee. Caring for her ruins his sex life, and he puts her up for adoption, but he cannot stop thinking about her and goes to take her back; when he sees how happy she is with her adoptive parents, he leaves her with them. Meanwhile, Stewie creates a dumbed-down clone of himself, Bitch Stewie, to serve as his assistant. Brian wants one too, but Stewie lazily lets his clone make it, and Bitch Brian turns out even less capable. Both clones prove unstable, fall apart and dissolve. In a minor subplot, Peter believes he is talking to the ghost of Ronald Reagan on a ham radio, but the voice belongs to the impressionist Rich Little. Genetics appears in two comic forms. In the main story, a paternity test confirms that the abandoned baby is Quagmire's daughter, which makes him face fatherhood; the episode then turns on whether he can raise her, and it ends with him letting her stay with the adoptive parents who love her. In the subplot, Stewie, the Griffins' genius baby, clones himself to get a simple-minded servant, and his clone in turn makes an even dimmer clone of Brian. The clones are deliberately inferior copies that deteriorate, lose body parts and dissolve, a running gag rather than a serious argument about cloning. Stewie is presented as a lazy, careless creator, but the episode passes no judgement on him. In reality, clones are genetic copies with the original's capacities, born as babies, and do not degrade in this way.

title: Splice
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras animal experimentation
text: Clive Nicoli and Elsa Kast, genetic engineers at the company N.E.R.D., splice animal DNA to create hybrids for medical use, including two large worm-like creatures, Fred and Ginger. When their employers forbid them to move on to a human-animal hybrid and order them to extract proteins for drug production instead, they secretly create one. The creature, Dren, grows rapidly and develops gills, wings and a stinger, and Elsa bonds with her as a mother. At a public presentation Fred and Ginger kill each other: Ginger had spontaneously changed sex. On Elsa's childhood farm, where they hide Dren, their relationship with her grows increasingly disturbed. Clive has sex with Dren and reveals that the human DNA came from Elsa herself. Dren apparently dies, returns as a male, kills Clive and two others, and rapes Elsa, who kills him. In the final scene, Elsa, pregnant, accepts payment from the company to carry the child to term. Genetic engineering is the film's subject. Clive and Elsa build hybrid organisms by combining DNA from different species, and they create Dren out of scientific ambition and, in Elsa's case, personal need: she secretly uses her own DNA, which makes Dren in effect her genetic daughter. Their employer, interested only in proteins it can patent, is equally reckless and ends by exploiting the outcome. The story plays on familiar fears about biotechnology: hybrids with unpredictable traits, unforeseen changes such as the creatures' sex reversal, and scientists who cross ethical limits and lose control of their work. Moving genes between species is routine in real laboratories; bacteria carrying the human insulin gene have produced insulin for decades. But, as a scientist reviewing the film for Discover noted, creating a viable creature that combines human and multiple animal genomes, as Splice shows, remains very far off.

title: The Day of the Triffids
text: In an alternative present-day Britain, triffids, large carnivorous plants able to move and to kill with a venomous sting, are farmed worldwide because their oil has become a clean fuel that ended climate change. Bill Masen, who works with triffids,, whose mother was killed by one of the plants, is in hospital with his eyes bandaged when a solar storm blinds more than 95% of the world's population. With the electric fences failing, the triffids escape and begin to hunt. Bill teams up with radio presenter Jo Playton and encounters groups of survivors, among them a religious colony led by Durrant and the brutal Torrence, who seeks to impose his rule. At Shirning House Bill finds his estranged father Dennis, who plans to genetically engineer a new triffid to neutralise the old ones, but the new plant attacks and kills him. Bill finally remembers a childhood trick, triffid poison applied to the eyes, which lets the group pass among the plants and reach a colony on the Isle of Wight. This two-part BBC adaptation of John Wyndham's 1951 novel uses biotechnology at two levels. The triffids themselves are an exploited resource, farmed industrially for their oil despite their danger, and the series hints at the human arrogance of relying on a creature that cannot be controlled. The main genetic element is Dennis Masen's plan to genetically engineer a new type of triffid that could neutralise the existing ones, a technological fix for a biological disaster; his son considers the idea absurd, and the experiment fails when the new plant kills its creator. The scientist is a lone, obsessive figure working outside any institution after the collapse of society. In the original novel the triffids' origin is uncertain, but Bill suspects they were bioengineered in the Soviet Union, and some editions link them to the theories of the Soviet agronomist Trofim Lysenko, a proponent of Lamarckism whose ideas were thoroughly discredited. In this version the triffids are instead tied to a story about energy and climate.

title: The Time Traveler's Wife
text: Henry DeTamble, a Chicago librarian, has a genetic disorder that makes him travel through time involuntarily, arriving naked and unable to change major events; as a child he survives the car crash that kills his mother by jumping back in time. In 1991 he meets Clare Abshire, an artist who has known his older self since she was a child, and they fall in love and marry despite his unpredictable disappearances. They are unable to have a child because Henry's condition makes the fetuses travel out of the womb, causing repeated miscarriages, and after seeking a renowned doctor's help Henry secretly has a vasectomy. Clare nevertheless becomes pregnant by a visiting younger Henry and gives birth to Alba, who inherits the ability but learns to control it. Henry learns from the future Alba that he will die when she is five; he is accidentally shot by Clare's father while hunting and dies in Clare's arms. The film adapts Audrey Niffenegger's novel and gives its fantasy premise a genetic label: Henry's time travel is described as a rare genetic disorder. Heredity matters to the plot. Henry's genes make the couple's fetuses time travel out of the womb, causing a series of miscarriages that lead them to consult a renowned doctor and Henry to have a vasectomy, and the daughter they finally have inherits the trait, though in her it is controllable. The film is a romantic tragedy, and genetics works as an explanation for an affliction and its inheritance rather than as a science that anyone practises or questions. There is, of course, no genetic basis for time travel; the film borrows the language of hereditary disease to make a paranormal condition feel like a medical one.

title: Unleashed
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering animal experimentation
text: Animal rights activists break into a laboratory and unwittingly release a creature, which follows them and kills them. The Fringe team, Olivia Dunham, Charlie Francis, Phillip Broyles and the Bishops, find marks from several different animals on the bodies, and a team of animal control workers is later killed too. When Charlie is attacked, Walter concludes that the creature is a man-made chimera combining traits of several species, including a lizard, a bat and a wasp. He had once tried to create such an animal without success, and the team learns that the creature was based on the work of one of his peers. One of the dead activists was the son of a scientist who carries out animal testing and had broken into his father's laboratory. The chimera has injected larvae into Charlie, who has less than a day to live. Walter, feeling responsible, confronts the creature alone in the storm drains and kills it, and its blood is used to cure Charlie. The episode is built around a laboratory-made chimera, an animal assembled from the genetic traits of several species. Walter Bishop, the series' scientist, admits he once attempted the same thing, and the creature turns out to be based on a colleague's research, so the episode continues Fringe's theme of scientists facing the consequences of past experiments. It also touches on animal research: the creature is released by activists breaking into a testing lab run by the father of one of them. The monster is pure fiction: combining whole body plans from reptiles, mammals and insects is far beyond any real technique. In real biology, a chimera is a single organism made of cells with different genotypes, for example from the fusion of two embryos, and artificial chimeras are produced for research rather than to combine features into a new predator.

title: Unloved
text: A 13-year-old boy is found kicked to death at Euston Station in London. Detectives Ronnie Brooks and Matt Devlin first take him for a runaway, but the autopsy shows he was well fed and healthy, and a press conference identifies him as Danny Jackson, a child in foster care whose mother is in a rehab clinic. Suspicion falls on the mother's former boyfriend, who is thought to have abused the boy, but the trail leads to another child, Jono Blake, who lived in the same care home. At trial, prosecutors James Steel and Alesha Phillips face Steel's old flame, the barrister Beatrice McArdle, who mounts an audacious defence: that Jono is genetically predisposed to violence. The episode is an adaptation of the American Law & Order episode 'Born Bad'. The genetic element is a courtroom argument: the defence claims that Jono's aggressive behaviour comes from his genes, so that he is not fully responsible for the killing. The series' synopsis calls the strategy bizarre and audacious and notes that, if accepted, it could upset the whole British legal system, since any defendant might blame his genes. The title points to the other side of the debate, the neglect suffered by children in care. The episode adapts the American 'Born Bad', whose defence rested on an extra Y chromosome; the available sources do not say which genetic evidence is used here or how the court rules. Twin and adoption studies show that aggression is partly heritable, but through many genes of small effect that interact with upbringing, and no genetic finding removes criminal responsibility.

title: Conviction
text: Based on a true story. Kenny Waters is convicted of the 1980 murder of a neighbour in Ayer, Massachusetts, on circumstantial evidence, testimony from his ex-wife and ex-girlfriend, and a blood-type match, and is sentenced to life without parole. His sister Betty Anne, a mother of two convinced of his innocence, puts herself through school and law school to become his lawyer, at the cost of her marriage. Realising that the new technique of DNA testing could prove Kenny's innocence, she contacts Barry Scheck of the Innocence Project. After a long search, she finds the blood evidence that was believed to have been destroyed, and the DNA results show that the blood at the scene was not Kenny's. The prosecutor still resists, but the two key witnesses admit that a police officer pressured them into lying, and in 2001 Kenny is freed. DNA forensics is what resolves the case, although the film is a legal and family drama rather than a story about science. Kenny was convicted when only blood groups could be compared, a test that can exclude a suspect but cannot identify one. Betty Anne's realisation that DNA testing can match blood to a single person is the turning point, and the decisive scene is the discovery of the stored evidence, which shows the importance of preserving biological samples after a trial. No geneticists appear on screen; the laboratory work is off screen and the expert voice is Barry Scheck's, co-founder of the Innocence Project, which uses DNA testing to challenge wrongful convictions. The case is one of the many exonerations obtained this way in the United States. The real story went further than the film: in 2025, further DNA testing identified Joseph Leo Boudreau, who died in 2004, as the murderer.

title: Dark Metropolis
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering post apocalyptic
text: Mankind has lost a 300-year war against the Ghen, a race of genetically enhanced people it created as soldiers and then abused and tortured. The Ghen now rule Earth from utopian underground cities, while the surviving humans on the surface are stricken by plague. The Ghen Baron Crecilius Pryme wants to be voted ruler and stokes fear of the humans above; he creates an elite force, the Ministers, which carries out brutal reprisals on the surface, and recruits his brother Aiden away from scientific research to join it, where Aiden discovers he enjoys the cruelty. On the surface, a woman named Mukayluh channels alien beings, the Kalendoah, who prophesy a figure who will bring peace between humans and Ghen. Crecilius tries to stop her, unaware that the prophesied one is close to home. The film, the second part of the 'Creation Wars' saga, ends with Crecilius escaping into the sunlight of the surface. Genetics provides the backstory: humans engineered the Ghen, a race with enhanced DNA, to serve as soldiers, mistreated them and were overthrown in a long war, so that the 'genetic supermen' now rule from below while plague-stricken humans survive on the surface. This is the familiar story of engineered servants turning on their makers, here with the roles of oppressor and oppressed reversed in the present, as the Ghen leadership becomes fascistic in its turn. No genetic work happens during the film; the story is about politics, prophecy and alien possession, and the Moria review judges the idea of a dystopia of genetic supermen unoriginal. No scientific detail is given about the enhancement.

title: El Clon
text: This Spanish-language remake of the Brazilian telenovela O Clone, co-produced by Telemundo, RTI Televisión and Globo, stars Mauricio Ochmann and Sandra Echeverría. Jade, a young woman of Arab descent, goes to live with her family in Morocco after her mother's death and falls in love with Lucas, the son of a wealthy Miami businessman, who is visiting the country. Cultural and religious barriers keep them apart, and Jade is married to Said. After Lucas's twin brother Diego dies in an accident, the scientist Augusto Albieri, devastated by the loss, secretly clones Lucas and implants the embryo in a woman, Dora, who gives birth to Daniel. Twenty years later, Lucas and Jade are drawn together again, and Daniel, the clone, now identical to the young Lucas, enters Jade's life, creating a love triangle between the man she loved and his younger double. Subplots deal with drug addiction and Islam. As in the Brazilian original, human cloning is one of the central storylines. The scientist Augusto Albieri clones a young man in secret out of grief for his dead twin brother, implanting the embryo in a woman, and twenty years later the clone, Daniel, grows up resentful and searching for the man he regards as a father. The geneticist is portrayed as a lonely, obsessive figure whose private grief overrides ethics and consent, and the story deals with the identity of a person who is a genetic copy of someone else but has a different upbringing and life. The telenovela uses cloning mainly to set up a melodramatic love triangle rather than to examine the science. Human reproductive cloning remains unachieved and widely opposed; a clone would, as here, be a genetic twin born decades later, not a copy of the original's mind.

title: Extraordinary Measures
text: John Crowley, a Portland advertising executive, and his wife Aileen have two children with Pompe disease, a genetic disorder that typically kills children before their tenth birthday. John contacts Robert Stonehill, a researcher at the University of Nebraska who has done innovative work towards an enzyme treatment. To raise money for the research and the required clinical trials, John devotes himself to the cause full-time and the two found a small biotech company, which they later sell to a larger firm, Zymagen, to finance development. There, Stonehill's temper, rivalry with other research teams and the company's profit motives repeatedly threaten the project and John's hope that his own children will be treated in time. The film is based on the true story of John and Aileen Crowley, as told in the journalist Geeta Anand's book The Cure, with names and some events changed. The film deals with a real inherited disease and with how treatments for rare genetic disorders are developed and paid for. Pompe disease, or glycogen storage disease type II, is an autosomal recessive condition in which a missing enzyme, acid alpha-glucosidase, lets glycogen build up in cells and damages muscle and nerve cells throughout the body. The treatment the characters pursue is enzyme replacement therapy, which supplies the missing protein rather than correcting the gene. The scientist, Stonehill, is a gruff idealist devoted to basic research, while the companies are shown as driven by money but essential to bringing a drug to patients. A review in The Scientist found the story told with remarkable accuracy, though it noted that the sick children appear healthier than real patients and that the film tends to dismiss basic research as idealistic. The real drug, Myozyme, was approved in 2006, and enzyme replacement has greatly improved the outlook for people with Pompe disease.

title: I'm Not Jesus Mommy
text: In this low-budget American thriller, also released as Devil's Angel, Dr. Kimberly Gabriel is a seemingly infertile young woman who will do almost anything to have a child. Through what the film calls the miracle of modern science, she obtains a cloned son, David. All seems well until David's seventh birthday, when disasters begin to strike the earth and appear to come from the boy himself. Dr. Roger Gibson then confesses a long-buried secret: the DNA used to clone David came from the Shroud of Turin, the cloth believed to have wrapped the body of Jesus. The secret cloning project was an attempt to bring about the Second Coming, but the child was born without a soul and is instead the Antichrist. The film presents itself as an interpretation of the Book of Revelation and the End Times. Human cloning is the premise. A secret project clones a child from DNA taken from the Shroud of Turin, in an attempt to reproduce Christ, and gives him to a woman desperate to become a mother; the result is a soulless Antichrist who brings disasters on the world. The film thus combines two worries about cloning, that copying a person is playing God and that a clone may lack a soul, in an apocalyptic religious frame. The only available source is a brief summary, so little is known about how the scientists are portrayed beyond Dr. Gibson's confession of the secret. In reality, any DNA surviving on an ancient cloth would be degraded and contaminated, far from what cloning would need, and the authenticity of the Shroud itself is disputed.

title: Megamind
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement nature nurture
text: Two alien infants are sent to Earth as their home planets are destroyed. Metro Man lands in a wealthy home and grows up to be Metro City's beloved superhero; Megamind lands in a prison, is raised by inmates, is bullied at school and becomes a supervillain. When Megamind seemingly kills Metro Man, he takes over the city but soon grows bored. Inspired by the reporter Roxanne Ritchi, whom he courts in disguise, he makes a serum from Metro Man's DNA to create a new hero to fight, but it is accidentally injected into Roxanne's cameraman, Hal. Coached by Megamind as the hero 'Titan', Hal turns into Tighten, a jealous, destructive villain. Metro Man, who faked his death to retire, refuses to help, so Megamind himself defeats Tighten, removes his DNA-derived powers and becomes the city's new hero. Genetics enters through a superpower serum. Megamind extracts Metro Man's DNA from a flake of dandruff on his cape, and the injected serum gives an ordinary man the hero's powers; a second device later strips them out. The serum shows that powers can be transferred but character cannot: the hapless, resentful Hal becomes not a hero but a worse villain than Megamind. The nature versus nurture theme lies in the two aliens' contrasting upbringings, and the film favours nurture: Megamind is a villain because he was raised in a prison and rejected at school, and he becomes a hero by choice. As science the serum is pure fantasy. Injecting someone else's DNA cannot copy their abilities into an adult's body; real gene therapy delivers specific genes to specific tissues, with targeted and usually modest effects.

title: Never Let Me Go
text: In an alternative history, a medical breakthrough in the 1950s has extended life expectancy beyond 100 years. Kathy, Ruth and Tommy grow up at Hailsham, an English boarding school whose pupils are encouraged to stay healthy and make art, the best of which is chosen for "the Gallery" run by the mysterious Madame. A new teacher tells them that they exist to donate their organs and will die young; she is dismissed. As young adults living in the Cottages, they learn that they are clones and hear rumours that couples truly in love can obtain a deferral. Ruth takes Tommy from Kathy, who leaves to become a carer for donors. Years later, Ruth, weakened by donations, reunites the three, admits her betrayal and dies. Kathy and Tommy become a couple and seek a deferral, but Madame and the former headmistress tell them that deferrals never existed: the Gallery was meant to prove that clones have souls. Tommy dies after his fourth donation, and Kathy awaits her own. Human cloning is the foundation of the society shown, but the film is not interested in how it is done. The clones are created and raised to supply organs, and the medical progress that allows ordinary people to live beyond 100 depends on their early deaths, which the system calls "completing". The real question is whether clones are fully human: the art collected at Hailsham was meant to prove that they have souls, and the guardians argue for better treatment while accepting the donation system itself. There are no scientists on screen; the responsibility lies with an entire society that prefers not to look. Some reviewers missed a fuller explanation of the cloning and the logic of this parallel world, while others have compared the clones' fate to that of farmed animals. Like the novel by Kazuo Ishiguro on which it is based, the film presents genetic identity as irrelevant to personhood; real cloning of mammals from adult cells became possible only with Dolly the sheep in 1996.

title: Resident Evil: Afterlife
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic cloning human enhancement human experimentation bioweapon post apocalyptic
text: Alice and an army of her clones attack Umbrella's headquarters in Tokyo. The Umbrella chairman Albert Wesker escapes and destroys the facility, killing the clones, and injects the real Alice with a serum that removes her superhuman powers before his plane crashes. Six months later Alice reaches Alaska in search of Arcadia, a rumoured safe haven, and finds only the amnesiac Claire Redfield, controlled by a device on her chest. In Los Angeles they join survivors trapped in a prison besieged by the undead, including Claire's brother Chris, and escape through the sewers after a giant axe-wielding monster breaks in. Arcadia turns out to be a ship used by Umbrella as a trap to collect test subjects. Alice and the Redfields free the prisoners and defeat Wesker, now struggling to control the T-virus in his body, who wants to consume Alice. Alice plans to make Arcadia a real refuge as an Umbrella squadron led by a mind-controlled Jill Valentine approaches. As in the rest of the series, the disaster comes from biotechnology. The T-virus, developed by the Umbrella Corporation, has turned most of humanity into zombies and gives superhuman abilities to the few, such as Alice and Wesker, whose cells bond with it. In this film Wesker has used the virus on himself and, unable to control it, believes that consuming fresh human DNA, and above all Alice, will restore his control. Umbrella also lures survivors to the ship Arcadia to use them as test subjects. Alice's army of clones, from an earlier Umbrella programme, appears only in the opening attack. Umbrella and Wesker are sinister and exploitative villains, and biotechnology appears mainly as the source of power and horror. A real virus could not produce zombies or superhuman powers, and the idea that eating DNA pacifies a virus has no basis in biology.

title: Sharktopus
text: The US Navy hires the geneticist Nathan Sands and his daughter Nicole to create a new weapon: S-11, an intelligent shark with the tentacles of an octopus. The creature is controlled by electromagnetic pulses from a device attached to its head, but during a test it discards the device and heads for Mexican waters in search of food, killing the people it meets. Andy Flynn joins Nicole in the hunt for the creature. After a long rampage, Andy shoots S-11 with a device that allows Nicole to hack the chip in its brain; she overloads it, the chip explodes and the creature dies. The Syfy television film was directed by Declan O'Brien and produced by Roger Corman. Genetic engineering is the premise of this deliberately absurd monster film. The Sharktopus is a cross between a shark and an octopus made in a private laboratory under contract to the Navy, and its creator, Nathan Sands, is a scientist working for military clients who loses control of his creation and then tries to cover up the damage. His daughter Nicole, also a scientist, ends up destroying the animal. The film follows the standard pattern of the creature feature, in which a hybrid made as a weapon escapes and turns on people, and it makes no attempt at realism. Sharks and octopuses are only very distantly related, a vertebrate and a mollusc, and their bodies are built on entirely different plans, so a functional hybrid of the two is impossible; real transgenic animals carry at most a few genes from other species.

title: The Bishop Revival
text: Fifteen guests suffocate at a Jewish wedding, all of them from the groom's side, whose grandmother survived the Holocaust; Walter Bishop concludes that the poison targeted a shared genetic trait. When customers with brown eyes die the same way in a coffee shop, fingerprints identify the killer as Alfred Hoffman, a Nazi scientist who is somehow still alive at over 100. Walter realises that Hoffman probably worked with his own father, Robert Bishoff, a German scientist who defected to the United States in 1943, on a toxin that, released as a heated gas, can be keyed to any trait using the DNA of the target, especially of those outside the "master race". The team finds Hoffman's laboratory and learns that he plans to strike a convention promoting world equality. Walter disperses his own toxin, tailored to Hoffman, and kills him. Peter later recovers his grandfather's papers, which include a photograph of Bishoff and Hoffman together. The episode imagines a genetically targeted weapon: a toxin that kills only people who share a particular inherited trait, such as brown eyes or the ancestry of a Jewish family. The villain is a Nazi scientist still pursuing the racial goals of the Third Reich, which places the story in the history of Nazi racial science, while Walter learns that his own father was involved in the original research before defecting to the Allies. The ending complicates the portrayal of the scientist as hero, since Walter uses the same technique to tailor a poison to Hoffman's DNA and kill him. The episode also reveals that the seahorse seen in the series' promotional images is a genetically encoded signature created by Walter's father. A poison that selectively kills people according to their eye-colour genes or ancestry is fiction.

title: The Crazies
text: In Ogden Marsh, Iowa, Sheriff David Dutten is forced to shoot a resident who walks onto a baseball field with a shotgun, and soon another man burns his wife and son alive in their farmhouse. David and his deputy Russell find a crashed military plane in a swamp and suspect the water supply, which David shuts off against the mayor's wishes. Communications are cut and the military quarantines the town; David's pregnant wife, Judy, the local doctor, is wrongly flagged as infected because of a fever. David and Russell rescue her and her assistant Becca as the troops abandon the infected and execute civilians. Becca is killed, and a captured government employee reveals that the plane carried 'Trixie', a prototype biological weapon on its way to be destroyed. Russell, himself infected, sacrifices himself at a roadblock. David and Judy escape as the military destroys the town with a huge explosion, but a satellite marks them, and nearby Cedar Rapids, for 'containment'. As in George A. Romero's 1973 original, which he executive-produced, the threat is a man-made bioweapon: 'Trixie', a prototype virus from the Rhabdoviridae family (the rabies family), escapes when the military plane carrying it for destruction crashes into the town's water supply, and after an incubation period turns people into calculating killers. The government that created it never appears as a scientist; it appears as the soldiers and officials who conceal the weapon, quarantine and execute both infected and healthy residents, and finally destroy the town, so the film's critique is aimed at the state that builds such weapons and the ruthlessness of its containment. The makeup of the infected was based on rabies, tetanus and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. No genetic detail of the virus is given.

title: The Gardener of God
text: This Italian drama, written and directed by Liana Marabini, follows the life and work of Gregor Mendel, played by Christopher Lambert, presenting him as a monk devoted to both prayer and science. Set in the Austro-Hungarian Empire of the nineteenth century, the film shows Mendel's struggle against the taxes imposed on monasteries and his efforts to convince others of the importance of his discovery about heredity. Mendel wonders whether faith and science can be reconciled, and whether his findings will benefit humanity or prove dangerous, since they could be used for eugenic purposes. His benefactor and friend, Princess Hanna von Limburg, supports him. Finally he publishes his conclusions and travels to the Vatican to meet the Pope, who welcomes his work. The film is a biography of Gregor Mendel, the Augustinian friar whose experiments with pea plants established the basic laws of heredity and who is regarded as the founder of modern genetics. It portrays the scientist as a man of faith for whom research and religion are compatible, and it has him foresee that knowledge of heredity could be misused for eugenics. According to Wikipedia's article on Mendel, his work, published in 1866, attracted little attention in his lifetime and was only recognised after 1900, when Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak independently confirmed his findings. The film's ending, with Mendel's work welcomed in Rome, contrasts with this history of neglect. The film offers a rare screen portrait of a real geneticist, told from a Catholic perspective.

title: The Kids Are All Right
text: Nic, an obstetrician, and Jules, who is starting a landscape design business, are a married couple in the Los Angeles area.
