Each gave birth to one of their two children, eighteen-year-old Joni and fifteen-year-old Laser, using sperm from the same anonymous donor. Laser wants to meet his biological father, and Joni, now old enough, asks the sperm bank to put them in touch. The donor, Paul, a relaxed, bohemian restaurant owner, is delighted to meet the teenagers, and the mothers invite him into their lives. Jules starts working on Paul's garden and they begin an affair, while Paul undermines Nic's authority with the children. When Nic discovers the affair, the family shuts Paul out, and after Joni leaves for college the two mothers reconcile. There is no genetic science in the film; it is about biological versus social parenthood. The children's wish to meet their donor drives the plot, and Paul enters the family as a charming outsider who shares the children's genes but none of their history. The story favours nurture. The biological link brings curiosity and some affinity, but when Paul tries to claim a place in the family, even asking Jules to leave Nic and bring the children to live with him, Nic calls him an intruder and tells him to start his own family. What endures is the family that raised the children. The film reflects real practice in donor conception: many sperm banks let donor-conceived people seek contact with their donor once they reach adulthood, as Joni does here.

title: Womb
text: As children, Rebecca and Tommy swear eternal love, but Rebecca moves to Japan with her mother. Twelve years later she returns and they resume their relationship. Tommy, an activist against biotechnology companies that are opening a park of cloned animals, is killed by a car on the way to disrupt its opening. Unable to live without him, Rebecca decides to have him cloned and to carry the clone herself; Tommy's father gives her his son's cells, despite his wife's objections. She gives birth to a son, also called Tommy, and raises him. Other parents shun clones, whom they call "copies", and Rebecca moves with her son to an isolated house. As an adult, Tommy increasingly resembles the original. When he brings home a girlfriend and the original Tommy's mother appears, he demands the truth; Rebecca gives him his predecessor's laptop, and he rapes her. The next day he leaves, thanking her for the life he has had. Womb is an intimate drama about human reproductive cloning used to bring back a lost loved one. Cloning is available in its near-future world, but socially stigmatised, as shown by the prejudice against children known as "copies". No scientist appears on screen; the film concentrates on Rebecca's decision and its consequences rather than on the technology. Its central question is identity: the clone grows up to resemble the original physically and in temperament, but he is a different person with his own life, and Rebecca's attempt to recover her lover through her son produces an impossible, incestuous relationship. The film thus explores nature versus nurture and the ethics of creating a person to fulfil someone else's wishes. Biologically, a clone is a delayed identical twin that shares its genome but not its memories or experiences. Mammals have been cloned from adult cells since Dolly the sheep in 1996, but human reproductive cloning has never been achieved.

title: Young Justice
themes: cloning human enhancement human experimentation mutants bioweapon
text: This animated series follows a covert team of teenage superheroes working under the Justice League's supervision. In the first season, Robin, Kid Flash and Aqualad investigate a fire at Cadmus Labs and find Superboy, a clone of Superman, together with the Genomorphs, creatures made as living weapons; with Miss Martian and Artemis they form a secret team and uncover the Light, a society of villains manipulating world events, and a Cadmus clone of the hero Speedy. The second season, Invasion, set five years later, pits the Team against the alien Reach, who have infiltrated Earth; Kid Flash dies stopping their bomb. In Outsiders, the Reach's revelation that humans carry a dormant 'meta-gene' that can be activated sets off an international arms race and the trafficking of teenagers with latent powers. Phantoms follows the original members into adulthood and ends with Superboy marrying Miss Martian. Genetic science is the source of several of the series' main threads. Cadmus Labs, a secret facility tied to the villains' society, the Light, creates Superboy, a clone of Superman who grows into one of the central heroes and struggles with his identity as a clone, as well as the Genomorphs, engineered creatures intended as weapons, and a clone of Roy Harper that has replaced the original. Later seasons introduce the 'meta-gene', a dormant gene that can be activated to give people powers; once the alien Reach reveal it, governments and criminal organisations traffic teenagers to exploit it, which the Team fights. Those who practise genetics are therefore clandestine laboratories, villains and exploiters, while sympathy goes to their creations, above all Superboy. The cloning and gene activation follow superhero conventions rather than real biology.

title: 7aum Arivu
text: The film opens with Bodhidharma, a Pallava prince skilled in martial arts and medicine, who travels to China, cures an epidemic and teaches the villagers medicine, hypnotism and the training that gave rise to Shaolin kung fu, before agreeing to die there. In the present day, the Chinese government sends the mercenary Dong Lee to Chennai to start "Operation Red", a biological war against India using the same virus Bodhidharma once cured. Meanwhile, Subha Srinivasan, a genetics student, believes Bodhidharma's abilities can be revived in a descendant whose DNA matches his, and finds a match in Aravind, a circus performer. Her professor rejects her idea and turns out to be secretly helping Lee for money. Lee hunts down Subha, Aravind and their friends and kills several of them. During the final fight, Aravind awakens Bodhidharma's powers, kills Lee and cures the disease with an ancient remedy. Genetics provides the premise for this Tamil science fiction action film. A genetics student believes that a historical figure's skills can be reawakened in a living descendant by matching their DNA, a version of the idea of "genetic memory", and the genetics professor is shown as a corrupt scientist who collaborates with a foreign bioweapons plot. The threat that drives the story is a biological attack with an ancient virus, the same strain Bodhidharma once cured, rather than an engineered one. The film links genetics with national pride, presenting ancient Indian knowledge as the answer to modern science. The notion that abilities or memories acquired by an ancestor can be inherited and reactivated through DNA has no scientific basis; learned skills are not encoded in the genome. Commentators compared the premise to the Assassin's Creed video games, and a critic in The Hindu noted that the telepathy and hypnotism were "comic book stuff". The film was also criticised for historical inaccuracies about Bodhidharma.

title: Attack of Mark's Clone
text: In the monster-filled New York of Ugly Americans, Callie Maggotbone of the Department of Integration clones her colleague Mark Lilly because he is a terrible bowler and she wants the department to win an upcoming tournament. The clone, blond instead of brown-haired and sadistic, locks the real Mark in his closet and takes over his life, turning Mark's therapy group into a fight club. A new assistant, Tad, banishes Callie to a sub-basement as a suspected saboteur but likes the clone's attitude. Reading Callie's diary, the clone learns that she plans to kill him after the tournament, so he murders Tad and frames her with her own trident. When Frank Grimes investigates and finds the real Mark, the clone shoots him in both legs. The real Mark tracks the clone to a tropical island, where he confesses; the clone is gassed and his parts give Grimes new legs and eyes. Cloning drives this comedy episode, which plays the archetypal evil-duplicate plot in the show's absurd style. Callie creates a copy of Mark for the most trivial of reasons, to win a bowling tournament, and plans to dispose of him afterwards; the clone turns out to be a nastier, more aggressive version of the gentle original and causes a murder, a frame-up and a shooting. The episode never says how or with what technology Callie makes the clone, and she refuses to tell Mark where it came from. The clone is finally gassed and recycled for spare body parts, a black joke that treats the copy as disposable material. Nothing about it is meant seriously as science; according to the series creator, the point was the fun of seeing the usually meek Mark as a jerk.

title: Concentrate and Ask Again
text: In this Fringe episode, a scientist at the pharmaceutical company Intrepus is killed by a blue powder that turns his bones to dust. The package is traced to a former Marine, Aaron Downey, who falls into a coma after being hit by a car while fleeing. To learn what he knows, Walter recruits Simon Phillips, a former subject of his childhood Cortexiphan trials, who has lived in isolation because he cannot control his telepathy; he is comforted by Olivia, whose mind he cannot read. Simon and Nina Sharp help uncover Project Jellyfish, a secret military bioweapon programme that developed a chemical agent that destroys skeletons. Downey and two other men had been inoculated against it, but their exposure passed to their children, who were stillborn without skeletons, and they are taking revenge on those responsible. Olivia stops the last two before they can attack a gala for Congressman Jim Thorn, the general who oversaw the project. The genetic element is the inherited damage caused by a military weapon. Project Jellyfish developed a chemical agent that dissolves bones; the soldiers who worked on it were inoculated and appeared unharmed, but their exposure was passed to their children, who developed without skeletons and were stillborn, and doctors told one of the fathers that he carried a DNA pathogen. The bereaved fathers turn the weapon against the scientists and officials responsible, and the episode presents them as sympathetic avengers whose revenge must nevertheless be stopped, while the general who ran the programme is now a politician. A second strand concerns the Cortexiphan trials, Walter's drug experiments on children that left Simon Phillips with uncontrollable telepathy, which the episode presents as a source of lasting suffering and guilt. Both stories show scientific programmes harming people long after the fact. A chemical that destroys bone and causes heritable damage of this kind is fiction, although some chemicals can cause birth defects.

title: Contagion
text: Back in Minneapolis from Hong Kong, Beth Emhoff dies of an unknown disease, followed by her young son; her husband Mitch is immune. As the virus spreads worldwide, the film follows several interlinked stories. At the CDC, Dr. Ellis Cheever sends epidemiologist Dr. Erin Mears to trace Beth's contacts, and Mears herself is infected and dies. Dr. Ally Hextall finds that the new virus, MEV-1, combines genetic material from pig and bat viruses; when a researcher in San Francisco defies orders to destroy his samples and finds a way to grow it in cell culture, she develops a vaccine and tests it on herself. A WHO epidemiologist traces the outbreak to Macau and is kidnapped by an official who wants vaccines for his village, and a conspiracy blogger promotes a fake cure, while society breaks down until the vaccine is distributed by lottery. A final flashback reveals how the virus jumped from a bat to a pig and to Beth. Genetics appears as a tool of virology and public health rather than as a theme in itself. Scientists identify the new virus by its genetic material, showing that it is a recombinant of bat and pig viruses, model how its mutations increase transmission and use that knowledge to make a vaccine. The film portrays scientists and public health workers in an unusually positive and realistic light: they are competent, overworked and willing to take personal risks, as when Hextall tests the vaccine on herself, while the obstacles come from bureaucracy, fear, misinformation and inequality of access. Made with advice from the virologist W. Ian Lipkin and the epidemiologist Larry Brilliant, it was praised by scientists for its accuracy. The chain of infection from a bat colony disturbed by deforestation, through pigs, to humans echoes the Nipah virus, which emerged in Malaysia in the late 1990s, and the film even uses a Nipah protein model on screen. Its relevance was underlined in 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic brought it renewed popularity.

title: Finale
text: In the two-part series finale of Smallville, Clark Kent and Lois Lane prepare to marry as the planet Apokolips descends towards Earth. Tess Mercer discovers that Oliver Queen is possessed by Darkseid and is captured by Granny Goodness. Meanwhile, the Lionel Luthor of a parallel Earth tries to bring back his dead counterpart's son, Lex, who has been surviving in the ruins of the Luthor mansion by grafting vital parts from his clones onto his own body; Lionel plans to use Tess's heart, and after she shoots him he makes a deal with Darkseid to restore Lex. At the wedding, the possessed Oliver tries to strip Clark's powers with a gold kryptonite ring, but Clark frees him. Lex reveals he always knew Tess was his sister and stabs her; dying, she poisons him with a neurotoxin that erases his memories. Clark finally flies, defeats Darkseid and pushes Apokolips away. Seven years later Lex is President and Clark is Superman. Genetics appears in a single strand of the finale: Lex Luthor's survival. Lex has kept himself alive by harvesting vital parts from his own clones and grafting them onto his body, which makes cloning the means of the arch-villain's return. The clones are treated as spare parts, a sinister use that fits Lex's role as the series' antagonist; his return also involves his father's bargain with Darkseid. The episode is otherwise about Clark accepting his destiny as Superman and defeating Darkseid, and the source gives no detail about how the clones were made. Growing a clone as a source of organs is a long-standing science-fiction idea; in reality a clone would be a separate person, and organ replacement research focuses on growing tissues, not whole copies.

title: George the Hedgehog
text: In this Polish adult animated black comedy, based on a comic, a professor's laboratory experiment produces a computer image of a hedgehog, and he sends his assistant to find a real one. The assistant hires two skinheads, Stefan and Zenek, to obtain the DNA of the anthropomorphic hedgehog Jerzy and then kill him. They get the DNA, but Jerzy survives. The lab clones him, having concluded that Jerzy has the full potential of a pop star but cannot be controlled. The clone assaults Jerzy's lover, Yola, who blames and leaves Jerzy, and the skinheads lure Jerzy under a Warsaw bridge, knock him out and throw him in the river; he is rescued by a prostitute, Lilka. While the clone becomes an international celebrity, Jerzy breaks into one of his concerts, exposes him and fights him until a falling beam crushes the clone. The assistant is arrested, Jerzy and Yola reconcile, and the surviving clone ends up cooked by two Vietnamese chefs. Cloning drives the plot of this crude satire. A professor and his assistant obtain Jerzy's DNA through hired skinheads and grow a clone, because their analysis says Jerzy has the makings of a pop star but cannot be controlled; the clone becomes a manufactured celebrity while the original loses his girlfriend and his name. The clone, a copy with none of Jerzy's loyalty, assaults Yola and takes his place, and the comedy turns on mistaken identity until Jerzy publicly exposes the impostor. The scientists are villains in the mad-scientist mould: they order the original's murder, the assistant ends up arrested, and the professor coolly abandons his creation. The film uses cloning as a vehicle for mocking celebrity culture and the media rather than as a subject in itself; the instant production of an adult clone has no basis in real cloning, which produces a newborn twin. The only source is the English Wikipedia plot summary.

title: Guilty Crown
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic evolution human enhancement religion post apocalyptic
text: In 2039, Japan is ruled by GHQ, an international body sent ten years earlier to contain the 'Lost Christmas' outbreak of the Apocalypse Virus, which arrived with a meteorite and crystallises its victims. High-school student Shu Ouma meets Inori Yuzuriha, singer of the group Egoist and member of the resistance Funeral Parlor, led by Gai Tsutsugami. When a vial of the Void Genome shatters on him, Shu gains the 'Power of the King', the ability to draw weapons called Voids out of people's hearts. GHQ's Anti-Bodies leader Shūichirō Keido unleashes the virus on Tokyo with a 'genetic resonance' broadcast. Shu learns that his sister Mana was the first infected and caused Lost Christmas, and that Inori was created as a vessel for Mana's soul, to bear a new human race. GHQ proves a front for Da'ath, an ancient cult seeking to force human evolution through the virus. Shu defeats Gai and Yu, Keido kills himself, and Inori sacrifices herself to destroy the virus. Genetics runs through this anime's science-fiction mythology. The Apocalypse Virus, which arrived with a meteorite, is turned into a tool by Da'ath, an ancient cult using GHQ as its front, to force mankind's evolution, and by Keido, who spreads it with a 'genetic resonance' broadcast. The pharmaceutical company Sephirah Genomics developed a vaccine and the Void Genome, a genetic weapon derived from the virus that grants the hero his power, and Inori's body was artificially created as a vessel to bear a new race with the soul of Shu's sister. Scientists appear on both sides: Keido is the villain, while Shu's stepmother Haruka, also from Sephirah Genomics, betrays GHQ to help him. The series treats forced evolution and genetic power as the source of oppression and catastrophe; its science is mystical rather than realistic.

title: Hanna
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering nature nurture human experimentation
text: Fifteen-year-old Hanna lives in the forests of northern Finland with her father, Erik Heller, a former CIA operative who has trained her since early childhood as an assassin. When she declares herself ready, she activates a beacon that alerts the CIA, and Erik leaves for Berlin. Captured and taken to an underground base in Morocco, Hanna kills a double of the CIA officer Marissa Wiegler and escapes, travelling across Spain and Europe with a British family on holiday while Marissa and the hired killer Isaacs pursue her. In Berlin she learns that Erik is not her biological father: he had recruited pregnant women into a CIA programme in which their children's DNA was enhanced to create super-soldiers, and when the programme was shut down all its subjects except Hanna were killed. Erik is shot dead by Marissa, and Hanna tracks Marissa down and kills her. Genetic enhancement is the secret at the heart of the story, revealed late in the film. Hanna is the surviving product of a covert CIA project that modified the DNA of foetuses to create super-soldiers with "high intelligence, muscle mass, and no pity"; when the project was shut down, the agency eliminated its subjects. The scientists remain off screen, but the programme is shown as a cold state enterprise that treats people as disposable. Much of the film's interest lies in the tension between Hanna's engineered nature and her upbringing: Discover magazine's Kyle Munkittrick called her a "transhumanist hero" who is nevertheless a good-natured person, and said she symbolises the contest between genetics and environment, nature versus nurture. Engineering complex traits such as intelligence or empathy in human embryos remains beyond current science.

title: Novation
text: In this Fringe episode, Peter Bishop has returned from an erased timeline and is held at Fringe headquarters. The Fringe team investigates the murders of Karen Truss and her boyfriend, the former wife and partner of Dr. Malcolm Truss, a biochemical researcher once at Massive Dynamic. The killer is Nadine, a new kind of shapeshifter who can pass for any human and who wants Truss's abandoned cell-cloning research. Posing as a patient, she finds Truss before the team does and forces him to synthesise a cure in his secret laboratory; he discovers her nature when she briefly takes his dead wife's form. Peter, from his cell, helps the team trace her through a tracking signal he finds on a recovered memory disc. When agents surround the laboratory, Nadine takes the serum, fakes her death by taking the form of a dead agent and escapes, then reports her success through a typewriter that warns that more shapeshifters are coming. The genetic element is Dr. Malcolm Truss's research on cell cloning, abandoned while he worked at Massive Dynamic, which a shapeshifter forces him to turn into a serum. Nadine belongs to a new generation of shapeshifters who can take any human form; she presents her need as a medical cure, mentions a daughter, and kills to obtain it, and the serum apparently stabilises or strengthens her abilities, making her harder to stop. Truss is a victim of coercion rather than a villain: he works under threat of death and is horrified when he learns what she is. The episode is mainly about Peter's return and Walter's guilt over his past experiments, so the cloning research serves as the engine of the case. The sources do not describe how the serum works, and cloning cells has nothing to do with changing shape.

title: Quarantine 2: Terminal
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic human experimentation bioweapon
text: On a night flight from Los Angeles, a passenger is bitten by one of the 'hamsters' that a man named Henry is carrying and turns violently ill, forcing an emergency landing. The passengers are sealed inside the airport terminal by soldiers and supposed CDC scientists. The infection, a rabies-like virus spread by bites, turns people into raging killers, and flight attendant Jenny, the boy George, the paramedic Shilah and others fight to survive. Officers who come in with drugs admit they belong to a Homeland Security bioterrorism unit, that the drugs are experimental antidotes and that the virus came from a quarantined bioterrorist lab in Los Angeles. George exposes Henry as a member of the terrorist cell, which spread the virus to cull humanity; Henry injects himself with the antidote, which fails. Jenny and George kill him, but Jenny is infected and only George escapes through a drainage tunnel, while an infected cat walks towards the Las Vegas Strip. The threat is a man-made pathogen: a rabies-like virus bred in a clandestine Los Angeles laboratory by an apocalyptic bioterrorist cell that wants to 'cull the human population', and deliberately spread by one of its members with infected lab rats. The government's response is no reassurance: the terminal is sealed with lethal force, and the survivors are treated with experimental antidotes, which fail, by a homeland-security unit that intends to study them. The film presents both the eco-terrorist use of biology and the state's containment as dangerous, and it ends with the virus escaping into Las Vegas. It is a sequel to Quarantine, the US remake of the Spanish film [REC], and gives no details of how the virus was made.

title: Rise of the Planet of the Apes
alt: El origen del planeta de los simios
themes: gene therapy animal experimentation engineered pathogens pandemic
text: In San Francisco, scientist Will Rodman is testing ALZ-112, a virus-based drug intended to cure Alzheimer's disease, on chimpanzees at the biotech company Gen-Sys. The drug greatly increases the intelligence of a female chimpanzee, but she is shot during a rampage and the project is closed. Will secretly takes home her newborn son, Caesar, who has inherited the drug's effects, and raises him as he grows into a highly intelligent ape. Will also treats his own father, who has Alzheimer's, and the drug restores his mind until his immune system fights it off. After Caesar attacks a neighbour to defend Will's father, he is sent to a brutal primate shelter, where he becomes the apes' leader. Gen-Sys develops a stronger gaseous version, ALZ-113, which proves lethal to humans. Caesar steals it, makes the other apes intelligent and leads them to freedom across the Golden Gate Bridge, while an infected man unknowingly spreads ALZ-113 around the world. The film's premise is a gene-therapy-like treatment that goes wrong. ALZ-112 is a virus-based drug designed to repair the brain in Alzheimer's disease; in apes it boosts intelligence, and its effects are passed from Bright Eyes to her son Caesar. Will Rodman is a sympathetic scientist, motivated by his father's illness, but he cuts corners by testing the drug on his father and raising Caesar at home, while his boss pushes the more powerful ALZ-113 into further trials despite the risks. The result is both the rise of intelligent apes and a pandemic lethal to humans, setting up the later films. The film raises questions about animal experimentation and corporate pressure on research. Modified viruses are in fact one of the main ways of delivering genes in real gene therapy, but no treatment can create human-level intelligence in apes, and Alzheimer's disease still has no cure.

title: Starbuck
text: In this French-Canadian comedy, David Wozniak, an amiable but irresponsible deliveryman for his family's butcher shop, owes $80,000 to thugs, and his pregnant girlfriend Valérie doubts he could ever be a father. Then a lawyer from a sperm bank tells him that the many donations he made under the alias 'Starbuck' in 1988 have produced 533 children, 142 of whom have filed a class action to learn his identity. Opening their files, David secretly seeks out some of his biological children, among them an actor, a recovering drug user and a disabled young man, and acts as their guardian angel. Passing himself off as a stranger, he even joins them on a camping weekend. In the end, after winning damages from the clinic, he reveals himself as Starbuck, reconciles with Valérie and is welcomed by his many children when his new son is born. Starbuck is about biological fatherhood rather than genetic science. The premise, a sperm donor who discovers that he has hundreds of children, raises questions about the anonymity of donors, the right of donor-conceived people to know their origins, and the risks of a single donor fathering very many children, such as accidental incest between half-siblings and the spread of genetic disease. The film presents the genetic tie as a powerful bond, and David's redemption lies in discovering a talent for fatherhood that goes beyond biology, so the story weighs heredity and upbringing together. The alias Starbuck refers to a famous Canadian Holstein bull whose semen sired a huge number of cattle. The writers raised the number of children to 533 after learning of a real donor with some 500 offspring.

title: Switched at Birth
text: In Kansas City, teenager Bay Kennish, raised by the wealthy John and Kathryn Kennish, finds in a school biology lab that her blood type is incompatible with her parents'. Genetic testing confirms that she was switched at birth with Daphne Vasquez, who is deaf after childhood meningitis and was raised by the single mother Regina Vasquez in a working-class neighbourhood. The Kennishes invite Regina, Daphne and Regina's mother Adriana to live in their guest house, and the two families try to come to terms with each other. Bay searches for her biological father, Angelo Sorrento, who, it emerges, had abandoned Regina after a DNA test showed that Daphne was not his child. Over five seasons the girls discover traits they share with their biological parents, Bay becomes an artist and Daphne a basketball player and cook, and the series follows their romances, careers and the Deaf community at Carlton School for the Deaf. Genetics sets the series in motion and frames its central question. A blood-type mismatch in a school biology lab, followed by DNA testing, reveals that Bay and Daphne were switched at birth, and an earlier paternity test had already led Angelo to wrongly conclude that Regina was unfaithful and abandon the family. The series then weighs heredity against upbringing: Daphne turns out to share John's athletic talent and Kathryn's love of cooking, and Bay shares Regina's artistic gift, yet each girl is shaped by the family and community that raised her, and both end up accepting both families as their own. Genetic testing is shown as a routine, reliable tool whose results carry great emotional weight rather than as science in itself. The series is better known for its portrayal of Deaf culture and American Sign Language.

title: The Hand That Rocks the Wheelchair
text: In this Family Guy episode, Bonnie Swanson asks Lois to look after her husband Joe and their baby while she visits her sick father, and Lois passes the job to Meg. Meg develops a crush on Joe, has Bonnie arrested at the airport by planting a gun in her luggage, and even throws herself in front of his police car hoping to end up in a wheelchair like him, before apologising and becoming his friend. In the second story, Brian tells Stewie that he has gone soft, so Stewie builds a machine to restore his evil nature. It seems to do nothing, but it has in fact created a truly evil clone of Stewie, who attacks Brian, overpowers Stewie and goes on a violent rampage. Stewie uses Brian as bait, and Brian shoots the clone after telling the two naked Stewies apart. Genetics appears only as a comic device in the Stewie subplot. Stewie's machine, meant to boost his own evil, instead produces a clone of him into which all his evil is concentrated, an idea borrowed from the Star Trek episode 'The Enemy Within'. The clone is a cartoon double rather than a product of genetic science: it appears instantly, fully grown and dressed, and the episode never explains how it was made. The other storyline, about Meg's crush on Joe, has nothing to do with genetics. The notion that a personality trait like evil could be separated into a copy has no basis in biology; a real clone shares a person's genome but not his character or memories.

title: The Skin I Live In
text: Robert Ledgard, a plastic surgeon in Toledo, has created an artificial skin resistant to burns and insect bites, which he calls "Gal" after his late wife, who was disfigured in a car crash and later took her own life. At a symposium he privately admits to having carried out illegal transgenic experiments on humans and is forbidden to continue. In his secluded estate he keeps a young woman, Vera, captive, helped by his housekeeper Marilia, who is secretly his mother. After Marilia's other son, Zeca, breaks in and rapes Vera, Ledgard kills him. Flashbacks reveal the past: six years earlier, Ledgard's fragile daughter Norma was assaulted at a wedding by a young man, Vicente, and later killed herself. Ledgard kidnapped Vicente and, over years of surgery and transgenesis, transformed him into a woman resembling his dead wife: Vera. Finally Vera kills Ledgard and Marilia, escapes, and returns to her mother's shop to say: "I am Vicente." Genetic engineering is the instrument of an obsessive revenge. Ledgard develops a transgenic artificial skin, presented at a medical symposium as a potential treatment for burns, but he has crossed the ethical line by testing his methods on humans, and when the scientific establishment forbids him to continue, he carries on in secret in his own clinic. The film portrays him as a brilliant, respected surgeon who uses his skill to imprison and remake another human being without consent, combining transgenesis with surgery to change Vicente's sex and appearance into a copy of his dead wife. Science here serves personal grief, control and punishment, and the film raises questions about bodily autonomy and identity, since Vera's body is transformed but Vicente's sense of who he is survives. Almodóvar described it as "a horror story without screams or frights". The transgenic skin and the transformation shown in the film are fictional.

title: The Terror Beneath
alt: Seeds of Destruction Semillas de destrucción
text: Two young environmentalists secretly filming at a Nevada mine to expose illegal toxic-waste dumping record an illicit sale of a seed whose leaves have remarkable healing properties. The deal goes wrong, the seller is shot, and the dropped seed instantly sprouts roots that spread at enormous speed. A covert government agency, SCOPE, calls in the palaeobotanist Dr. Jocelyn Stein, who recognises the seeds as coming from the Garden of Eden, which she and her colleague Dr. Jeremy Frame had been searching for. She realises that Frame has genetically modified the ancient seeds so that the plants absorb toxins, but that as a result they will spread over the whole planet, destroying all life in their path. In the manner of a television disaster movie, the heroes flee the spreading growth and opening fault lines, an obstructive official is devoured by the menace, and a discredited theory finally provides the means to stop it. The disaster is caused by genetic engineering. Dr. Jeremy Frame, a colleague of the heroine, finds ancient seeds from the Garden of Eden and modifies them so that the plants absorb toxins, an environmental aim, but the modified plants grow uncontrollably and threaten to cover the planet. The scientist who diagnoses the threat, the palaeobotanist Jocelyn Stein, is the heroine who works with a government agency to stop it. The only source available, a review, describes a cheap, formulaic disaster film mixing genetic modification with biblical themes, and gives few details about Frame's portrayal or the ending. Plants engineered to absorb pollutants are a real research field (phytoremediation), but nothing in it resembles a plant that spreads across a continent in days.

title: Wallflower
themes: genetic engineering human experimentation hybrids chimeras genetic disease dna identification
text: The Fringe team investigates a man found dead with his skin and hair turned completely white. Walter finds that the pigment has been extracted from his skin and detects both human and animal DNA. The human DNA belongs to a boy who supposedly died a week after his birth in 1989 of a rare condition that made his skin fatally sensitive to light. Nina Sharp admits that the baby was in fact taken to a pharmaceutical subsidiary of Massive Dynamic and experimented on for years, and that he escaped during a fire. Animal genes implanted in his skin let him survive light but also made him invisible. Now an adult, Eugene steals pigment from his neighbours in a condominium to become visible, although the treatment will kill him. Becoming visible at last, he is greeted by a woman he has secretly loved, and he dies smiling. Meanwhile Olivia, worried about her own capacity to feel, is drugged by Nina's agents. Genetics drives the case. A pharmaceutical subsidiary of Massive Dynamic took a newborn with an unknown genetic disorder that made light deadly to him, declared him dead, and kept him in a laboratory, where researchers implanted animal genes in his skin; he survived light, but his skin now blends perfectly with his surroundings and makes him invisible. The episode presents this experiment on a child as a corporate violation that turns its victim into a lonely, tragic killer, and Massive Dynamic's executive Nina Sharp ends the episode by having Olivia drugged to erase her memory. In contrast, Walter's analysis of the human and animal DNA left on a victim identifies the boy and solves the case. The science is fanciful: real gene transfer between species cannot produce camouflage that makes a person invisible, and pigment cannot simply be transferred from one person's skin to another's.

title: We Need to Talk About Kevin
text: Eva Khatchadourian, a former travel writer, lives alone, shunned by her neighbours, and visits her son Kevin in prison after he has killed students at his high school. In flashbacks she recalls her reluctant motherhood. From infancy Kevin seemed to target her: he cried incessantly only with her, rejected her affection and behaved like a model son in front of his indulgent father, Franklin, who dismissed her worries. Once, losing her temper, Eva broke Kevin's arm. After the birth of a sister, Celia, the girl's guinea pig disappears and she loses an eye in an accident with drain cleaner while Kevin is watching her, but Franklin defends him. Shortly before turning sixteen, Kevin kills Franklin and Celia at home and then classmates trapped in the school gym with his bow and arrows. Two years later Eva asks him why; he says he is no longer sure. There is no genetics in the film; it belongs here as a story that leaves open whether Kevin was born bad or made bad. Told through Eva's memories, it shows a child who seems hostile from birth, which points to an innate nature, but also a reluctant mother who struggles to love him and once injures him, which points to damage done at home. Because Eva is an unreliable narrator, the film never settles the question and gives weight to both: critics read it as a 'bad seed' story, yet it also invites the viewer to suspect the parenting, and Kevin's own final uncertainty about his motives leaves both explanations standing. Research on children with severe conduct problems finds that a child's temperament and the parents' responses shape each other over time, so neither inborn nature nor upbringing alone accounts for such a child.

title: X-Men: First Class
text: In 1944, at Auschwitz, the Nazi officer Klaus Schmidt sees the young Erik Lehnsherr bend a metal gate with his mind and kills his mother to make his power appear. In 1962, Erik, now a hunter of Nazis, is tracking Schmidt, who calls himself Sebastian Shaw and leads the mutant Hellfire Club. CIA officer Moira MacTaggert enlists the telepath Charles Xavier, a new Oxford graduate, and his adoptive sister Raven, a shapeshifter. Charles saves Erik, and with the CIA they recruit young mutants, including the scientist Hank McCoy. Shaw plans to provoke a nuclear war through the Cuban Missile Crisis, so that mutants can inherit the earth. Hank develops a "cure" for mutant appearance from Raven's DNA, but it turns him into the blue-furred Beast. The mutants stop the war and Erik kills Shaw, but Charles is paralysed and Erik, now Magneto, leaves with Raven and others to lead mutants separately. Genetics underlies the film's premise rather than its plot. In the X-Men universe, mutants are humans born with a genetic mutation, later called the X-gene, that gives them special powers. Most of the story concerns politics and the Cold War, but genetic themes appear in Shaw's belief that mutants are a superior species, which the film sets against its Auschwitz opening and Shaw's Nazi past, and in the debate over whether mutants should hide or take pride in what they are. Hank McCoy, a young CIA-funded scientist, creates a serum from Raven's DNA to make mutants look "normal", which she refuses and which backfires on him, a parable about trying to "cure" difference. The X-Men have often been read as an allegory of minorities facing prejudice. Real mutations do not confer powers of this kind.

title: Antiviral
text: In a near-future Toronto, Syd March works for the Lucas Clinic, which harvests viruses from celebrities and injects them into fans who want to share their idols' illnesses; the pathogens carry a 'copy protection' that makes them non-contagious. Syd smuggles viruses out in his own body and sells them to Arvid, who works at a butcher selling meat grown from celebrities' cells. After injecting himself with blood from the star Hannah Geist, Syd falls gravely ill, and Hannah is reported dead. He learns that she is secretly alive, that her virus was engineered to resist analysis and patented by the rival firm Vole & Tesser, and that a piracy gang wants to broadcast his death. Syd escapes, realises that Vole & Tesser infected Hannah to harvest their own virus, and joins the firm, which now grows her cells in a grotesque 'cell garden' and sells the viruses injected into them. Brandon Cronenberg's satire imagines biotechnology at the service of celebrity worship. Clinics harvest pathogens from stars and modify them before resale, adding a 'copy protection' that keeps them from spreading; a rival company engineers and patents a modified strain, deliberately infects the star with it so that it can sell her disease, and finally grows her cells into a deformed living 'cell garden' that serves as a factory for new viruses. Butchers sell meat cultured from celebrities' cells. The practitioners are corporations and their employees, presented as cold, mercenary businesses that turn bodies into products, and the protagonist ends by joining them. Like the film's grotesque body horror, the biotechnology serves to criticise consumer culture rather than to portray science. Copy-protected viruses are invented, though modifying viruses and culturing human cells and tissues are real techniques.

title: Cloud Atlas
themes: cloning genetic engineering religion post apocalyptic
text: The film interweaves six stories set in different eras, with the same actors playing different roles in each, suggesting souls connected across time. In 1849, an American lawyer befriends an escaped Moriori slave and becomes an abolitionist; in 1936, a young composer writes the "Cloud Atlas Sextet" for an ageing master; in 1973, a journalist uncovers a conspiracy at a nuclear power plant; in 2012, an elderly publisher is trapped in a nursing home. In Neo Seoul in 2144, Sonmi-451 is a "fabricant", a cloned human bred to work as a fast-food server. Rescued by a rebel, she learns that fabricants are recycled into the food that keeps the others docile, broadcasts the truth and is executed. In 2321, after a collapse of civilisation, the tribesmen of Hawaii worship Sonmi as a goddess, and a goatherd guides a woman from a technologically advanced people to a communication station. Genetics appears in only one of the film's six stories, but it is the one at its centre. In twenty-second-century Neo Seoul, fabricants are humanoid clones produced as an indentured workforce, and Sonmi-451 discovers that they are eventually recycled into the food that keeps the others docile. Sonmi-451's awakening and rebellion make her the founding figure of a later religion, and her story is the film's strongest statement against treating people as manufactured goods. The scientists and corporate leaders behind the system remain in the background; the film is concerned with the consequences of a society that classifies some humans as products. The fabricants are not a portrait of real cloning, which produces ordinary individuals rather than a servile caste; the story belongs to the tradition of dystopias in which manufactured people are treated as property.

title: Deranged
text: Bodies begin to appear in Seoul's Han River, killed by mutant parasitic horsehair worms, Yeongasi, which normally infect insects but now infect humans and control their brains, driving them to jump into water when the worms mature. Jae-hyuk, a former biochemistry professor turned pharmaceutical salesman, struggles to save his infected wife and children while his detective brother investigates. Ordinary anthelmintics prove deadly, and when one drug, Windazole, is said to cure the infection, supplies vanish and its maker, ChoA Pharmaceuticals, refuses to disclose its formula. The detective discovers that ChoA's former researchers had created the mutant parasite while studying brain control, and that after the company was sold, disgruntled researchers released it and hoarded the cure to manipulate the share price. The CEO is arrested, and Jae-hyuk realises that the active ingredient can be reproduced, so other companies quickly produce a cure. The epidemic is caused by an engineered parasite. A pharmaceutical research team created a mutant horsehair worm able to infect mammals in order to study how it controls its host's brain, hoping to find treatments for diseases such as Alzheimer's. After the company was taken over, researchers and the chief executive deliberately released the parasite and hoarded the only cure to profit from the stock market. The film is above all a critique of corporate greed: a legitimate research project becomes a weapon in the hands of people driven by money, while the hero, a biochemist, saves the day by recognising that the drug can be copied. Real horsehair worms do drive their insect hosts into water, but they cannot infect humans, and engineering one that could is pure fiction.

title: Errors of the Human Body
themes: genetic engineering genetic disease animal experimentation human experimentation regeneration
text: Geoff Burton, a geneticist known for identifying the rare genetic condition that killed his infant son, takes a post at a research institute in Dresden. There he meets again Rebekka Fiedler, a former colleague and lover, who is working on what she calls the "Easter gene", which allows cells to regenerate and which a colleague realises could speed natural regeneration in axolotls. Burton discovers that another researcher, Jarek Novak, has stolen samples from Rebekka's laboratory and is injecting the gene into mice in a secret lab. Burton takes one of Jarek's mice, finds that it can regenerate, and is bitten by it. He becomes infected, gains an extraordinary ability to heal, but then learns that the treated mice are developing tumours, and that he may face the same disease that killed his son. Haunted by his grief, he tries to find redemption as his condition worsens; the film ends on an unexpectedly hopeful note. Genetics and laboratory life are the subject of the film. It deals with gene transfer between species, the mouse lines used to test it, and the fine line between regeneration and uncontrolled growth: the gene that lets cells regrow also produces tumours. Its scientists are ordinary researchers rather than villains: Burton is driven by grief and guilt, Rebekka by her research, and Jarek by ambition, stealing a colleague's work and experimenting in secret; reviewers note its attention to disputed credit, plagiarism and unethical experimentation. Director Eron Sheean developed the project during several years as artist in residence at the Max Planck Institute of Molecular Cell Biology and Genetics in Dresden, where it was filmed in real laboratories with scientists among the extras and as advisers. He described it as fiction using real science as a starting point, and The Scientist reviewed it as more science drama than science fiction.

title: Evangelion: 3.0 You Can (Not) Redo
alt: ヱヴァンゲリヲン新劇場版:Q
themes: cloning evolution human experimentation post apocalyptic
text: Fourteen years after the Near Third Impact, Shinji Ikari is recovered from orbit inside Evangelion Unit-01 by WILLE, the anti-NERV organisation led by Misato Katsuragi. He learns that his earlier awakening caused a global catastrophe, that the Eva pilots have not aged, and that WILLE has fitted him with an explosive collar to stop him piloting again. Feeling betrayed, he goes with Rei Ayanami to the ruins of NERV, where his father Gendo wants him to pilot the new Unit-13 with the boy Kaworu Nagisa. Shinji bonds with Kaworu, but Kozo Fuyutsuki reveals that his mother Yui is sealed inside Unit-01 and that Rei is one of a series of clones of Yui. Hoping to undo the catastrophe, Shinji and Kaworu take Unit-13 to the depths of NERV, but pulling out the spears there starts a Fourth Impact, halted only when Kaworu lets the collar kill him. Asuka drags the broken Shinji away across a red desert. Genetics is one strand of this dense mystical science-fiction film. Its most direct genetic element is cloning: Rei Ayanami turns out to be one of the "Ayanami Series", copies of Shinji's mother Yui made by NERV, which is why this Rei has no memory of Shinji and only follows orders; the revelation breaks him. Gendo Ikari's larger plan, shared in rival form with the shadowy SEELE, is to force humanity's evolution through a mass extinction and reunite with his wife, and the pilots are stuck in an unaging state the film calls the "Curse of Eva". Science in the film is a tool of secretive organisations that manipulate and use people, especially children. The cloning and the evolutionary "Impacts" are fantastical, entangled with angels and religious symbolism rather than real biology.

title: Goliad
text: Shaken by a recent brush with death, Princess Bubblegum tells Finn and Jake that she has used science and her own DNA to create Goliad, a giant pink sphinx meant to rule the Candy Kingdom forever after her. Exhausted after 83 hours of teaching her about leadership, she asks the boys to show Goliad the world. At a preschool, Goliad sees Jake shout down unruly children and concludes that ruling means forcing others to obey; she reveals a third eye with which she can control minds and declares that the world would be perfect if she controlled everyone. When Bubblegum thinks of dismantling her, Goliad reads her mind and begins destroying the castle. While Finn and Jake distract her, Bubblegum creates a second sphinx, Stormo, from a hair plucked from Finn. Stormo refuses to join Goliad and locks her in an endless psychic duel that keeps her in check, and Finn realizes that Stormo is like a son to him. This Adventure Time episode is a fable about creating life and shaping character. Princess Bubblegum, the kingdom's scientist-ruler, makes an immortal heir from her own DNA, intending to secure her people's future; Goliad, however, learns from the first example of authority she sees, Jake shouting at children, and turns into a would-be tyrant who believes the strongest should control the weak. Bubblegum's remedy is another creation, Stormo, grown from Finn's DNA, who, she explains, has inherited Finn's heroic qualities and therefore sacrifices himself to contain Goliad. The episode thus sets upbringing against inheritance: one creature is corrupted by what she observes, the other is good because of whose DNA he carries. Bubblegum is a well-meaning but overconfident creator whose experiment nearly backfires. Critics read the episode as a story about absolute control and free will; the claim that heroism passes through a single hair's DNA is a comic simplification of heredity.

title: John Dies at the End
text: David Wong tells a sceptical reporter how he and his friend John were drawn into a supernatural war. After a party, John takes Soy Sauce, a black drug sold by a dealer named Robert Marley that gives users inhuman knowledge and throws them across dimensions and time; David injects himself by accident. Most of the people at Marley's party die or disappear, John apparently dies during questioning by the police and keeps contacting David telepathically, and creatures that only drug users can see begin to attack. With their friend Amy and her dog Bark Lee, the two pass through a ghostly door to an alternate Earth ruled by Korrok, a monstrous biological supercomputer worshipped as a god, which wants to devour them to learn how to travel between worlds. Bark Lee destroys Korrok with a bomb given to them by the psychic Albert Marconi, and David and John become reluctant demon hunters. Genetics appears only in passing. In the alternate Earth that David and John visit, the history that diverged from ours includes genetic experiments and the creation of animal-human hybrids, shown in a joke image of the Wright brothers flying a hybrid flying pig, and the god-like Korrok is described as a biological supercomputer. These details colour the absurd alternate world but play no part in the plot, which is driven by a hallucinogenic drug and supernatural forces.

title: Maattrraan
text: Ramachandran, an Indian geneticist working for the Soviet Union, tries to create a person with many talents through "baby designing". The result is his sons Akhilan and Vimalan, conjoined twins sharing a single heart. After the Soviet collapse he returns to India and becomes a billionaire with Energion, a best-selling children's energy drink. The twins are drawn into a conspiracy when a Russian spy claims that Energion is adulterated and could kill thousands of children, and is then murdered. Vimalan is fatally attacked, and his heart is transplanted into Akhilan when the twins are separated. In the post-Soviet state of Ukvania, Akhilan discovers that Energion began as a steroid to boost athletes that left Soviet Olympians critically ill, a scandal covered up with a faked plane crash. He exposes his father, who ordered Vimalan's killing, and who admits that the twins are the product of his failed experiment, made from several talented people's DNA. Genetics frames the story through a scientist whose ambition turns criminal. Ramachandran's "baby designing" is an attempt to engineer a multitalented child by combining DNA from several gifted people; the result is conjoined twins, whom the film presents as the cost of his failed experiment. He first works for the Soviet state and later for himself, and his Energion business repeats the pattern on a national scale: an enhancement product that harms the children who drink it, which he describes as using the whole of society as his research laboratory, and which he protects by murder, including that of his own son. A review in Behindwoods notes that the film dwells on the adverse effects of genetic engineering "when man starts thinking himself to be God". The premise is fanciful: a person cannot be assembled from the DNA of several donors, and conjoined twins arise when a single fertilised egg fails to split completely, not from genetic design.

title: Prometheus
themes: engineered pathogens human experimentation evolution religion bioweapon
text: In the distant past, a humanoid alien drinks a black liquid on a lifeless planet; its body dissolves into a waterfall and its DNA breaks apart and recombines. In 2089, the archaeologists Elizabeth Shaw and Charlie Holloway find matching star maps in several ancient cultures and interpret them as an invitation from humanity's creators, the "Engineers". The dying billionaire Peter Weyland funds an expedition aboard the ship Prometheus to the moon LV-223, where the crew find an Engineer structure, dead Engineers whose DNA matches that of humans, and cylinders of black liquid. The android David secretly infects Holloway with it; Holloway sickens and is killed, and Shaw, previously infertile, finds herself pregnant with a creature she removes by surgery. The base proves to be a military installation for a biological weapon intended for Earth. A surviving Engineer kills Weyland and prepares to launch, but the crew sacrifice themselves to stop him, and Shaw leaves to find the Engineers' home world. Genetics frames the film's question about the origin of humanity. The opening shows an Engineer's DNA breaking down and recombining in water, implying that life on Earth, or at least humanity, was seeded with his genes, and the expedition later confirms that Engineer and human DNA match. The same creators have developed the black liquid, a mutagenic biological weapon that rewrites living organisms and that they apparently intended to use to destroy humanity. The scientists on board are archaeologists searching for meaning, while the expedition is driven by a corporate magnate who hopes the Engineers can save him from old age, and by an android who experiments on the crew without their consent. The idea that intelligent beings deliberately brought life to Earth, known as directed panspermia, was proposed by Francis Crick and Leslie Orgel in the early 1970s, but there is no evidence for it, and human DNA fits within the shared genetic ancestry of all life on Earth.

title: Resident Evil: Damnation
themes: engineered pathogens human enhancement mutants bioweapon
text: In this computer-animated Resident Evil film, US agent Leon S. Kennedy enters the Eastern Slav Republic, a former Soviet state at civil war, to investigate reports that bio-organic weapons are being used. Captured by rebels, he discovers that their elderly leader carries a dominant Las Plagas parasite that lets him control monstrous Lickers. When the leader succumbs to the parasite, the former teacher Buddy, who hates the government for bombing his school and killing his fiancée and pupils, takes a new parasite to command the creatures. The spy Ada Wong, posing as an agent of a bioterrorism alliance, is in the country to steal a Plaga sample. President Svetlana Belikova, who produces the parasites in a bunker and has supplied them to the rebels to justify crushing them, unleashes Tyrants against Leon and Buddy. A Russian-American intervention ends the war; Svetlana resigns, and Leon frees Buddy from the parasite by shooting his spine, leaving him paralysed. The film is about bio-organic weapons from the Resident Evil franchise used in a civil war. Its key element is the Las Plagas parasite: a human carrying a dominant Plaga can command creatures created with the Progenitor virus or the T-virus, such as Lickers, while people infected with subordinate Plagas become controllable Ganados. President Svetlana Belikova mass-produces the parasites in a bunker built in an old nuclear silo, carries an enhancing Plaga herself, supplies the weapons to the rebels so that their use will justify her crackdown and win her foreign support, and sends monstrous Tyrants into battle. For the rebels, the parasites are a desperate weapon that consumes their hosts, and the sympathetic Buddy is saved only at the cost of his legs. The film presents these biological weapons as tools of political manipulation, coveted by every side, including the unnamed employer of the spy Ada Wong. Parasites and viruses with such powers are fantasy.

title: Resident Evil: Retribution
themes: cloning engineered pathogens human enhancement pandemic bioweapon
text: After an Umbrella Corporation attack on the ship Arcadia, Alice is captured and wakes in a vast underwater facility in Kamchatka, a former Soviet naval base where Umbrella mass-produces clones and stages simulated outbreaks of the T-virus in replicas of Tokyo, New York, Moscow and suburban Raccoon City to demonstrate its effects to buyers. During a power failure arranged by her old enemy Albert Wesker, she escapes with his agent Ada Wong while a rescue team led by Leon Kennedy breaks in from outside. In the suburban simulation Alice finds Becky, the deaf daughter of one of her own clones, who takes her for her mother. They are pursued by Jill Valentine, brainwashed by Umbrella's computer, the Red Queen, and by clones of Alice's dead allies. Alice frees Jill and escapes with Becky. At the White House, Wesker restores Alice's powers with the T-virus before a final stand against the Red Queen's monsters. Cloning and bioengineering are part of the film's background rather than its subject. Umbrella, a pharmaceutical company turned biological weapons maker, manufactures clones of Alice and her allies to populate its outbreak simulations, and some of the clones have false memories and family lives, raising questions of identity: Alice becomes a mother to the daughter of one of her copies. The T-virus and the Las Plagas parasite are engineered pathogens that create zombies and superhuman soldiers. Scientists appear only as anonymous employees of a corporation that no longer has any ethical restraint and is controlled by an artificial intelligence. The film treats cloning as an industrial process that produces adult copies on demand, which is pure fantasy: a real clone develops from an embryo and does not inherit memories. Its relevance to genetics is limited; it is primarily an action film built around video-game settings.

title: The Amazing Spider-Man
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human enhancement human experimentation regeneration
text: Years after his scientist father Richard disappeared, teenager Peter Parker finds his father's briefcase and learns that he worked with Dr. Curt Connors, an Oscorp scientist in the field of cross-species genetics. Sneaking into an Oscorp lab, Peter is bitten by a genetically modified spider and gains spider-like strength, agility and the ability to cling to walls. Connors, who has lost his right arm, is trying to regenerate limbs using lizard DNA, and Peter gives him a missing equation from his father's notes. After the murder of his Uncle Ben, Peter becomes Spider-Man. When Oscorp pushes for rushed human trials, Connors tests the serum on himself: his arm grows back, but he turns into a giant reptile, the Lizard, and plans to release a chemical agent that would turn the city's population into reptilian hybrids like himself. With help from Gwen Stacy, who creates an antidote, Peter stops him. Genetics is the origin of both hero and villain. Unlike the radioactive spider of the comics, Peter's powers come from a genetically engineered spider bred at Oscorp, and his father's work on cross-species genetics underlies the whole story. Dr. Curt Connors, the geneticist, is a sympathetic figure: he wants to use reptile DNA to help people like himself regrow lost limbs, and he initially resists his superior's demand to rush human trials, fearing harm to patients. The catastrophe comes from corporate pressure and from Connors's desperation to heal himself, after which he becomes a monster who wants to spread his transformation to everyone. Some vertebrates, including salamanders and some lizards that regrow their tails, can regenerate lost body parts, and researchers study the genetics of this ability for regenerative medicine. Transferring it with a serum, though, is fantasy, as is the instant and total transformation of an adult human body.

title: The Bourne Legacy
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering human experimentation
text: Six weeks after Jason Bourne's escape, the exposure of the CIA programmes Treadstone and Blackbriar leads Colonel Eric Byer, who oversees covert enhancement programmes, to shut down Operation Outcome and kill its agents and doctors. Outcome agent Aaron Cross, training in Alaska, survives a drone strike and fools his pursuers into thinking he is dead. At Sterisyn Morlanta, the pharmaceutical company behind Outcome, a researcher shoots his colleagues, leaving Dr. Marta Shearing as the only surviving scientist. Cross, running out of the pills ('chems') that sustain his enhancements, saves Shearing from assassins. She explains that a virus has already made his physical enhancements permanent, but he still needs pills for his mental ones. They fly to Manila, where Shearing infects him with the live virus at the company's lab. After he recovers, they escape the police and a 'Beta' super-soldier, LARX #3, through the city, and flee by boat. Genetic enhancement is at the heart of the plot. Operation Outcome, run for the US defence and intelligence apparatus with the pharmaceutical company Sterisyn Morlanta, creates super-agents whose physical and mental abilities are boosted by pills ('chems') and by a virus that makes the enhancements permanent; Cross depends on the blue pills to keep his raised intelligence. Dr. Marta Shearing, a scientist on the programme and the only one to survive its purge, becomes Cross's ally and uses the live virus to free him from the pills. The programme's overseers, led by Colonel Byer, treat agents and scientists as disposable and already have a next generation of super-soldiers. The film thus contrasts a sinister state enhancement programme with an individual scientist who turns the same technology to liberation. Viral vectors are real gene-therapy tools, but nothing like a single infection that raises intelligence exists.

title: The Other Son
alt: Le Fils de l'Autre El hijo del otro
text: On a night of bombing in Haifa, a Franco-Israeli woman and a Palestinian woman give birth to sons in the same maternity hospital, and in the confusion of moving the babies to shelters, the boys are switched. Eighteen years later, Joseph Silberg is about to start his Israeli military service when routine tests show that his blood type does not match his parents'; DNA testing confirms that he is not their biological son. The hospital's investigation reveals the switch, and the Silbergs learn that their biological son is Yacine Al Bezaaz, raised by a Palestinian family in the West Bank. The fathers, Alon and Saïd, resist the truth, while the mothers, Orith and Leïla, are more ready to get to know the sons they bore. As Joseph and Yacine become friends, both families are forced to rethink their beliefs, prejudices and sense of identity against the backdrop of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict. The genetic element is DNA identification: a routine blood test before military service, followed by DNA testing, reveals that Joseph is not the biological son of the family that raised him, and the hospital traces the switch. The film uses this revelation to ask what makes identity, family and nationality: biological origin or upbringing. The two young men, each born on one side of the Israeli–Palestinian divide and raised on the other, must reconcile the families and peoples they were born into with those that shaped them, and the film suggests that both bonds matter, while exposing the arbitrariness of the hostility between the communities. Genetic testing is presented as an accurate, neutral tool whose results unsettle religious and national certainties; no geneticist plays a role.

title: The Viral Factor
text: During a mission in Jordan to escort a scientist who has stolen a sample of smallpox virus, International Defense Commission agent Sean Wong betrays his team, killing agent Jon Man's girlfriend and leaving Jon with a bullet in his brain that will paralyse him within weeks. Sean escapes with the virus and plans, with the arms dealer Tyler, to turn it into a biological weapon and sell a vaccine to a corrupt pharmaceutical company. Jon learns that he has a long-lost brother, Man Yeung, a criminal in Malaysia who is working for the gang. Yeung forces Rachel Kan, a doctor at the Asian disease control centre, to steal a sample of another virus, and Sean has her combine it with smallpox. The brothers clash, then join forces when Sean injects the new virus into Yeung's daughter and holds the antidote. After chases and gunfights ending on a ship, Yeung kills Sean, and Jon's fate is left uncertain. The plot turns on a man-made bioweapon. The rogue agent Sean Wong steals smallpox virus and plans to mutate it into a biological weapon, unleash it and profit by selling a vaccine through a corrupt pharmaceutical company; to do so he forces Rachel Kan, a disease-control doctor, to combine smallpox with a second virus, the Carnot virus, under threat to her mother. He then infects a child with the new virus to blackmail the heroes. The scientists in the film are a thief who dies early and Rachel, a coerced victim; the villainy lies with the agent, the arms dealer and corrupt police, who treat the virus as a commodity. The film does not explain how the two viruses are combined; the engineering is a thriller device rather than a subject of the story.

title: Underworld: Awakening
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering human enhancement human experimentation eugenics
text: After the existence of vampires and Lycans is revealed, humans wage a campaign of extermination against both. Selene is captured and spends twelve years in cryogenic suspension at Antigen, a biotechnology company. Freed by a mysterious telepathic girl, she finds that the girl, Eve, is a vampire–Lycan hybrid and her daughter with Michael Corvin. Eve is hunted by Lycans, and a vampire coven that gives them refuge betrays her. Selene learns that Antigen, officially devoted to killing vampires, is run by Lycans posing as humans. Its director, Dr. Jacob Lane, wants Eve's DNA to perfect the Lycan race; his son Quint is already a genetically enhanced 'Super-Lycan' immune to silver. Selene and her allies storm Antigen, Selene kills Quint and Eve kills Lane, but Michael's cryogenic tank is found empty. Genetics drives the plot of this fourth Underworld film. Eve is a hybrid carrying the 'Corvinus strain', and the villain, Dr. Jacob Lane, is a Lycan posing as a human scientist who runs the biotechnology company Antigen. He keeps Selene and Michael in cryogenic storage as research subjects, has engineered his son into a near-invulnerable Super-Lycan, and wants Eve's DNA, or according to some sources her eggs or a forced pregnancy, to breed a perfected Lycan race. The film presents this as a sinister programme of human experimentation and racial improvement inside a corporation, a front that also misleads governments, and both Lane and his son are killed. Reviewers noted that the cloning and genetic experiments are invoked with little explanation. Its genetics is entirely fantasy: vampires and werewolves do not have genes for silver resistance.

title: Universal Soldier: Day of Reckoning
alt: Soldado Universal 4: El día del juicio final
text: John wakes from a months-long coma to learn that his wife and daughter were murdered in a home invasion, and FBI Agent Gorman tells him that the killer he remembers is Luc Deveraux, a former Universal Soldier (UniSol) who now leads a separatist group of rogue UniSols against the US government. Searching for answers, John meets a stripper, Sarah, who claims to have known him in a life he cannot remember, while he is hunted by Magnus, a cloned UniSol sent after him. John discovers that he has superhuman strength and that his severed fingers grow back. At a riverside cabin he finds an exact duplicate of himself, the man Sarah knew, and kills him. Deveraux's scientist, Dr. Su, reveals that John was synthetically created weeks earlier and that his family is an implanted memory. Driven mad, John kills Deveraux's followers and Deveraux himself, then kills Gorman and takes over the group, deploying a clone of Gorman to infiltrate the government. Cloning is used here as a technology for mass-producing soldiers. The government's UniSol programme produces clones of its soldiers, gives them implanted memories and conditions them to obey, and Deveraux's separatists need only stolen hardware to make clones of their own. The film's horror lies in the discovery that the hero's identity, family and grief were manufactured, and it treats a clone as a disposable copy that can be killed and replaced by another one. Scientists appear as technicians of this system: Dr. Su, a former programme scientist, now serves the rebels and offers to cut John's emotional ties surgically. The film does not explain its cloning in genetic terms, and its adult clones with implanted memories and regenerating bodies are pure science fiction. Its connection to genetics is limited to the general idea of copying human beings for use as weapons.

title: Age of Dinosaurs
text: In Los Angeles, the biotechnology company Genetisharp uses flesh-regeneration machines to create living dinosaurs and pterosaurs from strands of DNA. The creatures escape and spread through the city: a giant Ceratosaurus, raptor-like Carnotaurus, a Spinosaurus that climbs buildings and a Pteranodon. Gabe Jacobs, played by Treat Williams, is among those caught up in the chaos, which culminates in a final battle around the Hollywood Sign. The dinosaurs are finally destroyed when, drawn by a scent, they are lured into a collapsing building. The film was produced by The Asylum and directed by Joseph J. Lawson. The film uses genetics as the premise for a creature feature in the tradition of Jurassic Park. Genetisharp's technology turns ancient DNA into living animals almost instantly through "flesh regeneration", and the company is a familiar figure: a commercial biotech firm that shows off a spectacular product without adequate safeguards and loses control of it, with the city paying the price. No scientific detail is offered beyond this. In reality, recreating dinosaurs is not possible: DNA degrades over time, and the older and more degraded a sample is, the more fragmented its DNA, which is why even well-preserved woolly mammoth remains, only thousands of years old, yield little usable genetic material. Dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, far beyond the survival of DNA, and current de-extinction projects aim instead to edit the genomes of living relatives of recently extinct species.

title: Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.
themes: human enhancement human experimentation mutants heredity
text: Agent Phil Coulson, secretly brought back to life after his death in The Avengers by a S.H.I.E.L.D. project using alien Kree blood, assembles a small team of agents, among them the scientists Leo Fitz and Jemma Simmons and the hacker Skye, to investigate strange cases. They uncover Project Centipede, which creates super-soldiers by combining the Extremis substance with alien DNA, and discover that Hydra has infiltrated S.H.I.E.L.D. Coulson rebuilds the agency as its Director. Later seasons introduce the Inhumans, people whose latent hereditary powers are unlocked by Terrigen crystals; Skye learns she is the Inhuman Daisy Johnson and leads the Secret Warriors against the ancient Inhuman Hive. Subsequent arcs involve android Life Model Decoys and a virtual world, a dystopian future in 2091, the alien Chronicoms and time travel, ending in the team's victory over the Chronicoms. Over seven seasons the series returns repeatedly to biological enhancement. Coulson owes his life to a secret S.H.I.E.L.D. programme that resurrected him with alien blood; Hydra's Project Centipede injects people with Extremis and alien DNA to make super-soldiers, often with lethal results; and Hydra scientists experiment on captured Inhumans. The Inhuman storyline turns on heredity: powers lie dormant in certain bloodlines until Terrigen crystals trigger a metamorphosis, and the series uses the newly powered as a metaphor for prejudice and fear of the other. Against these misuses stand S.H.I.E.L.D.'s own scientists, above all the biochemist Jemma Simmons, who studies alien and Inhuman biology to heal and protect, so the series presents science as a double-edged sword. Its biology belongs to the Marvel universe: alien DNA cannot be injected to make soldiers, and no crystal activates hidden genes.

title: Boyz Crazy
text: Mabel and her friends Candy and Grenda want to see the boy band Sev'ral Timez, but the concert is sold out, so they sneak backstage. There they discover that the band members are clones kept in cages like animals by their owner, Ergman Zarazin, who scolds them for a poor performance and threatens to replace them with a new batch. The girls smuggle the boys out and hide them at the Mystery Shack, where Mabel, wanting to keep them for herself, pushes her friends aside; Zarazin comes looking for the band and ends up arrested after Soos removes his car's licence plate. Meanwhile Dipper, jealous that Wendy has given Robbie another chance after he sang her a song, discovers with Grunkle Stan that the song hides a hypnotic message, and Wendy breaks up with Robbie. Moved by a song the band writes for her, Mabel apologizes to her friends and the clones are set free in the woods. Cloning is the joke and the moral of the episode's main story. The boy band Sev'ral Timez is made up of clones owned by their manager, Ergman Zarazin, who keeps them caged and replaces any batch that performs badly with fresh copies. The episode never explains how the clones are made; cloning serves as a satire of the manufactured, interchangeable boy bands of the pop industry and of treating people as products. Zarazin is a cartoon villain who is arrested, and the clones are presented as sympathetic victims who are finally freed, although Mabel herself is tempted to keep them as her own possessions. Real clones would be ordinary individuals born as babies, not ready-made adult copies.

title: Dark Medicine
text: A group of college students break into an abandoned school to explore it. Once inside, they discover that the building is not completely abandoned, because of a eugenics programme that has gone horribly wrong. The only available source, a very short Wikipedia entry, gives no further details of the story; it says only that the film builds to a twist ending that one reviewer thought would surprise most viewers. Eugenics is the film's premise: the abandoned school that the students explore hides the remains, or the survivors, of a eugenics programme that 'has gone horribly wrong'. The only available source, a two-sentence plot summary in English Wikipedia, does not say who ran the programme, what it did or how the film presents it, so this summary cannot go further than noting that the programme serves as the source of horror in a low-budget teen horror film, now known as Dark Medicine and originally titled The Eugenist. Reviews quoted by Wikipedia were poor.

title: Decoding Annie Parker
themes: real science genetic disease heredity genetic testing
text: The film follows two parallel stories over several decades. In Toronto, Annie Parker loses her mother to breast cancer as a child, and later her father and her older sister, Joan, who dies of the same disease. Married young to Paul, an aspiring musician, Annie is diagnosed with breast cancer herself, undergoes surgery and chemotherapy, and becomes convinced that the cancer in her family cannot be chance. Her marriage breaks down when Paul has an affair with her friend. Meanwhile, at the University of California, Berkeley, the geneticist Mary-Claire King sets out to show that some breast and ovarian cancers are hereditary. Despite the doubts of many in her field, she collects families with many cases of the disease and in 1990 links a susceptibility gene, BRCA1, to a region of chromosome 17. Annie survives two further cancer diagnoses. The film dramatises a landmark in human genetics: the finding that some breast and ovarian cancers run in families because of inherited mutations in a single gene. Helen Hunt's Mary-Claire King is a wholly positive portrait of a geneticist, a persistent researcher whose work with affected families eventually benefits patients like Annie. The method shown, family studies and genetic linkage, matches the record: King's group reported in 1990 that early-onset familial breast cancer was linked to markers on chromosome 17. The gene itself was cloned in 1994 by a team at Myriad Genetics, after a race between laboratories. The real Annie Parker, diagnosed with breast cancer in 1980 and ovarian cancer in 1988, was offered testing after the gene's discovery and tested positive, which she saw as proof that her family's cancers were not bad luck. Testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations is now standard practice for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.

title: Delivery Man
text: David Wozniak, an amiable underachiever who drives deliveries for his family's butcher shop in New York, owes $80,000 to thugs, and his girlfriend Emma, a police officer, is pregnant. A lawyer for a fertility clinic informs him that the 693 sperm donations he made as a student, under the alias 'Starbuck', have produced 533 children, 142 of whom are suing to learn his identity.
