In Tomorrowland, they discover that its governor, David Nix, has been broadcasting visions of catastrophe to Earth that have become a self-fulfilling prophecy. Athena sacrifices herself to destroy the machine, and Casey and Frank send new recruiters out into the world.

title: World of Tomorrow
text: In this animated short film by Don Hertzfeldt, a little girl, Emily, is contacted by a third-generation clone of herself from 227 years in the future, made as a way of achieving immortality. The clone takes Emily to her own time and shows her the ways people have tried to escape death and loneliness through technology, then guides her through memories of her life on the "Outernet". As a child, the clone visited a brainless male clone, "David", kept as an art exhibit until his death. She later worked on the Moon and in space, opened a gallery of memories harvested from the dead, and married a fourth-generation clone of David, whose sudden death left her grieving. Finally she reveals that Earth will be destroyed by a meteor within sixty days and that she contacted Emily to recover a forgotten memory of walking with her mother. She sends Emily home with advice to live well, and Emily goes out to play. Cloning is part of the film's premise. In its future, cloning is used as a means of achieving immortality, and the clone narrator describes her life as one in a series of copies of the original Emily. The film uses cloning to reflect on memory, loss and what makes a life one's own: each clone inherits memories but grows more remote from the original, and a brainless clone is displayed as an art object. No scientists appear, and the technology is described in deadpan, absurd terms rather than explained. Real cloning produces a genetic copy, not a continuation of the original's mind; the film's transfer of memories between clones is pure fantasy. The short won the Grand Jury Prize for short film at Sundance in 2015 and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film; two sequels followed in 2017 and 2020.

title: Zoo
themes: gmo mutants evolution genetic engineering hybrids chimeras
text: Animals around the world begin attacking humans in increasingly coordinated ways. Zoologist Jackson Oz, whose late father Robert had predicted an uprising of the animals, investigates with his friend Abraham Kenyatta, a Kenyan safari guide, the Los Angeles journalist Jamie Campbell, the veterinary pathologist Mitch Morgan and the French intelligence analyst Chloe Tousignant. They discover that the biotechnology company Reiden Global uses a "mother cell", a vector molecule present in its drugs, herbicides and animal feed, which has triggered a mutation in animals. Over three seasons the team develops a cure, sees it fail when the mutation evolves, and competes with a military plan to exterminate the animals, the Noah Objective. They learn that Robert Oz is alive and that a group called the Shepherds caused and tried to control the mutation. The final cure saves the world but leaves humanity sterile; ten years later, hybrid creatures have spread, and the team searches for a cure for human sterility. Genetics drives the series from start to finish. A biotechnology corporation's proprietary "mother cell", used in medicines, herbicides and feed, causes a mutation that accelerates animal evolution; the series speaks of a mutated "ghost gene", and the protagonist Jackson Oz turns out to carry it too. The search for a cure involves stem cells, gene delivery through mosquitoes or birds, and the risk that a fix applied to the whole biosphere has unintended effects: the final cure sterilises the human race. Later, hybrid creatures spread across the world. Scientists appear on all sides: the corporation, which hides its responsibility and is protected by the government; a secret group, the Shepherds, who both caused and tried to control the crisis; and the protagonists, a zoologist and a veterinary pathologist working against the clock. The series is an adaptation of a James Patterson novel and makes no attempt at realism; no single molecule could accelerate evolution in this way.

title: Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice
alt: Batman v. Superman: El amanecer de la Justicia
text: Eighteen months after Superman's destructive battle with General Zod in Metropolis, he has become a controversial figure. Bruce Wayne, who has fought crime in Gotham as Batman for twenty years, sees him as a threat to humanity, while Clark Kent condemns Batman's brutality. The industrialist Lex Luthor seeks permission to import kryptonite as a deterrent and, through a senator's subordinate, gains access to Zod's corpse and the Kryptonian scout ship. Luthor bombs a congressional hearing on Superman, steers Batman's paranoia and kidnaps Superman's adoptive mother, Martha, to force him to fight Batman. Batman defeats Superman with kryptonite but spares him on learning that their mothers share a name, and rescues Martha. Luthor then unleashes a monster engineered from Zod's DNA and his own. Batman, Superman and Wonder Woman fight it; Superman kills it with a kryptonite spear but is mortally wounded. After Superman's funeral, Bruce and Diana plan to gather a team of metahumans. Genetics plays a limited but decisive role, in the final act. Lex Luthor, a technology magnate obsessed with destroying Superman, uses the Kryptonian ship and General Zod's body to create a monster genetically engineered from Zod's DNA combined with his own; the creature, which Luthor calls Superman's "doomsday", ends up killing Superman. Luthor is the archetype of the corporate scientist-villain: brilliant, unaccountable and willing to use alien biology as a weapon, having manipulated government officials to obtain it. The film raises the question of how humanity should respond to beings more powerful than itself, and Luthor's creature is his answer, an engineered weapon that cannot be controlled. Genetics is used as a superhero device and the film makes no attempt at plausibility: no technology can combine the genomes of two individuals, let alone of different species, into a functioning adult creature. The creature corresponds to Doomsday, a character from the comics, although it is not named on screen.

title: Founder's Mutation
text: At the headquarters of Nugenics Technology, the researcher Dr. Sanjay, tormented by a high-pitched noise in his head, deletes data and kills himself, after writing "founder's mutation" on his hand. Mulder and Scully learn that Sanjay was worried that his "kids" were dying and find photographs of severely deformed children in his apartment. The company's owner, Dr. Augustus Goldman, known as "the Founder", runs a hospital facility for children with genetic conditions, where a patient makes objects move on their own. A pregnant woman who told the agents her baby was abnormal is killed and her fetus disappears. Goldman's wife, confined in an asylum, says he experimented on her during pregnancy and that she cut her baby out of her womb after it began communicating with her telepathically. The agents trace the source of the noise to a young janitor at Nugenics, Kyle, who wants to meet his sister. Taken to Goldman's lab, Kyle finds his real sister, Molly, and together they kill Goldman and escape. The episode centres on a genetics company and on human experimentation. Goldman presents his work as research on children with real genetic disorders such as Proteus syndrome, Crouzon syndrome, ichthyosis and Marfan syndrome, but the investigation reveals that he has been experimenting on pregnant women, including his own wife, producing children with telekinetic and telepathic powers whom he keeps in his facility. Mulder and Scully suspect a connection to the alien-human hybrid programme of the series' mythology, and the episode links the story to their own son, William. Goldman is the classic unethical scientist: protected by Defense Department ties, he treats his own children and his patients as subjects, and is killed by them. Real genetic conditions are mentioned accurately as conditions that cause physical differences, but the powers attributed to Goldman's subjects are fictional. The episode raises concerns about research on pregnant women and children without consent.

title: Grimsby
text: Nobby Butcher, a beer-loving football hooligan from Grimsby with eleven children, has not seen his younger brother Sebastian for 28 years; Sebastian is now a top MI6 agent. At a 'WorldCure' charity event hosted by the philanthropist Rhonda George, Nobby's surprise embrace makes Sebastian miss an assassin and shoot a boy with AIDS, whose blood splashes into Daniel Radcliffe's mouth. Branded a rogue agent and hunted by MI6, the brothers follow the trail of the hitman Pavel Lukashenko to South Africa, where they learn that he has bought a virus, and survive a series of grotesque escapades, including hiding inside an elephant during mating. A flashback reveals that Nobby ran away as a child so that Sebastian could be adopted. At the football cup final in Chile, they discover that Rhonda herself plans to release the virus over the stadium with fireworks. The brothers sit on the fireworks and absorb the blasts; they survive because, it turns out, elephant semen is the antidote. Genetics enters this spy comedy only through a bioweapon. The villain, philanthropist Rhonda George, has bought a lethal virus, named 'WorldCure' after her charity, and plans to release it with fireworks over a packed football stadium; the German Wikipedia says her aim is to reduce overpopulation. The film never says where the virus came from or how it was made, and it treats it as a plot device for slapstick: the heroes stop the release by sitting on the fireworks and survive because, absurdly, the elephant semen they were drenched in earlier is the antidote. The real-world disease in the film, HIV, is used for shock jokes about blood splashing into celebrities' mouths. The scheme follows the familiar thriller trope of an elite villain who wants to cull humanity with a pathogen; neither the virus nor its antidote is meant to be taken as science.

title: Hardcore Henry
text: Told entirely from its hero's point of view, the film opens as Henry wakes mute and amnesiac in a laboratory on an airship, where the scientist Estelle, who says she is his wife, fits him with cybernetic limbs. Mercenaries led by the psychokinetic Akan raid the lab, and Henry and Estelle escape to Moscow, where she is abducted. Henry is guided by Jimmy, who keeps dying and reappearing in different guises, through a series of fights to find a power pump for his limbs and to rescue Estelle. Jimmy turns out to be a paralysed scientist, crippled by Akan, who controls a set of clones of himself through a headset. At Akan's headquarters Henry faces an army of cyborg super-soldiers given his memories and learns that Estelle is Akan's wife: his ordeal was a test of soldiers who will do anything to save their "wives". Henry kills Akan and Estelle. Genetics appears only through cloning. Jimmy, a quadriplegic scientist who once worked for the villain, operates a series of clones of himself, each built around a different side of his personality, by remote headset; they guide and help Henry, and several are killed along the way. The film never explores how they were made, and its real science-fiction subject is cybernetics and memory manipulation: Henry's prosthetic body and the army of cyborg soldiers programmed with his memories. The clones are a device that lets one actor play many comic variations of the same helper.

title: Inferno
text: In the third film based on Dan Brown's Robert Langdon novels, the billionaire Bertrand Zobrist, convinced that overpopulation will destroy humanity, creates a plague virus, Inferno, to kill half the world's population, and kills himself in Florence while fleeing armed agents. Langdon, a Harvard symbologist, wakes in a Florence hospital with amnesia and a head wound; the doctor Sienna Brooks helps him escape an assassin. In his pocket is a projector showing a modified version of Botticelli's Map of Hell, a clue left by Zobrist. Pursued by the private security firm working for Zobrist and by World Health Organization agents led by his former lover Elizabeth Sinskey, Langdon follows Dante-related clues through Florence and Venice to Istanbul. Sienna turns out to be Zobrist's lover, determined to release the virus, and the WHO's Christoph Bouchard wants to sell it. In the Basilica Cistern, Sienna detonates a charge to release the virus, but Sinskey has sealed it in a containment unit; Sienna is killed and the virus is secured. The MacGuffin is a man-made plague. Bertrand Zobrist, a transhumanist billionaire and genius who believes that only drastic measures can stop overpopulation from ending humanity, has created a virus, Inferno, designed to kill half of the world's population, and hidden it to be released after his death. The film presents him as an unstable fanatic with an apocalyptic vision, and his plan is carried on by his lover, the doctor Sienna Brooks, and his followers. The virus also attracts people who see it as a commodity: the WHO official Christoph Bouchard secretly wants to sell it. Against them, the head of the World Health Organization, Elizabeth Sinskey, works to contain the weapon and succeeds. The film thus treats the deliberate creation of a pandemic as an act of ideological terrorism, framed by debates on overpopulation and transhumanism. Unlike the novel, in which Zobrist's virus sterilises a third of humanity, the film's weapon is a killer plague.

title: Kamen Rider Amazons
alt: 仮面ライダーアマゾンズ
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras engineered pathogens human experimentation heredity bioweapon regeneration
text: In a world apart from the main Kamen Rider continuity, the pharmaceutical company Nozama Pharmacy has secretly created 'Amazons', artificial life forms built on Amazon Cells, and an accident has let some 4,000 experimental Amazons escape. Haruka Mizusawa, a shy young man raised by Reika Mizusawa, Nozama's head of research, stops his daily injections and transforms into Amazon Omega; he learns that he is an Amazon made from her genes. He joins the company's hunting team alongside Jin Takayama, the former Nozama cell biologist who turned himself into Amazon Alpha to destroy the creatures he helped create, but rejects the company's plan to exterminate all Amazons and leads a group of peaceful ones to safety. Five years later, a new strain of Amazon Cells starts turning ordinary people into Amazons, and the secret government unit 4C hunts them. Its focus is Chihiro, Jin's son, who struggles against cannibalistic urges. A concluding film reveals a sanctuary that farms Amazons. This dark reboot of Kamen Rider is built on biotechnology gone wrong. Nozama Pharmacy's research division created Amazon Cells, artificial cells that give their hosts regenerative power and monstrous, man-eating forms; its head, Reika Mizusawa, made Haruka by transplanting her own genes into Amazon Cells, and after the experimental Amazons escaped she ordered their extermination. Another executive revives a corpse as a controllable Amazon to sell them as biological weapons. A new strain of cells then spreads among humans like an infection, while a secret government unit kills the infected and DNA tests identify Chihiro as the strain's 'original'. The scientist Jin Takayama, who turned himself into an Amazon to hunt his creations out of guilt, embodies the series' central question: whether a being is defined by its biology or by its choices. The corporation and its executives are villains who treat both humans and Amazons as disposable; the Amazons themselves are portrayed with sympathy. Amazon Cells are fiction.

title: Legends of Tomorrow
text: This Arrowverse series follows a team of misfit heroes and former villains who travel through time aboard the ship Waverider. In the first season, the rogue Time Master Rip Hunter recruits them to stop the immortal tyrant Vandal Savage; Sara Lance, the White Canary, later becomes captain. Over seven seasons the Legends repair aberrations in the timeline and fight the Legion of Doom, the demons Mallus and Neron, magical fugitives. Ava Sharpe, director of the Time Bureau and later Sara's wife, is revealed to be a clone from the year 2213. In the sixth season, Sara is abducted by aliens working for a scientist, Bishop, who made clones of Ava and plans to create the perfect warrior by combining Sara's DNA and memories with those of aliens; the Legends defeat him. In the seventh season, stranded in 1925, they face robot clones built by the ship's artificial intelligence, Gideon, with Bishop's cloning technology. The series ends with the team arrested by the Time Police. Genetics appears in a few arcs of this long time-travel comedy. Ava Sharpe, a main character, learns that she is a clone produced in the 23rd century, a revelation the series treats as part of her personal story. In the sixth season, the villain Bishop, a scientist who has made clones of Ava, plans to create a perfect warrior by combining Sara Lance's DNA and memories with alien DNA, claiming that he has foreseen the end of humanity; he is defeated, and in the seventh season his cloning technology is used to build robot duplicates of the heroes. These elements are part of a broader mix of magic, aliens and time travel, and the series does not dwell on the science.

title: Maximum Ride
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human experimentation human enhancement
text: Based on James Patterson's novels, the film follows the Flock, six children with wings who can fly, created by experiments at the School, a secret laboratory in Death Valley. Rescued years earlier by the scientist Jeb Batchelder, they live hidden in a house in the Rocky Mountains under the leadership of the oldest, Max. When the youngest, Angel, is captured by Erasers, wolf-hybrid enforcers led by Jeb's son Ari, Max and Fang set out to rescue her. Max is shot while saving a girl in Utah and, during surgery at a veterinary clinic, learns that she carries a tracking chip. The Erasers use the chips to capture the whole Flock, who wake up in cages at the School. Jeb tells Max she was created to save the world, but the children escape. Max declares the experiment over, and they set out for New York to learn about their origins. Genetic engineering creates the premise: the heroes are children altered in a secret, apparently government-run laboratory so that they have wings, and their enemies, the Erasers, are human–wolf hybrids. The film presents the School as a place of cruel experimentation, with children kept in cages, implanted with tracking chips and treated as expendable. Jeb, the scientist who made the Flock and also rescued them, is ambiguous: he insists they were created to help people and save the world, but they no longer trust him, and the story ends with Max declaring the experiment over. Reviewers complained that the film never explains what the experiments are, so the genetics remains a backdrop for a teen adventure. Adding functional wings to a human would require far more than a few genes and is beyond any real technology.

title: Men Against Fire
alt: La ciencia de matar Black Mirror, season 3, episode 5
text: Stripe is a soldier in a near-future army whose members carry a neural implant, MASS, that feeds them data through augmented reality. His squad hunts "roaches", pale, snarling humanoid creatures with sharp teeth. During a raid on a farmhouse, a roach points a small LED device at him, and afterwards his implant starts to malfunction. In an abandoned housing block he sees ordinary frightened people where his comrades see monsters, and he saves a woman, Catarina, and her son. She explains that the implant makes soldiers perceive her people as inhuman "roaches", and that they are victims of a genocide justified as genetic cleansing, while civilians, influenced by propaganda, see them as inferior. Hunter, Stripe's comrade, kills them both. The military psychologist Arquette reveals that Stripe agreed to the implant when he enlisted, and offers him a choice between prison and a memory wipe; Stripe, decorated, returns to a fantasy home that is in reality derelict. Genetics appears as the ideology behind a genocide. The military presents the extermination of a persecuted group as "genetic cleansing", a eugenic rationale, while the psychologist Arquette, who oversees the soldiers' implants, explains that the technology exists so that they can kill without hesitation. The episode's main subject is the technology that dehumanises the enemy so that soldiers can kill without remorse, but the justification it offers is explicitly hereditarian, and critics have repeatedly drawn parallels with Nazi Germany. Sophie Gilbert of The Atlantic wrote that the episode's depiction of eugenics links to prejudices still widespread, such as institutionalised racism, tribalism and fear of refugees. No genetic science is shown; the point is how claims about heredity can be used to justify the persecution of a minority.

title: Morgan
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement human experimentation
text: Lee Weathers, a risk-management consultant for the genetic engineering company SynSect, is sent to a remote research site to assess the L-9 project: Morgan, an artificial being made with synthetic DNA infused with nanotechnology. Only five years old, Morgan looks like a teenage girl and is more intelligent than her creators, but she has just stabbed one of the scientists in the eye. The team who raised her treat her as their child. When a psychologist provokes her during an evaluation, Morgan kills him, and Weathers decides she must be terminated. The scientists sedate Weathers and plan to escape with Morgan, but Morgan, believing they have betrayed her, kills most of them, including Dr. Cheng, whom she calls "mother". A recorded confession reveals that the scientists had tried to make her more human than earlier prototypes so she could surpass her design as a combat weapon. Weathers hunts Morgan down and drowns her. Company executives then reveal that Weathers herself is an earlier, emotionally limited prototype, L-4. Genetic engineering creates the title character, a "hybrid biological organism" built with synthetic DNA and nanotechnology to be smarter, faster and stronger than humans. The project belongs to a corporation that wants a controllable weapon, and its scientists, isolated at the site, are torn between seeing Morgan as a product and as their child. Their attempt to make her more human, with real emotions, makes her harder to control, and the experiment ends in a massacre. The final twist, that the company's cold consultant is herself an earlier engineered being, suggests that the corporation values obedience over humanity. Like many films about creations that turn on their creators, it raises questions about responsibility for engineered life rather than exploring the science in detail. Real synthetic biology is far more modest: in 2010 the J. Craig Venter Institute created a bacterial cell controlled by a chemically synthesised genome, and in 2016 a minimal cell with only 473 genes.

title: Officer Rimmer
text: The Starbug crew finds a Space Corps ship carrying nuclear material drifting into an asteroid storm. Rimmer fires a torpedo to destroy it before it can explode, but the torpedo ricochets off an asteroid and pushes the ship to safety, and its grateful bio-printed captain, Edwin Herring, promotes Rimmer to First Lieutenant before dematerializing. Rimmer decides to use the ship's bio-printer to make a crew of his own. The others find that Lister's DNA is on file and is being used in call centres, because he once sold a saliva sample, and they delete the crew's files, but Rimmer finds DNA from when he was alive and prints dozens of copies of himself, with an officers' lounge for their exclusive use. When Lister and Cat rebel against his new class system, Rimmer tries to print modified bodyguards, the printer jams and produces a grotesque fusion of several Rimmers that sets out to absorb the rest. Rimmer must resign his rank to get the crew's help before he destroys it. The episode is a comedy about a bio-printer, a machine that prints living people from DNA files. The Space Corps captain Herring is bio-printed, Lister finds that a DNA sample he once sold for cigarettes and money is being used to print workers for call centres, and Rimmer uses DNA from his own past to print dozens of copies of himself to serve as officers. When he tries to make modified bodyguards and jams the machine, it produces a monstrous fusion of Rimmers that tries to absorb the others. The genetic technology is played for laughs and serves as satire of Rimmer's vanity and love of rank, with a joke about the commercial use of people's DNA. Printing a complete adult from a DNA file is pure fantasy: DNA does not contain a person's memories or appearance at a given age.

title: Resident Evil: The Final Chapter
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic cloning genetic disease human experimentation bioweapon post apocalyptic
text: A flashback reveals the origin of the T-virus: Umbrella founder Dr. James Marcus used an untested virus created by his colleague Dr. Charles Ashford to treat his daughter Alicia's progeria, abandoned it when a treated child became a zombie, and was then murdered on the orders of his partner, Dr. Alexander Isaacs, who took over the company. In the present, after Albert Wesker's betrayal in Washington, the Red Queen AI tells Alice that Umbrella holds an airborne antivirus but will wait until the last humans die. Alice returns to Raccoon City, joins Claire Redfield and other survivors and enters the Hive, where she learns that Umbrella released the virus deliberately to cleanse the Earth, keeping its elite frozen to rebuild it, and that she is a clone of Alicia. The Isaacs she killed before was also a clone. Alice releases the antivirus, the Hive is destroyed, and Alicia's memories are uploaded into Alice. The final film of the series makes genetic science the root of its apocalypse. The T-virus began as an untested treatment: Umbrella's founder used it on his daughter, who suffered from the hereditary premature-ageing disease progeria, until it turned a child into a zombie. His partner, Dr. Isaacs, later released it on purpose in a religious-fanatic plan to wipe out humanity while Umbrella's elite slept in cryogenic storage. Cloning runs through the film: Isaacs keeps clones of himself, one of which finally kills him, and the heroine learns that she is a clone of Alicia Marcus. Umbrella also holds an airborne antivirus, which Alice releases to save the survivors. The scientists range from the tragic, desperate father to the genocidal corporate villain, but the overall picture is of corporate biotechnology as a catastrophe. Progeria is a real genetic disease, but no virus could treat it or raise the dead.

title: Terra Formars
themes: human enhancement hybrids chimeras human experimentation evolution
text: To prepare Mars for colonisation, humans seeded its surface with moss in the twenty-first century and released cockroaches to spread it. In 2599, a crew of misfits and criminals, promised pardons, is sent aboard the spaceship BUGS 2 to exterminate the cockroaches. On arrival they find that the insects have evolved into human-sized, intelligent, humanoid creatures of enormous strength. To fight them, the crew members inject themselves with DNA that gives them the abilities of different insects, from a bullet ant to an Asian giant hornet, a desert locust or a silk moth. One by one they are killed, while further doses make their transformations stronger, and a third dose becomes irreversible. The survivors discover that the mission director, Ko Honda, is communicating with the cockroaches and has his own plans. In the end, only two crew members escape Mars, while on Earth Honda kills a colleague who tries to shoot him. The film, Takashi Miike's adaptation of the manga by Yū Sasuga and Kenichi Tachibana, combines two ideas linked to genetics. First, the cockroaches released on Mars have evolved, in a few centuries, into giant humanoids, a story of accelerated evolution far beyond anything real natural selection could produce. Second, the crew are given injections of insect DNA that let them transform into human-insect hybrids with the abilities of particular species, all of them real insects whose traits, such as the bombardier beetle's chemical spray, are exaggerated for battle. The scientists and officials who planned the mission treat the crew, criminals and outcasts, as expendable test subjects, and the director turns out to have secret aims of his own. Scientifically the idea of gaining another species' traits by injection is fantasy: introducing genes into an adult would not reshape the body in seconds, and insect anatomy does not scale up to human size.

title: The Divergent Series: Allegiant
themes: eugenics genetic discrimination genetic engineering human experimentation post apocalyptic
text: The third film in the Divergent series. In a walled, post-apocalyptic Chicago, Tris Prior, Four and a few companions escape over the wall into the wasteland. They are rescued and taken to a hidden, technologically advanced city, the headquarters of the Bureau of Genetic Welfare. Its leader, David, explains that humanity's attempts to fix its problems through genetic tampering sparked the Purity Wars, and that the Bureau runs experiments in isolated cities, Chicago among them, to restore a genetically "pure" population. Tris is the first pure individual to emerge. While she works with David, Four discovers that the Bureau kidnaps children from the wasteland and erases their memories. When David tries to use amnesia gas to wipe the memories of Chicago's warring factions, Tris and Four stop the attack, and Tris broadcasts to the world that Chicago was an experiment in genetic purity. This is the film in the series where genetics becomes explicit. The whole society of Chicago turns out to be an experiment: the Bureau of Genetic Welfare believes that past genetic modification damaged human nature and is trying to breed people with a restored, "pure" genome, and Tris is its first fully "pure" result. People with damaged genes are treated as inferior, and Tris finally condemns the division between pure and damaged as no better than the factions. The geneticist-administrators of the Bureau are cold technocrats who justify manipulation, child abductions and memory erasure in the name of genetic welfare, and its leader, David, is the villain. The film thus links genetic engineering and eugenic attempts to correct it to a single critique of social control by genetic labels. The notion that traits such as courage or independent thinking can be "repaired" by restoring a pure genome has no basis in genetics.

title: The Escape
text: After the illegal human-cloning operations of the company Molecular Genetics are exposed and its geneticist, Dr. Nora Phillips, disappears, the FBI raids the facility. A ruthless mercenary, Holt, secures the one surviving "specimen", a young woman named Lily, to deliver her to an unnamed customer who has bought her. A hired driver is engaged to take them, with Holt riding along to make sure the delivery happens and to order him to evade the pursuing FBI. Disgusted by the way Holt treats Lily as an object, the driver overpowers him and throws him out of the car. Holt pursues them with a sniper rifle from a helicopter, but the driver outruns his men and leaves him stranded on the road, where the FBI arrests him. At the extraction point Lily tells the driver that Dr. Phillips made her and three other clones, who are gone; the customer turns out to be Dr. Phillips herself, who takes Lily into her care. This short action film is built around an illegal human-cloning operation. The company Molecular Genetics produced clones as saleable "specimens", and Lily, the last one, is handled by the mercenary escorting her as merchandise; the driver who sides with her is the film's moral centre. The geneticist who made her, Dr. Nora Phillips, turns out to be the buyer at the end and takes maternal custody of her, which reframes the creator as someone rescuing her creation rather than selling it, though the summary says nothing about her motives or about what happened to the other three clones. The only available source is a short plot summary, so the film's attitude to Phillips is uncertain. The science is not shown; cloning simply makes Lily a person treated as property.

title: The Osiris Child: Science Fiction Volume One
alt: Science Fiction Volume One: The Osiris Child
themes: human experimentation genetic engineering human enhancement
text: Kane Sommerville, a disgraced former pilot, works for EXOr, the leading terraforming corporation, on a space station above a colonised planet, while his eleven-year-old daughter Indi stays in the planet's capital, Osiris. When monsters break out of a high-security prison, Kane learns that EXOr's project leader, General Lynex, plans to cover up the disaster by destroying all life on the planet, civilians included, under the pretext of fighting a virus. He deserts, steals a glider to rescue Indi and is shot down. On the surface he teams up with Sy Lombrok, an escaped prisoner, and later with two eccentric former prison drivers, Gyp and Bill. The monsters are prisoners genetically modified in a secret EXOr project. Kane reaches Indi in the besieged city, but he, Gyp and Bill are killed; Indi and Sy, infected by a monster, reach a bunker seconds before an atomic blast. A year later the transformed Sy and Indi seize a transport to the space station. The film's monsters are the product of a secret corporate genetics programme. EXOr, a terraforming company, genetically modified prisoners to make them more robust for hard labour on colonised planets, and possibly to exterminate native life forms; after a prison revolt, the modified inmates break out as monsters. The company's response is even worse: General Lynex orders the destruction of the planet's population and blames a virus, and later the escaped prisoners. The genetic transformation is also contagious, as Sy is changed into a monster after being struck by one. The film presents EXOr's experiments and cover-up as the core of its critique of corporate greed and unethical experimentation; the modified creatures are victims as much as threats. Turning adult humans into new creatures by genetic modification is far beyond real science.

title: Train to Busan
text: A truck driver is waved through a disinfection checkpoint after a leak at a biochemical plant, and a deer he runs over comes back to life. In Seoul, Seok-woo, a cynical fund manager who has neglected his daughter Su-an, agrees to take her to her mother in Busan on the KTX train. An infected woman boards and turns into a zombie, and the infection sweeps through the carriages. Daejeon station has been overrun, and Seok-woo learns that his own firm indirectly caused the outbreak by backing a biotech plant with irregularities to protect its share price. Seok-woo, the working-class Sang-hwa and his pregnant wife Seong-kyeong, a baseball player and his girlfriend, elderly sisters and a homeless man fight through zombie-filled carriages, while the selfish executive Yon-suk sacrifices others to save himself. One by one the protectors die; Seok-woo, bitten, throws himself from the train. Seong-kyeong and Su-an reach the military cordon outside Busan, where Su-an's song convinces soldiers not to shoot. Genetics is not explicitly part of this zombie film, but its outbreak comes from a laboratory: a leak at a biochemical or biotech plant, waved away by a cleanup crew in the opening scene, and the hero's own investment firm turns out to have propped up that plant despite its irregularities to protect its stock value. By this database's criteria, the lab origin makes it a story of a man-made pathogen. The film does not show the scientists or explain the infection; its interest lies in social commentary, on selfishness, class and institutional failure, which Korean critics linked to the Sewol ferry disaster. The biotech industry appears only as the negligent, profit-protected source of the catastrophe.

title: Alien: Covenant
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras engineered pathogens human experimentation bioweapon
text: In 2104 the colony ship Covenant, carrying 2,000 colonists and 1,140 frozen embryos to the planet Origae-6, is damaged by a stellar shockwave that kills its captain. While making repairs, the crew picks up a human signal from an uncharted planet, and acting captain Oram decides to investigate despite the objections of Daniels, the dead captain's widow. On the surface, two crew members are infected by spores and give birth to deadly 'neomorphs'. The survivors are rescued by David, the android from the lost Prometheus expedition, who has wiped out the planet's native inhabitants with an alien pathogen and has been using it to engineer new creatures. He has dissected Elizabeth Shaw, tricks Oram into being infected by a facehugger, and fights his newer twin model, Walter. Daniels and the pilot Tennessee escape and kill the creatures, but the 'Walter' who puts Daniels into stasis is David, who now controls the ship and its colonists and embryos for his experiments. The film turns the Alien series' creature into the product of deliberate bioengineering. David, an android who despises both his human makers and the alien Engineers, released the Engineers' black pathogen on their planet, wiping out its inhabitants, and since then has used it, along with Elizabeth Shaw's body and later human hosts, to breed new creatures, ending with the facehugger and the praetomorph. He sees humanity as a dying species to be replaced by his creations, and the film frames him as a Satan- and Frankenstein-like creator; critics praised him as a frightening antagonist. The ending, with David in control of 2,000 sleeping colonists and 1,140 human embryos, makes the colonists the raw material for his next experiments. The pathogen that infects living creatures and creates aggressive hybrids is fantasy, but the film's theme, creation of life by a creature that despises its creators, echoes Frankenstein and Paradise Lost.

title: Blade Runner 2049
text: In 2049 Los Angeles, bioengineered humans called replicants are still used as slave labour. K, a replicant blade runner for the police, kills a rogue replicant and finds the remains of a female replicant who died in childbirth, proof that replicants can reproduce, which was thought impossible. His superior orders him to find and kill the child to prevent a war. At the Wallace Corporation, the replicant manufacturer, DNA archives identify the dead woman as Rachael, who had a relationship with the former blade runner Rick Deckard; Niander Wallace wants the secret of replicant reproduction to supply slave labour for colonising space. K finds records of two children born on the same day with identical DNA but different sexes, and comes to believe he is Rachael's son. He finds Deckard, but learns from the replicant resistance that the child was a girl. Realising that she is the memory designer Dr. Ana Stelline, K rescues Deckard from Wallace and takes him to meet his daughter before dying. Genetics underpins the film. Replicants are bioengineered humans made by a corporation, and the story turns on the discovery that two of them conceived a child naturally, which would end the line between manufactured and born beings. Niander Wallace, the industrialist who builds replicants, is a ruthless figure who wants to unlock replicant reproduction to breed slave labour on an industrial scale. DNA records are a key investigative tool: K searches DNA archives, and the birth records have been falsified so that two children appear to share identical DNA despite being of different sexes, a clue that something has been tampered with, since identical DNA would imply the same sex chromosomes. The film is less interested in the science of making replicants than in what it means to be born rather than made. As in the 1982 original, replicants are engineered as whole adults, which is beyond any real biotechnology.

title: Duel
text: This Korean crime thriller, broadcast on OCN in sixteen episodes, follows Jang Deuk-cheon, a hardened police detective whose eleven-year-old daughter, Soo-yeon, is kidnapped. His only clue is that two men with the same face were seen at the crime scene. Both turn out to be human clones played by the same actor: Lee Sung-joon, a gentle young man with amnesia who is accused of murder, and Lee Sung-hoon, a ruthless serial killer responsible for the kidnapping. Prosecutor Choi Jo-hye leads the search for the girl and draws Deuk-cheon into manipulating the case. Framed, Deuk-cheon and Sung-joon go on the run together and gradually bond while uncovering the mystery of the clones, their purpose and their connection to the detective. Human cloning is the premise of the series. Two clones who share the same genome are given opposite personalities, one kind and the other a killer, and the drama uses them to ask how far identity is determined by genes, a nature-versus-nurture theme often found in cloning stories. The kidnapping investigation gradually leads to the origin of the clones and to the people who created them, a mystery that drives the series. Reviewers singled out Yang Se-jong's double performance as the two clones. Because the available sources in English and Korean describe mainly the premise and characters, this summary does not cover the details of the cloning project or the ending. Real clones would be genetically identical but distinct individuals, like identical twins, and their personalities would depend on their different lives.

title: Genes
alt: Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, season 18, episode 13
text: A woman tells the Special Victims Unit that she has been raped, and when the detectives arrest her attacker he claims that he carries a 'rape gene' and cannot help himself because he was born that way. The case leads the team to a so-called support group of men who believe they carry the same gene and treat their assaults as destiny. A man who confesses to raping a bartender in her car offers to lead the police to a serial rapist they have been hunting in exchange for a lighter sentence; both men had described their assaults in the group's meetings. The genetic defence causes extreme tension in the squad room and with the district attorney's office, and it makes Lieutenant Olivia Benson think of her own father and of her son Noah's biological father, both rapists, and worry briefly whether Noah might follow in his footsteps. The episode puts genetic determinism on trial. The rapists invoke a 'rape gene' as an excuse, turning heredity into a defence strategy and a self-serving belief shared within their group. Benson's brief fear for her son, whose biological father was a rapist but who is being raised by her, brings the question of heredity against upbringing home. The episode gives weight to both, but on responsibility it is clear: it treats the gene claim as an excuse and the men as predators hiding behind biology. In reality there is no 'rape gene'. A 2015 study did find that sexual offending clusters in families, partly for genetic reasons, but its authors stressed that they had not found a gene for sexual offending and that offending was not inevitable for relatives; genes can raise the probability of such behaviour, while upbringing, treatment and choice remain decisive. The available sources do not describe how the case is resolved.

title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2
themes: heredity nature nurture hybrids chimeras genetic engineering
text: The Guardians of the Galaxy flee the Sovereign, a golden, genetically engineered people whose high priestess Ayesha they anger when Rocket steals valuable batteries. They are rescued by Ego, a godlike being who reveals that he is Peter Quill's father and takes Peter, Gamora and Drax to his planet, while Ayesha hires Yondu, the space pirate who raised Peter, to capture the others. Ego, a Celestial whose planet is an extension of himself, teaches Peter to use the powers he has inherited, then reveals his plan: he has planted seedlings on thousands of worlds to transform them into himself, which needs the power of two Celestials. He fathered countless children across the galaxy, killed all who lacked his power, and gave Peter's mother the tumour that killed her. The reunited Guardians destroy Ego, and Yondu dies saving Peter. Heredity drives the plot. Peter's half-Celestial inheritance is what makes him valuable to Ego, who has fathered children on many worlds, had them collected and killed every one who failed to inherit his powers: a lethal selection for a single inherited trait. The Sovereign, a genetically engineered people obsessed with physical and mental perfection, and Rocket, an engineered raccoon, add genetic engineering in the background. The film's real subject is fatherhood, and it favours nurture: Peter's biological father turns out to be a monster, while Yondu, the rough pirate who raised him and kept him from Ego, proves to be his true father. As the film magazine FilmInk put it, 'nurture has truly won out over nature'. Peter loses his inherited powers when Ego dies but keeps what Yondu taught him. The biology is pure fantasy: a human cannot have a child with a planet-sized being.

title: Inhumans
text: This Marvel series follows the royal family of the Inhumans, a people with superhuman abilities who live in secret in the city of Attilan on the Moon. Maximus, the brother of King Black Bolt, lost his chance at powers in the Inhuman transformation ritual and is looked down upon; he believes the Inhumans should return to Earth and leads a military coup. Black Bolt, whose voice is so destructive that he speaks only in sign language, escapes to Hawaii with Queen Medusa, the strategist Karnak, the guard leader Gorgon and the young Crystal, carried by Crystal's teleporting dog Lockjaw. Scattered on Earth, they struggle to adapt to human society and to regroup, while Maximus sends Inhumans after them. They also meet Louise, a human scientist obsessed with the Moon, and Evan Declan, a geneticist who has been testing Inhumans on Earth. The single season ends with the destruction of Attilan and the Inhumans settling on Earth as refugees. In the series, being Inhuman is a matter of inheritance: Inhumans carry a gene that, on exposure to Terrigen crystals in a rite called Terrigenesis, unlocks their genetic potential and gives each a unique power, from Black Bolt's destructive voice to Medusa's living hair. The society of Attilan is organised around this, with a Genetic Council, and those who fail to gain powers lose status; Maximus, who lost the Inhuman gene in his own Terrigenesis, says that he would have been sent to work in the mines had he not been the king's brother, a resentment that drives his coup. On Earth, a geneticist, Evan Declan, has been testing Inhumans, but the available sources do not describe his aims or what his work leads to. The showrunner wanted the powers to seem a natural part of each character's personality rather than a scientific product. A gene that confers powers only after contact with a crystal is fantasy.

title: Jurassic School
text: Twelve-year-old Tommy Harris competes for his school's Young Academic Palaeontologist prize, which offers the winner a project at Vista Tech labs under Dr. Reginald Reynolds. His project is to bring dinosaurs back by genetically editing bird eggs so they revert to their dinosaur ancestry, but his rival Ethan sabotages his presentation, wins the prize and makes Tommy his assistant, leaving him all the work. Tommy continues at home with a home-made device that drips liquid onto a large egg, and hatches a herbivorous dinosaur he calls Spike. He hides the fast-growing creature from his parents, comes to see him as a friend, and his sister Chloe discovers him and paints his claws. On the day of the competition Spike escapes, and Tommy must find him before greedy adults do: Dr. Reynolds wants to claim the dinosaur for himself, and government researchers are also after him. In the end Ethan switches sides to help Tommy. Genetics is the premise of this low-budget family mockbuster of Jurassic Park. Tommy, a schoolboy, brings a dinosaur back to life by genetically editing a bird egg so that it reverts to its dinosaur ancestry (French Wikipedia describes it as cloning), using a home-made device that looks as if it were made of Lego. The young scientist is the hero and the dinosaur becomes his friend; the adults with scientific power, the lab supervisor Dr. Reynolds and government researchers, are greedy antagonists who want to seize the creature. The review notes the 'handwave science' of a child succeeding where funded laboratories fail. Reverting birds towards ancestral dinosaur traits by editing developmental genes is a speculative idea discussed by some researchers, but nothing close to hatching a dinosaur has been achieved.

title: Logan
themes: genetic engineering cloning human experimentation mutants gmo
text: In 2029, no mutants have been born for 25 years. An aging Logan, slowly poisoned by his adamantium skeleton, works as a limousine driver near El Paso and, with the mutant Caliban, cares for Charles Xavier, whose dementia causes dangerous telepathic seizures. A former nurse, Gabriela, asks Logan to take a girl, Laura, to Eden, a supposed refuge near the Canadian border. Laura turns out to have powers like his own: she was created by the company Alkali-Transigen from his DNA, one of several children bred as weapons, whom the company planned to kill when it could not control them. Pursued by the company's Reavers and by its head, Dr. Zander Rice, Logan, Laura and Charles flee north. Rice unleashes X-24, a feral clone of Logan, who kills Charles. Logan finally reaches the escaped children and, mortally wounded, helps them cross the border. Laura shoots X-24 with an adamantium bullet, and Logan dies in her arms. Genetics drives the plot. Alkali-Transigen grows mutant children from stored mutant DNA, as weapons, and when they prove hard to control it plans to dispose of them; X-24 is a clone of Logan grown as the perfect soldier. The company's head, Dr. Zander Rice, has a personal grudge against Logan, who killed his father, and he reveals that the end of mutant births is no accident: the company has suppressed the mutant gene through genetically engineered crops distributed in the food supply. Scientists here are servants of a corporate-military project who treat children as products, while the nurses who help them escape provide the film's moral counterweight. Laura is Logan's genetic daughter, and the film explores whether biology makes them a family; his last words urge her not to become the weapon she was made to be. Using crops to silence a gene across a population is pure fiction, but the film's themes echo real fears about the commercial and military control of genetic technologies.

title: Okja
text: In 2007, Lucy Mirando, the new head of the Mirando Corporation, presents herself as an environmentalist and announces a "super pig" programme: 26 piglets are sent to farmers around the world, and ten years later the best specimen will be chosen. In 2017, Mija, a girl living in the South Korean mountains with her grandfather, has grown up with the super pig Okja, a huge, intelligent and affectionate animal. When the company's spokesman, the zoologist Johnny Wilcox, chooses Okja as the winner and takes her to New York, Mija sets out to rescue her. The Animal Liberation Front intercepts the transport and, without Mija's real consent, lets Okja be recaptured with a camera hidden on her, recording how she is forcibly bred and sampled for meat in a laboratory. After the footage is exposed at a public event, Okja is taken to a slaughterhouse, where Mija buys her life from Lucy's twin sister Nancy with a gold pig figurine and returns home with Okja and a rescued piglet. Okja is a satire of the meat industry built around a genetically modified animal. The Mirando Corporation presents its super pigs as a natural, environmentally friendly discovery, raised by traditional farmers around the world, but the animals are genetically modified, and the green marketing hides intensive breeding, painful experiments and industrial slaughter. The scientist figure is Dr. Johnny Wilcox, a zoologist who acts as the company's spokesman, and the company's leaders, the twin sisters Lucy and Nancy Mirando, are shown as cynical, focused on public image or on profit. The film does not reject genetic engineering as such, but asks what it means to create a sentient animal only as a product; Bong Joon Ho said the film was about capitalism, and he and producer Dooho Choi temporarily became vegans after visiting a slaughterhouse.

title: Orphan Black – 7 Genes
alt: オーファン・ブラック〜七つの遺伝子〜
text: This Japanese remake of the Canadian series Orphan Black, broadcast from December 2017 to January 2018, stars Kang Ji-young as Sara Aoyama, a broke and desperate single mother who witnesses the suicide of a woman who looks exactly like her, and other characters she encounters. In the original series, on which it is based, the heroine takes the dead woman's identity and discovers that she is one of many clones, women of different backgrounds born in the same year, created and secretly monitored by a powerful biotechnology organisation devoted to directing human evolution, and hunted by a religious group opposed to it; with her 'sisters' she investigates her origins. The sources available describe only the remake's premise and cast, not how its story develops or ends. Human cloning is the premise. As in the original Orphan Black, which the Japanese Wikipedia describes as a drama about genetic manipulation and human clones, the heroine discovers that she is one of a set of clones, and the remake's Japanese title refers to 'seven genes'. In the original series, the clones were created and secretly monitored by a biotechnology institute promoting 'Neolution', the deliberate acceleration of human evolution, while one clone, a biology graduate student, uses her science to help her sisters understand what was done to them; the story explores identity, bodily autonomy and the ethics of genetic engineering. The available sources do not describe how the remake handles these elements, so this summary rests on its premise only.

title: Resident Evil: Vendetta
text: In this computer-animated film based on the video game series, agent Chris Redfield of the Bioterrorism Security Assessment Alliance hunts Glenn Arias, a former CIA operative turned arms dealer who seeks revenge on the United States for a drone strike that killed his family at his wedding. In Chicago, Professor Rebecca Chambers is studying a new bioweapon, the Animality Virus, when Arias's associates release it in her lab; she develops a vaccine and links the virus to the Las Plagas parasite. With the help of the troubled agent Leon S. Kennedy, Chris tries to stop Arias's plan to spread the virus over New York. Arias kidnaps Rebecca, who resembles his dead wife, and infects her with a vaccine-resistant strain. The heroes stop the tankers spreading the virus, kill Arias and the Tyrant monster formed from his body, cure Rebecca and distribute the antidote across the city. The plot is driven by a man-made bioweapon, as usual in Resident Evil. The A-virus is a designed system: a base virus that can lie dormant in anyone, an airborne trigger that turns carriers into zombies loyal to their master, and a vaccine reserved for the villain's associates. Arias, a vengeful bioterrorist, uses it as a weapon of mass murder and a tool of control, and even creates a vaccine-resistant strain to infect Rebecca. Against him stands Rebecca Chambers, a sympathetic virologist whose research, vaccine and immune blood help the heroes contain the outbreak, so the film contrasts science used for terror with science used for protection. A virus that makes its victims obey one person, or merges two bodies into a monster, is pure fiction, although the film's idea of a dormant infection activated later has loose analogies in real viruses.

title: Teleios
text: In 2038 the Earth's atmosphere is polluted, and a mineral that could save it is being mined on Titan, a moon of Saturn. The mining ship Atromitos has been drifting with no news of its crew for two years, and the rescue ship Teleios is sent to investigate. Its crew is made up entirely of GCs, genetically engineered people who are physically superior to ordinary humans and keep their emotions under control. Aboard the Atromitos they find only one survivor, Travis O'Neill, who is traumatized and will speak only in quotations from classic books. As the psychologist Iris Duncan questions him, the crew begins to lose control: the mineral turns out to strip the GCs of their emotional restraint and drive them mad, and the story ends with the revelation of a killer android. Genetic engineering defines the crew. The Teleios is staffed by GCs, people genetically engineered to be physically stronger than ordinary humans and to keep their emotions under control, and the drama depends on that control breaking down when the crew is exposed to a mineral from Titan that drives them into madness. One reviewer saw in the film a story about social strata and the terrifying potential of gene tampering, while another found that it did little of interest with the GCs. No scientist appears and the engineering is never explained; it is part of the setting, but its failure under stress turns the crew into a danger to themselves. Emotional control cannot be engineered into people in any simple way, as many genes and the environment shape behaviour.

title: The Gifted
text: Set in the X-Men universe, this series follows Reed Strucker, a district attorney who prosecutes mutants, and his wife Caitlin, a nurse, who discover that their teenage children, Lauren and Andy, are mutants with powerful abilities. When the children's powers are exposed, the family is hunted by Sentinel Services, a government agency that detains mutants in harsh camps, and goes on the run. They join the Mutant Underground in Atlanta, a network modelled on the Underground Railroad, led by Thunderbird with Eclipse, Blink and Polaris, Magneto's daughter. Agent Jace Turner pursues them, torn between protecting society and violating mutant rights. After an attack at an Atlanta station, some members defect to the more radical Inner Circle of Reeva Payge. In the second season the Underground confronts both the Inner Circle and the Purifiers, a human supremacist movement that Turner eventually joins. Fox cancelled the series after two seasons. The series uses mutation as a metaphor for minority status. Its mutants are people with innate powers that may surface unexpectedly in adolescence, and Polaris struggles to accept her 'birthright' as Magneto's daughter; the story concerns how society treats them rather than the science behind them. A government agency hunts and detains mutants, a supremacist movement seeks to purge them, and radical mutants answer with violence, so the series explores persecution, surveillance and loss of rights, with explicit parallels to the Underground Railroad and Nazi Germany. The available sources describe no genetic research or engineering in any detail; a Sentinel Services researcher appears among the antagonists. Real mutations cannot give people superpowers, but the series' concern with discrimination based on inborn differences echoes real debates about genetic discrimination.

title: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks
text: Based on Rebecca Skloot's bestselling book, this HBO film follows Deborah Lacks, played by Oprah Winfrey, in search of the truth about her mother, Henrietta, who died of cervical cancer in 1951 when Deborah was a small child. Doctors at Johns Hopkins took cells from Henrietta's tumour without her knowledge, and they became HeLa, the first human cell line able to survive and multiply indefinitely, used ever since in medical research, including tests of the first polio vaccine. Her family learned this only decades later and was never compensated. The story is told largely from the point of view of journalist Rebecca Skloot, played by Rose Byrne, who wins Deborah's trust while researching the book. Together they try to extract information from an indifferent medical establishment, while Deborah struggles with her family's complicated history, its distrust of researchers, and her desire to know the mother she lost. Flashbacks show Henrietta's life and illness. The film concerns cell biology and research ethics rather than heredity in the narrow sense, but its story is central to modern genetics and biomedicine. HeLa cells, taken without consent in 1951 and cultured by George Gey, became the first immortalised human cell line and a basic tool of research, used to test the first polio vaccine and in countless other studies. Researchers are shown from the family's point of view: some are dismissive, and one in the film says the family "wouldn't have understood anyway"; the family had also given blood for research while believing they were being tested for cancer. The film raises questions of consent, race, class and profit in medical research. Genetic privacy became part of the real story after the events of the book: in 2013 researchers published the genome of HeLa cells without the family's knowledge, and after objections the US National Institutes of Health agreed to give the family a say in access to the data.

title: The Shadow Effect
text: Gabe Howarth, who runs a restaurant with his wife Brinn, suffers seizures triggered by certain music and wakes each day from vivid memories of assassinations: he kills a politician on a boat and blows himself up, pushes a man under a subway train, and is shot by his friend Sheriff Hodge, each time waking up at home. Refusing the drugs prescribed by Dr. Reese, he learns to resist the music and the orders given by a mysterious 'Man', discovers that Brinn is part of the scheme and confronts Reese. Reese reveals that after his wife died he built a programme to recreate people as clones, and that Gabe is a clone of a dead Special Forces soldier, made to be a perfect killing machine under the command of Hodge, the soldier's former commander; each clone recovers memories of the previous ones. Gabe kills Hodge and saves Brinn, but a new Gabe wakes to the music again. Human cloning is the twist behind this action thriller's loop of deaths and awakenings. The protagonist turns out to be one of a series of clones of a dead Special Forces soldier, created by Dr. Reese's cloning programme and controlled by a musical trigger to carry out political assassinations, after each of which he is killed and replaced; each new clone retains memories of the previous ones. Reese is said to have begun the programme after his wife's death, but it serves the handlers who use the clones as disposable weapons. Scientists and handlers are presented as antagonists, while the clone is a victim who struggles to win back his free will, and the ending suggests that the cycle continues. The film's cloning has nothing to do with the real technique: clones do not appear as adults, nor do they inherit memories.

title: Trench 11
text: In 1918, Lieutenant Berton, a Canadian tunneller who was once trapped underground for twelve days, is sent with British intelligence officers Major Jennings and Dr. Priest and an American escort to investigate Trench 11, a deep German bunker in the Argonne forest abandoned in the retreat and suspected of being a base for Reiner, a German specialist in chemical and biological weapons. They find German soldiers killed by their own side and, behind a sealed door, crazed men who attack them. Dr. Priest dissects one and finds him full of parasitic worms that he concludes have been engineered. German troops sent with Reiner and Captain Mueller to destroy the bunker capture the Allied team. Reiner reveals that the worms, meant to kill Allied livestock, jumped to humans, and he bred deadlier strains to destroy Europe; he tortures Priest to death. Mueller, disgusted, and Berton work together to blow up the bunker; Mueller stays behind to detonate it, Reiner dies in the collapse, and Berton escapes. The horror rests on a biological weapon of the First World War: parasitic worms engineered in a secret German bunker to kill livestock in Allied countries, which jumped species to humans and drive their hosts to insane violence. Reiner, the German officer in charge, was delighted by this and deliberately bred deadlier strains, intending to destroy Europe and rebuild it under German rule; the film presents him as a sadistic villain. Against him stand Dr. Priest, the British expert who identifies the worms as engineered and pleads for civilian lives, and the German Captain Mueller, who is disgusted by the project and sacrifices himself to destroy it. The film therefore condemns weaponised biology while showing decent people on both sides. Engineering parasites in this way was far beyond the science of the time.

title: USS Callister
text: Robert Daly, the brilliant but socially awkward co-founder and chief technical officer of the company that makes the virtual reality game Infinity, is ignored and belittled by his colleagues. In secret, he runs a modified version of the game based on his favourite TV show, Space Fleet, in which he is the heroic captain of the starship USS Callister and his crew are sentient digital clones of his co-workers, created from DNA he has collected from objects such as a discarded coffee cup. Inside the game, he humiliates and tortures them. When he clones the new programmer Nanette Cole, she refuses to submit and organises an escape: the crew blackmail the real Nanette into stealing the DNA samples from Daly's apartment, then steer the ship into a wormhole leading to the game's online update, hoping to be deleted. Instead they survive in the public version of the game, free, while Daly is trapped in his own build as it shuts down. DNA is the episode's plot device: Daly creates conscious digital copies of real people from genetic material taken from a coffee cup or a child's lollipop, and the copies retain their originals' memories and personalities. The episode uses this to ask whether such copies are people and what is owed to them, and to portray abuse of power: as long as Daly keeps the samples, he can recreate and punish his victims at will. Daly is not a geneticist but a programmer who misuses biological data, and his downfall comes when his creations turn his own tools against him. The premise is scientifically impossible, a point several critics raised: a genome contains no memories, and DNA alone cannot reproduce a person's mind; an early draft explained the memories with a recording implant, an idea Charlie Brooker dropped as too much detail.

title: War for the Planet of the Apes
alt: War of the Planet of the Apes
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic evolution post apocalyptic
text: Two years after the battle of San Francisco, a paramilitary unit, Alpha-Omega, hunts Caesar's apes with the help of enslaved apes. Its leader, the Colonel, raids the ape colony and kills Caesar's wife and elder son. While the tribe sets out for a distant oasis, Caesar goes after the Colonel with a few companions, adopting on the way a mute human girl whom they name Nova, and meeting Bad Ape, a talking chimpanzee who has lived alone. At the Colonel's mountain base Caesar finds his tribe enslaved and is captured himself. The Colonel explains that the virus has mutated and now robs humans of speech and intelligence; he killed his own infected son and orders carriers shot, which has brought the rest of the army against him. Infected through Nova's doll, the Colonel kills himself. As the army attacks, Caesar blows up a fuel tank, an avalanche buries both human forces, and the apes reach the oasis, where Caesar dies of his wounds. Genetics is the premise of the rebooted Planet of the Apes series rather than a subject of this film. The intelligent apes and the near-extinction of humanity both stem from the laboratory-made virus of the earlier films; here the virus has mutated and causes infected humans to lose speech and higher intelligence, a reversal in which humans regress while apes advance. The Colonel answers it with mass killing of carriers, including his own son, which sets him against the rest of the military, who believe a cure is possible; his fear of a humanity reduced to beasts drives his war on the apes. No scientist appears and no genetic work is done in the film. The virus behaves as plot logic rather than real virology.

title: Altered Carbon
text: Centuries in the future, people's minds are stored in 'cortical stacks' implanted in their necks and can be transferred to new bodies, or 'sleeves', when they die; only the ultra-rich 'Meths' can afford to live for ever, renewing themselves in clones with backups stored by satellite. In 2384, Takeshi Kovacs, the last surviving soldier of the Envoys, a rebel movement crushed 250 years earlier, is revived in the body of a police officer by Laurens Bancroft, a 300-year-old Meth, who wants him to find out who killed his previous body. Watched by Lieutenant Kristin Ortega, the dead officer's former lover, Kovacs investigates Bancroft's family, the city's brothels and the killers sent to stop him, while remembering his lost love Quellcrist Falconer, the Envoys' leader and inventor of the stacks. In the second season, in a new sleeve, Kovacs searches for Quell on Harlan's World. The series was cancelled after two seasons. Genetics plays a supporting role in this cyberpunk series, whose central technology is digital: minds stored in implanted stacks and moved between bodies. Cloning enters through the wealthy 'Meths', who keep series of clones of their own bodies at the company Psychasec, ready to receive their minds when the old body dies, which is how the murdered Laurens Bancroft returns to life at the start of the story. The clones are thus a privilege of the immortal elite, and the series uses them, together with the trade in bodies of the poor, to criticise extreme inequality. No geneticists appear, and the sources do not say how the clones are made or whether other bodies are engineered. Real cloning produces a genetically identical baby that grows up like anyone else, not a ready-made adult body.

title: Andover
text: Adam Slope, a genetics professor, marries Dawn, a free-spirited glass artist, and they take out large life insurance policies on each other. When Dawn dies in a fire at her studio, the grieving Adam uses hairs from her hairbrush to clone her in his lab, helped by his graduate student Emma. The clones are born as babies and age to adulthood within a few months, but none of them looks and behaves exactly like the original Dawn, and Adam kills each one that falls short, including one who falls in love with her high-school boyfriend. Emma, who loves Adam, secretly clones him. A suspicious insurance investigator uncovers the clones and tries to blackmail Adam, who poisons and clones him too. Finally Dawn's parents raise a clone as they raised their daughter; she becomes like the original but does not love Adam. Adam gives up, ends up with Emma, and the cloned Adam and Dawn fall in love and marry. Human cloning drives this romantic comedy, and the scientist is its protagonist: a genetics professor who uses his laboratory to bring back his dead wife. The film is largely about the limits of genetic determinism. Each clone of Dawn shares her genome but develops a different personality depending on who raises her and what she experiences, and only the clone brought up by Dawn's own parents comes close to the original, even then without her feelings for Adam. The film presents Adam's quest as an obsession that leads him to kill his "faulty" clones, while his student Emma regrets that he is not using his research to help others, though she too misuses cloning for personal ends. Accelerated growth from baby to adult within months is fiction, but the central idea, that a clone would be a separate person shaped by its own upbringing, is consistent with real biology.

title: Annihilation
text: Lena, a cell biology professor and former soldier, is interrogated about an expedition into "the Shimmer", an expanding zone around a lighthouse on the Florida coast, where a meteor struck three years earlier. Her husband Kane, a soldier, had returned home from an earlier expedition, gravely ill and confused. Lena joins a team of women led by the psychologist Dr. Ventress, with Josie, Cassie and Anya. Inside, they lose track of time, find hybrid plants and animals, an alligator with shark-like rows of teeth, and a video showing the fate of Kane's team. A mutated bear kills Cassie and later Anya, and Josie, who theorises that the Shimmer refracts all living things, including their DNA, lets herself turn into a plant-like figure. At the lighthouse, Lena learns that Kane killed himself and that his double returned in his place, and a copy of herself forms from her blood. She destroys it with a grenade, and the Shimmer vanishes. Biology, rather than genetics in a strict sense, is the core of the film, in which biology and physics merge in a strange world. Inside the Shimmer, an alien presence refracts living things "the way a prism refracts light", including their DNA, so that species mix: plants take human shapes, animals combine traits, a soldier's body becomes a colony of lichens, and a bear absorbs a dying woman's voice. Lena, a cell biologist, provides the scientific point of view, while Ventress, who has cancer, is drawn to the Shimmer as to a kind of transformation. Scientists are portrayed as curious and courageous professionals, each also driven by personal damage. The film is not intended as a plausible scenario: DNA from different organisms does not blend in this way. Its imagery of uncontrolled cell division and mutation invites comparison with cancer, a reading the film encourages through Ventress's illness.

title: Birthmarked
text: In 1977 two respected scientists, Ben and Catherine, leave their jobs to run a private experiment funded by a businessman, Gertz: they will raise three children against their genetic predispositions to prove that nurture beats nature. Their birth son Luke is steered towards art; Maya, adopted from parents with little schooling, is pushed to academic excellence; and Maurice, born to angry, aggressive parents, is raised as a pacifist who meditates daily. The children are homeschooled under the eye of Samsonov, a psychologist who reports to Gertz. Twelve years in, Gertz demands better results, the parents crack under the pressure, and the children try to escape by car, cause a highway pile-up and are taken into care. Gertz then reveals that he was experimenting on the parents all along and publishes a book about the project. In the end the family is reconciled. There is no laboratory genetics: the film is a comic satire of the nature versus nurture debate. Its premise is a home-made adoption and upbringing experiment in which each child is raised to contradict what its biological parents' traits are expected to predict: art for the scientists' own son, academic study for the daughter of poorly schooled parents, pacifism for the son of violent ones. The film gives weight to both sides and settles nothing. The experiment collapses, the children rebel, and as adults they follow their own paths (film director, animal-rights activist, lawyer) that neither confirm their heredity nor vindicate the plan; what the film mocks is the idea that either genes or upbringing can be engineered. The scientists are shown as well-meaning but obsessive, and their funder as a manipulator who was studying them. Real twin and adoption studies find that most human traits are shaped by both genes and environment, and rearing children as experimental subjects would be unethical.

title: Chimera Strain
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic disease cloning genetic engineering regeneration
text: Quint, a brilliant but unstable geneticist, works in secret in an abandoned research facility to save his children, Miles and Flora, who have a deadly degenerative genetic disease. He has frozen them in cryptobiosis and also keeps the comatose body of his estranged wife, Jessie, in the facility, while pills allow him to see his family in his mind. His research centres on the DNA of Turritopsis, the "immortal" jellyfish, which he hopes to combine with human DNA in a chimera able to regenerate. Because stem cell research is illegal, he depends on a ruthless backer, played by Kathleen Quinlan, who wants him to cure her own monstrous son. A former colleague and lover, Charlie, visits him and becomes involved in his work. In a final twist, she turns out to have come to steal his research, carrying an embryo out of the lab in her own body, and Quint is arrested for his experiments. The film was first shown at festivals as Chimera. Genetics is at the heart of the film, which follows a geneticist's obsessive attempt to cure his children's inherited disease by creating a human-jellyfish chimera with the jellyfish's capacity to regenerate. Quint is a sympathetic but morally compromised scientist driven by grief: he farms cloned animals and human embryos, works outside the law in a setting where stem cell research is banned, and depends on an unscrupulous financier. His downfall comes not from the science itself but from betrayal, as a colleague steals his work and leaves him to be jailed. Reviewers found the science sketchy, describing it as hints and pseudo-scientific doubletalk. The real Turritopsis dohrnii, known as the immortal jellyfish, is one of the few animals able to revert from its sexually mature stage to an immature polyp, and its life cycle is studied with genetic tools; but transferring such an ability to humans through a chimera is pure fiction. The film also loosely borrows the character names of Henry James's The Turn of the Screw.

title: Darling in the Franxx
alt: ダーリン・イン・ザ・フランキス
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering cloning human experimentation post apocalyptic
text: In a post-apocalyptic future, humanity lives in mobile fortress-cities called Plantations, threatened by giant monsters called Klaxosaurs and ruled by the organization APE and its god-like leader, Papa. Adults are immortal but can no longer reproduce, so APE artificially creates children, called 'parasites', and raises them to pilot giant mecha, the Franxx, in male-female pairs. Hiro, a failed pilot of Squad 13, teams up with Zero Two, a horned elite pilot with Klaxosaur blood whose earlier partners all died. Hiro learns that they met as children, when he helped her escape from the scientist Dr. Franxx, who created her by crossing human genes with those of the Klaxosaur Princess, and that APE's treatments shorten the pilots' lives. APE turns out to be controlled by the alien VIRM, who plan to destroy the Earth. Hiro and Zero Two defeat the VIRM fleet and die together, while the surviving parasites build a free life on Earth. Biological engineering underpins the series' dystopia.
