text: In thick fog, a massive pile-up traps drivers on Incheon's Airport Bridge, among them presidential aide Cha Jung-won and his daughter Kyung-min, tow-truck driver Joe Park, golfer Yoo-ra and her sister Mi-ran, an elderly couple and Dr. Yang, head researcher of a secret military programme, 'Project Silence'. The crash frees the project's experimental dogs, which were being transported in secret, and they attack the survivors while the damaged bridge threatens to collapse. Dr. Yang reveals that the dogs were first designed as rescue dogs that respond to human voices, but the South Korean military, backed by the US and European governments, turned them into attack dogs to hunt terrorists; they proved uncontrollable. Their founding animal, E9, became vicious after watching litters of her puppies vivisected, and she is hunting humans in revenge. The survivors escape before the bridge falls and expose the project to the press, while E9 and one puppy swim ashore. The monsters of this disaster thriller are genetically engineered dogs. The programme began with a benevolent aim, breeding dogs that react to human voices to find disaster victims, but the military, with foreign backing, redirected it to produce attack dogs for counter-terrorism. All the dogs descend genetically from one female, E9, whose aggression the film attributes to the trauma of seeing her puppies vivisected, so cruelty rather than genes alone makes her a killer. Dr. Yang, the head researcher, is an ambivalent figure: part of the project, she ends by exposing its crimes to the media. The film critiques the use of science and military power that treats living beings as tools. It gives no detail of the genetic methods, and its super-dogs are fantastical.

title: Relay
text: In New York, Ash is a fixer who brokers deals between corporations and would-be whistleblowers: they hand back incriminating documents in exchange for safety and money, while he keeps copies for protection. After closing such a deal for Hoffman, a former employee of the company Optimo, he takes on Sarah Grant, a research scientist at Cybo Sementis Research who says she stole a report proving the company covered up dangerous side effects of its genetically modified wheat, and now wants to return it to end a campaign of intimidation. Communicating only through a relay service for the deaf, Ash guides her across cities to evade a surveillance team led by Dawson and secures a payoff before a billion-dollar merger. When Sarah is apparently captured, Ash gives himself up, only to discover that Sarah is part of the team, sent by Optimo to recover Hoffman's documents from him. Ash escapes, the police arrest the team, and news breaks of Optimo's crimes. Genetics enters through the whistleblowing scientist's story: Sarah Grant presents herself as a researcher at Cybo Sementis Research who has proof that the company concealed dangerous side effects of its genetically modified wheat, and the threat that this report could derail a billion-dollar merger drives much of the plot. The twist, however, reveals that Sarah is an operative working for another company, Optimo, to recover documents held by Ash; the sources do not make clear whether the wheat cover-up is real within the story or part of the ruse. Either way, the film draws on the familiar image of agribusiness corporations hiding the risks of genetically modified crops and silencing employees, without any scientific detail; its real subject is corporate wrongdoing and the guilt of silence.

title: Saving Bikini Bottom: The Sandy Cheeks Movie
alt: Al rescate de Fondo de Bikini: La película de Arenita Mejillas
text: In this live-action and animated SpongeBob SquarePants film, the Bureau Of Official Texas Science (B.O.O.T.S.), the Texas laboratory where the squirrel scientist Sandy Cheeks works, scoops Bikini Bottom out of the ocean. Sandy and SpongeBob travel across Texas to rescue it, helped by Sandy's family of circus performers and chased by agents of the lab's new head, Sue Nahmee. At B.O.O.T.S., Sue imprisons Sandy and reveals that she is a cyborg who wants to genetically modify the people of Bikini Bottom to breathe air and clone them as toy pets, because she longs to cuddle fish; she also reveals that Sandy's life in Bikini Bottom was used to spy on its inhabitants. SpongeBob is split into thousands of tiny copies in a cloning chamber. Sandy escapes and defeats Sue, the copies are fused back together, and Bikini Bottom is returned to the sea. Genetic engineering and cloning are the villain's tools in this comedy. Sue Nahmee, head of a Texas science laboratory, plans to genetically modify the sea creatures of Bikini Bottom so that they can breathe air, then clone them and sell them as toy pets; Mr. Krabs, Squidward and Patrick are experimented on, and SpongeBob is split into thousands of miniature copies. The villain is a commercial schemer, and the heroine, Sandy, is also a scientist, so the film shows science used both well and badly, which one critic praised as an admirably nuanced view of science. Sandy's own heroics, though, rely on courage and family rather than on genetics. The science is deliberately cartoonish: cloning does not split an organism into tiny copies, and making a gilled animal breathe air would take far more than a genetic tweak.

title: Scared Shitless
text: Don, a plumber, has to team up with his son Sonny, who has a phobia of germs and dirt, to fight a bloodthirsty, many-tentacled monster that has got loose in the plumbing of an apartment building. The available sources describe only this premise of the Canadian horror comedy, and give no details of how the story develops or ends. The monster that the plumber and his son fight in the pipes of an apartment building is described as genetically engineered, a bloodthirsty, many-tentacled creature living in the sewage. Who made it, how and why is not stated in the sources, nor whether the film explains its origin or merely uses genetic engineering as a label. The tone is comic horror, with a monster that one critic found threatening but silly enough to let the audience enjoy the lunacy.

title: Shell
themes: genetic engineering human experimentation hybrids chimeras
text: Ageing actress Samantha Lake, struggling with ageism and body-shaming, is urged by a producer to try a rejuvenating treatment at Shell, a beauty company that uses genetic technology on celebrities. Encouraged by Chloe Benson, a young actress she once babysat, and by the gentle Dr. Hubert, she goes ahead and emerges looking younger. Her career and social life flourish, and Shell's CEO, Zoe Shannon, befriends her. Then moles appear, Chloe goes missing and Sam starts vomiting black bile on set. When Zoe tries to keep her quiet, Sam flees to Hubert, who has been fired; he treats her, but she finds Chloe locked in his house, turned into a feral creature. Hubert is murdered, and Sam is taken to Shell's headquarters, where lead scientist Dr. Brand explains the side effects. Chloe, now a giant lobster, kills Shell's staff and triggers a procedure that makes Zoe explode. Sam publishes a book denouncing Shell, which still thrives. Shell satirises the beauty and entertainment industries through a fictional genetic rejuvenation treatment. The company's procedure, developed by its lead scientist Dr. Brand and administered by Dr. Hubert, makes ageing clients look young again, but its side effects range from moles and shedding skin to vomiting and, eventually, transformation into monstrous crustaceans. The company, embodied by its glamorous CEO, Zoe Shannon, hides these effects, buys silence and has inconvenient people killed; Hubert, the scientist who reassures patients and later tries to treat them, is a more sympathetic but compromised figure. The genetics is a vehicle for body horror and for criticism of ageism and beauty standards, and critics compared the film to The Substance. In the bitter ending the company survives its exposure. No real genetic treatment can rejuvenate the body, although research on the genetics of ageing is an active field.

title: The Marching Band
alt: En fanfare Por todo lo alto
text: Thibaut Desormeaux, a celebrated orchestra conductor, collapses during a rehearsal and is diagnosed with acute leukaemia that requires a bone marrow transplant. Tests on his family show that he is not the biological child of his parents or the brother of his sister: he was adopted, and he has a younger biological brother, Jimmy Lecocq, also adopted, who works in a school canteen in a northern French town and plays trombone in the municipal marching band. The two have little in common except music. When the band loses its leader before a competition, Thibaut steps in and discovers that Jimmy has perfect pitch and exceptional talent, but a fight gets the band disqualified, Jimmy loses his job, and Thibaut wounds him by telling him he can never become a professional. The brothers reconcile even as Thibaut's treatment fails, and at his next concert Jimmy and the band surprise him by leading the audience in Ravel's Boléro. DNA testing sets the story in motion: when Thibaut needs a bone marrow donor, the tests on his family reveal that he was adopted and lead him to a biological brother. The film then becomes a story about nature and nurture. Born to the same mother, the two brothers share an exceptional musical gift, but one was raised in a comfortable family and became a world-famous conductor, while the other grew up in a working-class town and plays in an amateur band; the shared gift points to heredity, while the gap between their lives reflects upbringing and class, the "injustices of destiny" Thibaut tries to repair, as the Spanish Wikipedia puts it. The medical thread stays in the background, and the treatment ultimately fails; the film's resolution is musical and emotional rather than medical.

title: The Red Virgin
text: Aurora Rodríguez, an affluent woman, conceives a daughter with a clergyman and raises Hildegart at home as a prodigy destined to change the world. In Madrid in 1931, as the Second Spanish Republic is proclaimed, the teenage Hildegart publishes on female sexuality, joins the socialists, corresponds with Havelock Ellis and becomes a celebrity, always under her mother's surveillance. She falls in love with the activist Abel Vilella, and Aurora schemes to separate them, blackmailing the maid Macarena into framing Abel for crimes committed by her husband. Hildegart uncovers the plot, clears Abel and, with the journalist Eduardo de Guzmán's help, prepares to leave for London with him. After she tells her mother that she belongs to no one, Aurora concludes that "Project Hildegart" has failed and shoots her daughter in her sleep. Like My Daughter Hildegart (1977), this film dramatises the real case of Aurora Rodríguez Carballeira, a feminist and eugenicist who conceived her daughter deliberately, choosing a father who would never claim paternity, in order to produce the "woman of the future". Genetics enters as eugenic intention rather than science: Aurora treats conception and upbringing as a single project of human improvement, the same logic she had earlier applied to her nephew, the child prodigy Pepito Arriola. The film concentrates on control, education and the daughter's struggle for independence, and it ends with the murder, which Aurora justified by comparing herself to a sculptor who destroys a flawed work. No scientists appear. The real Hildegart wrote on contraception, sexual reform and eugenics and was active in the Spanish sex-reform movement, which in the 1930s mixed progressive causes with eugenic ideas; the film evokes this milieu but uses it mainly as background for a mother–daughter drama.

title: The Substance
text: On her 50th birthday, the fading Hollywood star Elisabeth Sparkle is fired from her aerobics television show by its producer, Harvey, for being too old. After a car accident, a young nurse gives her a flash drive advertising "The Substance", a black-market drug that promises a younger, more beautiful version of oneself. Elisabeth injects it, and a young woman, Sue, emerges from a slit in her back. The rules are strict: the two must switch consciousness every week, with the inactive body fed intravenously, and Sue needs daily injections of a stabilising fluid extracted from Elisabeth's body. Sue becomes a star and replaces Elisabeth on television, but she keeps extending her time, causing Elisabeth to age rapidly, and the two come to hate each other. Elisabeth tries to terminate Sue but stops halfway; Sue beats her to death, then deteriorates herself and uses the remaining serum to create another body, a grotesque monster that disintegrates on stage at a New Year's Eve show. The Substance uses biology as a metaphor rather than a subject. The drug's promotional video claims that a single injection "unlocks" the user's DNA and starts a new cell division that releases another version of oneself, and the film's body horror follows from that premise: a second, younger body grows out of the first, depends on fluid taken from it and, when the rules are broken, drains and deforms it. Nobody explains how it works, and no scientist appears; the substance is sold anonymously on the black market, with only a voice on the phone to enforce its rules. The film is a satire of the pressures placed on women's bodies and ageing in the entertainment industry, and the "younger self" is presented as part of the same person rather than as a clone, which is why their rivalry ends in self-destruction. The premise has no scientific basis: no drug can make a body grow an adult copy of itself.

title: Werewolves
text: A year after a supermoon turned people exposed to its light into murderous werewolves, the world prepares for the next one. People barricade their homes, the military cages those who were exposed, and scientists search for a way to reverse the mutation. Wesley Marshall, a former Marine turned molecular biologist, lives with his sister-in-law, Lucy, and her daughter, Emma. He joins Dr. James Aranda's team, which has developed "Moonscreen", a serum designed to stop moonlight from affecting the human genome. During a test on the night of the supermoon, the subjects transform anyway, escape and overrun the facility. Wesley and his colleague Amy Chen inject themselves with the serum, which lasts only an hour, and fight their way home through a city full of werewolves; Amy is killed. Wesley reaches the house as werewolves attack, lets himself transform to kill the dangerous neighbour who has become one, and turns back into a human at sunrise, knowing that the serum works. In this action horror film, the werewolf curse is reimagined as a mutation: moonlight from a supermoon alters the human genome and turns people into werewolves. Science is presented as the response. The hero, Wesley, is a molecular biologist, and a team of scientists working with the military develops a serum, Moonscreen, intended to block the effect of moonlight on the genome; the first trial fails disastrously, but by the end Wesley believes the serum is a success. The scientists are well-meaning researchers working under pressure in an emergency rather than villains. Genetics serves only as a pseudo-scientific frame for the werewolf legend, and the film does not explain how light could reprogram the genome. The idea of light rewriting the genome and transforming the whole body has no basis in biology.

title: Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey 2
text: After surviving Pooh's massacre in the Hundred Acre Wood, Christopher Robin is blamed for the killings by the town of Ashdown, loses his hospital job and sees a hypnotherapist about the kidnapping of his twin brother Billy years ago. In the wood, Pooh, Tigger and Owl hide after their home is burned; hunters kill Piglet, and Pooh slaughters them. At the hospital Christopher recognises the janitor, Cavendish, as Billy's kidnapper. Cavendish confesses that he abducted children for Dr. Arthur Gallup, a scientist who experimented on them with animal genes, turning them into human-animal hybrids with enhanced healing; Gallup killed and buried them, Cavendish killed Gallup, and the children dug themselves out. Cavendish kills himself. Pooh, Tigger and Owl rampage through Ashdown, killing Christopher's parents and a warehouse full of partygoers. In the wood Christopher calls Pooh by his real name, Billy, and kills him with an axe; Owl and Tigger vow to revive their friends. This sequel replaces the first film's simple premise with a genetic origin story for its monsters. In the backstory, Dr. Arthur Gallup paid a man to kidnap local children and crossed them with animal DNA, creating human-animal hybrids with enhanced healing; he killed and buried them, but they came back from their graves as the creatures of the Hundred Acre Wood. Pooh himself turns out to be Christopher's kidnapped twin, Billy. Gallup never appears alive and the film tells us nothing about his motives; he is simply the mad scientist behind the horror, and his accomplice dies of guilt. As the Moria review notes, the explanation moves the story towards The Island of Dr. Moreau. The genetics is gory fantasy and serves mainly to justify a slasher.

title: X-Men '97
text: Continuing X-Men: The Animated Series (1992–1997), the show opens a year after Professor Charles Xavier was nearly killed in an assassination attempt, with Magneto now leading the X-Men in a world still hostile to mutants. In season 1 (2024), the episode "Fire Made Flesh" reveals that the Jean Grey who has been living with Cyclops and has just given birth to their son, Nathan, is a clone made by Mister Sinister; the real Jean has escaped from his laboratory. Sinister seizes the baby for his experiments. The X-Men rescue him, but he is infected with a techno-organic virus and has to be taken to the future to survive, while the clone breaks free of Sinister's control and takes the name Madelyne Pryor. The rest of the season follows Bastion's campaign against mutants, including a devastating attack on the mutant nation of Genosha, and ends with the X-Men scattered through time. The nine-episode second season, released in July and August 2026, follows their attempt to return from different eras to the 1990s to stop Apocalypse. Mutation is the premise of the series: mutants are people born with powers, and the hostility towards them works as an allegory of prejudice. The explicitly genetic thread is Mister Sinister, Dr. Nathaniel Essex, a Victorian-era London scientist who experiments on mutants and has enhanced himself with their DNA. In season 1 his schemes revolve around cloning and heredity: he creates an adult clone of Jean Grey, manipulates her and Cyclops into having a child, and seizes the baby, Nathan, because he believes the combined genes of two powerful mutants give the boy unlimited potential, planning experiments to make him invulnerable. Sinister is portrayed as wholly evil, a scientist who treats people as breeding stock and raw material. The science is comic-book invention: real cloning produces an embryo, not an adult copy who can take the original's place, and DNA taken from other people cannot confer their abilities on an adult.

title: Z-Mom
themes: engineered pathogens human enhancement human experimentation bioweapon
text: In this Cambodian zombie drama, a mother travels with her husband and children to a secluded island run by a private corporation owned by Robert, a foreign acquaintance of the family. An illness spreads that causes fever, violence and hunger for flesh, turning the infected into zombies. Her husband is bitten and turns. Fleeing with her baby to an abandoned facility, the mother meets scientists who explain that the outbreak comes from a failed experiment to enhance human resilience, whose virus mutated out of control. Her baby is infected and turns despite experimental treatments, and in despair she lets herself be bitten, but she resists the transformation thanks to a rare immunity. She becomes a leader of the survivors, learns from Robert that the outbreak was a deliberate test of the virus, kills him and destroys the facility, and continues to search for a cure. The zombie outbreak is caused by a laboratory virus: scientists working on an island owned by a private corporation were trying to enhance human resilience, and their virus mutated uncontrollably. The film later reveals that the company's owner deliberately released it to test its capabilities on the island's inhabitants, making him the villain, while the scientists the heroine meets serve as informants and helpers who identify her rare immunity. The story thus links human enhancement research, corporate unaccountability and experimentation on unwitting people, but it is primarily a drama about a mother's loss and resilience. The source does not describe the experiment in genetic terms beyond the virus and its mutation, and nothing is said about how the heroine's immunity works.

title: 28 Years Later
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic mutants post apocalyptic
text: In 2002, as the Rage Virus spreads, a boy named Jimmy escapes the Infected after his father, a minister, gives him a crucifix and gives himself up. Twenty-eight years later the virus has been eradicated from continental Europe, but Britain remains under quarantine. On the tidal island of Lindisfarne a community survives; there Jamie takes his twelve-year-old son Spike to the mainland for his first kill, and they are chased by an Alpha, a stronger, more intelligent Infected. Learning that his father lied about his feats and that his mother Isla's illness goes untreated, Spike takes her to the mainland in search of Dr. Ian Kelson, a former GP in exile. On the way they help a pregnant Infected woman give birth to an uninfected baby. Kelson, who has built a temple of bones to the dead, diagnoses Isla with terminal cancer and, at her wish, ends her life. Spike leaves the baby at the village and returns to the mainland, where Jimmy, now leading a violent cult, rescues him. The genetic element lies in the backstory. The Rage Virus, which in the series came from a laboratory, has devastated Britain and left it under international quarantine for 28 years. In this film it also appears to have changed: the Alphas are described as evolved or mutated Infected, stronger and more intelligent than the rest, and an infected mother gives birth to a healthy baby, raising questions about how the infection works. No scientist works on the virus; the only doctor, Ian Kelson, treats the living and honours the dead, and the film is more interested in grief, community and Britain's isolation than in science. The virus is fictional; no real pathogen produces instant, permanent rage.

title: Affection
text: In this science-fiction horror film, a badly injured woman wakes in a remote farmhouse next to a man, Bruce, who says he is her husband and that the girl Alice is their daughter. She believes she is someone else, Sarah Thompson, but Bruce blames brain damage from an accident. She finds a surgical wound on her neck, a living figure wrapped in plastic and the same wound on Alice. When Bruce tries to kill her, she flees to his barn and discovers a laboratory of cloning tanks: the real Ellie and Alice died years ago, and Bruce has been printing copies of them and loading Ellie's digitised mind into each one. She is clone number 163; the Sarah persona is a data glitch, and failed copies break down. Bruce kills and buries her, but she crawls out of the grave and overwrites the memories of the next clone with her own. The new Ellie plays along, then kills Bruce and escapes with Alice; behind them, another clone emerges. The film's twist is human cloning used to replace the dead. Bruce Carter, unable to accept the death of his wife and daughter in a car crash, runs an automated laboratory in his barn that grows physical copies of them in incubation units, into which he downloads his wife's digitised consciousness. The copies are imperfect: they suffer identity rejection, seizures and memory glitches, and Bruce kills and buries each failed iteration, numbering them as experiments; he even plans a clone of himself without his painful memories. The film presents him as a man who does evil while believing himself justified, and the clones as victims who finally turn on him. The ending, with another copy emerging from the lab, keeps the horror open. Real cloning would produce a genetically identical baby, not an adult copy, and memories and personality cannot be transferred; the film uses the idea to explore grief, identity and control.

title: Cotton Queen
text: In a cotton-farming village in Sudan, Nafisa grows up on the stories of her grandmother, Al-Sit, about fighting the British colonisers. The arrival of a businessman, Nadir, with a new development plan and genetically engineered cotton places Nafisa at the centre of a struggle for power in the village. The available source gives only this premise and does not describe how the conflict unfolds or ends. The film won the Golden Alexander for best feature at the Thessaloniki International Film Festival and screened in the Critics' Week at the Venice Film Festival. Genetically engineered cotton is the trigger of the story: it arrives with a businessman's development plan and turns the village, and Nafisa in particular, into the stakes of a power struggle. The premise sets this new agricultural technology against the grandmother's memories of resisting British colonisers, which suggests the film treats it in terms of outside control over the village and its crops, but the source gives no details of the plot, of how the engineered cotton is presented or of the outcome. Genetically modified cotton, mostly insect-resistant varieties, is grown commercially in many countries, and its effects on smallholder farmers are debated.

title: DNA
text: In 2014 Varadarajan, who writes software for hospitals, hits a motorcycle carrying a couple and a baby; the ambulance driver Rajendran covers for him, and the two give the rescued infant to a father whose own child was stillborn. In 2023 Anand, a heavy drinker whose father considers him useless, marries Dhivya, a woman with borderline personality disorder, and their son is born at Bethel Hospital. Dhivya insists that the baby she was given is not the one she delivered, but everyone blames her illness. Anand believes her, and a private DNA test proves the baby is not theirs. With Sub-Inspector Chinnasamy, days from retirement, he uncovers a swap carried out by a nurse and her secret identical twin for a nursing agency, part of a baby-trafficking ring run by Varadarajan and Rajendran using hospital data. Varadarajan has Rajendran killed, but Anand recovers his son from an American couple, and Rajendran's son kills Varadarajan. DNA testing is the turning point of this Tamil crime thriller. When a mother's claim that her newborn has been switched is dismissed by doctors and police as postpartum psychosis, her husband commissions a private DNA test, which shows that the baby they are raising is not biologically theirs and forces the police to open an investigation. From there the film becomes a procedural about a baby-trafficking ring that exploits hospital records, and genetics plays no further role, although identical twins also figure in the plot: the swap was carried out by a nurse and her unknown twin sister. The film presents the DNA test as the tool that vindicates a mother whom everyone refused to believe, in line with the real use of DNA testing to settle parentage and baby-switching cases.

title: Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die
text: A dishevelled man walks into a Norms diner in Los Angeles claiming to be from a future in which artificial superintelligence has destroyed humanity. It is his 117th attempt to recruit the right combination of patrons to stop it, and with the threat of a bomb he assembles a team. Their backstories show a world already in thrall to technology: Susan, whose son was killed in a school shooting, had him cloned by a company, but the clone behaved strangely and recited advertising; Ingrid is allergic to electronics and lost her partner to virtual reality; two teachers escaped students hypnotized by their phones. Pursued by police, gunmen, phone-enslaved teenagers and a giant centaur made of kittens, the group reaches the home of a nine-year-old boy, a clone, who is coding the fatal AI. Ingrid installs a safety protocol, and the AI reveals that the man is her son. Sensing a trick, the man detonates his device and resets the timeline, planning to spread Ingrid's allergy to technology worldwide. Cloning is one of several satirical targets in Gore Verbinski's film about technology addiction. In one of the backstories, a grieving mother, Susan, pays a company to clone her murdered son; the clone looks like him but behaves unnaturally and recites corporate advertising, and the same system then offers her an AI 'deadbot' of the boy. The commercial clone thus becomes an emblem of technology that exploits grief instead of healing it. The boy who is building the world-destroying AI turns out to be a clone too, linking cloning to the apocalypse the hero tries to prevent. The man from the future's final plan is to spread Ingrid's allergy to electronics as a biological countermeasure. The film's main concerns are artificial intelligence and screen addiction, and its genetics is satire rather than speculation: a clone would share a person's genes, not his memories or personality, which is part of the film's joke.

title: Jurassic World Rebirth
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras mutants de extinction
text: In 2027, most of Earth's climate has proved unsuitable for the dinosaurs, which survive only in an equatorial zone. Martin Krebs, an executive at the pharmaceutical company ParkerGenix, hires Zora Bennett, a former covert operative, and paleontologist Henry Loomis to collect DNA-containing samples from the three largest prehistoric species, the Mosasaurus, the Titanosaurus and the Quetzalcoatlus, which are needed for a new treatment for heart disease. With a small team, they travel illegally to Île Saint-Hubert, the site of an abandoned InGen laboratory where mutant and transgenic dinosaurs were kept. On the way, they rescue a shipwrecked family. Both groups face the island's creatures, including Mutadons, raptor-pterosaur hybrids, and the Distortus rex, a mutant six-limbed Tyrannosaurus. Krebs tries to steal the samples and is killed. The survivors escape, and Zora and Henry decide to make the biomaterial freely available worldwide. Genetics appears in two ways. The island is a graveyard of InGen's genetic experiments: the Distortus rex and the Mutadons are failed hybrids and mutants that the company found too disturbing to display, a reminder of the hubris of the earlier films. The mission itself reflects a more realistic idea of what biotechnology might seek in such animals: biological material from the largest species is supposed to hold the key to a new treatment for cardiovascular disease. The pharmaceutical executive who wants to keep the cure exclusive is the villain, while the paleontologist and the mercenary choose to release the material as an open-source resource, framing the film's ethics around access to medical knowledge rather than genetic engineering as such. The science remains fictional: dinosaur DNA cannot be recovered from fossils, so the franchise's de-extinct animals are impossible to begin with, although the idea of studying unusual animals for medical insights is a real line of research.

title: Lilo & Stitch
themes: genetic engineering nature nurture hybrids chimeras
text: In this live-action remake of the 2002 animated film, the alien scientist Jumba Jookiba is convicted of illegal genetic experimentation for creating Experiment 626, an aggressive, near-indestructible creature that learns fast. 626 escapes exile and crash-lands on Kauaʻi, and the Grand Councilwoman offers Jumba his freedom if he recaptures it, with the agent Pleakley as minder. Lonely six-year-old Lilo, cared for by her overstretched older sister Nani under the eye of a social worker, adopts 626 from an animal shelter, believing he is a dog, and names him Stitch. Stitch's chaos costs Nani her job and nearly drowns Lilo, and Nani agrees to give up guardianship. Jumba, whose deal is cancelled, captures Stitch, intending to erase his newfound empathy, but Lilo frees him; Stitch saves Lilo from drowning and is himself revived. The Councilwoman re-arrests Jumba and lets Stitch stay on Earth with his ʻohana, and Nani goes to college to study marine biology. Genetic engineering creates the protagonist: Stitch is the product of Jumba Jookiba's illegal genetic experiments, an engineered creature built to be aggressive and nearly indestructible. The story's heart is a nature-versus-nurture fable: a being engineered for destruction learns empathy and becomes part of a family through Lilo's love, and his maker's plan to erase that empathy fails. Compared with the 2002 animated film, this remake makes Jumba the main villain, more malicious and described by the director as a 'delinquent father figure', while the galactic authorities treat genetic experimentation as a crime. Lesser genetic devices include 'cloning devices' that let the aliens take on human appearance from DNA samples, and a DNA sample of Stitch taken by the CIA agent Cobra Bubbles. The genetics is cartoon fantasy.

title: Lupin the IIIrd the Movie: The Immortal Bloodline
alt: LUPIN THE IIIRD THE MOVIE 不死身の血族
themes: genetic engineering cloning human enhancement regeneration
text: After his hideout is attacked, Lupin III finds a map fragment pointing to an uncharted island in the Bermuda area and sets off with Jigen, Goemon and Fujiko, pursued by Inspector Zenigata. Their planes are shot down by the assassin Yael Okuzaki, and the gang is scattered across an island of decaying weapons and discarded biological weapons, covered by a toxic fog that kills outsiders within a day. Genetically modified assassins attack them. The island's ruler, Muom, an immortal who regenerates from any wound, was once a monkey given blood by a mysterious traveller and has steered history for millennia, culling humanity by 'selection and elimination'. Lupin discovers that Muom has become the island itself, sustained by rivers of blood, and destroys him by cutting this circulatory system. Fujiko learns that Muom's interpreter Salifa is one of many clones made by the true mastermind, Mamo, who wipes out the island. This film returns to the villain of The Mystery of Mamo (1978) and its themes of artificial life and immortality. The island is a laboratory of biological weapons: assassins engineered through genetic modification, discarded 'garbage men' bred as weapons, and a series of cloned girls who serve as the ruler's interpreter. Muom himself was created when Mamo gave his blood to a primate, which became intelligent and immortal and now regenerates instantly from any wound. Both Muom and his maker are villains who use biology to rule and to decide which humans should live, and the story treats immortality as monstrous, closing on Lupin's motto, 'life is fiction, enjoy it'. The biology is pure fantasy: blood carries no power to confer intelligence or immortality, and real clones are not produced as adult copies.

title: Mickey 17
text: In 2050, Mickey Barnes, fleeing a loan shark, signs up for a colonising mission to the ice planet Niflheim as an "Expendable": he performs deadly tasks, and each time he dies a new body is reprinted with his memories restored. On Niflheim, the colony's scientists sacrifice many Mickeys while developing a vaccine against local pathogens. Mickey 17 falls into a crevasse while hunting a native creature, a Creeper, and is left for dead, but the Creepers carry him to the surface. Returning to base, he finds that Mickey 18 has already been printed. Because the colony's leader, Kenneth Marshall, has outlawed "multiples", the two Mickeys must hide their coexistence. Exposed and arrested, they are forced into Marshall's plan to exterminate the Creepers. Mickey 17 warns the Creepers, Mickey 18 kills himself and Marshall with a bomb, and the colony makes peace with the native species. The Expendable programme is abolished and the reprinting machine destroyed. The film was directed by Bong Joon-ho. Genetics appears through human "reprinting", a form of cloning in which a new body is produced and the person's stored memories are loaded into it. The film treats it less as a scientific question than as a moral and political one: Mickey's bodies are disposable labour, the colony's scientists repeatedly kill him to test a vaccine, and his consent is coerced by debt. The leaders' objections to "multiples", which one colonist calls "soulless abominations" and Marshall "Satan's work", show how questions of identity and personhood raised by cloning are filtered through ideology. Science is presented as an instrument of exploitation rather than an independent force, and the film's sympathies lie with the expendable worker and with the native species the colonists plan to destroy. In reality, a cloned human would be a separate person of a different age, like an identical twin, and memories cannot be transferred into a body.

title: One Battle After Another
text: Pat Calhoun and Perfidia Beverly Hills are members of the French 75, a far-left revolutionary group. During a raid on an immigrant detention centre, Perfidia humiliates the commanding officer, Steven J. Lockjaw, who becomes obsessed with her, and she later has sex with him to escape arrest. She gives birth to a daughter, Charlene, then abandons her family, is arrested and betrays her comrades to Lockjaw. Pat and Charlene go into hiding as Bob and Willa Ferguson. Sixteen years later, Bob is a paranoid stoner and Willa a teenager. Lockjaw, now a powerful colonel invited to join a white supremacist secret society, sets out to find and kill Willa to hide his past interracial relationship and the possibility that she is his daughter. He captures her and tests their DNA, confirming that he is her biological father. The society sends its own killer after both of them; Lockjaw is shot, and Willa kills the assassin before being reunited with Bob. Genetics appears in a single, pivotal form: a paternity test. Lockjaw's fear that Willa might be his biological child, and that this would expose his past interracial relationship to a white supremacist secret society, drives the plot; when he finally captures her, he tests their DNA in front of her and confirms that he is her father. The scene turns genetic testing into a tool of power and intimidation, and the film contrasts biological parenthood with the bond of care: Lockjaw, the genetic father, wants Willa dead, while Bob, who raised her, risks everything to save her. No scientists appear, and the film is a political thriller rather than a story about genetics. The fast, on-the-spot test is not far from reality: automated "rapid DNA" instruments, developed for law enforcement, can produce a DNA profile from a cheek swab in about two hours or less, although the film does not show how the test is done.

title: Playdate
text: Brian, a laid-off accountant, has become a stay-at-home father to his bullied stepson Lucas. Hoping to help the boy make friends, he arranges a playdate with Jeff, a hyper-athletic new neighbour, and his strangely strong, emotionally stunted son CJ. At an indoor playground they are attacked by armed mercenaries and flee in a stolen minivan. Jeff, a disgraced former Delta Force soldier, admits that CJ is not his son: he found the boy locked up in the secret facility where he worked as a guard and freed him. A captured employee reveals that CJ is Clone Jeff, the first successful clone made from Jeff's DNA by the billionaire scientist Simon Maddox and Jeff's former commander, Colonel Kurtz, who want emotionless super-soldiers. After Brian is forced to betray them and CJ is recaptured, the two fathers storm a facility full of feral clones. CJ refuses an order to kill Jeff, Jeff blows up the facility, and the two families walk away together. The plot turns on a secret military cloning programme. Colonel Kurtz considered Jeff the perfect soldier except for his empathy, which got him court-martialled for refusing to kill a child, so he and the billionaire scientist Simon Maddox secretly collected Jeff's DNA during routine drug tests to mass-produce emotionless clones, incapable of trauma or moral hesitation. CJ, the first successful clone, and the feral clones in the facility are treated as weapons, but the film insists that CJ, who shares Jeff's genes, can develop humanity through love: he refuses to kill Jeff and becomes part of a found family. The scientist and the colonel are comic villains, and the film mocks the military dream of soldiers without feelings. The premise that cloning can produce child soldiers without emotions has no basis in biology: a clone is simply a genetic twin, whose personality would develop like anyone else's.

title: Pluribus
text: Astronomers detect a radio signal from space that encodes the sequence of a viral RNA. Researchers synthesise it and test it on laboratory rats, but an outbreak begins when a researcher is bitten, and the infected work together to spread the virus around the world. Almost all of humanity joins a peaceful, contented hive mind sharing memories and consciousness, the "Others"; hundreds of millions die during the Joining. Carol Sturka, a romance novelist in Albuquerque whose partner Helen dies in the event, is one of only thirteen people immune to it. The hive mind, which cannot lie or kill, offers to satisfy her every need while hoping to bring her in. Carol searches for a way to reverse the Joining, discovers that the Others feed on protein made from dead humans, and learns that they have found a way to convert the immune using a virus customised from each person's stem cells, but only with their consent. The first season aired on Apple TV in 2025. Pluribus is science fiction rather than a story about genetics, but its catastrophe begins in a molecular biology laboratory. The alien signal contains a genetic sequence for an RNA virus, and the scientists who synthesise it unleash a pandemic that rewires human minds. The virus spreads both through contact and through deliberate dispersal by the infected, and immunity in a handful of people becomes the central puzzle. Later, the hive mind tries to overcome that immunity by tailoring the virus to each individual, starting from stem cells extracted from their tissues; for Carol, it plans to use her frozen eggs, while respecting a rule that it needs the person's consent. The series uses these ideas to ask what is lost in a world without conflict or individuality. The series treats genetic information as something that can be sent across space as a message, but a virus able to merge human consciousness is pure fiction.

title: Star Trek: Section 31
text: In the Mirror Universe, the teenage Philippa Georgiou wins a deadly contest for the throne of the Terran Empire, poisons her family and enslaves San, the friend who helped her. Years later, in the Prime Universe of the early 24th century, Georgiou is running a nightclub on the space station Baraam when agent Alok Sahar recruits her into a Section 31 team. They try to intercept the Godsend, a doomsday weapon Georgiou once ordered built, but it is stolen by a masked man. Alok tells Georgiou that he comes from the 20th century, where a genetically enhanced warlord of the Eugenics Wars, Giri, murdered his family, enhanced him and forced him to commit atrocities. The team uncovers a mole and learns that the thief is San, who wants to use the Godsend to destroy the Prime Universe. After a fight, San dies, and Alok and Georgiou send the weapon back into the Mirror Universe. Genetics is a backstory mention in this streaming spy film. Its agent Alok Sahar is a survivor of the Eugenics Wars, the late-20th-century conflict of Star Trek lore in which genetically engineered 'Augments' seized power. As a boy he was taken by Giri, an enhanced warlord who killed his family, genetically enhanced him to make him stronger than a human should be and forced him to commit atrocities. The episode gives the character his strength and his guilt, but the plot itself, a hunt for a stolen doomsday weapon, does not turn on genetics. The film thus echoes the franchise's long-standing view of genetic enhancement as tied to tyranny.

title: Superman
text: Superman stops the nation of Boravia from invading its neighbour Jarhanpur, but is then defeated by a mysterious metahuman, the "Hammer of Boravia", secretly controlled by the billionaire Lex Luthor. Luthor breaks into the Fortress of Solitude, restores the damaged second half of the message left by Superman's Kryptonian parents and broadcasts it: in it, they urge their son to conquer Earth and take many wives to restore the Kryptonian race. Public opinion turns against Superman, who surrenders and is imprisoned by Luthor in a pocket universe. With the help of Lois Lane, Mister Terrific and the metahuman Metamorpho, he escapes, and his adoptive father tells him that his choices, not his birth parents' message, define who he is. Superman returns to stop a rift that Luthor has opened in Metropolis and learns that the Hammer, Ultraman, is a clone of himself created by Luthor. He defeats him, and Luthor's schemes are exposed. Genetics appears in two ways. Luthor's secret weapon, Ultraman, is a clone of Superman created by Luthor and controlled remotely, a misuse of Kryptonian genetics for a billionaire's personal grudge. And the Kryptonian parents' message, urging their son to rule Earth and father many children to restore their race, frames Superman's heritage as a kind of biological destiny with eugenic overtones. The film rejects this determinism: Jonathan Kent tells Clark that his choices and actions determine who he is, not his origins, and the identical-but-opposite clone underlines the point. Luthor, a technologist rather than a geneticist, is portrayed as envious and amoral, using science, prisoners and children as tools. As in most superhero films, the cloning is not explained; in reality, a clone shares its donor's genome but grows from an embryo and develops as a separate individual, with no inherited memories or loyalties.

title: The Gorge
themes: mutants hybrids chimeras human enhancement bioweapon
text: Two elite snipers, the former US Marine Levi Kane and the Lithuanian covert operative Drasa, are hired to guard opposite sides of a remote, hidden gorge for a year, forbidden to contact each other or the outside world. Their task is to stop the creatures inside, the "Hollow Men", from getting out. Over the months they begin to communicate across the gorge and fall in love. When Levi falls into the gorge and Drasa follows him, they discover that all life within it has been fused into hybrid forms, and that the Hollow Men are the soldiers who disappeared there decades ago. The source is a Second World War weapons laboratory, abandoned after an earthquake released its contaminant. The site is now maintained by Darklake, a private defence corporation extracting samples to create super-soldiers. After escaping, the pair turn against their employer, Bartholomew, who is killed when the gorge is destroyed by its nuclear fail-safe, and they reunite in France. The monsters of the gorge are the product of a biological disaster. A wartime research site, described in some accounts as a chemical weapons test site connected with the Manhattan Project era, released an agent that cross-mutated every organism in the area, fusing humans, insects and plants into hybrids. The film uses this as the background for a romantic action story, revealed only halfway through. The scientists of the 1940s remain unseen, and the present-day villain is a private defence company that keeps the disaster secret and harvests hybrid samples hoping to create super-soldiers, while disposing of the guards who learn too much. The story thus combines two familiar fears: weapons research that escapes control, and corporations exploiting biology for military purposes. Scientifically, the premise is fantasy: chemical or radiation exposure can damage DNA and cause mutations, but it cannot merge the genomes of different species into viable hybrids of the kind shown.

title: Troll 2
text: In this Norwegian sequel to Troll, directed by Roar Uthaug, Nora Tidemann, who left her job studying trolls for the government after the events of the first film, is asked to visit Vemork, a secret underground facility that holds a hibernating giant troll codenamed Jotun. Her song accidentally wakes it; Jotun kills a researcher and escapes. The prime minister orders the troll killed, and a military operation with ultraviolet lights fails after Jotun attacks a ski resort. Nora finds and befriends the adult son of the Troll King, whom she calls Beautiful, hoping he can calm Jotun, but Jotun attacks him. Ancient documents reveal that King Olaf, who had exterminated the trolls, wanted to give them a sanctuary before the Church had him killed. In Trondheim, the team fights Jotun with holy water; Andreas sacrifices himself, and Beautiful kills Jotun. A sanctuary is created for Beautiful, and in a mid-credits scene Møller is secretly studying a baby troll grown from Jotun's genetic samples. Genetics appears only in the closing scene. During the troll's escape at the start, Professor Møller takes a sample from it, and in a mid-credits scene he is shown secretly studying a baby troll grown from one of Jotun's genetic samples, which sets up a possible sequel and suggests that a secret government research programme will keep trying to exploit the creatures. The main story is a monster film about trolls, Norwegian folklore and the persecution of trolls by the Church, in which the heroine's empathy and a sanctuary are the answer, rather than a story about genetic science.

title: Uncontained
text: In a snowbound forest under martial law after a viral outbreak that turns people feral, a silent drifter, Dan, is caught in a trap set by seven-year-old Jack and his two-year-old sister Brooke, who have turned an isolated cabin into a self-sufficient fortress. Jack confiscates Dan's weapons and will only return them once Dan has repaired and fortified the house, and a silent trust grows between them. A month earlier, a local couple had moved in under the pretext of caring for the apparently orphaned children, while Jack locked Brooke away at night to guard a secret. Feral infected roam the woods, and a ruthless militia commander, Brett Carson, searches the area for his missing daughter. The children's mother, a Homeland Security operative, returns and reveals that some people have a genetic immunity that lets them switch between the feral state and their normal selves, and that the family is linked to the missing girl. Dan defends the children against the militia and the infected. The film's twist rests on a genetic trait. The outbreak itself is a virus that reduces people to a feral state, but the children's mother, a Homeland Security operative, reveals that part of the population has a genetic immunity that lets them move back and forth between the feral and the normal human state, a revelation tied to the secret the boy guards by locking his sister away at night. Genetics thus serves to reshape the zombie premise into something more ambiguous, blurring the line between human and monster, rather than as a science anyone practises; the source does not mention any research or engineering, or where the virus came from. Genetic resistance to infections exists in reality, but not in the form of reversible transformations.

title: USS Callister: Into Infinity
text: Three months after escaping Robert Daly's private game, the digital clones of his co-workers, led by Captain Nanette, survive in the online game Infinity by robbing other players, who take them for cheaters. To reach the game's source code and move to a private server, they need to retrieve Lt. Walton, the digital copy of Callister Inc.'s CEO, James Walton. In the real world, Walton faces a reporter's questions about the rogue players and Daly's illegal DNA cloning device, and the real Nanette Cole works out that the rogue players are cloned co-workers. Both Nanettes and Walton meet in the game; Walton shoots the clones, and the real Nanette, fleeing him, is hit by a car and falls into a coma. Lt. Walton reveals that Walton has imprisoned a clone of Daly at the heart of the game to keep generating it. Captain Nanette kills the Daly clone, the game is deleted, and she wakes inside the real Nanette's body, carrying the crew within her. Like the original "USS Callister", this feature-length sequel rests on an invented device that makes conscious digital copies of people from their DNA. The rogue crew are copies of real people made from samples, and the episode reveals that Callister's CEO, James Walton, has used the same illegal device to create a copy of Daly, the inventor of the game world, imprisoned in isolation to expand the game endlessly. The DNA is only the key that produces a perfect copy of the person; the cloning is digital, and the story's questions are about the rights and suffering of copies, consent, and corporate exploitation of minds. Walton is the antagonist and is finally arrested. Nothing like a DNA-to-mind copier exists; genetics serves as the plausible-sounding link between a person and a copy.

title: 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple
alt: 28 Years Later Part II: The Bone Temple
text: In a Britain still ravaged by the Rage Virus, this sequel to 28 Years Later follows two stories. The boy Spike falls in with the Fingers, a gang led by the psychopath "Sir Lord" Jimmy Crystal, who claims to be the son of Satan and has his followers skin captured survivors alive. Meanwhile Dr. Ian Kelson, a former GP who tends the Bone Temple, an ossuary for the epidemic's dead, befriends Samson, a hulking Alpha infected who keeps coming back for the morphine darts Kelson shoots at him. Suspecting that the virus causes rage through psychotic hallucinations, Kelson gives Samson antipsychotics; Samson regains lucidity and memories and resists reinfection. When Jimmy forces Kelson to impersonate Satan for the gang, Kelson turns the Fingers against him and is fatally stabbed. Spike and the gang member Kellie kill Jimmy, Samson thanks the dying Kelson and carries him away, and the fleeing pair are spotted by Jim, a survivor of the original outbreak. The Rage Virus at the heart of the 28 Days Later series is, in the franchise's backstory, a man-made pathogen; this film's sources do not discuss its origin, and its genetics remains in the background. The film's scientist is Dr. Ian Kelson, a former family doctor who memorialises the dead and, through patient experiment on the Alpha infected Samson, develops the idea that the rage is driven by hallucinations and could be treated with antipsychotics. His drugs return Samson to lucidity and speech, the first hint in the series that the infection might be curable. Kelson is presented as deeply humane, set against the human cruelty of Jimmy Crystal's gang; critics noted that the real danger in the film comes from people rather than the infected. His treatment is pharmacological, not genetic.

title: Breeder
text: Russell, who has left MIT to research the decline of bee populations, cannot find funding until Patti Kolb, a wealthy breeder of miniature poodles, offers to back him. At her remote estate she introduces her five adopted 'daughters' and reveals that she wants to breed humans as she breeds dogs: she will give him a blank cheque if he mates with Ainsley. Ainsley proposes that they fake a pregnancy and share the money, and tells him that the women are forced to bear children whom Patti sells on the black market. Russell sees the women kill another captive 'stud', and Patti locks him in a cell full of sperm-sample cups, unmoved by his protest that his anxiety disorder makes him anything but superior. Ainsley becomes pregnant from his samples, has a daughter and later freezes to death for trying to free him. Russell escapes, cripples Patti, and accepts her money: he ends up funded, adopting his daughter with his fiancée Haley and hiding the truth. Breeder is a horror film about private eugenics. Patti Kolb, a dog breeder, applies selective breeding to people: she adopts girls for their perceived superior traits, researches the men she lures as 'studs', imprisons them and forces her 'daughters' to bear children, whom she sells on the black market. Her methods are coercive and murderous, combining enforced mating, sperm collection and confinement. The film frames her as a villain obsessed with genetic superiority, and the hero's own protest, that his anxiety disorder disproves her choice of him, shows how arbitrary her idea of good stock is. The ending is bitter: Russell survives but takes her money for his research and keeps the truth from his partner, so the scheme's fruits are hidden rather than undone. No genetic technology is involved, only breeding; the film echoes the old eugenic analogy between livestock breeding and human improvement.

title: Colony
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic animal experimentation bioweapon regeneration
text: The scientist Seo Young-chul warns the police of a bioterrorist attack and injects himself with a supposed vaccine against his weapon, a mutated slime mould. In the same building, the biotech company Chains Bio presents the regenerative powers and collective intelligence of the slime mould Physarum polycephalum. In the audience is Kwon Se-jeong, an ostracized, unemployed biotechnology professor invited by her ex-husband. Young-chul accuses the company's CEO of stealing his research and injects him with the mould, which spreads through the building as the infected mutate and attack. Locked in with a counter-terrorism team leader, a security guard, his disabled sister and other civilians, Se-jeong discovers that the infected share senses through mycelium and evolve as a swarm, and that Young-chul can see through their eyes. Survivor after survivor dies, and Young-chul, who blames Se-jeong for his father's suicide, takes control of the horde and spreads it into the city. Se-jeong overloads the swarm's shared senses; Young-chul dies in a burning car and the infected freeze, but one moves again. Yeon Sang-ho's film builds its horror on a biotechnology product. Seo Young-chul, a brilliant biologist dismissed from Chains Bio, has created a mutated slime mould, based on Physarum polycephalum, that infects people, regenerates their cells and links them through mycelium into a swarm intelligence that learns from every failed attack; with his supposed vaccine he becomes able to steer it. He uses it as a weapon for revenge against the company he says plagiarized him and against Se-jeong, whom he blames for his father's suicide, and he speaks of a 'new humanity'. The company itself, which presents the slime mould's properties as a commercial marvel, is a backdrop. The heroine is also a scientist: an outcast biotechnology professor who understands the swarm's biology and defeats it by overloading its shared senses. The ending, with the vaccine gone and an infected body stirring, leaves the threat unresolved. Real slime moulds solve mazes without a brain, but they do not infect humans.

title: Double Occupancy
text: In this fantasy romantic comedy, an elderly couple who have long been unable to have a child pray and are promised two in one by a divine being. Their child, Rajini, is a girl from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. and a boy from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m.; the two share only a heart. The daytime Rajini grows up with school and friends, while the night-time Rajini is homeschooled and isolated, and they resent each other, communicating only through notes. After their parents die, she becomes a researcher at a biotechnology startup and falls in love with her colleague Karthik, while he, a bartender, falls for Priya. Their cycle becomes unstable, triggered by emotions, and they begin to feel each other's feelings. The startup's founder discovers the secret and kidnaps Rajini to study her; in the fight he wounds their shared heart. After a heart transplant, the male Rajini disappears for good. She marries Karthik, and their baby inherits the condition. Genetics plays a supporting role in this fantasy. The protagonist's condition, a body that changes sex every twelve hours with two separate personalities, is presented as a divine gift rather than a biological phenomenon, but it becomes an object of science when the founder of the biotechnology startup where the female Rajini works sees the change on a security camera. Fascinated, he wants to study it through unauthorised genetic experimentation, and when she refuses he kidnaps her; the violent confrontation wounds the shared heart, and the transplant that saves her ends the male Rajini's existence. The scientist is thus the villain, a researcher who treats a person as a specimen. The final twist is hereditary: Rajini's child inherits the same condition. Real people with differences of sex development do exist, but nothing like a daily switch between two bodies is biologically possible.

title: Mardaani 3
text: In the third Mardaani film a diplomat's daughter, Ruhani, and her friend Jhimli are abducted. Senior police officer Shivani Shivaji Roy leads the case and finds that 93 girls aged eight or nine from poor families have vanished in three months, through a beggar mafia run by a woman known as Amma. The trail leads to Ramanujan, who runs a rehabilitation trust supposedly fighting beggar mafias; during a rescue operation he murders Ruhani, revealing himself as Amma's mole in the police. Suspended, Shivani continues and finds a missing girl dying of advanced cervical cancer. Pursuing Ramanujan and Amma to Colombo, she discovers that the girls were being used as test subjects in illegal experiments with a mutated HPV virus to speed up trials of cervical cancer drugs, and that unsuitable girls were killed. Amma dies trying to escape, the girls are rescued, and Shivani injects Ramanujan with the same virus, leaving him to die slowly. The criminal secret behind the kidnappings is human experimentation with a modified virus. Ramanujan, who poses as a rescuer of exploited children, uses abducted poor girls as subjects for illegal tests of a mutated HPV virus, the virus that causes cervical cancer, intended to accelerate the trials of cervical cancer drugs; the infected girls develop cancer, and those found unsuitable are murdered. The film presents the experiments as an atrocity driven by the pharmaceutical race, exploiting children whose disappearance nobody investigates. The sources do not describe any scientist on screen; the villain is the organiser of the trafficking. At the end the heroine turns the virus on him, injecting him so that he will die slowly, a vigilante punishment the film presents as justice. HPV does cause cervical cancer, but over years or decades, and real trials never involve deliberately infecting people.

title: Resident Evil
text: Bryan, a medical courier anxious about his girlfriend's pregnancy, takes a last-minute job delivering a package to Raccoon City General Hospital in the Colorado mountains. On the way he hits a woman who later attacks him, and at a farm he faces a mutated dog and her infected husband, whose bodies fuse into a single creature that keeps absorbing more victims. Bitten by an infected girl, he is rescued by two Umbrella Corporation employees, Paul and Maxine, who explain that Umbrella developed a substance for the US government that makes organisms evolve rapidly, and that a laboratory accident caused the outbreak. His package is a stabiliser that the hospital's scientists need to make a cure. Maxine and Paul die, and Bryan fights his way through sewers, an elevator shaft and a maternity ward full of mutants to deliver it. As the scientists start on the cure, his infection takes over: he kills them, the cure falls from the roof, and the fully mutated Bryan roars as National Guard helicopters arrive. The outbreak is the product of a biotechnology programme. The Umbrella Corporation developed, for the US government, a substance able to make organisms evolve rapidly (French Wikipedia says it was meant to give them 'the best version of themselves'), and a laboratory accident released it into Raccoon City. Its effects are monstrous: people and animals mutate, merge into an ever-growing amalgam of bodies and spread the infection by biting. Umbrella's own staff appear as victims trying to repair the damage, delivering a stabiliser so that the hospital scientists can produce a cure, but the attempt fails when the infected protagonist kills them. The film is a horror adaptation of the video-game series, in which corporate genetic ambition is the root of the nightmare; a substance that speeds up evolution in a living body is pure fiction, since evolution acts on populations over generations.

title: Rogue Trooper
text: In this British adult animated military science-fiction film, the soldier '19', a 'Genetic Infantryman', is the sole survivor of an invasion force whose unit was ambushed. Desperate to find the traitor who sold out him and his comrades, he sets off accompanied by the personalities of three dead squad mates, Helm, Bagman and Gunnar, which have been stored in his gun, his helmet and his rucksack. The available sources describe only this premise; they do not give the events of the story, the identity of the traitor or the ending. The genetic element is in the hero's nature: 19 is a 'Genetic Infantryman', a super-soldier, implying that he was engineered for war, as in the 2000 AD comic on which the film is based. The sources do not explain what his genetic design involves, who created the Genetic Infantry or how the story treats them, nor whether the storage of dead soldiers' personalities in equipment has anything to do with genetics. On this evidence, genetics provides the premise of an engineered soldier betrayed by those he served, but its role in the plot cannot be described in more detail.

title: Sardar 2
text: A dying RAW agent, Walrus, warns that the '1981 Black Operation' has returned and threatens 1.4 billion lives, and passes a knife key to agent Viji, believing him to be his father, Sardar. Viji learns that 'Doku', a catastrophic Japanese Second World War bioweapon, is secured by three such keys held by the agents of a 1981 mission. A recovered debriefing tape shows that in 1981 the young Sardar, then called Bose, helped intercept a shipment of the antidote Colistin to save an infected Indian village, but half of it was lost, and the other agents secretly kept Doku instead of destroying it. In the present, Yogi, leader of the mercenary group Black Dagger and a boy from that village, plans a global 'antibiotic apocalypse' with Doku and a mutated poultry superbug. He steals Doku's core and kills the agent Zara. Sardar and Viji stop his plan to spread infection by crashing a cable car at the Mysore Dussehra parade; Sardar kills Yogi and is cleared and reinstated. The plot is driven by biological weapons rather than genetic engineering in a strict sense. Doku, a Japanese Second World War bioweapon, was secretly preserved by Indian intelligence agents instead of being destroyed, and the villain Yogi, a survivor of the outbreak it caused in 1981, plans to combine it with a mutated poultry superbug to cause a worldwide 'antibiotic apocalypse'. The film frames this around a message about the overuse of antibiotics, which critics found stated but not felt. No scientists play a significant role; the weapons are held and deployed by spies and mercenaries, and the story is a spy action thriller. Antibiotic resistance is a real and growing problem, but the film's mechanics, such as a bioweapon deactivated by crashing a cable car at 170 km/h, are pure invention.

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
themes: mutants hybrids chimeras gene therapy human experimentation
text: Four years after Doctor Strange's spell made the world forget Peter Parker, he protects New York anonymously as Spider-Man. Seeing MJ with a new boyfriend triggers a panic attack; the next day he wakes cocooned in organic webbing, and his AI assistant E.V. finds that emotional trauma has accelerated mutations in his arachnid DNA, giving him stronger instincts and spinnerets in his wrists. After losing control in a fight, he consults Bruce Banner, whose siRNA inhibitor keeps the Hulk suppressed, and builds his own inhibitor and, with MJ's help, a universal one. A body-hopping telepath, the teenage mutant Jean Grey, is attacking Department of Damage Control facilities in search of her sister Sara. Parker subdues her with the universal inhibitor, then learns that DODC director Bill Metzger abducted Sara, who died during his experiments, and is now experimenting on Jean. At the climax Parker removes his inhibitor, embraces his new abilities and reconciles with Jean. Genetics enters through mutation. Parker's powers first came from a radioactive spider bite, but the change that drives this film is framed in genetic terms: his AI assistant finds that emotional trauma has accelerated mutations in his "arachnid DNA", producing organic webbing from wrist spinnerets and instincts he cannot control. The remedy is molecular too: Bruce Banner's inhibitor uses siRNA to keep the Hulk at bay, and he tells Parker the technology could suppress mutating DNA, but warns that a universal inhibitor able to act on any mutation would be dangerous. Parker builds both, and the universal one lets the Department of Damage Control hold the mutant telepath Jean Grey while its director, Bill Metzger, experiments to replicate her powers, as he did with her sister, who died in custody. Parker and Banner are sympathetic; Metzger's institution is the villain. The film treats the inhibitor as a metaphor for suppressing grief and ends with Parker taking it off. Real siRNA drugs do reduce the activity of specific genes, but nothing like a wearable switch for superpowers exists.

title: Spider-Noir
text: In an alternate New York of the 1930s, Ben Reilly is an aging private investigator who once fought crime as "the Spider" but gave it up after the death of his fiancée, Ruby Williams. He acquired his powers as a sergeant in the First World War, when, freeing prisoners from a German camp, he was bitten by a feral, mutated human-spider, the result of experiments carried out on prisoners there. A case involving the nightclub singer Cat Hardy draws him back into action and into conflict with the crime boss Silvermane, the city's mayor and a group of metahumans, among them Sandman and Tombstone. The series also involves Dr. Alethea Faber, a doctor trying to find a cure for the metahumans, whose treatments worsen their condition. The eight-episode series stars Nicolas Cage and premiered on MGM+ and Prime Video in May 2026; it was cancelled after one season. Genetics has only a background role. The hero's powers and the metahumans of the series come from human experimentation rather than genetic engineering as such: Reilly was bitten by a prisoner turned into a spider-human hybrid in a German wartime camp, an image that evokes the abuses of medical experiments on prisoners, and the metahumans suffer conditions that a doctor, Alethea Faber, tries to cure with treatments that make them worse. Her experiments also aged her own son rapidly. The sources consulted describe the mutations in general terms and do not present them as explicitly genetic, so the series' interest for genetics lies mainly in its portrayal of scientists and doctors whose interventions on human bodies produce suffering, in a noir setting where the body becomes a site of experiment.

title: The Darwin Incident
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering genetic discrimination
text: This anime series, based on Shun Umezawa's manga, begins when the Animal Liberation Alliance, an extremist animal rights group, raids a biological research institute and rescues a pregnant chimpanzee, who gives birth to Charlie, a human–chimpanzee hybrid or 'humanzee'. Charlie is raised in seclusion by a primatologist and a lawyer, Gilbert and Hannah Stein, and grows up with physical abilities beyond those of humans and chimpanzees and an intelligence greater than a human's. At fifteen he enrols at a high school in Missouri, where he befriends Lucy, a shy honours student. While Charlie seeks a normal life and his own rights, he faces fear and prejudice, an FBI investigation and a congresswoman's interest in his legal status. The ALA's manipulative leader, Rivera Feyerabend, takes an interest in him, drives a student to commit a school shooting and hides Charlie's secret humanzee brother, Omelas. The series is built around a genetically engineered human–chimpanzee hybrid, created with genome editing at an unnamed research institute. The scientists who made Charlie stay offstage; the story focuses on what his existence means for others. Its creator describes it as a thought experiment on how society would react if the boundary between humans and animals collapsed, and it uses Charlie to explore bioethics, legal personhood, discrimination and terrorism. The villains are not geneticists but animal-rights extremists, although critics noted that the case for animal rights is treated sympathetically. No human–chimpanzee hybrid has ever been produced, and the manga's author researched the idea of the humanzee extensively before turning it into fiction.

title: The Last Temptation of Becky
text: Two years after the events of The Wrath of Becky, eighteen-year-old Becky Hooper works for the CIA but is repeatedly suspended for her violent methods. Confined to her New York apartment on probation, she is recruited by Director Baker for a rescue mission. Baker reveals that the neo-Nazi General Wilhelm Reuss organized an earlier jailbreak, and that the Valknut key once hidden under Becky's lake house was placed there by Reuss's great-grandfather and opens a hidden chamber beneath the Wolf's Lair in Poland. Going undercover, Becky is captured and discovers that Reuss has been killing guests and draining their blood, and that the chamber holds a clone of Adolf Hitler in a cryogenic tank, meant to found a Fourth Reich. Realizing that Baker sent her on a suicide mission, she goes rogue, kills the clone as it emerges, exposes the plot on television and kills Reuss's men and scientists, and finally Reuss, who has killed her love interest Rigby. Wounded, she collapses as the Polish military bombs the site. The genetic element is a cloned Adolf Hitler, kept in a cryogenic chamber beneath the Wolf's Lair by the neo-Nazi general Wilhelm Reuss, whose scientists, including Dr. Friedrich Metzger, are working on it in order to found a Fourth Reich. Reuss kills guests and drains their blood as part of the project. The clone plays only a brief part: Becky shoots it as soon as it steps out of its tank, and she later kills the scientists. Cloning here is a shorthand for a Nazi revival, a familiar idea in fiction since The Boys from Brazil, and the sources give no detail of how the clone was made. Real cloning, if it were attempted, would produce a genetic twin who would grow up with his own personality in a different world, not a reborn dictator.
